A simple, but pleasant strategy game. It contains a little bit of everything: tactics, economy, stationing, improvement for units and buildings, reckless attack and indestructible defense.
It has a few flaws due to the simplicity, the largest of which are: battle results are calculated randomly (so you can capture a few castles in a row, but fail to capture an empty area with five armies) and AI constantly start fighting with each other, if you do not attack them (even if you have more than any other territories and can destroy them all after a couple of days).
Result: easy game to feel yourself like a strategist and conqueror for those who do not like difficult to mastering strategy games or who just want to spend a little time for a tactical game.

It is pretty decent, a thousand times better than the old ugly clunky janky Thief games that were made four hundred years ago. I remember Thief came out around the time Quake 3 was out and nobody I knew wanted to play them because at that time Quake 3 was God. The original Thief games I do not understand their hit cult status and don't care. I really like this new game, especially compared to the older games because they are so incredibly janky.
Sound, music, effects, and controlls are all good. The art direction of the people and the city is all very well done to be dark and gloomy in a time of extreme poverty and struggle. The streets and people are very filthy looking, especially the bums and the whor-s. The main guy is like-able and so are most of the other characters around him. I understand what they said about this game holding your hand while you play, but it isn't that bad, and it does give you some freedom of how you want to do missions. You can kill guys, knock them out, or avoid them. I couldn't help myself and through the whole game I sneakily knocked out all the guys in the levels, only killing if I had to or felt like it.
The sneaking part is done well, kills/knockouts are fun, and the weapons and gadgets are great. It is awesome breaking into a random place and stealing all of their stuff to pawn off for cash. What is cool about that though is that when you pick something up it just turns into cash for convenience. Getting around town could have been a bit more parkourish but it is fine like it is. Melee combat isn't so great. In fact melee combat sucks bad. Every fight plays out exactly the same: strike at your foe to make them do a sword block and instant counter attack, dodge their counter attack and then strike for a hit, repeat until he is dead. If you run into two guys at once you might as well reload a save because your♥♥♥♥♥is grass since you can't take two guys at the same time. Try to never engage in hand combat because it is just extremely awkward, easily the worst part about the game. The sub-weapons are fun to use in different situations and the game has a pretty easy to learn upgrade system. The map system could have been done better too because getting around town is trial and error and a lot of memorization since the map makes no sense because it does not show if someplace is blocked off or inaccessible. You will find that out on your own and have to find a alternate route to your destination since the map system kinda sucks. However traveling around the dark, gloomy, creepy and foreboding city is a pleasure. The city serves as a hub for missions that you can start then go to their instanced-off area and do them.
Don't let the Thief 1 & 2 fanboys on here fool you. I am having a good time with this because it was mostly well made. The last boss fight is a cop out and is pretty dumb, but oh well since the game leading up to it was fun. I see no reason to give it below a 7/10 because in general terms it is not a bad game. It could have been better, namely the suck balls melee combat, but for what it is, is easily worth at least ten bucks on sale.

I'm terrible at shmups but I like this game.  Developer "Quadsphere" has made a casual mode for scrubs like me to practice on before I graduate to the three higher difficulties.
What sets this game apart from your average schmup is the ability to collect tech as you play.  Unlike your typical game which gives you a short boost, these upgrades are permanent and may be better than your  existing shields, weapons, and missiles.  If so, you can switch them out at the end of each level.  If you're playing casual difficulty, you can also switch gear if you die before the level is finished.  Any of your items can be sold for cash if desired and there is a cash shop available to purchase additional items.
You accumulate experience points to level up and build the type of ship you want -- Attack/crit, defense/armor/resists, or tech/special weapons.  For example, you can increase the damage of your weapons, increase your crit chance, add armor or increase the amount of tech you receive.
My only complaint with the game is the items in the cash shop are usually low quality weapons  aside from maybe one of two items that may not have the weapons or stats you need.  In addition, the items in the shop do not change until you complete a level.  This can be a problem if you're stuck on a tough level with weak equipment both on your ship and in the shop.
My tips?
Decide on your preferred playstyle (Attack, Defense, or Tech) in advance.
Pick the ship that matches your playstyle best.
Invest at least 21 skill points for your playstyle to get the maximum buff.
Always max Bullet Resistance with skill points regardless of playstyle
Try to buff up Tech Find with your equipment to keep a steady stream of gear flowing.

Pretty fun little scrolling bullet hell.
Has some interesting additions to customizing your ship and gameplay. You have RPG aspects to upgrade your skills, you get boosts to stats with skill points, and it has a complete weapon and accessory system like an RPG with the colored levels and whatnot. Special skills, secondary weapons, XP and tech pickups, and quite a few non-upgradable stats that are boosted by the equipment you find and buy.  (shield regen, crit. %, pickup distance, etc.).
You pick up weapon parts, shields, and modules to give yourself different stats and it is kind of randomized like a Diablo/Borderlands as it says on the  store page. It's defintiely NOT an adventure RPG game, its a SHMUP, but it has that style of item value so there isn't much other way to describe it. White, green, blue, purple...yadda yadda. xD
Music and the backgrounds aren't great. You can dim the backgrounds though so it makes it a lot easier to see enemies and stuff through bullets and the background graphics. Sounds, music, and backgrounds make it feel Indie and it does make the presentation feel a little less than amazing.  Options to force V-sync, change resolution, and a few other video options like changing to windowed and landscape. Audio is standard volume so you can shut the music off if you want. I think that the gameplay and mechanics are solid enough to recommend this, however. Watch the store video if this is a major issue for you.
It also has the option to turn on auto-fire so your main weapon fires constantly. This is actually pretty much what I use because you wouldn't stop firing in this game regardless. No reason to bother turning it off imo. You also have a speed up button to skirt out of tight spots much faster.
It's not a AAA made SHMUP by any stretch, but defintiely has a lot of great qualities that aren't common in this genre. Getting it from a bundle I am pleasantly surprised, and the low price isn't something I'd cry about if I had bought it either.
The gamepad controls are OK, but not great until you rebind them. Initially, before you are able to rebind them they feel very awkward trying to move around the menus (they actually do work in the menus, but may not seem like it the way they are bound). They do become easier to use once you figure out how to bind them and that the cursor is being moved by the left stick, or D-Pad. Trigger buttons, are not available to bind, at least on my PS3 gamepad using 360 emulation, but the shoulder buttons work fine. There aren't enough controls to worry about this, however. Unless you turn off auto-fire the only other in-game buttons you need are "Special" and "Speed Up/Boost" So you don't need the triggers anyways. Once you bind them everything works fine and you don't need to worry too much. You are dodging a TON bullets (bullet hell obviously) and picking up loot so not worrying about firing is nice. :P

Icarus-X has seen it fit to introduce that most traditional of gaming mechanics - The Grind. Even in scrolling shooters, a branching skills tree could perhaps be labelled uncommon if hardly new, but I've not seen many looting system within the genre. Games like Borderlands and Diablo are liberally name-dropped as comparison models, and not completely unfairly. Either by defeating enemies and picking up drops or purchasing from the in-game store, you can deck out up to four equipment slots including primary and secondary fire, as well as a core chip and a shield.
It all works pretty well; though physically there’s not a huge amount of variation. For example, the primary fire is purely distinguished by the rate of spread, the more focused the collection of bullets, the more powerful they usually are. Secondary fire has a little more choice to it, offering homing missiles or a collection of lasers with a small variety of tricks ranging from vanilla constant beams to a circling weapon that rotates constantly around your craft. Things like armour rating, shield power, tech drop rates, critical hit percentage and power consumption are also tracked through your equipment making any alteration you go for more of a balance trade off rather than a straight swap. That new laser might be more powerful, but it does chip away and your shield regeneration rate and make your hitbox slightly bigger.

You level up, get some loot and allocate points in skill trees with the usual critical strike, armor, shield and such stats you would find in a typical Diablo-like. So while it's not the big adventure you might expect, there is some interesting theorycrafting to be made.
Pros
Super smooth framerate
Good variety of loot and stats
Weapons feel great
You get a massive regenerating shield which is a relief when tons of bullets are fired your way
Controls fine with a gamepad
Pretty cool music
Cons
The backgrounds are really minimalist and repetitive
Some bosses are op, some are jokes, could use some balancing
Gamepad in menus controls the mouse cursor, might as well use the mouse?
All in all I'd recommend it, just don't expect a full blown RPG but rather a small top-down shooter with Rpg mechanics.

I've played this before on the interwebs. Might as well toss out a token review.
For a game that causes grown men to go into fits over the dreaded ess-jay-dubyas, this isn't a terrible intersectional game. The main character doesn't have any money concerns, has a steady job, a supportive girlfriend and at least one supportive family member, hits the jackpot on their first time visiting a therapist (it took me about four or five tries to find one that clicked), lives in a location that allows them to keep a cat, and doesn't seem to suffer any ill effects from race, religion, physical disability, age, or gender.
As a long-time sufferer of depression's smaller cousin, dysthymia (if depression is a big black dog sitting on your chest for stretches of time, dysthymia is an overweight cat that lays on your head and never leaves), I recognized a lot of the situations presented in the game, and the options for action described pretty well actions I might have taken. Although I really wish getting help were as easy as clicking a link in a Twine game...
All in all this game doesn't merit the hate it gets. So thusly I give it a recommendation. It's not a Half-Life-esque landmark game... but it deserves to be appreciated for what it is.

The feeling of having no motivation, getting no enjoyment from anything, and believing that by getting help you're just inconviencing others, are all things that this game tries to portray as well as it can. So while it does fall short in terms of length and actual gameplay, it at least makes a effort to try and emulate the real ways that depression slowly eats away at you like a crippling disease.
The fact is that in the end it actually displays the effects of depression better than most other games, movies, and TV shows. Because depression is a monster in your closet that you can't ever be rid of. No matter how much people say things like "Just go get help" or "Do something to not be depressed", that's just not possible because that beast called depression will always be in the back of your mind chewing on your thoughts and making it seem like every possible choice will just make you a burden on others. Often people suffering from depression will never seek help, and the best help they can receive is by their friends and family noticing the problem and getting them that help (sometimes whether they want it or not).
To sum up:
Gameplay: 3/10 (Pretty much non-existing)
Story: 5/10 (Could be much longer and more compelling)
Experience: 10/10 (For anyone who has actually experienced real depression and been diagnosed, this game may or may not be relatible to your own experiences)
Fun: 0/10 (This game is about depression and doesn't have a happy ending)
Worth it? (Price): 10/10 (It's a free game)
Length: 1/10 (Short and simple)
Overall: 2/10 as a game, but a 8/10 in terms of actual effort and care that was put into it. I wouldn't say that this is a all-time "Must play" kind of experience, but rather on par with playing through a brief educational game.
In the end I will say that it's good attempt at approaching a serious subject, and that It is unfortunately a forgettable experience.

Now, the game is well written, explaining in detail things even when I was depressed I couldn't express, and the choice based system is nice. It is a good interactive novel.
While I had such an unique experience, game could improve upon some aspects, I'd like to say that sometimes there were things which were crossed out, but if I was in the protagonist's shoes I would do just that, which sucks as I could relate better if game allowed me to do the crossed out things.
I understand everyone's experience with depression is different, I could actually quite relate to many parts of the game. The best part is that this game is free so please give it a try.

You know how some people say "I really want to like X, but no matter how hard I try I can't"?  Well, for me, Dungeons of Dredmor is the opposite.  I really don't want to like it.  It's a 2D rougelike, top-down, turn-based-ish dungeon crawler with an odd sense of humor (it's hit and miss) and a 90's feel to it.  While each floor is randomized, each room is a template of sorts, so after a few hours of gameplay, you'll start to see the same rooms pop up over and over (just with different loot sometimes).  It doesn't feel like there's enough content for a game like this.  And yet, I can't stop playing it.
On normal, the game is easy enough to lure you in until you find yourself suddenly dead (health is mostly gained by eating food, but it replenishes 1 point per turn (usually for 10 or so turns, depending on the item) so you need to be careful when getting into combat.  The enemies are unusual, yet somewhat bland, but they will sometimes insult you (via text above them) that is actually pretty charming ("You smell like diggle pee" or "I hope they nerf your playstyle").  The biggest draw for me, though, is the item collecting.  There's all kinds of random loot to find, better equipment or something to sell for money so you can buy better equipment.  It's actually sort of relaxing.  All this on top of crafting (which could have been done better, to be honest), leveling and basic (go here and kill this mostly) sidequests that are there to parody the RPG genre.  Plus, you regain magic by drinking alcohol.
In the end, I suppose Dungeons of Dredmor feels like a poor man's Torchlight, but I find it to be a little more likeable than Torchlight.  The music is good, the graphics are decent and it's pretty easy to pick up and play.  I recommend this game!

Now Man Flies! Isn’t that a surpise? Well, no since by “now”, you could debate that the first flight of an object heavier than air and still capable of lifting a human being, either occurred during Antiquity in Asia (giant kites) or 18th century France (the Montgolfière hot air balloon). For all his brilliance, Leonardo’s 15th century aerial screw “helicopter” was never a feasible design. Back to our game for now. It’s a casual 2D title which has entertained me enough to overlook its flaws. The second Steam project for developer Epic Fire and the publishing debut for DNB Media.
I can’t really say much for the story since not even a title screen is present, once you boot up the game. From what I could notice however, the “protagonist” can be regarded as a collective character in the form of a space ship which surely needs a crew in order to be maneuvered the way it is. Initially a red rocket which can be switched into a blue one, after 100 planets have been reached. The antagonists are also the obstacles between failure and success in Now Man Flies. Both homing missiles and static satellites will get in the way or even hinder your space exploration efforts.
Even if it might be another Unity-powered title, Now Man Flies fails to mention this and the biggest sin it has commited in my opinion, is the limited Steam Overlay support that it features. Sure, the frame rate counter is present and unsurpringly, it never drops below 60fps even on my native 4K resolution. At least it has Vsync enabled and thus, spares me of having to play at a thousand frames per second. Yes, the graphics aren’t much to look at yet it didn’t bother me one bit. Casual genre is never synonymous with “eye candy”. It’s priced accordingly afterall. Well, in most cases anyway. Now Man Flies won’t allow me to take any screenshots of it through the Overlay and I really can’t understand why some Steam titles still obstruct an innocent feature that can promote the game in question.
The soundtrack is comprised of just two songs which reminded me of mall elevators. Not repetitive enough to become annoying yet still nothing special. To make matters worse, one song gets unlocked after you pass the aforementioned planet threshold. No voice acting or sound effects are present.
Without any story to begin with, you’d be right in the assessment of the gameplay. It has to compensate the lack of a narrative and in the case of most casual games, that is not an issue. Now Man Flies is not an exception from the rule per se, yet it does become rather repetitive within half an hour, provided you can tolerate its gameplay mechanics for that long. No change of scenery, foes and even controllable ship until you’ve discovered a set number of planets. You might say that the incentive to keep playing is exactly the promise of that new song, ship skin and increased challenge through the unlockable Survival Mode. Reaching it, is only part of the challenge. Now Man Flies has an open-ended structure which means that you can keep on playing for as much as you’d like. And you’ll have to play A LOT until you finally unlock the Steam Achievement for over 32 hours of playtime. To put things into perspective, I’ve seen all that this game has to offer, without even reaching 2 hours of playtime. Good luck dodging the same looking obstacles for another 30!
You’ll have to endure and even grind through the Classic Mode which has the red rocket travel from planet to planet, all the way to the 100th discovery before the blue vessel takes over. While not a planet for certain, the encounter which makes this transition and marks the culmination of the “campaign”, is a location that resembles the Death Star from Star Wars. What I couldn’t explain was how can so many satellites interfere with space exploration, especially since we’re being led to believe that we’re breaking new grounds with each subsequent discovery. Also, why and who would try to stop these space pioneers through the use of so many guided missiles? If the answer you’re imagining is “aliens”, no other ships or structures are ever encountered. Just the red/blue rocket you’re steering and the far-too-similar-looking blue satellites along with grey projectiles that seem to follow players at an obviously greater velocity than their target.
Monotony is never setting in, simply because you have to become creative, by the time you’ve passed your 50th discovered planet. Beyond the sheer number of obstacles, the randomly generated levels ensure that even if you fail a certain stage repeatedly, you’ll still have to ambition yourself to overcome your mistakes, without having to replay in the same conditions over and over again. Also, the booster mechanic helps plow through foes and reach your destination sooner It can be used as a “I win” button on lower levels. By the time I reached stage 100 though, the booster was only a minor assistance, as instantly covering 10 thousand out of 30 thousand kilometres (only the Metric system is featured in-game) still gave me 20 thousand “reasons” to remain focused on the digital onslaught ahead. Indeed, it was challenging and for this reason alone, I reconsidered my initial intention of slamming this game through a much lower rating.
It’s not going to impress you and it certainly won’t keep you as entertained as an excellent RPG or RTS, yet casual games have their very own niche on PCs. We’re not talking of the lazy cash grabs that are prevalent to smartphone “gaming”. Steam needs to host casuals and fortunately, even Now Man Flies is priced within good measure and reason, in perfect balance with its offerings. You get what you pay for, yet it’s still up to you to appreciate the game’s fun factor. Just don’t judge it for its first few levels. If you’re an Achievement collector, it goes without saying that you’ll enjoy this game thoroughly. At the time of this writing, there are five thousand Steam Achievements, waiting to be unlocked within Now Man Flies. With my limited playtime or not, I still managed to gain over three thousand. A considerable number, perhaps even crazy, since I haven’t collected that many in all the Steam games I played in the past combined.
+ Steam Achievements.
+ Adequate scaling of the difficulty factor.
+ Decently priced title offering exactly what it advertises.
- No Steam Trading Cards nor Overlay screenshot support.
- Inherently repetitive gameplay.
- Limited sound selection.

Scenic Kyrat: home to vibrant landscapes, varied wildlife, Kyrati Films, and enough backstabbing to make Julius Caesar empathetic.  Thrust into a rebellion led by the Golden Path against the tyrant Pagan Min, you play Kyrati-American Ajay Ghale on a mission to return his mother’s ashes to Lakshmana.  Ajay is immediately intercepted by the Royal Army upon trying to enter the country and brought to Min’s fortress, along with his guide Darpan.  Presumably due to the fortress’s lack of a TSA invasive search, security fails to recover the cellphone Darpan promptly uses to text the Golden Path for help.  Min then has his lieutenant Paul “De Pleur” Harmon take Darpan to be tortured for information and tells Ajay to enjoy some Crab Rangoon while he tends to other business.  Bearing the attention span of a goldfish, Ajay immediately gets up (how rude, am I right?) as you take control to find the exit where you first encounter Golden Path leader Sabal.  You are guided to the village of Banapur, the home of the Golden Path and its state of disrepair.  Here, Amita is introduced as the Path’s other leader.
Far Cry 4’s story is certainly present and purposeful, but doesn’t really have the slew of decisions it claims to have.  The appearance of variety in the choices one can make establishes itself in the conflict between Amita and Sabal; Amita wants to bring Kyrat into the modern era of equality, whereas Sabal wants to keep old tradition alive.  This implies arranged marriages, a ritual to instate a young girl as an avatar to the god Kyra, and I assume accusing disobedient women of being witches.  It is established that Ajay is the son of Mohan Ghale, the man who founded the Golden Path, putting him in the influential position to decide whose plan to follow.  For you, this means picking to do one mission or another which ultimately leads to different endings.  Implicitly this means that one would have to play the game through twice for the different endings, and the game’s lack of more than one save slot or ‘new game plus’ means removing any progress made in the first play through.  I played through both endings and didn’t feel it was worth the time, as the ‘different’ missions end up being in the same areas with different objectives.  Especially considering the extra missions that can be done besides the story (more on those later), it ends up being more satisfying to beat the game once and then just look up the different endings.
Which brings me to my only small gripe with the story; the cut scenes, dream, and drug sequences are unskippable.  I’ll avoid spoiling more than the type of events I’m talking about, but it felt strange playing a game rooted in reality and suddenly have Ajay tripping harder than a soccer player faking an injury.  You’re forced into these a few times with the option of going again (more with the extra missions), but in a different spot.  I found the sequences directly relevant to the story the most frustrating as they ended up just being trial and error while trying to be cinematic.  Admittedly, I could just be bad at the game to the point where the allure of those sections weren’t fun, but that was my experience nonetheless.  I still found each to be put together well despite my dislike of having to do them.  This would be attributed to the fact that the world you get put into for certain trips is consistent in pace, environment, and appearing truly surreal and out of this world.
Where the story lacks replayability, the side missions provide the tasty, tasty filler.  For starters, Kyrat has 24 outposts and an option in the game’s settings to reset them all for recapture as well as each post having Outpost Master where you can top your friend’s high scores.  Each outpost will also have one of the following side missions:
Eye for an eye: kill the target with the designated weapon and take a picture of the body.
Assassination: kill the target with the bonus objectives of stealth of body disposal.
Hostage Rescue: take out all the captors and free the hostages unharmed.
Hunting Supplies, Control, and Survival: kill the designated animal with arrows/bolts/blades for hides, kill all designated animals, and keep at least one civilian alive during an animal attack, respectively.
That doesn’t even cover everything at every outpost, let alone the rest of the tasks by the story’s side characters.  There is much more to be said about the racing, hunting, bomb disposal, and sabotage offered by the various interesting side characters that won’t be spoiled in this article.
When you inevitably reach the point where taking outposts and strongholds begins feeling more like a chore than the fun of shanking baddies, multiplayer adds the comfortable dynamic of conquest with a friend.  To remove the element of breezing through missions with the aid of a second veritable super power, cooperative play is restricted from advancing the story.  Instead, you can collaborate on capturing outposts and carrying on the side quests within.  The simple addition of being able to flank, divert, and synchronize kills manifests a whole other realm of possibility.  It’s hard to beat raining Molotov’s at the enemy with your friend in tow on a grappling hook, only to drop him off directly on a survivor for a drop assassination.  Unfortunately, I didn’t find competitive multiplayer to be nearly as engaging.  Each mode features combat between the Rakshasa and the Golden Path.  On one end, the Rakshasa have supernatural abilities such as summoning wild animals, teleporting, and invisibility.  On the other end, the Golden Path have modern weapons and explosives.  It makes for an interesting battle, but the splendor of that detail was squelched for me when that ended up being the only type of combat.  No standard team deathmatch, no guns versus guns, just a clash of arrows and powers against bullets and bombs.  Don’t get me wrong; I was impressed with the original setup and balance of the combat, but I was underwhelmed with the lack of variety.  Far Cry multiplayer in general hasn’t been too impressive to me since FC2, where the online community of FC3 died before I got the opportunity to delve into that.  In short, competitive multiplayer is well-put-together, but also all there is.
Overall, Far Cry 4 is truly impressive.  Every time I play, I can’t help but stop every once in a while just to take in the scenery.  The way the sun shines through the trees of the forests, the sprawling green of the valley, and the snowy Himalayas all draw me into to a staggeringly immersive experience. Barraging outposts with a buzzer and a grenade launcher, then landing to mop up the mess with a WWII era MG42 really inspires a Flight-of-the-Valkyries-esque feeling to the already exhilarating bloodbaths. Driving next to someone just so you can hop into their vehicle, stab them in the throat, and shove them out the door so you can keep driving created some ‘OH,♥♥♥♥♥♥’ moments in itself, and that’s just one of the many styles of takedowns. Memorable, fast-paced, and high-caliber, Far Cry 4 is certain to leave a gratifying sense of victory on your pallet.

Thief is a very solid stealth game, dripping with atmosphere.
You are Garrett, the master thief and immediately from the beginning of the game you can be as invisible as a ghost for your adversaries. Stealth is the key to all of your actions, as you are a very weak combatant when exposed. The game focuses on what a thief does, stealing items of worth for his own gain. So if you like looting and looking for loot, especially the well hidden sort, Thief offers plenty of this.
The main story is supported by nicely animated cutscenes and very good voice acting, even in the german version. Like Deus Ex this is clearly one of Square Enix' strengths. Levels are well designed and you usually have more than two ways to deal with obstacles.
My only real problem with the actual gameplay is that you don't have many options to deal with actual enemies. Garrett has a form of "magic" which is called focus, but it is barely any more than passive buffs which enhance your abilities, like slowing the time or extending shadows. In most cases you are limited to a hide and seek gameplay with the options of distracting, killing or knocking out enemies but nothing more. Dishonored, for comparison, offers a wide variety of "magic" abilities and tools to help you overcome your foes.
That said, what Thief does, it does it pretty well and it's a nice looker on top.
I had some performance issues with strange loading stutters, but apart from that it runs well on my old machine even on very high settings. So I guess even older machines can play it well, if you tune the options a bit.
Grab this game if you like the atmosphere, which it really practically radiates, if you like stealth gameplay and stealing stuff.

This was an unique game, and an interesting opportunity to connect with how I see  Depression. I myself have been diagnosed and struggle with clinical (or major) depression. I downloaded and played through the game today, read all of the note from the producers in about 1 1/2. My experience, and the choices that I chose throughout the game really helped me connect with the same behaivors, and the impact of my choices in real life. While the game itself may not be for everyone- and may insult or desenitize others with depression or similar diagnosis- I would say it in my mind very similar to what I myself have experienced as a person diagnosed with Depression.
I would simply like to thank the producers for their involvement in this project, and while I may not ever touch this game again, I would recomend it to some friends- their outcomes, their resolutions may not go well, but maybe they might just be able to grasp how difficult depression can be to handle from day to day. One choice can affect everything, making positive choices- even when you feel empty, guilty, hurt, embarrest- like you are a failure or ugly inside, and don't know how to tell anyone else- That is one of the hardest things to do. No ammount of telling someone to try harder or be a better person will change if they don't trust themselves to feel safe, or to feel loved, beautiful, or capable to live as they want to. The only reason I have this ability is because I made that choice to open up no matter how afraid I was everything I did would fail.
This might be a game to some people, but for me, it's like reliving a part of my life that I didn't know how to connect to before. So Thank you.
I know some people may not agree with my review, but please respect that this is my opinion, you don't have to agree with it, but please don't bash it.

The game makes a very important point at the end: there is not a "true" end to depression, as it is something that just happens and you can't plan it. There is so much stigma and ignorance against mental illness and I find that the game portrayed it very well, as well as the feelings of desperation, self loathing, mind feeling numb and blank all the time, and making those little efforts that although they are absolutely important to someone with a disorder, it feels like we did nothing. I found the game particularly real and it felt like reading the diary of someone that actually feels the way I do.
The scratched out choices, who were like "the best choices for yourself" were scratched out and that makes a powerful statement: you can't just shake off depression or any other disorder, because it is  a chemical imbalance in the brain, an illness, no different than any other and it consumes you slowly.
I hope Zoe Quinn will still produce beautiful content like this in the future.

ASWD to move, left click shoot, right click alt fire, 1-2-3 for special weapons options, call in support for dollars, it's very very basic even for a touch-pad port.
As it's been said, the "campaign" is nothing more than disjointed, generic missions played sequentially. Missions on maximum difficulty can be completed effortlessly the first time you see them, provided everyone but your main unit means nothing to you. I'm guessing that the "challenge" is that you can only control the head of your squad and all other members move like a snake behind him. Therefore, when you are trying to avoid fire, you have to do so in a way that does not allow the other members of your party to get hit when they arrive at your location two or three seconds later. Basically, it's inevitable that your main unit will be grossly overpowered and everyone else will be new and inexperienced.
Really, I would sum this game up by saying it's just not very good and be done with it. However, it's struck me right from the main menu that this is intended to be something like 3D, isometric Call of Duty for eight year olds. I don't really mean that in a condescending way, and this isn't really a game that I'd give and eight year old to play unless I was trying to explain military strategy of the Iraq war (run in with thousands of troops, shoot up locals, watch your troops die, and accomplish nothing yet make a lot of money). But really, the maturity level conveyed and depth from the game definitely makes me think ages 8 - 10 and lord knows I can think of better options than this for somebody's childhood.

I like Hammerwatch, but I don't love Hammerwatch

I can't quite put my finger on what it is about Hammerwatch that I love so much. The endless dungeon crawling should get tedious, but it doesn't. The lack of variety in enemies should get boring. The oh-so slow grind of upgrading powers should be faster. The huge difficulty spikes of boss battles should be frustrating.
But somehow, Hammerwatch manages to be more than the sum of it's parts, and provides an answer to all of the potential failings I've mentioned.  The lack of variety in enemies is offset by the fact that there's an enormous number of them, which come at you in various combinations, and the interaction with the level design keeps each encounter fresh. While the character upgrades are very slowly drip-fed, that means that you have ample time as the player to master nuances of each before having more powers laden on. The boss difficulty spikes are offset by the fact that the game provides you plenty of extra lives, notably handing you a stack of five at the end of each boss fight, presumably to make up for the slew of them you lost during said fight.
It's that balance that only starts to shine through a few hours into the game. Hammerwatch rewards and demands careful, smart play. Wade into a battle without an exit strategy in mind and you'll quickly be swamped by 50 enemies. Get surrounded, and you're toast. But go in knowing that you've cleared the hallway behind you so you can retreat that way, kiting the enemies into a more manageable grouping, and that you can trigger a combo with one power and use a combination heal/AoE with the other. and you'll stroll through the encounter.
The only possible downside is that once you've got your build mastered and your careful approach strategy down, the challenge can slacken off (with the exception of the punishing boss battles). Though to be fair, there are harder difficulty levels that I've not yet explored that may solve that issue.
I'll also note that I haven't even tried the co-op, which I expect will change up the feel of the game dramatically.

Do you like the 70's? Do you like love stories? Do you like limos? Do you like spinning around violently? Do you like dr... uh.... candy induced trips from a plastic skeleton? Then this is the game for you!
Roundabout takes the excort mission to new levels by having you play as the world's most aspiring revolving limo driver in this tale of love and revenge.

Drive for 30 yards. Explode violently because you touched a lamp post. Respawn. Drive for 25 yards. Explode violently because you touched a curb. Drive for 30 yards. Explode violently because you touched another car.
Seriously, this game is an exercise in frustration.
Okay, the story is kind of fun, told almost entirely through FMVs. Apparently the team couldn't afford any decent props so they decided to just add some film grain and turn it into a cheesy 70s pastiche. Even though, aside from a few references to Jimmy Carter and disco, it really has no effect on the game whatsoever. It's basically Kuru Kuru Kururin crossed with GTA. Navigate your spinning limo around the city delivering people from A to B, trying not to burst into a flaming wreck on the way.
But you'll finish story mode in about an hour, and after that, unfortunately there isn't a whole lot to do. You can replay the individual missions and try and achieve a better score, or you can try and collect some of the hundreds of extra items within the game world. You can buy some of the 23 properties within the game world. What do they do? Well, they give you money every now and then, but you have to go back and collect it. Or you could try and find the 127 piles of cash in the game world. They...give you cash. What do you do with all the cash? You buy 'hats' and paint jobs for your limo, which make NO difference to the gameplay and are purely cosmetic. So, money is useless. You can try and find all of the 157 "Sick jumps", which are similar to the jumps in the GTA games. I don't think anything at all happens when you find them all besides a Steam Achievement. Or you can try and find all 49 horns. Which, again, are purely cosmetic.
The story mode itself is also incredibly linear, with no branching, and almost no variety in the order missions can be completed in. So...about an hour of story mode which consists almost entirely of driving from A to B, with the occasional pedestrian killing-spree thrown in. And then there's 333 optional extras you can find. Which don't do anything useful. There's no additional vehicles or anything like that. Oh, and there's half a dozen or so minigames, most of which you'll have already done as part of main missions.
The only modifications you can make are unlocked in garages as you play, and can do things like let you float/dive in water, or alter which way you spin. None of which you need for the missions.
It's a nice enough game and the presentation is very well done, but there isn't really much here to do once you've finished the main game. It's really just a mini-game that's been expanded into a full-length game without reason. If there were optional missions (taxi missions, anyone?), or upgrades that radically altered the way the game works (what if, say, certain missions were only available after certain mods to your limo, like the rich guy won't get in unless it has tinted windows added), or if the collectables DID something (like the hidden packages in GTA) then there might be a reason to keep playing after the end. But, there really isn't. Except for bragging rights.
It's also quite buggy...often a respawn will either drop you miles from where you were, bypassing all the closer checkpoints, or it'll respawn you partially inside a building or vehicle causing you to explode immediately. This might happen 3 or 4 times before you can regain control. I also once had my balance switch to £0.01- for absolutely no reason, and was also told that the garage was earning me money and was 23% complete....even though that's not possible in-game.
It's worth playing. For about an hour. But there isn't any replay value unless you want the Steam Achievements.
Oh, and the developers seem to think that taking drugs and driving under the influence is funny.

- Having a A WORKING MATCHMAKING SYSTEM in an F2P FPS
- User Interface is easy to navigate
- A WORKING LEADERBOARD
- The hideout (Combat record, or player card equivalent) has a large amount of stats to look over to see how well you've been performing.
- Aiming down your sights actually works use it > hip fire. learn HOW and WHEN to do both.
Cons:
The Shop:
-  LOW GUN SELECTION. Game just came out more will be added sooner or later.
-  Most of those guns on the market must be purchased via gems which is the real world currency for the game. Not enough to players are going to play long enough to buy those guns without a larger selection of guns purchasable through in game currency.
-  There needs to be paint skins and other items that can be purchased permanently. It's a f2p game players like flashy items, the GP items obviously should be less fancy.

In game:
-  There needs to a larger incentive for players to play the object, in object based game modes. Players tend to just go for kills in Search and Destroy rather than planting or defusing because it's obviously easier, but there isn't a large exp reward for planting or defusing, grabbing the flag in CTF, etc.
-  NERF THE KRISS THERE IS NO WAY A SMG SHOULD HAVE THAT TIGHT OF A SPREAD WITH A FIRE RATE THAT HIGH OP

My feelings towards the new Thief are complicated. I'm probably going to post an unpopular opinion.
And that opinion is: Thief 2014, on its own, is a good game.
I'm saying 'on its own', because if you bought it expecting to relive the memories of Thief games of old, you'll be sorely disappointed. Exploration, while interesting, doesn't offer nearly as much choices as the classic games. Levels are not as sprawling and intricately designed. The ambient music is just a shadow of Eric Brosius' masterpieces. No Stephen Russell. Also, you can't jump non-contextually. You can only shoot rope arrows at designated spots. Which sucks.
However, please hear me here: you need to look at Thief 2014 as a game completely of its own. It is a reboot, after all, not a sequel. (Even though it's filled to the brim with nice shout-outs to the classics + I'm pretty sure it is actually set in the same continuity). And the truth is, when seen without the prism of its predecessors, it's a very decent game. Graphics are very good and pleasingly gritty - even though they take a while to load - and The City feels deliciously grimdarky. And I actually liked the new Garrett very much; he's just as witty and darkly humorous as the Garrett we knew. Plus, let's not forget what the main source of fun in Thief has always been: stealing! This game managed to appease my inner cleptomaniac completely; looting feels fun and satisfying.
So, all in all, give Thief 2014 a shot, especially if you haven't played the classic ones (maybe you'll come to appreciate them afterwards). Think of it as Dishonored without Blink. It's a very fun bit of obsessive-compulsive stealing that should keep you occupied until we get a new, better stealth game. Until then, I give Thief a solid 7/10.
PS. By the way, if you feel that this game has been 'dumbed down' and made 'too easy' in comparison to the classic Thief... There is an option to play with a completely custom difficulty setting. You can make the game literally harder than hard. Like, Super Meat Thief level hard.

To fully enjoy it I recommend the following:
1) Play on Master difficulty.
2) Forgo the (frankly bizarre) combat upgrades and focus only on stealth).
3) Remove as much of the UI as you feel comfortable with (I got rid of all the locking helper stuff)
4) Use a gamepad!
At first I really disliked this game, the voice acting is a little wobbley, the story is weak at best, the AI can sometimes be a bit daft and yes I've noticed more than a few bugs. It falls short in many areas.
However, there is so much to like about it and at it's best moments Thief is a stunning game. For instance the tactile nature of your interaction with the world. Letting the player see Garrett's hands and feetfrom a first person perspective was a masterstroke. Every quick grab for loot, every scramble over an object, every tentative peek around a corner or gentle slide along the frame of a painting connects you to the action in a way I've just not experienced in a game before. The "swoop" mechanic as well is brilliant, a very nuanced and well implemented addition to Garrett's abilities.
In many ways this game reminds me of Hitman because it suffers from the same problems. Like Hitman it is at it's best when you are doing standalone contract missions (the many side jobs on offer), when you are playing the role of a 'Master Thief' trying to use the environment and the tools at your disposal to steal the prize...
...and like Hitman at it's worst it's reduced to a terrible 'hero tale' through shlocky writing and forced confrontations.
I can see why long time Thief-fans have their noses bent out of shape by it, but frankly having played the previous Thief games this was a series that had problems long before this particular installment.
What gets me is that people rarely stop to think that a development team, a team of PEOPLE, poured their heart and soul in to this game for probably 2+ years of development and it's been so readily dismissed. It boggles the mind, especially when there is so much here to enjoy.
Would I pay £19.99 for it? Admittedly, no.
But if you like stealth games, next time you see this in the sales do yourself a favour and pick it up.

cons: lag spikes & horrendous stuttering especially during cut scenes/scripted scenes, stability issues (the game would not even launch at times), QTE in opening windows & moving wooden blocks, some audio goes out of sync, some voice audio varies in volume, map does not tell you which windows or narrow pathways leads to a map transition, map does not allow you to visualize areas you've already explored other than the specific area you are in, there are plenty of side quests - but they do not differ at all (always sent to "take this thing from that person"), scripted parts with instant death scenarios especially on the last 2 chapters, movement/controls can be clunky at times, once you knock out a guard you are unable to grab his loot without being forced to carry his body first, sometimes guard patrols bug out, boss battles are horrendous & the ending was a disappointment

I tried this game expecting a result that would match some of the critics I read, and honestly, I'm baffled. This game is absolutely fine. I have gone through a few playthroughs, and I think it depicts depression (and only depression, not linked to any kind of PTSD or any other mental or emotional disease) with a simple and neat outline. Obviously, it doesn't cover everything it could cover, and as it states at the forenote, it's not recommended for people still struggling with depression.
However, it puts simply the basic functioning of depression, it's limiting capacity and how it works as a neverending cycle if you don't step out of it, which is something most people without depression or closeness to someone with depression can't understand.
So yes, I do recommend this game, because honestly, the basics are great, and it makes some clear statements that, judging from other reviews, not even people with depression know, and everybody should understand them.
, the makers are skilled with the subject, know how it works, and produced a neat outline to display the basics of how depression feels and works, and also how to keep it on track.
The protagonist comes across more like an attention seeker than somebody who is actually depressed. There's no option to set up a Patreon account and make other people pay for your dysfunctions.

Far Cry 4's mechanics don't stray very far from how Far Cry 3 worked. You've got outposts to liberate. You've got radio towers to unlock. You've got animals to skin. You've got bad guys to shoot. Like Far Cry 3 the easiest path to take is usually going from point A to point B through the jungle. Why? Because every road and town is filled with things that want to kill you (most of the time). The animals in Far Cry 4 are much stronger than those in the previous game. You can and will die to animal attacks and luring animals for your benefit is a standard tactic in this game. Out of all of the animals the worst animal is the eagle. As soon as you're attacked by one you'll quickly learn why every NPC is scared of them. If you see a bird with a predator label shoot it. Next in the line of evil comes wolves, who will attack in packs and often are relentless in their pursuit of you despite (or because of) killing all of them.
The largest change between Far Cry 3 and Far Cry 4 is really the terrain. The mountainous regions make navigating difficult and turn what should be a short trip into a long one simply because you needed to change your elevation. It also makes outposts and other enemy strongholds more difficult to take because they have natural barriers. Generally when viewing an enemy outpost from a distance your vision of the area will be obscured from below and above making tagging enemies or taking stealth shots much harder. And stealth is also one of the big changes between 3 and 4. It is rather difficult to take down outposts completely silently and knocking out alarms will give you the "no alarms" reward. The game gives you a chance to replay outpost captures without losing control of the outpost but unless you really need that stealth capture to unlock one of the later skills there isn't much point to it. However it should be noted that the A.I. of the enemies remains strong whether you are trying to sneak in or capture the base through sheer force.
The RPG elements of the game are rather generic. Some require certain achievements. Some require being so far along in the story before they'll unlock. Spend experience points to increase your health points. Spend experience points to heal a little more.  Most of these are on the elephant side of the skill tree which deals with using herbs to make power-ups. Power ups do actually take time to make and you should stock up before going into battle. However I really only found the hunting power up, which allows you to see all enemies, to be useful. On the tiger side of the skill tree you have various takedowns and other combat oriented skills.
I enjoyed this game but I couldn't help thinking "This is a repackaged Far Cry 3". I was actually disappointed by the amount of "pop-ups" and textures fading in. I was expecting beautiful landscapes on max settings and was instead treated to trees and mountains popping into existence and appearing slightly better as I got close. I was very disappointed with the main narrative. You play the role of a young male on a trip to fulfill his mother's dying wish of taking her ashes to her homeland. From the moment you land you know this is not a good place to be. Now the game introduces the laughable "big bad" Pagan Min who gets a lot of overacted dialog which continues throughout the game even when you aren't doing a task related to the main story at all.
As for the main story there are several endings which I will not spoil but I will say that the idea of choice in the game has almost no weight towards what happens in the end. Sure the narratives are slightly different but there are basically one of two endings that the average player will see and neither is rewarding. The main character is a generic white male. His voice actor is good but the character is not well developed. His backstory is repeated over and over again in the game and this is possible because there is so little of it.
While I recommend the game I do not recommend any of the DLC. Both of the "expansions" are made of very linear maps with little to no gameplay changes outside of your hub. In one of the DLCs you have a base that can be upgraded and needs to be defended nightly but actually defending it isn't that fun. Either you'll be well defended enough to take out the waves of enemies with ease or you won't be and you'll probably die from a rush of enemies. In one of the DLCs you get to see Yetis. These are nothing more than giant tanks and while you might get a bit of excitement from having to hide or run from them unarmed, you won't be too worried if you see one in the wild. The DLC weapons are half decent when you are just starting the game but will quickly be outclassed. The HURK DLC is just a few missions in a different zoned area and your ultimate payoff is a harpoon gun that is really only good for laughing at corpses pinned to walls. Unfortunately you'll have to be rather close to use it.
In summary: This is Far Cry 3.5. The groundwork of the game series is still enjoyable but so little has changed that it seems to be missing that "WOW" factor that makes a good game into a great game.

The one downfall to this game, is it's tie to Horribad Uplay. U-play is clunky, buggy, crashes and has a horrible interface. I almost didn't buy the game because it was on U-play. Other than that, very solid RPG elements incorporated into a good storyline with the feel of progression as you advance.

Having clocked a good ~77 Hours into the game, including the DLCs, I gotta say the gameplay is quite addictive!
To put it midly, FC4 has nothing related from previous Far Cry games, storywise and lore speaking, so you cannot be "lost" in the game in that aspect. Whether that's good or bad, it's up to you but in game sequels, I like to have some continuation, to keep me invested in the franchise but sadly, you won't find this here.

Drive for 30 yards. Explode violently because you touched a lamp post. Respawn. Drive for 25 yards. Explode violently because you touched a curb. Drive for 30 yards. Explode violently because you touched another car.
Seriously, this game is an exercise in frustration.
Okay, the story is kind of fun, told almost entirely through FMVs. Apparently the team couldn't afford any decent props so they decided to just add some film grain and turn it into a cheesy 70s pastiche. Even though, aside from a few references to Jimmy Carter and disco, it really has no effect on the game whatsoever. It's basically Kuru Kuru Kururin crossed with GTA. Navigate your spinning limo around the city delivering people from A to B, trying not to burst into a flaming wreck on the way.
But you'll finish story mode in about an hour, and after that, unfortunately there isn't a whole lot to do. You can replay the individual missions and try and achieve a better score, or you can try and collect some of the hundreds of extra items within the game world. You can buy some of the 23 properties within the game world. What do they do? Well, they give you money every now and then, but you have to go back and collect it. Or you could try and find the 127 piles of cash in the game world. They...give you cash. What do you do with all the cash? You buy 'hats' and paint jobs for your limo, which make NO difference to the gameplay and are purely cosmetic. So, money is useless. You can try and find all of the 157 "Sick jumps", which are similar to the jumps in the GTA games. I don't think anything at all happens when you find them all besides a Steam Achievement. Or you can try and find all 49 horns. Which, again, are purely cosmetic.
The story mode itself is also incredibly linear, with no branching, and almost no variety in the order missions can be completed in. So...about an hour of story mode which consists almost entirely of driving from A to B, with the occasional pedestrian killing-spree thrown in. And then there's 333 optional extras you can find. Which don't do anything useful. There's no additional vehicles or anything like that. Oh, and there's half a dozen or so minigames, most of which you'll have already done as part of main missions.
The only modifications you can make are unlocked in garages as you play, and can do things like let you float/dive in water, or alter which way you spin. None of which you need for the missions.
It's a nice enough game and the presentation is very well done, but there isn't really much here to do once you've finished the main game. It's really just a mini-game that's been expanded into a full-length game without reason. If there were optional missions (taxi missions, anyone?), or upgrades that radically altered the way the game works (what if, say, certain missions were only available after certain mods to your limo, like the rich guy won't get in unless it has tinted windows added), or if the collectables DID something (like the hidden packages in GTA) then there might be a reason to keep playing after the end. But, there really isn't. Except for bragging rights.
It's also quite buggy...often a respawn will either drop you miles from where you were, bypassing all the closer checkpoints, or it'll respawn you partially inside a building or vehicle causing you to explode immediately. This might happen 3 or 4 times before you can regain control. I also once had my balance switch to £0.01- for absolutely no reason, and was also told that the garage was earning me money and was 23% complete....even though that's not possible in-game.
It's worth playing. For about an hour. But there isn't any replay value unless you want the Steam Achievements.
Oh, and the developers seem to think that taking drugs and driving under the influence is funny.
Way more fun than it has any right to be. Super silly and doesn't hide that fact. My only criticism is that the soundtrack can get repetative. Other than that, it's super great.

Roundabout is a top-down platforming game. They describe it as a '70s B-Movie and you'll find that everywhere. Expect 'bad' humor, 'bad' scenes/acting, 'bad' plot, etc. It has a very particular style of humor throughout the game that I think you'll either like or hate.
Pretty simple premise: you have a car that always rotates/spins and you have to maneuver it, avoiding obstacles, to your destination. The car itself doesn't control like a vehicle; you can jump, move in any direction (with a slight delay to reverse direction or reach max speed), and choose to spin faster. Collide with enough objects enough times you'll explode, no regenerating health. You drive through the same world where story missions take place. Missions are generally 'avoid obstacles, follow checkpoints until you get to the destination' missions.
There are plenty of collectables scattered across the world when you're not in a mission so there are things to do while travelling in-between missions.
A lot of the time one hit leads to another (no real invulnerability period after a hit) so you can destroy the limo pretty quickly. It's pretty frustrating when you almost get to a checkpoint before getting caught on one obstacle that destroys the car.
I would have liked a fast travel option or a way to just start missions. Maybe an easy-mode hot-air balloon type of thing to fly over the world just to activate missions (and be unable to get collectables).
It was a little annoying when I died multiple times trying to go fast through the city and just wanted to get to the next mission area. There are areas that I found a pain to get through which is fine for a mission but annoying for world travel.
Because the game plays almost top-down, I found myself looking a lot at the minimap for pathing and the main screen only to dodge/manuever. You can't really tell what the best path is because it's zoomed in enough that you may make a leap of faith into a deadly series of obstacles. I found out later that you can press +/- on the keyboard to zoom out a little but it's still not quite enough for me.
In rare cases (after dying) you'll respawn in a bad location that causes you to immediately take damage again.
Worth a look if you like platformers and you think you'll like this variant. Even if you enjoy cheesy cutscenes you're going to have to platform your way through the world and through several dozens of missions to see the story (which is B-movie mediocre). If you're not enthralled by the gameplay you're probably not going to keep interest long enough to get to the ending.

Roundabout is a cheesy low-budget FMV game starring a limousine driver, a mechanic, a lady in a hat, and a $40 skeleton bought off of
with surprising entertainment value.
In Roundabout, you control a constantly rotating limousine. You play as Georgio Manos, the world’s first revolving limousine driver. Your limousine is constantly rotating at all times, which forms the core of the game’s gameplay – you know how to get from point A to point B, but your constant revolution makes your life a lot more difficult. Early on it is fairly simple, navigating your way around stationary obstacles, but as the game progresses, things get increasingly more difficult, with moving obstacles, barrels which cause you to bounce in the opposite direction after striking them, platforming (done while spinning all the while), and the odd unique gameplay challenge to make things harder.
The core of the game are the “rides”. At the start of each ride, Georgio picks up a passenger, each of whom has a little bit of dialogue to start things off – a reason for going from point A to point B. There’s also a narrator, who chimes in, and both the narrator and the passengers are pretty chatty – every mission contains numerous lines of dialogue, as well as at least two FMV videos, one at the start and one at the end – with some rides having additional FMVs interspersed in the middle.
The passengers are deliberately terribly acted – every character acts in a very cheesy way. The videos are shot to look like something made in the 1970s, and the game itself is set in the 1970s, with references to Jimmy Carter and Disco present throughout the game, and a 70s aesthetic to the entire world.
But while the characters are campy as heck, they have a certain degree of Narm Charm to them – the acting in this is one of those “So Bad It’s Good” sort of things, and deliberately so, and it more or less works. It is impossible to take the game seriously, and the game knows it, and so plays it to the hilt, with “serious” events being comically ridiculous due to context, acting, and the very low budget of the game.
The game itself outside of the FMVs looks reasonable – it is not the highest quality of graphics, but the cars have an iconic quality to them, and while there’s nothing particularly special about the graphics in the game, they’re very serviceable and look decent enough.
While you can play through the game and just beat it, the game is not very hard in and of itself – the game is very generous with checkpoints, and it is impossible to fail at a ride. The real challenge in the game comes from completing optional objectives on the various rides. These include speed running the ride, beating a ride without getting hit at all, collecting all the coins in each ride, and beating the ride in various more difficult ways (no jumping, no using your alternate abilities). You can complete one or several of these challenges in any particular go at a ride, and you need not complete them all in a single ride.
Additionally, there are various collectables. Beyond being able to buy skins and limo hats via in-game currency which is not terribly difficult to collect (I ended up with $4k in the bank at the end with nothing to spend it on), you can also purchase properties… which periodically give you more money (oh boy!). But there are also piles of money in the environment to collect, “sick jump” icons which are in places you must jump to (ranging from inanely easy to reach to quite difficult, requiring multiple distant leaps), and horns which make different sounds when you honk them.
You also can unlock a bunch of items which allow your vehicle to do different things. There’s a raft which allows your car to float on water and dive beneath it, there’s an ability which slows down time, there’s an ability which reverses your direction of rotation just as if you’d hit a barrel, there’s an ability which makes your limo play ice cream truck sounds to pull in pedestrians to run over… there’s even an ability to shrink down your limousine, unlocked only after you beat the game, which makes a few things a lot easier (and is required for beating a few of the speed run times). These unlockables are either unlocked as you progress through the game, or (in most cases) unlocked by completing some sort of special challenge, such as running over 2,500 pedestrians or bouncing off of those direction-reversing barrels 100 times. While some of these sound tedious, I actually ended up unlocking almost all of them in the first of three major areas in the game.
All in all, this game is remarkably fun for how low budget it is. It rolled with its low-budget nature and did not take itself seriously at all, and as a result, it actually ends up having its cheesy story work to some degree – you can’t help but be amused by the terribly campy characters and the overdramatic narrator, and all the terrible, terrible puns. The gameplay itself is competent enough, though 100%ing the game is pretty tough, especially the speed run and no hit challenges.
If the core gameplay mechanic seems interesting to you, then this might be worth checking out.

You play as Georgio Manos, driving your clients around town in a crazy spinning limousine while trying to avoid obstacles and pick up items. A controller is strongly recommended.
It's a non-linear open world game with storyline attached. You head towards one of the animated stars on the mini map to pick up your next client. There's a short film (FMV) of a real-life character actor on the back seat telling you where he/she wants to go and why, then off you go following a big yellow arrow, trying to avoid all the cars and other obstacles in your way. If you hit 5 obstacles your car bursts into flames and you respawn at your last checkpoint, of which (thankfully) there are many.
Dotted around the streets there are spots where you can get a full repair. These are useful when they're in the middle of a particularly difficult stint but mostly redundant since you constantly just die and respawn anyway.
At the end of each successful trip there's another FMV as the character's personal story progresses. There's no overall storyline, the various threads are all unconnected apart from the fact that Georgio drives them all around.
At a certain point in the game jumping your limo becomes a thing, and the tasks increasingly require it.
There are many items to collect all over the place:
It's certainly recognisable as 70s. The generic background music (twanging bass and fast trumpet) from all 70s cop shows gives it away immediately, but if you're looking for period drama or insightful commentary on 70s culture then I'm afraid you're out of luck. There are some wing collars, tasteless sports jackets and I heard a pedestrian yell something about Jimmy Carter but that's about as far as it goes. There's a groovy disco tune on the main menu; I would have liked to hear more pieces in-game but sadly not even Disco Sylvain managed to produce any, and there's no punk at all.
Crowds of pedestrians shout angry comments wherever you go. They all end up in your wake as a bloody mess (don't worry, no close-up gore). There's no penalty for murdering innocent civilians, in fact one of the upgrades requires you to mow down 2,500 of them. It seems counter-productive for a driver to cull potential clients though doesn't it?
... is (intentionally?) bad and the storylines are a bit wacky and inconsequential. There are quite a few characters with a different actor for each. The star of the show is a plastic skeleton, which indicates the general standard of acting here. These FMVs, though I wouldn't find them very impressive in any other context, do bring the game to life and I've enjoyed every cheesy minute of it. Georgio herself never utters a word. No idea why not.
For the first few hours I was bursting into flames literally every 5 seconds. Towards the end my stamina increased to 10 seconds and occasionally even to the dizzying heights of 15 seconds (please resist any filthy comments). Deaths cost nothing though, unless you're trying for a deathless achievement. After a while it becomes part of the game and you're often repeatedly trying to make it to the next checkpoint without dying. Checkpoints are numerous enough that you can still make good progress despite frequent deaths.
Overall it's a good challenge. Difficult but no rage-quit due to the plentiful checkpoints.
Smooth and responsive, no glitches found on either Windows or Linux. The artwork of the game is clear and cartoony 3D, good quality but not overly artistic. The FMV is like watching TV (not flatscreen, ofc). There are a few cutscenes within the FMV which are deliberately fuzzy film snippets of cars exploding at the bottom of cliffs and suchlike. No problems at all.
It took me 7 hours to finish the story with 31% completion. Bear in mind that my controller skills are abysmal. The story is really only a means to show the player the entire town, afterwards you can continue in sandbox mode to collect further upgrades, hats, horns etc. Not to mention the achievements and mini-game leaderboards. All in all I'd say it's well worth the full asking price.
5 trading cards. 40 achievements. Steam cloud. Steam leaderboards. It's got the lot. Cross-platform is the cherry on the cake.
7 hours was more than enough for me - towards the end I was starting to find it tedious. I'm not blaming the game for this, it's just that I usually prefer some mental stimulation in my games whereas this is pure fun with no brainwork required. There's only so much fun I can take before I feel the urge to torture myself with some masochistically difficult puzzles.
This is a unique game, unlike anything else you've ever played (probably). If you like the idea of using a controller to grapple with a spinning limo then I highly recommend it, you'll have hours of fun. The many extra features flesh out the core gameplay nicely and it runs smooth as silk on all platforms.

I was skeptical of this game at first - I'm a fan of pixel graphics, but the bullet hell aspect of it seemed to lack depth from the previews and screen shots. I was very wrong  about that- the bosses and regular minions are challenging and take a lot of strategy (mainly the bosses) and learning of their attack patterns to defeat (some bosses are downright impossible without teammates and change up their patterns a lot, but they're beatable alone once you find a strategy that works).
The skills for each class fit each class nicely and make each class play very, very differently, which is great for variety and the team aspect of the game. These skills allow you to grow you character as you see fit; you can do more damage, do that damage more often or upgrade/purchase unique skills, or buy skills that allow you to be more durable in different ways. These skills play to each class' particular strengths, and as a result, they are all pretty balanced, but there are also weaknesses that can be overcome with time or teammates. It's a simple setup and skill tree, and it works extremely well for character balance.
The music is nice, but I ended up turning it off in favor of my own playlist, but aside from that, there really are no discernable negatives to this game.
I think this game was made by gamers, for gamers, and incorporates a lot of good ideas into a very streamlined, good product.
Highly recommend.

When you realize the garage door opening at five in the morning at night was the boy's mother going to the gym to cheat on the father. Depression is watching your whole entire world fall apart. This game just makes it look like you smoked a bit of weed and are lazy and sleepy. This game has nothing special other than depression. I don't believe anyone on that team had ever experienced depression. Because the real thing about depression is. There is no escape. It will follow you around and whenever you're having a happy moment you remember the bad moments, you always do. Even when I had no will to live, when I just wanted to end it all. I still soldiered on, I hated myself. I thought I was♥♥♥♥♥♥ like everything was my fault. I soldiered on because people cared about me, people loved me. People talked to me. They taught me how to love myself, they taught me how to be myself again. Talking in this game doesn't help, it doesn't solve anything and it doesn't help your character which is a total and utter lie. So at the end of third grade the boy was depressed. By fifth grade the boy was happy. And by sixth grade the boy was loved. From one depression survivor from another, don't kill yourself. You might think nobody cares about you, but really all you had to do all along was open your eyes and experience the good. Therapists are overrated, talk to a dog and or cat. They're much better listeners. I love all of you in a brotherly way survivors and sufferers. Don't give up. Let age knock at your door, not a stool and rope.

Fun, beautiful, but short (and too easy). Recommended, but not highly so.
This game is absolutely beautiful and oozes atmosphere like few others do. For this alone, I can recommend it and this outweighs the downsides.
Despite the game being low on dialogue (or any direct story telling), the atmosphere through what is given and through the art and level design itself is simply very well done.
The story actually has a surprising ending (if you get the true ending, that is) and you do want to see how it ends.
The controls are fluid and easily learned. The game quite simply fun to play.
The music and sound effects are top notch as well.
And finally, there are some quite interesting secrets to find, most of which will make you think "Ok... what was that about?!".
There aren't too many downsides here, but those that are, are pretty glaring, making this only a barely recommended game despite all the good.
It is too easy. Really. When you play a game and beat the final boss on the first try without even using all your items, and it was the hardest boss, too, then you know you have played a pretty easy game.
And since I'm mostly a mouse+keyboard purist, I'm really not that well versed with controllers.
Bosses in general are little more than HP sponges that require to dodge a few times.
This is also probably the biggest letdown for people seeing all the Dark Souls comparisons and wanting to play the game for the challenge. There just isn't much here.
The combat never evolves. Both your melee and ranged attack will always be the same, except for some minor damage upgrades (and one charge upgrade for the ranged).
Again, seeing it compared to Dark Souls, Castlevania or Metroid - in all of those your weapons change
- this is quite the letdown.
It is too short. My playtime after not 100% completion, but collecting all ivory bugs and all vitality items was barely five hours.
The game is sold at 10€, but short playtime is always a downside.
In such a short time, it is of course hard to implement a proper difficulty curve as well as more interesting upgrades.
I really hope this game will get a sequel of sorts. One that is longer so it actually has some space for more weapon, enemy and boss variety as well as adding more challenge.
PS: Yes, you do punch a witch to the boobs until she turns you into a cat.
