TL;DR A sprite based game that wants to be Dark Souls / Metroidvania but comes up short due to mechanical issues.
What it’s worth: $3-$5
Pros:
A. Beautiful animations
B. A unique main and side weapon combo (Strong, short range, 3-combo leaf and weak, long range, infinite ammo bow)
C. Smooth and polished, the game never felt choppy or internet flash game like.
Neutrals:
A. Setting is pseudo creepy castle town with a few extra locales. (Not unique, but not bad)
B. Characters are interesting from a visual perspective, but pretty bland from a writing perspective.
C. Difficulty is considerable, but not unbeatable. Your character has VERY little health, save points are few and far between, and minions respawn as soon as you leave a room, but minions really aren’t that bad if you use the terrain to your advantage and careful use of healing items will get you from save to save without much trouble.
Cons:
A. Combat options are EXTREMELY limited as you get NO NEW WEAPONS (Imagine a Zelda game where you got a sword and slingshot and nothing else for the entire game).
B. The combat animations are very poor from a mechanical point of view. Again they LOOK beautiful, but you will often find yourself taking damage from an attack whose animation you’re cleared of or at a different time then when the enemy looks like it is attacking. In addition your ONLY defensive technique which is a roll gives no indication whatsoever of when you’re safe or when you’re not (compare to risk of rain where it says “INVINCIBLE” on your health bar when you are).
C. Boss fights are incredibly boring, which is my main bone to pick with this game. The bosses are just giant health sponges that you just roll to dodge, then pound with your one and only 3-hit, one button, combo (a game that has precisely one combo shouldn’t style itself with “Impressive combos”). That’s literally it. Hit, roll, hit, roll, hit, roll, hit. No finding an elemental weakness, no finding a chink in the armor, no using terrain, no selecting the right item, no blocking, countering, or even picking a different attack. You’re put in a tiny box and play a glorified Mario party minigame.
Conclusion:
Maybe I needed to crank up the difficulty to make the game feel more intense, but that doesn’t make a game better. A hard game does not equal a good game. A game must be enjoyable, which this game wasn’t.

Far Cry 4's mechanics don't stray very far from how Far Cry 3 worked. You've got outposts to liberate. You've got radio towers to unlock. You've got animals to skin. You've got bad guys to shoot. Like Far Cry 3 the easiest path to take is usually going from point A to point B through the jungle. Why? Because every road and town is filled with things that want to kill you (most of the time). The animals in Far Cry 4 are much stronger than those in the previous game. You can and will die to animal attacks and luring animals for your benefit is a standard tactic in this game. Out of all of the animals the worst animal is the eagle. As soon as you're attacked by one you'll quickly learn why every NPC is scared of them. If you see a bird with a predator label shoot it. Next in the line of evil comes wolves, who will attack in packs and often are relentless in their pursuit of you despite (or because of) killing all of them.
The largest change between Far Cry 3 and Far Cry 4 is really the terrain. The mountainous regions make navigating difficult and turn what should be a short trip into a long one simply because you needed to change your elevation. It also makes outposts and other enemy strongholds more difficult to take because they have natural barriers. Generally when viewing an enemy outpost from a distance your vision of the area will be obscured from below and above making tagging enemies or taking stealth shots much harder. And stealth is also one of the big changes between 3 and 4. It is rather difficult to take down outposts completely silently and knocking out alarms will give you the "no alarms" reward. The game gives you a chance to replay outpost captures without losing control of the outpost but unless you really need that stealth capture to unlock one of the later skills there isn't much point to it. However it should be noted that the A.I. of the enemies remains strong whether you are trying to sneak in or capture the base through sheer force.
The RPG elements of the game are rather generic. Some require certain achievements. Some require being so far along in the story before they'll unlock. Spend experience points to increase your health points. Spend experience points to heal a little more.  Most of these are on the elephant side of the skill tree which deals with using herbs to make power-ups. Power ups do actually take time to make and you should stock up before going into battle. However I really only found the hunting power up, which allows you to see all enemies, to be useful. On the tiger side of the skill tree you have various takedowns and other combat oriented skills.
I enjoyed this game but I couldn't help thinking "This is a repackaged Far Cry 3". I was actually disappointed by the amount of "pop-ups" and textures fading in. I was expecting beautiful landscapes on max settings and was instead treated to trees and mountains popping into existence and appearing slightly better as I got close. I was very disappointed with the main narrative. You play the role of a young male on a trip to fulfill his mother's dying wish of taking her ashes to her homeland. From the moment you land you know this is not a good place to be. Now the game introduces the laughable "big bad" Pagan Min who gets a lot of overacted dialog which continues throughout the game even when you aren't doing a task related to the main story at all.
As for the main story there are several endings which I will not spoil but I will say that the idea of choice in the game has almost no weight towards what happens in the end. Sure the narratives are slightly different but there are basically one of two endings that the average player will see and neither is rewarding. The main character is a generic white male. His voice actor is good but the character is not well developed. His backstory is repeated over and over again in the game and this is possible because there is so little of it.
While I recommend the game I do not recommend any of the DLC. Both of the "expansions" are made of very linear maps with little to no gameplay changes outside of your hub. In one of the DLCs you have a base that can be upgraded and needs to be defended nightly but actually defending it isn't that fun. Either you'll be well defended enough to take out the waves of enemies with ease or you won't be and you'll probably die from a rush of enemies. In one of the DLCs you get to see Yetis. These are nothing more than giant tanks and while you might get a bit of excitement from having to hide or run from them unarmed, you won't be too worried if you see one in the wild. The DLC weapons are half decent when you are just starting the game but will quickly be outclassed. The HURK DLC is just a few missions in a different zoned area and your ultimate payoff is a harpoon gun that is really only good for laughing at corpses pinned to walls. Unfortunately you'll have to be rather close to use it.
In summary: This is Far Cry 3.5. The groundwork of the game series is still enjoyable but so little has changed that it seems to be missing that "WOW" factor that makes a good game into a great game.

The one downfall to this game, is it's tie to Horribad Uplay. U-play is clunky, buggy, crashes and has a horrible interface. I almost didn't buy the game because it was on U-play. Having just started Far Cry 4 two weeks ago, I must say, this game has sucked me in like no other.
While I've never been the biggest fan of the way Ubisoft makes games (DRM, mandatory companion apps, downright hostile customer relations), I really cannot fault their ability to make an interactive graphics stress-test. In this, their craft has gotten markedly better, as their games have been steadily getting more game-like while still maintaining the level of visual fidelity one expects from a Cryengine title.
So where does this trend leave us with Far Cry 4? Essentially GTA set in the Himalayas.
Please understand, this is not a bad thing. In fact, I can think of no better setting for those of us who love the open world chaos of Grand Theft Auto but are tired of the city surroundings. Once the prologue is finished, players are set loose in a gigantic world in which random and scripted events mesh in a way that breathes life into the gameworld. Point in fact, in a very early portion of the game, I was getting ready to sneak into an enemy encampment when suddenly a leopard chased a pack of dogs into the area. The enemies, as scripted to do so by the game engine, immediately opened fire on the dogs, who went from running from the leopard to attacking the humans, while the leopard also went into full human attack mode. I watched in awe as 3 dogs and a leopard set about completely clearing the enemy camp that I had been seconds away from attacking. Once all the humans were dead, I knocked the leopard down with an arrow and ran down to collect all my loot. I hadn't thrown any bait, I didn't otherwise lure the animals into the camp. This was a wholly organic situation that arose from the sheer insanity of having so many game systems in place at once. These situations are not rare, but all are unique, entertaining, and immersive.
FC4 feeds on this dynamic. The sheer number of things to do in this game is mind-boggling, from discovering new locations, to finding thousands of items scattered across the gameworld, to partcipating in hundreds of missions, quests, and distractions. Granted, some people may be turned off by such a multitude of activities, but each mission is so fun, and the ability to engage a situation so open, that all players will find a way to have fun in FC4. So many times have I marked a waypoint on the map and told myself that I would just do that one run before logging off and doing something else, then found myself playing a solid 2 hours later. The game is built for this, as on your way to any objective, you will run across random events such as villagers being attacked by enemies, a garrison of troops just ripe for stealth-killing, or the appearance of an animal you need to finish crafting a bigger ammo pouch. What starts as a quick diversion can quickly turn into an enemy chase that leads you halfway across the map, exposing you to yet more objectives, loot, insanely gorgeous vistas, and myriad opportunities to crouch at the top of a ridge and rain sniper bullets or arrows down on unsuspecting targets.
The story--thus far at least--is quite good, and I'm continually drawn in by the suave, flippant psychopath that is Pagan Min. Backstory is elegantly told through collectables such as Mohan's Journal entries, which help flesh out the conflict currently raging in the fictional country of Kyrat. Other items, such as the masks of Yalung and the pages found near them, expand the scope of the story, revealing a serial killer with dark religious motivations, adding a chilling, mysterious side-story to the game. All of the characters are well voiced, and the mostly tight script helps to move the game along without getting in the way too much. Power Struggle missions are often difficult choices that help move the game narrative in a direction selected by the player, adding a layer of interactivity to the plot that a great number of other games lack. Choosing between collecting enemy intel or saving the lives of a group of rebels is a surprisingly difficult one, and the choice you make will affect who sides with you and what future missions you'll get to play.
As already mentioned, the graphics, particularly on a system that can handle it, are incredible. When I bought this game, I was running a rather old GTX 550Ti, and I was still able to make the game look great. Just a few days ago however, I took the splash and invested in a GTX 970, and I'm constantly blown away by how unabashedly gorgeous this game is. As usual, the Cryengine is capable of some positively dazzling displays of nature, and standing just about anywhere in the game, the player will be slapped across the face with the realization of: "I'm PLAYING this visual feast". For the feeling of immersion, Far Cry 4 cannot be beat, even on lower spec hardware.
Of course, no game is perfect, and yes, something as vast and complex as FC4 is going to have its share of issues, from a slightly unbalanced difficulty curve, to bugs, poorly defined missions, and at times spotty hit detection. One thing I can say, the wingsuit has upset me more than a few times. Often have I been in the middle of a firefight with the enemy, and in a bid to get clear of enemy fire have I run toward a very short ledge (small enough that you could climb up from the other side). Unfortunately, if you hold the run button as you go over the edge, you'll automatically open your wingsuit and since short ledges like that are frequently mirrored by cliffs, you will fly right into the cliff or the ground and instantly die. Not exactly the way I'd like to lose in a firefight. Same story with trees. Get too close to a tree in your wingsuit, and you'll soon be watching the loading screen, even if you never actually hit the tree itself. Other times, a hazy mission objective, or even the sometimes wacky pathfinding for waypoints has resulted in a game over screen when it shouldn't have. Fortunately, these issues are usually minor and can be overcome with practice (let go of the run button near cliffs unless you MEAN it!).
When taken as a whole, FC4 has way more ups than downs and as an evolution of the franchise is one of the finest in the series, and despite the continued and adamant reliance on the Uplay companion app (seriously Ubi, no one likes it...please STOP), this game is a worthy addition to any PC library. I most certainly recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun, beautiful open world challenge with tons of stuff to do between missions.
Cheers/Game on.

As a game it has a simple premise, navigate your spinning car around an obstacle filled town.
What makes this game memorable is the over-the-top FMV cut scenes that are full of wonderfully silly acting, all by a host of colourful characters. A true hidden gem.

When you look at the Roundabout trailer, it looks like a colourful crazy havoc in style of old Carmaggedon. Driving over people, blood everywhere, explosions. But it is not only about it really, only when you do few quests where you have to run over somebody. The main goal of the game is to get from one point to another and don’t crash with your car. And it's not easy as it sounds, because your car is a limousine that continuously spins around and occasionally just jumps.
Roundabout is essentially a logical platformer, where you need with the help of spinning avoid tricky deployed obstacles, including tires, which change direction of spinning of your limousine. In garages, which are scattered throughout the town, you can use removable upgrades like swimming or temporarily slow down time. You can also jump and quickly accelerate, but all at a constant spinning.
Even though this sounds like a strange feature, developers No Goblin were inspired by another game and they took it on their own. And it’s very funny. The environment is beautifully coloured and you will drive … I mean spin through several parts of the town, from the beaches to snowy mountains. You need to obtain missions in some parts of town and it feels like sort of an open world. You earn some cash for doing missions and tricks which can be spend to improve the quaint decorations on the roof and funny honking sounds.

What is the main advantage, however, is the story. It is narrated through FMV sequences that are very endearingly amateurish. Small studio due to their "budget" accommodate videos as short monologues of passengers with a female driver Georgio. Amateur actors take their roles with passion and you look forward to see more of it.
I haven’t encountered any major bugs while playing, just when the limousine jump into the air. I don’t mean when you crash, moreover, it takes only about five bumps into obstacles before the car explodes and returns to a nearby checkpoint, or to a repair shop in the garage. And I swear you’ll do this a lot. I am thinking of using the jump and jumping over roofs. Several times it happened to me that the car was stuck in the texture, flew into the building and blew up or crashed into invisible barriers.
Roundabout is truly indie game, the graphic design and movie sequences feels cheap, but it’s followed by the irreplaceable charm, from which some other little studios can inspire. This is an ambitious project that may look strange on paper, but in practice it works very well, because Roundabout doesn’t take itself seriously. Storyline is short and lasts for several hours, but the game is trying to prolong the game with pile of challenges plus the percentage performance of missions, which allows you to play again to achieve 100% in it. And you need to really try and endure dozens of explosions to achieve it. At these times, the game can be frustrating, but there’s no other game with a similar theme, nor a sense of humour so I can recommend it.

It's a serviceable game, I suppose. A rather linear stealth action game where combat is heavily discouraged, though possible if you plan ahead. Combat shouldn't be glossed over, you have a few arrows and a short bow, as well as a blackjack to cudgel your enemies. Not much use outside of contextual sneak attacks, if you end up in a straightforward fight you will lose health but survive a single enemy. Maybe even two. Running away though is the only real option. That's fine, bar the context thing, I ended up feeling as though I had limited control over combat because of that.
There is a set way to do most things and get most places, and deviating will get you nowhere. Occasionally, you'll have the choice of sneaking through a vent or picking a lock (and avoiding enemies on the ground) as opposed to taking the rooftops, but more often than not there is the way, and you will take that way. Rope arrows can only be affixed to certain beams, you can climb set points (with white markers on them, mostly. Nothing with something vague like jars or small boxes atop it despite having an edge), and are railroaded to a destination. There are several points where I was left utterly confused on how to get somewhere nearby, to find I had to travel around the map, and on occasion into another cell to get there due to a locked gate I could not climb.
The story also appears to have been designed by committee, it seems like plot lines were dropped but the initial set up is still in the game. Without spoilers, the Asylum and the vast deal of "documents" found there have provoked many reactions. Alongside who exactly the Queen of Beggars is and why the Thief-taker General finds you wherever you are. Perhaps it makes sense with context from past games, but as a reboot it certainly shouldn't be necessary to have to ask what exactly the characters are, outside of a flimsy plot device.
Honestly, though I can't get past that and it would've been a recommend if not for the contextual movement, I have repeatedly fallen to my death in jumps that should be entirely possible. Button mashing E to open windows to get in or out of most buildings. When combined with the linearity it feels less like you are the player-character, and more that you are simply riding on his back. I barely had to think to complete the game and I am terrible at stealth. Even pressing the spacebar to "swoop" is annoying (though useful.) You don't really seem to do much, it's more of a "press space to do something awesome" form of movement.
So, really from a gameplay standpoint... it's a no. It's a game that's unsure whether it wants to commit to stealth or stealth action and that really shows, pure stealth it could've been great, proper exploration, more routes to escape and find enemies etc. Pure stealth-action, good too - they could've fixed combat and movement. But as it stands watching the world through Garret's eyes felt like I had no agency in this game, I felt relief over triumph at the end of a mission. For that, it's a no.

Hammerwatch is a well crafted and entertaining traditional top down 2D action game in the style of Gauntlet.  Alone or online with up to three friends, choose one of 6 different classes and work your way through Castle Hammerwatch, filled with traps, secrets, and of course thousands of monsters to destroy, while spending your hard earned gold on upgrades for your characters.
Hammerwatch is at its normal or hard difficulties a punishing, yet rarely unfair game that gives a real sense of mastery as you get better, but it also has an easy difficulty as well as custom mutators you can set to tailor your game experience exactly how you like it.
The game is presented in simple top down 2D sprite graphics that have a retro feel to it, which may be offputting to some but I personally adore the art style.  The controls are simple, the action is fast and the Castle itself is very well designed with tons of secrets and puzzles to solve between all the killing.
I'm having a great time playing this game, at time of writing having finished the main game in a private co-op group and just getting started on the (free) expansion.  While the game is fun if you're going it alone, it definitely shines the brightest in multiplayer, especially if you want to play a melee character as certain situations are very, very tricky to pass without proper ranged damage.
While I haven't looked at it myself yet, there is also a level editor included and the Steam Workshop has a whole bunch of community created adventures you can play, potentially adding a heckton of hours to the longevity of the game.
If you see the game at a discount somewhere I can safely recommend a purchase if you like some throw back, uncomplicated dungeon crawling action.  Especially so if you have a few friends you can pass around 4 pack copies to and drag along for the fun!

German Fortress 3D is a broken and buggy mess of assets cobbled together to make a Wolfenstein 3D clone.
As far as I can tell, this game was made using no assets created by the developer themselves.
The sprites are mod assets created by Wolf Skevos-Jones for use with Wolfenstein 3D fan creations. The developer does credit this in the game but I highly doubt the sprites were intended to be used for commercial purposes.
The rest of the game seems to be entirely comprised of Raycasting Game Maker stock assets, including the UI, weapons and environment. The developer has also attested to this in the past.
While the developer has acknowledged this in the past, it still shows that they are incapable of creating a proper game themselves, as is evidenced by the terrible main menu in the game, which is most likely the only thing the developer made themself.
This game (along with all the other games by Ghost_RUS), was listed as incompatible with Greenlight and not allowed to pass through the system. The likely reason being infringement on copyright in their various submissions, or possible vote tampering/botting.
Okay, so enough about that. What is the game actually like? Well, it's a broken mess that is nearly unplayable.
The controls in the game don't work properly with a modern mouse. If you move your mouse at a speed faster than a snails pace, it simply won't register as you moving it at all. This makes aiming or turning with the mouse extremely frustrating and broken. You can also aim with the arrow keys on the keyboard, but there are no keys on your keyboard that allow you to fire your weapon. You can only fire your weapon with the left-mouse button, so using the arrow keys is completely useless.
The levels are very simple, you shoot everything, find a key then go to the next level. What makes it difficult is the awful A.I that simply start nuking down your health when you see them without any sort of combat loop. Your health just melts constantly and you can't do anything about it due to the broken controls.
Overall, avoid this game at all costs. There is nothing here to enjoy if you like old school style games. This is simply a quick cash-grab. There are many mods for Wolfenstein that are many times better than this trash.

The puzzles seem similar to older games like crazy machines. You put missing parts in machines and fix them. The game always gives you clear instructions what the machine should do, there is never any confusion about the goal. Most of the problems are timing related, which can be solved by trial and error, but also with a little bit of thinking ahead. For someone who loves games like spacechem and infinifactory, the puzzles are pretty easy to solve, but still fun.
There is not much of a story so far, but this is only episode 1.
The artwork looks pretty good, and suits the game perfectly. The same can be said about the music and sounds. It just has this nice atmosphere, that fits perfectly with the game.
But, without rushing, reading every dialog, and playing around with the machines after i build them, it still only took me about one hour to finish the game. Mostly because of the easy puzzles, I never had to think to hard or was stuck for longer then 30 seconds. The whole game just feels like the tutorial for me. But a good one.
Is it worth it?
For the current price and considering the time to complete the game, i would compare it to going to a movie. About the same price per hour. (At least where i'm living).
If you are looking for a relaxing puzzle-game, with no time pressure, no frustration and no danger of overheating you brain, this game is for you.
If you are looking for a something spacechem / infinifactory difficult, or just want a lot of playtime for you money, this is not it.
Would I recommend it: YES, if you like mechanical puzzles and don't mind spending the same amount of money as you would spend on a movie.
Am i going to buy episode 2: Already done.
Edit: After playing episode 2:
The puzzles get more complex and difficult to solve. The gameplay lasts a bit longer. The puzzles are still very good, based around a different theme this time. After playing the second episode, it seems that the first one was indeed just the tutorial in how to play the game. The second episode has all the good parts from the first, and improved the one complaint i had. So, even better than the first part.

So lets just get this out of the way, yes the game is free, yes its by mojang, no being a free game does not exempt it from being criticized.
The game is a clone of the old Risk games, you start your turn with a finite number of actions indicated by Gold, every action costs varying amounts of it with basic attacks only costing one and fortification upgrades costing upwards of 6 gold. Now you get more gold by capturing neighboring nations and holding them, in fact it takes a turn before they start producing gold for you.
However producing gold is all they do, they confer no bonuses to attack or defense, no price reduction in actions, there is no way to affect the outcome of an action, the game gives you fortifications you can place which supposedly increase one's defensive capabilities, but in a game powered strictly by RNG with no skill involved these fortifications mean little when they can fall in a single action and an empty node can stand the test of time and weather an entire turn worth of actions.
As I said previously, there is no strategy, there is no thought to this game (either in production or playing), the game is essientially a clicker game, just keep clicking nodes you don't own and eventually you'll win
Pros
None
Cons
*Terrible Music and repeditive sound effects quickly become irritating within minutes of starting.
*Terrible controls, yes thats right a mouse driven game with terrible controls. Clicking works whenever it chooses to and seems to be affected by the same RNG that controls the rest of the "game".
*RNG, literally what the game should had been called. you click tiles to try and capture them, you keep clicking till either A) you run out of gold or ,B) the game decides to give it to you. No way to swing the favor, no way to mitigate risk, or anything.
Tldr
Free game that can and should be avoided, only enjoyment one can derive from the game is reviewing the steam reviews and laughing at the people trying to defend this dreck on its sole merit of being f2p. But no really, even in the most heinous of f2p wreckage of games they usually have something going for them
but this is essientially nothing but a clicker game trying to masquerade as a strategy game.

Far Cry 4. First off lets just get this out of the way. It is not as good as Far Cry 3. Not due to the gameplay or the graphics (which are beautiful BTW if you have a high end machine) For the most part the gameplay is almost exactly the same as Far Cry 3, which is a very good thing. The Crafting is fun. You can spend hours just trying to upgrade your stuff, driving around in cars and helicopters, the whole bit, and just have a blast. The Outposts have improved with the AI looking to retake the ones you have already captured. However it is a bummer that it only does it next to outposts that you are around, so essencially they never retake it unless you just ignore the plea for help, with you being like literally 2oo ft awayfrom the battle. So that was a hit/miss in my opinion. The game has beautiful graphics, and moments where you are playing and feel amazing, like when you are Jumpsuit flying through the Hymilayas...super amazing, you feel as if you are really there. Just wonderful.
Ok, now that that is out of the way, why is this not up to Far Cry 3, main point is STORY LINE. Right from the get go in 3 you feel this pull to the story. Your friends are captured, your brother killed, you have this crazy man named Vas after you, who lets admit is one of the top 10 villians in gaming. In 4 you dont feel that. You dont feel that growing ability to not only survive, but to be a real Bad♥♥♥♥♥as you try and save your friends. And while they dont have "friends" so to say in this one that you need to save, they try to pull you into the politics of the world, with you picking sides of either the chick who wants to be modern, or the man who wants to hold on to tradition, all the while you are fighting Pegan Min, who you find yourself actually wishing you could join his side of things because he is the only really likable person in the game (although he is a crazy dictator)
Long Story Short, if you liked Far Cry 3 then you will enjoy 4. But dont expect to be pulled into caring about the story line like you were in 3.

The complexity of the genre is still there in Dredmor, but it's more accessable.
All in all, if you need an introduction to the Roguelike genre, or simply want something you can take a bit less seriously but still enjoy as much as the Hack's and Dungeon Crawl's that are the current staple of the genre, Dungeons Of Dredmor is a good choice.
Also, it's entirely worth the $5 pricetag. Don't bother waiting for a sale, if you think you'd enjoy the game.

Here's the thing, if you're really fiending for some sort of metriodvania styled game and you've already played Axiom Verge and Hollow Knight, then maybe its ok for you to drop some money on this game itch that scratch for a weekend.
Even then, I find it a bit odd that this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews. I found it to be incredibly average.
What I think this game has going for it is that it does have some pretty impressive pixel artistry and some very good animation, and I don't think the game is really all that "bad", its a complete game which is something I can't say for a lot of games now days. Hell, I'm even fine that its a short game, it can take about 4 hours to beat. The problem is that it kind of lacks personality for a game that is supposed to be story driven, all I know about the game is that your trying to kill a queen because a curse spread to your land and thats litterately it. The combat was incredibly bland, all you have are arrow shots, a roll, and the same 3 hit combo to get you throughout the entire game. What makes it challenging is the artifical difficult of being hit about 3 times is enough to kill you and reset your progress.  Knowing where to travel next was a pain because, unlike other metriodvania's, this game doesn't really give you new power ups that warrant a reason for you to explore previous areas. You just get a key and have to try to remember which door you might have passed earlier that its supposed to fit to. The soundtrack of the game was ok, there was a song I liked in there somewhere but too much of it felt like generic japanese fantasy music.
I think my biggest gripe is that you can tell this game wants to be Dark Souls but fails to come close capturing the essence of the series. When you use your bellflower its the exact same animation as crushing a soul gem. There's a fight where the boss lights her sword with the exact same animation as using Charcoal Pine Resin in dark souls. The background of Karst Castle looked like I was back in Kanehurst from Bloodborne.Now, there's not problem borrowing ideas from other games, it shows your influences and there's a reason why so many games nowadays are borrowing mechanics and the overall vibe of the dark souls games. The problem is that I didn't see anything in Momodora that made me feel like I was playing a game influenced by Dark Souls but rather a game trying to be Dark Souls with a chibi aesthetic.
Look, the guy who made this game is a talented indivdual. I can't make a video game, I've tried, I don't have the patience and I'm not as good of an artist as he is. I want to see what else he puts out in the future, but here's advice as to what can be improved upon.
As far as Metriodvanias are concerned, the games are usually about the journey of the hero and watching as they, and the player, grow more powerful throughout their journey. Provide some upgrades that improve the way the character moves throughout the world. Some of the basic stuff seen in other games is additional jumps, wall jumping, sprinting, climbing, etc. Also, use these upgrades as reasons to include environmental puzzles for the players to return to and solve. Use these upgrades are reasons for a player to be able to progress to a new area they otherwise wouldn't have been able to access yet.
As for what makes Dark Souls special, its not just the combat, its the world. Leave a trail of breadcrumbs for the in areas that maybe have some sort of significance to the story. Tell a story to the player without using words. Especially with how great of an artist this guy is, I feel like that would be his strong suit here.
So yeah, overall, I played the game through to completion and I appreciate that it was a short game, but I think there's a lot of progress that can be made on future games. The main reason why I'm marking this as a game I don't recommend is because there's already games out there that do the same thing but do it better, and while I'm the type of person to spend a ton of money on steam, if a friend has 10 bucks and asks me which game to buy between Hollow Knight and Momodora I'm going to say Hollow Knight.

It's entertaining, but don't expect it to be as good as Cannon Fodder 1/2. It lacks the fluidity and speed present in CF, also you can't split up squads. Such a comparison would usually be unfair, but Tiny Troopers is basically an unashamed attempt to be an "inspired by Cannon Fodder" type of game.
However it's better than the real Cannon Fodder 3. I'd also say it's better than Foreign Legion or Bunch of Heroes, so buy it if you were thinking of buying any of those. (If you're looking for something slightly less arcadey, look up 'recruits'. It's been greenlit but is not on the store yet. It's on Desura though. Also lookup running with rifles)
The campaign is weird. There's a persistent set of points/money used, which is gained by completing missions. But if you repeatable fail missions not only do your troops die (and therefore you get poorly skilled replacements) but you don't get any money. You often need to spend money to get some one-time only extra troopers, but if you fail the mission and therefore they die. It's as if the mission has cost you negative money! The game has an angry-birds style ability to choose to replay previous missions (complete with a 3-star rating) so I imagine players can grind old missions for money if they need to cash to buy some uber-force for later ones. I didn't have to do that when doing 'campaign 1'. A quick google and I see it's an iOS game with IAP. Now I'm not surprised by the odd campaign structure. ;)
The mouse controls are tricky to use, but very faithful to CF if you've played it. With the mouse, you click and ALL troops immediately go in that direction. If you want to walk one way whilst shooting the other a great amount of mouse dexterity is required (especially to keep a constant speed up). This was one of the major sources of difficulty in the original Cannon Fodder on later bullet-hell style levels and one of the main adrenaline producing factors.
Switching to WADS removes that sense of urgency but presents its own problems. (They're also non-rebindable, grr). The keyboard controls are strange and differ from the mouse controls in that all the people no longer move at once. They turn it into a semi twin stick shooter crossed with 'snake'. i.e. you only move the front guy and the rest follow, meaning that if you change direction most of your squad will staying in place for a second or so as the lead guy moves past them, which makes them easy bullet sponges for the enemy. It's pretty annoying.
I don't know if that quirk of the WADS control scheme is to make it more 'balanced' (as all troops instantly moving in the same direction would substantially reduce the likely-hood of your trailing guys getting shot yet be easier to control), or if it just wasn't thought about at all.
Also: The camera is a bit annoying when shooting, especially on the zombie level.
Overall it's quite fun. If they were to up the walkspeed of everything, make the projectiles slightly smaller, make the projectiles faster, make better walk animations, and fix the annoying WADS snake issue I'd say they'd have a very entertaining games on their hands.

Dungeons of Dredmor, as a rogue-like, is somewhat easier than many I've played in the past. Nethack, Crawl, and others can be trickier. But while not quite as difficult per se, it nevertheless achieves a substantial amount of challenge with its own system. Though the in-game help is somewhat useless for many skills--it takes a wiki to sort through things and understand what things actually do--the flavor text used is just one small part of the game's overall sense of charm and humor. This is not a game that takes itself seriously in any sense of the word. It happily mocks and makes fun of any and everything, with tongue-in cheek descriptions of every item and monster in the game in such a way as to make you think you've wandered into a comedian's dream by mistake. The gameplay is particularly satisfying, especially when you conquer Monster Zoos, which are giant rooms filled with anywhere from 50 to 200 monsters. The modding community is rich, with gads of useful additions and fun additions to please all kinds of fans who want to see their favorite work in video games. I highly recommend this rogue-like for many many hours of fun dungeoneering.

I have a few aspects that in my opinion, should be in every video game sequel.
- The game must not CHANGE the story of the previous game/s.
- The game's story should not be EXACTLY the same as the previous games* (* can be excused at times, such as a game in parts or a linear continuation).
- The game must retain aspects of the previous game/s.
- The game should have NEW aspects to freshen the experience, while still holding similar ones.
- The game should have a FEW differences that completely change the experience for the better.
- The game must be fun and difficult (duh...).
- The game must be either short and sweet or long and enduring.
- The game should have events that make it interesting and have minimal cliche`es.
If you ask me, Thi4f meets these requirements pretty well, and so therefore make it worth all the money to me, and it should to you as well.
Thi4f has a great story, adapts the characters very well, and has an atmosphere seen only in masterpieces, all wrapped together in a warm sheet with badass soundtracks and lots o' loot. However, I won't lie: it's not the best game ever. I was quite disappointed when I got the game from pre-order, and here's why:
- No sword or even dagger. I can live without 'em cause it is a stealth game, but still :(
- Not the kind of parkour I was looking forward to (come on, at least let me slide!)
- The world isn't AS open as I would have liked.
- The storyline, while still interesting, is not the same as it was announced when the game was revealed.
The game is OK, but all in all, it could have been better. I personally think it's quite underrated, but it's also not the amazing game I had hoped for.

Depression Quest provides what I feel is a very fair representation of some of the thought patterns and attitudes prevalent in those experiencing depression.  Calling it a game however, is a bit of a stretch in my opinion considering depression itself is not a game.  I am seeing lots of reviews that are written by people that seem to think that the "solution" choices being unavailable is ridiculous, but from my experience wtih type 1 bipolar disorder the lack of those options is nothing short of realistic as a representation of the workings of the mind of the severely depressed.  Hell, I would even argue that the options presented *aren't hopeless and dark enough!*  That, however, is just reflective of my personal experiences with very intense and deep depression where hygene and food intake are put completely on hold and every other thought that goes through my head is self deprecating or suicidal.  However, the authors explained the choices and decision options very well in the description when they stated that eveerybody experiences depression differently, and it is quite simply not possible to cover every single possible decision and experience angle.  Besides, if they DID manage to cram in... say 100 different decision options, it would result in the game not being what it is supposed to be - a glimpse into the mind of one "average" depression afflicted individual for the purpose of educating those unfamiliar or curious about what could be on the mind of a depressed person.
Is this title for everyone?  Hell no.  There is no happy ending or real control illustrated in the text... this is EXACTLY how MANY, MANY people with depression feel and see the world and is completely intentional.  The only goal of the seriously depressed is to make it to the next minute of their life.  The princess is NOT in another castle... she bled out in her bathtub last week.  If you expect a sunshine and lollipops style ending with just the right combination of choices, you're in the wrong place.
Does this title reflect poorly on the depressed, making them appear lazy?  Only to the grossly uninformed or those with a deeply misguided view on depression as a weakling's illness that's cured with force.  (Please F*** right off - you only perpetuate or worsen the problem)  The described emotions herein are very true to life and the lack of a real "ending" is truly reflective of the illness.
Should people give this a try for s**** and giggles?  If you are truly looking for giggles or a sense of accomplishment after  completing this, you are looking in the wrong place.  Trust me.  Uncertainty orbits the depressed mind like a moon and often eclipses the soul from the light.  People curious about the depressed or those faced with living with a depressed person absolutely should give this a go.  The reality of the depressed person won't make you smile or laugh, so this game will not either.  Reality's a ♥♥♥♥♥ like that.
Do I reccomend people try this out?  Definitely.  Just know what you are getting into, and that everybodies experience and attitudes are going to be different.  Don't be a jerk - realize what the goal of this project is, and not what you want it to be:  education, not entertainment.

I think the biggest thing people don't consider with this game is that it isn't about a specific kind of depression. It isn't something so easily defined. It is about the player, and how they cope with certain situations, and how hard life seems to be when crippled by their own thoughts. It is meant not to be a realistic break down of depression, but to show key points in the process, and to show those small moments that most people think won't matter, and how they really do make all the difference.
I honestly loved this game, and it felt nice to see a happy ending, without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t romanticization.

As a longtime fan of the Katamari games, Roundabout was the perfect game for me.  The story is quirky and intentionally told like a bad-B movie through FMV cutscenes, which gives the game a certain flair I haven't seen in anything else.  The actual controls for the game are precise (well, as precise as a rotating limo can be) and while the game is tough, I never felt like it was being unfair.  If I have any complaints, it would primarily be the lack of a fast-travel system to get from place to place (the map is really large), and the story is overall too short for my tastes.  Even still, I highly recommend this game to someone looking for a unique game with a style all its own.
Update:  I just nominated this game for the self-created category in Steam where I simply called it "Weirdest game ever".  That's really the only way to describe it.

Mini Metro is a strategy game with a very minimalistic interface and set of rules.
You're a designer of a city's subway lines, and you have to keep passengers flowing through stations as they continue to pop up all over a city. Every week, you earn an additional train engine and one of two items, that could be an additional car (holds more passengers), a tunnel to navigate through waterways, a new line (with a maximum number allowed per city).
The object is to move as many passengers as possible, without letting any passenger wait at a station for too long.
Though still not ready for prime time, what is in the game is well-built and very challenging. The best laid plans constantly need to be changed to fit around passenger needs. You can't rest while the city grows around you.
If you're a fan of train, simulation or strategy games, I highly recommend this title. If you just want a casual challenge and like minimalism, I would also recommend this game. Try it out.

I don't know why, but I just love games about making dots move on lines. I own many such games and Mini Metro is the one best right now. The dots on these lines come in different shapes, which is exciting, and the lines can be controlled entirely by the player, with some restrictions. Seeing your dots move efficiently rather than piling up is very gratifying.
What makes this game particularly clever, in the dots-on-lines genre, is that the dots represent passengers and the lines connect between stations on real world city geographies. The game can be very challenging, but in a very fun sort of way. There are decisions to make along the way and I feel like these are very important decisions. Don't forget you can always remove and rebuild lines when you find yourself struggling. What was most efficient at the start of the game may not be the most efficient halfway through.
I would recommend this game. There are bugs, and it's Early Access, but it's fun.

Ok, so.
In a vacuum, this game isn't bad.  Probably even recommended.  The controls are weird and floaty, but the gunplay is designed with those controls in mind.  You absolutely need to get more than one jump to take advantage of the game feel, but
However.
In a world where Ziggurat and Immortal Redneck exist, this game fails to measure up.  It's not difficult enough, allowing players to rush through rooms with little downside and with enemies and attack patterns that don't challenge people used to these types of games.  The overuse of stationary turrets instead of varying, moving enemies (and the ones who do move are significantly slower than the player) mean that the frantic nature of the movement and gunplay mechanics are at odds with the actual challenges of the game.  And the liberal downpour of upgrades meant that I sprinted through the last floor and had no incentive to stop and fight enemies, since I had 3 health bars, double the starting movement speed, four jumps, a max-level gun that stunned enemies, and an AOE room clear ability that I barely even needed.  I beat the final boss without breaking a sweat, and he was the hardest boss in the game.
Also, the game is ugly as hell.  While that's not a deal-breaker for me, it means that this game has literally nothing to offer.
I appreciate this game as an early example of the genre, but it hasn't aged well.  Play Ziggurat or Immortal Redneck instead.  Hell, even Paranautical Activity is better than this garbage.
I refunded this game.  There isn't enough replayability to justify the price tag even on sale, much less full price.

In brief, it has a large library of drums, synths and vocals clips which you can rearrange on the sequencer with multiple tracks to add layered sound and contruct the music. There is enough variety of phrases to make interesting music.
The virtual instruments including Robota, so called virtual synthesizer are all just different ways to create drum sounds i.e drum machines. There is a virtual keyboard but it doesn't generate any sound nor does it pull  instruments / voices from the  sound card. Basically i don't know if the keyboard has any useful purpose. I may be wrong about this since i've not delve deeply into it yet. Currently i'm using and external USB sound device Sound Blaster X-Fi so that might be the reason the virtual keyboard couldn't hook into the sound instruments.
The virtual keyboard is somewhat useful because you can only link it with one of the VST intruments; Urban Drum kit.
You can import MP3 files but you'll most likely have to adjust the tempo detection, especially on tracks that don't have consistent drum beats. Basically the software slices your music file into sound bytes so you can rearrange it anyway you want. I was hoping that it is advanced enough to extract individual instruments and phrases automatically. In other words de-contruct the music but what do i know; first time using a music production software. Maybe there isn't a software that can do that.
There is an easy way to create music with just one click. Just select the instruments from the library and the generator creates a complete piece very quickly with no need to get into the nuts and bolts of it but if you want more creative control, you'll have to use the cut and paste method with the sequencer.
It's an interesting sofware to try and even though for me the learning curve is steep, it's worth the price i paid for it.
Disclaimer: Since i have no musical intrument nor completed a project yet, i cannot comment on the record and export function.

For a game trying so hard to be Dishonored, you'd think it take some of the things people liked about Dishonored. The level design was the standout part of Dishonored, with open, expansive levels with plenty of paths and secrets. At first glance, Thief's levels look like they have a taken a page from the same playbook Dishonored copy-pasted from, but once you explore a little, you'll realize that there is never more than two paths on each level. There is a level where you have to sneak into a mansion. There were two obvious paths into the mansion: one through the front door, surrounded by about six guards with the intelligence of a Michael Bay fan; and another path leading to a vent, which was completely unguarded. I first went through the vent but, upon realizing that the vent just put me behind the front door, I reloaded and played the other path.
Another bonus of Dishonored were the abilities, each of which had their own use for exploring the levels. Thief's abilities are almost all boring passives, that I didn't upgrade at all after the initial level. Thief's abilities have no use in the levels, they open no new paths. There is almost no point to stealing things after the first few levels, as once you have the wrench and the wirecutters, the upgrades are almost completely useless. The focus is lifted right out of Hitman: Absolution because originality is hard.
The game pretends to encourage different playstyles but anything other than pure stealth is completely unreasonable. The only way to kill guards is the bow and all of the lethal arrows are absurdly expensive. I'm alright with a game being a stealth game, Square Enix, you don't need to cater to the ritalin popping droolers who get bored when their fellow man isn't being exterminated at a rapid pace. Have some backbone and stick to your guns: If you want to make a stealth game, make a stealth game.

Roundabout is a game about cars going about in circles. The presentation is charming and silly, in a harmless, lo-fi, FMV, "were they all high while making this game?" sort of way. It takes the Kuru Kuru Kururin (google it) gameplay concept of guiding a rotating object (in this case a limousine) across an obstacle course within a time limit and gives this woefully underused old premise an open-world, FMV, funky, cartoonish twist. The result is about just as crazy as it sounds.
The FMV video footage is deliberately cheesy and funny, and it mostly works. The basic gameplay mechanic is solid (as it always has been) and well-implemented in an open-world setting. The whole city turns into a big circus for your freaky car acrobatics! You also learn how to jump! JUMP! The game world is pretty big and sprawling, with multiple unlockable areas, minigames, collectibles and bonuses. Unfortunately the main missions can be played through faster than you can spin your car ten times, but for HC spinning afficionados there are plenty of fun bonuses to unlock to make the most of your time there. I didn't feel compelled to go back after finishing the main story, but I enjoyed my short time with it.
Rating: 8/10

Its weakness is the game itself, it isn't bad by any means but I didn't find it quite strong enough to carry the game once the cutscenes are over. The main issue being that the car is fragile and routes narrow so it forces you to try and drive with a level of precision that to me never felt like it fitted with the themes or the polish of the game itself (particularly the hit detection). It demands a level of seriousness and respect for the game that it never earns.
Still the FMV carries it through and it is well worth it for the 4 hours or so it takes to get through the story. What it lacks in length of play I'm quite certain it'll make up for in terms of how long it'll live in the memory so for all its faults it is still highly recommended.

Mini Metro is a game that allows the player to teach all those transportation moguls how to properly setup a metro grid, or how to properly fail at doing so. Odds are it will be the latter.
It's an incredibly fun and challenging game, that will leave the player looking for the best possible routes.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Mini Metro.
If riding a metro is part of your daily routine, you'll either be extremely interested in trying Mini Metro out, or completely uninterested.
The goal is to "survive" as many days as possible by having customers happy, which means providing them transportation without having to spend much time waiting for it. As you can easily imagine, that's pretty simple to do, but as the game goes on, not only will the map increase, more stations will also start appearing, which can, sometimes, force the player to redo all the lines.
At the end of each week there will be a couple rewards, from more locomotives, to carriages, tunnels and extra lines, all of which can be used to make life easier. But choose wisely, as you may find yourself in need of either reward sooner than you think.
It's up to the player to make sure they don't end up like all the metro companies in the world, full of angry customers.
Considering it's an Early Access (EA) game, I've decided to add a "Neutral" category, for details I consider important, but not gamebreakers, and could easily improve the gameplay if attended.
Not much to point out "Cons" wise, as the game is pretty solid.
I'd give it a
, as it offers the player a nice and relaxing experience, as well as a nice change from the current gaming trend.

Momodora: Reverie Under The Moonlight is an innovative, refreshing approach to Metroidvania/Platformer games. It's gameplay is smooth and simple without getting stale thanks to several items, both active and passive, being spread throughout the game. It's fun and interesting to try out different combinations of passive items together, and the active items are helpful especially at higher difficulties.
The map is very large and open as in many Castlevania games. Exploring it is rewarded through several hidden items and Health upgrades. The map is divided in different areas with different enemies and visuals. The great strength of the game are it's bossfights, they are challenging, fair and look amazing. They all play differently aswell.
The game's a little short but it offers a lot of replayability thanks to different difficulties and a new game+ feature. The plot of the game is not explained in detail, which means that you'll be left with a lot of unanswered questions. There are also some confusing decisions regarding level design. Sometimes you'll find a room with seemingly no real use in gameplay whatsoever, the map shows very few details which means you'll sometimes get lost, and there are several NPC's that don't really seem to have any use either. They'll just say a single sentence and feel kind of useless otherwise, maybe they were intended to make the rooms feel less empty.
However, all in all the game is great. Bossfights all feel unique and challenging, there is a wide range of difficulties, exploring the map and experimenting with different items is well rewarded, and the gameplay is heavily focused on timing and reflexes. The music is ambient and beautiful and fits the visuals very well.
All in all it's a great game.

Don't be put off by the first few tutorial levels. Until you get access to all your actions, the game comes across as a shallow RNG slog, but the strategy is in there -- you'll just need some options besides "attack" and "fortify."
Don't worry about the low Steam rating either. A lot of players are checking this out because it's "by Mojang!" and not quite getting that it's "a free spare-time project by one of Mojang's artists!"
The screenshots communicate exactly what you're in for. If you like things like this, you'll like this example of the sort of thing that it is. Why not give it a try? You can always get a Steam refund for your zero bucks.

Gone are the careful footstep sounds of Thief: The Dark Project; instead, it's either regular ground no matter what you walk on, wet dirt, or ♥♥♥♥ing glass bits. Who is dropping these pots? Who is on the warpath to litter the world of Thief with ♥♥♥♥ing glass shards? Why can't Stealer Guy Steals Things 2014 be about tracking down this nefarious glass bit left-behind-er? Furthermore, is anyone going to ♥♥♥♥ing sweep this♥♥♥♥♥♥up? What if a baby falls in it? Who will defend the baby? Stealer Man? Certainly not him, he's currently shoving his feet into glass in an attempt to replicate someone opening a bag of chips.
Actually, can we go back to the story? It really is ridiculously stupid. Roundabout is a game about a chauffeur called Georgio who owns a limousine that always spins in circles. It takes this simple idea and puts it into a cartoon like open-world  with a few upgrades, some cosmetics and a few basic game mechanics mainly obstacles which you have to dodge, drive around and even jump over. At first, the game seems fun, colourful and quite funny. The map seems huge and the people you drive around seem fun and wacky. So why the negative review? Well…
The game just doesn’t work. At least for me it doesn’t. It’s not that the gameplay doesn’t match the story of the vibe of the world doesn’t match the characters. It’s just that there are too many things wrong with the game. Bugs and glitches are very common, I found myself easily once every 5 minutes getting wedged between 2 small objects or getting hit by something that I didn’t actually touch. When jumping onto things the limousine gets stuck and sometimes glitches slightly into the ground instantly killing you. That’s just PART of the reason why this is a negative review.
Let us start of with the gameplay. The gameplay starts off very fun and feels fluent and awesome, but after a few missions, it just starts to get so repetitive. Pick up X get to checkpoints A B C drop off at Y and dodge around a bunch of stuff along the way. There was no variation in the game. Even the challenges were just so boring after a little while. The gameplay did not fit in with how the world worked. It was just too easy to get hit too easy to die. It made the game frustrating and at some points feel unplayable.
The story, while being alright, was only 2 ½ hours long, there are only a few characters that you pick up throughout the game and they’re all wacky and funny and stuff but it’s just so freaking short. Other than the story, there wasn’t much stuff to do other than the few challenges and going back to 100% all of the story missions completing tasks such as “Complete in under 30 seconds” or “Complete without hitting anything.” There are upgrades and hats and paint jobs you can unlock and buy but the best upgrade can be acquired within 2 minutes of finishing the tutorial mission. The rest are just cosmetics.  I mean if you want to get literal about it. You can complete the 8 F*CKING HOUR challenge that is basically “Desert Bus” but with this game’s art-style. What is Desert Bus you ask? It’s a game where you sit in first person in a car tapping left every so often so you don’t fly off the road, for 8 real life hours, and this game has a replica of it.
So let’s get to another issue I have with this game. Who is it aimed at? At first you’d think children because of the colourful world and the wacky cartoonish characters, but the game is very difficult and frustrating. Not to mention the part where you run over pedestrians creating giant pools of blood on the road. So, achievement hunters? I guess, but it seems like even if you are an achievement hunter you wouldn’t waste your time with this game and have to sit there tapping left for 8 hours straight just to get that 1 achievement. So people who just want to play a short low budget indie game? Then why is it 15 dollars? I just don’t understand.
The music is alright, very cartoony and upbeat, it’s good for this game. Nothing too crazy and like with a lot of games with not great music. I just put on my own music in the very small amount of time I spent driving around this game’s open world.
The game looks cute, the real life cutscenes are very nice and compliment the game’s atmosphere. All the characters are brought to life by their costumes, and I generally I enjoyed the game and how it all looked.
Now the final part I want to go over is how the game runs. The game DOESN’T run at 60 FPS most of the time. Which I find crazy because I reach the minimal and recommend requirements for a game that isn’t very tanky graphics wise so it is just straight up poorly optimized. Also, micro stuttering from time to time.
Roundabout has a simple concept that it applies to a funny open world. The gameplay is frustrating, there are bugs and glitches everywhere. It’s extremely short and the entire game just doesn’t feel very complete. Also it’s way overpriced for the amount of content in it. This game will stay dead in my library never to be played again, by me at least.

Picked this up in a bundle and wasn't really expecting much out of the game. However, I would highly recommend it for both the absurdist gameplay that seems initially impossible but quickly becomes ... not normal... but oddly compelling once you do get the hang of it.
In addition, the storyline is told through equally absurdist 1980's low budget TV format, with some really good tongue in cheek "acting" going on.
Nothing about this game is normal and it isn't going to keep you occupied for more than a few hours if you just play the storyline, but my wife and I found ourselves genuinely laughing throughout.

The intentionally awful FMV in Roundabout will have you spinning out of control in laughter, but you'd better recover quickly, because the hard-as-nails arcade action never steers you wrong. This solid gameplay enables the rest of the game to be as eccentric as possible, and this wholly original title asks players to navigate the world's first revolving limousine through a series of increasingly (open-world, birds-eye view) missions. Crazy Taxi has nothing on this, and even Grand Theft Auto pales in comparison to the cartoonish vehicular manslaughter committed in the sake of maintaing a combo multiplier.
Casual gamers will feel welcomed and encouraged by the generous checkpoints, but an increasingly difficult series of bonus objectives for each mission will ensure that hardcore players don't have to take a comfortable backseat. Short of a few technical issues with the audio now and again, there's not a thing here that I wouldn't wholly recommend.

Being a huge fan of the old school rogue-likes, a la Nethack, ADOM and Angband, I've had my eye on this game for quite some time. I finally decided to pick it up and I am so happy I did. From my short playtime of the game, I am already in love with it.
Dungeons of Dredmor contains all manner of thinly veiled pop-culture references, right down to the title screens for the game, one of which is styled after the DOOM 1 box art, and another which resembles a classic Star Wars movie poster. If you are knowledgable about these kinds of things, you'll find A LOT to appreciate.
Aesthetically speaking, the game has a boatload of charm. The visuals are crisp and vibrant. The sounds are just right. The music is superb. It has got to be one of my favorite soundtracks I've ever heard in many years of gaming.
Don't let the cartoony visuals fool you though, because under the hood lies a deep and engrossing numbers game. There are quite a bit of stats, buffs, and skills to worry about. The skills are one of my favorite things about the game, as most of them are hilarious. For example, Emomancy. There, now go buy the game.
The amount of content you get for under 10 bucks is insane. Did you buy it yet? Go. Do it.

I downloaded this game to see if it would live up to the hype (for better or worse), and I decided to take an objective look. What I noticed first were some typographical errors, which would be negligible if not for this game being almost exclusively text-oriented. Also, since I find it difficult to concentrate on large areas of text for long periods of time, I think having a save state of some sort would have been a nice addition to the game, especially since the developer was generous enough to include a graphic showing how to "play" this game with a controller.
As far as content goes, I think that since the protagonist is supposed to be you (the player), I think that “Alex” (your girlfriend in the game) should have been a neuter character so people of all sexual orientations (not just lesbians) could better relate – there was a huge opportunity to do so, what with “Alex” being a unisex nickname, and since this game is meant to simulate what it feels like to be clinically depressed, I think it would have better immersed the player in that world.
Other than these few minor nitpicks, it does have a semi-interesting story, and as someone who has suffered from clinical depression myself, it does have relatable elements. I didn't finish because it was too long for me to complete in one sitting and I couldn't find a way to bookmark my place to pick it up later (as I stated before, save states would have been useful). I think this game could use more development, but it does have potential, and I can honestly say I got what I paid for from Depression Quest.

Before talking about the actual game, I want to emphasize the first sentence of this game's description: "Depression Quest is an interactive fiction game where you play as someone living with depression". If you're expecting anything more than a text based game, think depression is just 'people being lazy' or simply don't like reading, this is not a game for you.
I've seen some reviewers complaining the character you control is gloomy, lazy, paranoid, clingy... Well, welcome to the ugly ugly world of depression! I don't think the people complaining about the crossed choices quite get the point of the game. Depression is a downward spiral of negative thoughts and emotions, where even the things you once loved cheer you up. Everything is exhausting, even something as simple as making dinner or talking to someone. You want to ask for help, but instead shut down and distance yourself from others, genuinely believing you don't deserve their attention. Asking why you can't choose the better option is the same as asking why poor people don't buy money.
I think the good and bad endings could have benefited of more differences between them, simply to emphasize the importance of getting help and support during these times. Otherwise it was a good, short, free game. 8/10

While exploring a castle dungeon, the collapse of a bridge have left you (and a few friends) stranded on your own. With the main party lost without your presence they decide to wait for you to find your way back to them. So off you embark on a journey of fortune and glory as you travel deeper into the dungeons of Castle Hammerwatch.
Set in a beautiful pixel-art world, Hammerwatch provides a challenging hack and slash adventure offering a fun solo and local co-op experience with a nice selection of classes to choose from, each with different abilties and playstyles. With plenty of hidden secrets and Easter Eggs, there is plenty to explore. With an extended campaign to the Sun Temple as well as user-created campaigns with the workshop, Hammerwatch offers a fun, but challenging experience.
+ Beautiful pixel artwork
+ 2 campaigns as well as workshop support
+ Several classes to choose, each with their own abilities
+ Character progression
+ Hidden secrets and Easter Eggs
+ Controller support for a great couch co-op experience
+ Different difficulty modes (as well as extra challenge/help settings)
+ An auto-attack toggle in the settings (I found out about this way too late)
- The main campaign's level layout is always the same (can be considered good and bad)
- The Sunwatch Temple campaign has pretty unfair bosses that may cause some frustration (while soloing at least)
- Online co-op community is quite inactive
- The Millionaire and Genocide achievements can be quite grindy

Tower of Guns is a roguelike FPS where you climb a tower (made of guns) and shoot every single robot inside while collecting ludicrous powerups and experience silly non-stories while doing a run. However, pretty crap graphics for Unreal 3 standards and mediocre gunplay turn a great concept into a forgettable experience.
Tower of Guns starts you off with some peashooter guns and perks (except bluegrass which is the best perk) until you complete objectives to unlock (arguably) better weapons and perks. Even then, collecting extra jumps and other upgrades to soar through a generated level is undoubtedly more fun than upgrading your gun in a runthrough. The combat ranges from "eh" to "GOD DAMN" as enemy numbers and furthermore projectile numbers increase egregiously through your tower climb. The guns and enemies barely give feedback, limply glowing orange when you hit them as they stand still (or fly in a lazy hovering pattern) until either the enemy or the player dies. Environment hazards range from bottomless pits to bottomless pits but filled with liquidized death, as levels are typically platform-heavy but don't really provide a challenge in the way that the enemies do. Level mechanics are sparse to fit in with the procedural generating level designs as well.
If you desperately want to break Deus Ex's record on how many times you can just leave a level and find garbage the dev left on the sides of an unfinished wall, that is certainly provided for you with Tower of Guns. If you want to find a good roguelike FPS, this isn't it. Overall, it's not a terrible game but (ironically) this procedural-generated roguelike isn't worth replaying either. You see everything the game has to offer you in 5 hours max, and the raw moment-to-moment gameplay won't impress anyone who's played a more visceral or mechanically-inclined shooter.

Thief series, & Dishonored
Thief is a reboot of the old first person stealth game series Thief. In Thief you play the role of a master thief who in an odd twist of fate has been forced into the role of hero for the city. You will be stealing and breaking into places while trying to either avoid detection or taking out the guards. You will be rated at the end of each lvl on wether you are an opertunist, predator, or ghost play style. Between levels you will be able to take on side quests and purchase equipment. The master thief has a magic eye that allows for you to see hot spots on the level and much more. Arrows can kill guards from a distance, put out flames, provide rope areas to climb, light things on fire, ect ect.
The animations and environment feel amazingly immersive. The game allows for many types of play styles by offering multiple routes. The voice acting is top notch. The puzzles in the game are well done. There is plenty to steal which is important in a game called Thief. The equipment adds an additional layer of depth to the game.
The level design are uneven. Some are absolutely brilliant offering at least four ways to enter a building while others offer about 1.5 ways in. The equipment is great, but isn't always given a chance to shine. The master thief could have been allowed more takedown moves. I don't believe you should have to purchace a wire cutter, razor, and a wrench since a thief would have those in his tower by default aka tutorial.
Thief is good at what it does most of the time and unlike the previous titles gives you a descent enough story. The consistancy of the levels were done better in the past thief titles though. It doesn't offer a whole lot new to the formula, but did it really need a drastic change? I think not.
I value Thief as a $15 game. Get it in a bundle or on sale.
