Although it does have its minor bugs which Bamco can't be bothered to fix, this is a fantastic collection, but not at full price. Wait for a sale. Final result of the games in the collection:
Pac-Man: Probably not the best idea if you have the Arcade Game Series like I do, but you can still play it if you only bought this collection for the other games, like I did.
Pac-Mania: Pac-Man, with the ability to jump and crave powerups, tapped against FIVE GHOSTS (There's more in Pacman's Park onwards)?! Challenge accepted.
Pac & Pal: Love it. Miru can help you out, but if you want most points, grab the item she's carrying off of ya before she takes it to the ghost home. Plus, powerups. I love to stun ghosts in front of Pac (Who I play as)!
Pac-Land: 80's platforming action, Pac-Man Style! But it's a race against time, which makes it better! Lovin' it!
Super Pac-Man: Decent. Super Pellets make it better. Break through walls like Superman from DC Comics! (Only if you consume the Super Pellet)
Pac-Attack: If you've played Tetris Ultimate by Ubisoft or Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine by Sega, you'll love THIS! Also good for those new to the puzzle genre. Has more music than the GBA Pac-Attack.
Pac-Man Battle Royale: Fun to play by yourself, and even better if you play local MP with Family and Friends! (You'll most likely need more than one controller for MP) Seeing that Pac-Man Battle Royale originated in the Arcades, there's no Online MP there. I hope that clears things up.
Pac-Man Arrangement: I'm very bummed that this Arrangement is not the GBA Arrangement which I loved as a kid, but the Museum's Arrangement kinda holds the GBA Arrangement's spirit and adds some new features. That allows me to enjoy the game.
Pac-Man Championship Edition: Original Pac-Man, but with bigger maps that change with every fruit munched on and a touch of "Gotta Go Fast!". Harder than DX+, however. (I can imagine that Championship Edition 2 (Not in the Museum) is probably harder.)
The Hub is in the shape of the Ghostly Adventures Cartoon you can find on Disney XD (If you live in the UK) or on Netflix. There, the character designs are Bad@$$! Pac, Cylindria, Spiral, Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde etc. all look amazing! You start with nothing in your hub. You need to earn stamps to earn items based on that cartoon. In the words of Game Freak: Gotta catch' em all! (And I'm talking about stamps, not Pocket Monsters by Nintendo.)
Plus, There's a Ms. Pac-Man DLC which you should NEVER BUY if you have that game in the Arcade Game Series. (That's not a part of the 3-pack)
This should've been on Wii U and 3DS, tho. ( ; - ; )

Thief (2014) has hints and touches of what could have been considered a great sequel to the first three games. Although I recommend it, it must be said that Thief has major flaws that for some will not be acceptable and will downright ruin their experiences. Most of those flaws were overcome by the time I hit the 3rd Chapter “Dirty Secrets”. For fans of the earlier franchise, it isn’t until this chapter that the game will pay dividends (and will be hit or miss on further levels). However, I’ll list below what could make some people quit before that.
If you consider the below are deal breakers, then this game should not be purchased (minor spoilers ahead):
•	No free-to-jump-at-anytime mechanic: Over time, the controls will become familiar and allow for some tense chases through the streets, however when you open your game with a rooftop level, not being able to jump sticks out like a sore thumb. Immediately, you’ll be scrambling to figure out why this wasn’t incorporated. It doesn’t upfront explain very well how the movement system really works.
•	Rope arrows are limited to certain points: This is also confusingly just thrown into the opening segment and you’re left wondering “Is this really going to continue like this, or was this just an example of how to use rope arrows?”
•	Restrictions to free roam: This was discussed, but after a pretty good jewelry story section at the beginning, you’ll come to an impasse when Garrett will say he cannot come back once he goes through a window. Why? These back-tracking restrictions are found here and there and are mostly poorly designed.
•	Poor sound mix: I actually did not like a lot of Deadly Shadows’ mechanics and level designs, but the sound design of that game appealed to me and was quite memorable. This Thief game goes backwards in time. The flaws are so immediately apparent during the first cutscene that you’re immersion will be lost and won’t come back fully for a few hours. (In my case, Chapter 3)
•	The story is laughably bad and poorly executed: On the surface, the concept worked very well for an addition to the Thief series: The City has undergone political turmoil and through a magic artifact a plague has run rampant and older factions have lost political power. Garret finds himself at the heart of the problem as he attempts to retrieve said pieces of artifact and deals with the grief of Erin. This would all fit nicely in with the first three and could reboot the series without dismissing any of the earlier entries. *Spoilers somewhat* it’s so poorly done that it’ll make you want to destroy your computer and shake the writing staff. The story’s flaws could have been so easily fixed and so obviously tweaked to make the experience better, but it wasn’t done. It’s infuriating at times.
•	Gratuitous swearing: I would argue some swearing could fit into the Thief universe, but when you first encounter Basso you’ll wonder why they even bothered to include it.
So if you know the above will ruin it, this won’t work out for you. In my case, I was lucky not to have read through the companion app before being roughly 90% of the way through the main campaign. The first 2 Thief games were elevated to amazing heights by the community that expanded the lore and offered amazing custom missions. The world was just ambiguous enough to allow the community to form its own worlds around it. In the case of the reboot, the companion app overthrows all of that and forces a view on you. So I suggest skipping it entirely prior to playing.
Why do I recommend it?
For the moments of brilliance that can be found. Clearly, there are times when you can see and feel that a portion of the team was working on an amazing sequel to one of the most amazing franchises. When you’ll get those visual cues that tie in with earlier games you’ll immediately see the potential this game had. Case in point, the second chapter (spoilers) has you going through the Foundry. This level is so poorly designed that it feels like a simple name drop and obnoxious wink at fans. Then you’ll get The Cathedral or The House of Blossoms which has many elements that make you realize this game easily could have worked its way into the franchise. Even though the outing to the repurposed Angel Watch is incredibly short lived, the design of it is spot on.
Some of the side missions are also welcome additions; the labyrinth house holds clues to the past. The Bank Heist has some mechanist devices that will make you realize just how frustrating the fact that this isn’t canon is!
The look of The City is brilliant. The level of details is astonishing. They really managed to create a claustrophobic city with sharp turns and dark corners. It’s very easy to get immersed in this world, lots of small loot places and secrets and is very pleasant to explore.
Under the surface, there are times where this game needs to be experienced to fully see how dedicated part of the team was. There was a lot of work and details put in to really give original fans the sequel they deserved. Odd choices were done in the end and poorly implemented mechanics hurt this one real bad. However, with an appropriate update that would retcon those poor story decisions (and this should be easy to do) and an update to mechanics that would remove some of the constraints, you could have a descent Thief canon entry, albeit it being the least creative of the 3, but the best looking.

Ever remember those old badly acted fmv (full motion video) games back in the 1980's and 1990's, those games sadly died down when gaming moved to better technology and better cutscenes and very few games nowadays come out using the classical full motion video technique
Then Roundabout comes along and I must say, it was a fun ride! The game basically follows a limo driver whose name is Georgio (but played by a gal, awesome!) who drives around areas of Roundabout City and its outskirts picking up passengers and dropping them off at their destinations and falls in love with one of his (or her) passengers, Elizabeth (Beth is mentioned in the game)
The plot does sound cliche but does use its gaming mechanics to make the game more fun and interesting, such as, that new technology makes limo cars turn round, like a roundabout, and basically you have to drive about with a turning limo, which is pretty fun but does have its flaws
I died or crashed... a lot, and it made me frustrated, sometimes it could be my fault, but it can also be due to bad timing, environmental elements blocking your limo, etc... this did annoy me sometimes but there are some upgrades that can help you on the way. The game does suggest that you use a controller, but I found it just fine to play with a mouse and keyboard
Now onto the fmv scenes, they are not bad, but they are not good. You can say that this game is so bad its good, but bad in a good way. Some of the actors did look like they were inexperienced and had no idea what was going on, for example, the date couple were the worst, they gave no character and looked like they were relying on each other for cues. Mike, the mechanic was also another one who gave very little character and also looked like he was relying on the script to give out his lines
The only two characters who I actually liked were Elizabeth, who although, did look like she was relying on the script but did give out some character and the quiet Georgio, who gives out his/her character brilliantly by just turning round, and looking at his/her passengers which made me giggle inside
The narrator was also good, giving out a character in his voice. The filming was mediocre and the sound editing did vary in some fmv scenes, sometimes they were okay and sometimes they were bad. I liked the addition of stock footage to replace the things the passengers were talking about
The game is pretty short, overall the main story is 2-3 hours long with some side missions here and there
Overall, this game is so bad its good, it has some memorable fmv scenes, and some great yet annoying gameplay, and a few characters that you will love till the end. It is highly recommended if you can take the type of games that they are so bad they are good type

Visit the city of Roundabout and help Georgio Manos, who is clearly not a woman, fight against an evil rival copycat chauffeur, the police and centrifugal forces, and maybe even help him find love!
Framed by gloriously trashy 70's style FMV sequences, the gameplay of Roundabout comes as advertised with a twist. Causing mayhem on the streets comes naturally when trying to maneuver a car that never stops spinning. Inspired by games such as Kuru Kuru Kururin, controls are responsive, yet actually controlling where you drive is challenging.
One can play through the main story fairly quickly, yet that is only part of the game. Numerous fun challenges await, there are collectibles en masse to be found, and a good amount of customizations to be unlocked. As a finishing touch, there's several goofy extra options, such as the Roundabutt mode.
If you are looking for a unique gameplay experience, and enjoy indie games that take themselves seriously, but have a lot of fun while doing so, Roundabout might just be your kind of game. The store page offers a demo, so go ahead and see if revolving is your thing as well.
Simple without being braindead, funny without being referential. Cool FMVs, creative premise, fun. Not a long game by any means unless you want to aim for mastery and 100%.

Roundabout is a fun little game about a limousine service in the 70s.
You are Georgio Manos and your limousine is ... spinning. All the time. Because.. obviously!
You basically spend the game maneuvering your spinning limousine through the obstacle courses of Roundabout City. Five collisions and you, as well as your clients die a fiery death as your vehicle explodes. Everday business!
While the game is surprisingly hard, the checkpoints are always fair, so that you don't really have to be perfect at the game.
The most charming feature about the game are its story and its FMV cutscenes.
Keeping in touch with the 70s flair of the game, the cutscenes are ridiculous and full cheesy acting. But these cutscenes, where several weird, quirky characters enter Georgio's limousine are where the heart of the game is located.
The game is incedibly hilarious with its story about love, glory, vengeance and redemption. Kate Welsh does an amazing job as silent Georgio Manos, who is interacting with the passengers using mostly facial expressions. But everyone else is on top of their game as well while trying to be as cheesy and hammy as possible. Not to enjoy these cutscene is almost as bad a crime as destroying someone else's car.
Seriously, buy this game. You will enjoy it, even if just for its story (which isn't very long unfortunately.)

This game is a total riot. A hilarious roguelike game with funny gear and creatures. Fantastic music tracks. The graphics are pixely retro in a good way. Dungeons of Dredmor is an intelligently designed Rogue-Like, it's very hard and extremely satisfying. You choose between a variety of perks when you start off your character, and it's crucial to pick a good build, because that's what you're stuck with for the entire run. The game has a moderatly strong sense of humour that come up in incredibly surprising places, the soundtrack is enjoyable, there's lots of enemy, item and level variety, but most importantly, there's no spiders (as far as I've been).
Overall, I think that Dungeons of Dredmor is a very good game if you enjoy rogue-likes  and that you should pick it up with the DLC.

Disclaimer: I friended the dev of the game after finding and trying the beta builds on IndieDb. I did buy my own copy of the game however, and wrote this review of my own accord.
Think Payday: The Heist meets Hotline Miami, with some Diablo-esque gear system thrown in. That's really the easiest/simplest way to describe the game.
Controls are tight, gameplay can be challenging, and the skill system allows for a diverse set of play styles. Whether you want to be Solid Snake, the TF2 Engineer, or Rambo, the game has weapons and classes supporting that play style.
The game also records global theft amounts, and has systems in place to reward the playerbase as they steal more and more, creating a good system for community sense of achievement.
Yes, the game has bugs here and there, but the developer is very responsive, and often fixes bugs found with a good amount of speed.
All in all, Cash_Out is a great game to waste a few minutes (a single level or two) or a few hours on, enjoying yourself the entire time... except for maybe if you die on a career character after getting them through a couple hours worth of levels. But hey, just like Dwarf Fortress taught me, losing is FUN!!

CASH_OUT is a recently released, 5 dollar early access game on steam. it is made by my friend UNTOUCH and i think you should play it.
CASH_OUT is a top down shooter that plays a little bit like hotline miami with a lot more emphasis on stealth and guard detection. things like bottles clinking on the floor, bloody footprints, and your own shadow can reveal you to the guards.  the objective of the game is to get in, and get out with as much cash as you can. levels are randomly generated with randomized loot.
one of the many things that makes CASH_OUT unique is the skill system. when you start your cash_out ‘career’, you pick your class. each class focuses on something different, like stealth, durability, speed, power, accuracy, etc. etc. each class has its own set of skills as well. you get to pick two class skills and two universal skills that any character can get. this allows for you to take your own unique approach to the levels which only get harder and harder as you progress.
well, you got the cash, you got out, what do you do with it. you buy upgrades, items, weapons, anything that can help you get cash and get out even better.
the game is in early access at the moment and is kind of unpolished, i’m not gonna lie. sound  and graphical design need work, and some bugs are prominent. but, it’s an extremely cheap game and it has a ridiculous amount of potential. and even in this early beta state, it can still be played and still be really fun and enjoyable. i can’t wait to see what it will blossom into and i want to support my buddy UNTOUCH as much as i can.
i fully believe this game can be the next sleeper hit on steam. please support my bud.

I just want to know why you can't kill yourself?? The warning at the beginning mentions suicide as a trigger, so why isn't that even mentioned by the character? If you want to make a more realistic game about depression, at least give the option to kill yourself. Sure that's not what EVERY depressed person contemplates, but had a content warning for it, so what's the problem? When nameless-MC is so deeply depressed he can't get out of bed 90% of the time, why can he not kill himself. Why. Regardless of what's right or wrong or whatever, it's reality.
But that aside, I found it to be pretty accurate for depression- at least for the way I experience it. I'm probably just griping about the suicide option because that's the main difference between the depression depicted here and my personal depression, because no matter how good I feel I still want to die. I realize that this game was based on the creators' experience with depression, but I find the trigger warning to be out of place. I did a playthrough making the worst possible choices to see if he could off himself, and it was hardly different than if he was happy, save for the fact that MC was spending a buttload of money on therapy and medications on the happiest route. There should be a more drastic difference between the endings to show just how much a few decisions can make someone's life pan out differently.

Seeing a lot of reviews whose main complaint is that this "isn't like depression." It's actually a lot like my experience of it. Funny thing, depression can present itself in a lot of different ways to different people.
It's not a FUN game, and it's not EVERYONE's experience of depression. But if you don't know what depression is like, it's an excellent starting point for educating yourself. And since that's the point of the game, job well done.
If you are trying to get depressed playing it, you better read the rushed reviews about this game instead.

But once you get a gun that fits your play style, the game gets a LOT better.  This game has a lot of advantages over other roguelike games, such as being mostly skill based (with a bit of RNG luck), the fact that every enemy killed gives you a reward of some sort, the gun and perk unlocks, the fact that you usually get a big health boost to bring you back into the fight at the end of each level, not having to worry too much about micromanagement, etc.
I'm not sure this game is worth $14.99 (I got it as part of a Humble Bundle), but it's unquestionably good, and YMMV on what constitutes value anyways.  If you want a good FPS roguelike with challenge and good rewards, or just something where you blow stuff up without having to think too hard, you could do a lot worse than this.

The game is filled with powerups so I feel like this balances out the insane amount of enemies very well. As you play you unlock more guns for your next attempt. You can only choose 1 gun per round but as you kill you upgrade the 1 weapon you have. There are a wide variety of guns, I havent unlocked them all yet, but from my personal experience, not all guns are versitile enough to get the job done in all scenarios. Tower of Guns is a nice indie hidden gem that appears to be a labor of love and it will easily give you hours of enjoyment.

A simplistic and slightly buggy game that absolutely feels like the jam-game (a game created in a short amount of time, usually in a distracting party environment) it is.
For starters, clicking doesn't quite work right. Sometimes clicks just won't register, other times the hit detection just doesn't quite align with the displayed cursor. Managing to mess up the act of pointing a mouse and clicking on things - something that's been handled with grace and relative aplomb since approximately the mid-1980s - is bad enough, but in a game consisting mostly of clicking it's borderline unforgivable.
There's an RNG element which is utterly frustrating - sometimes you'll waste an entire turn trying to attack an undefended territory and repeatedly losing, then watch the AI attack one of your fortified strongholds and capture it on the first try. RNG absolutely *can* spice things up when used sparingly, but this game offers no real strategic choices to mitigate the RNG. You can't choose between a high risk / high reward or low risk / low reward technique, and territories don't have any form of a hitpoint system, so attacking multiple times isn't necessarily going to chip away at a wall of defenses. You're basically just rolling a d6 and if it's 2 or higher you win, or natural 6 to capture a fortified territory.
Furthermore, because of the RNG and simplistic (as in "virtually non-existent") strategic element, the broader game quickly collapses into which side manages to capture the most territory on the first turn. More territory = more money = more attacks = more territory. Sure, that's the basic gist of every 4X game and RTS on the planet, but - for example - in Civilization I can place cities in better territory for defense and economic bonuses, and easily hold back an opponent with twice as many cities in poor locations. In Starcraft, I can use recon to see an enemy is weak against air, and focus my research and unit creation into air units, making the best of what may be a bad situation and eventually turning the tables. Hell, even old-school DOTA (even before all the comeback mechanics) wasn't quite as much of a snowball as this game - and nothing is more tedious than playing out the last few turns when you're in an unwinnable situation, or even the last few turns when the enemy has just one territory left and you can't tickle the RNG into giving you your justly-earned victory.
It's single-player only, and the AI is about as bland as it gets. You don't see certain opponents prioritize defensive fortifications and others going for larger acquisition - it's just a cacophony of attacks and random tile improvements. It's the worst sort of AI - not smart enough to bother planning ahead for, and even worse, not predictably dumb enough to manipulate.
To top it off, there's seemingly no options menu, which means you're stuck listening to the bland and repetitive music throughout the experience. It's a bit like the songs in a Koei game from the SNES era, except far shorter and far, far more repetitive. No full-screen option either - hell, you can't even change your character color away from blue.
All in all it reminds me of the "games" that might be bundled with a Linux distro ten years ago - sort of a tile-based Liquid War, except Liquid War had more map variety and, hell, you could even change your color and name.
It's free and I think it's still a little bit overpriced.

You're mostly buying this for Battle Royale
Let's not beat around the bush here -- with the new Pac-Man Museum compilation, you're getting a bunch of really old games you've most likely played before, a few you probably already own, and Pac-Man Battle Royale. Royale is a bit of a unique release, as it's only been playable outside of Japan at special events and arcades, and has been highly sought out by fans of the genre.
To be blunt, this is the perfect opportunity to wait for a sale just to pick up Royale.
Pac-Man Museum (PC, PS3, Xbox 360 [reviewed])
Developer: Namco Bandai Games
Publisher: Namco Bandai Games
Released:  February 25, 2014
MSRP: $19.99
Reviewing a collection of old games can be tough, so let's start at the iconic, timeless classic: the original Pac-Man. It still holds up today, and although Museum doesn't pack a ton of nuanced options to fundamentally change the game, it does have few extras like the ability to select a starting level (once you earn it), and increase your life and bonus life thresholds.
Having said that, I know a lot of people who hated the original Pac-Man until they played the Championship Edition of the game which really helped them "get it" -- since it was pretty much better in every way. While CE is fully included in the Museum, sadly the DX upgrade that came later is not. Why Namco would opt to give you an inferior, outdated version of Championship Edition is beyond me, and counts as a strike against Museum's quality.
Next up is Pac-Mania, which is similar to the original, just with an isometric view, expanded boards, and the ability to jump. Pac's leaping power is a lot more useful than you'd think, as he can change his trajectory mid-air and jump around corners, making for a more action-oriented feel.
The problem is since the view is at an angle, you can't actually see the whole board, and it's frustrating to have to track down that last pellet you can't even look at. Because of that, you'll have to change up your strategy fundamentally and go on specific routes, clearing pellets along the way. Pac-Man Arrangement is very similar in that it offers up jumping capabilities (with a classic view), but it goes a step further with other power-ups like speed boosts. Both are fun, but not nearly as engaging as Championship Edition.
Then you have the decidedly dated Pac & Pal and Super Pac-Man, which don't hold up today, as they essentially operate like the original, but with convoluted additions such as "keys" and other weird concepts. With Pal you have a ghost that steals items and with Super, Pac-Man grows really big and can speed up to smash through walls -- that's about it.
When it comes to Pac-Land and Pac-Attack, they're anything but familiar. Land is basically the black sheep of the franchise, taking the form of an odd 2D platformer in which Pac needs to escape from ghosts chasing him in vehicles like old-timey cars and UFOs.
It's got a perfect "so bad it's good vibe" going on, although you probably won't want to play it more than a few times. Pac-Attack is basically a clone of Dr. Mario, with Pac-Man pieces eating the ghosts (viruses) instead of the requirement to match up colors. It features a two-player versus mode, which is just about the only way you're going to get mileage out of this game.
Again, Battle Royale is the main reason you're probably interested in this pack. There's no surprise here -- the concept of putting four Pac-Man players in an arena and forcing them to eat each other is good fun. It uses the Championship concept of automatically arranging levels in real time around you, and it speeds up over time to increase the tension. Even if people aren't Pac-Man fans, they can still enjoy the fast-paced, simple gameplay of Royale. Thankfully, it also supports solo play against an NPC, but you'll definitely want to find three local friends for this one (mostly because Museum doesn't have an online component).
Museum as a whole supports full leaderboards for every game, an in-game Stamp Book achievement system, and a "Pac-Room" to mess around in that stores collectibles. Visually on consoles the game looks fine, but every game outside of CE and Royale will support a tiny native resolution while a border takes up the rest of the screen. As a side note, if you buy the game before the end of March, you'll net the wonderful Ms. Pac-Man for free, which sweetens the deal.
Pac-Man Museum has a bunch of middling pieces, but the addition of Battle Royale is the icing on the cake. If you've never played Championship Edition before and thus do not have DX to compare it to, it's a perfect way to re-acclimate yourself to the franchise, while you use Royale to spice up your next local gathering. Everyone else who lacks friends on-hand or has already played CE should wait for a sale, or pass this one up entirely.

It would've been nice to get a new Namco Museum game for PC, considering the only one we actually have besides this uses a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DRM and only works on Windows XP or lower (I'm looking at you, 50th Anniversary). Maybe we could've gotten an HD remake of the old PS1 titles (Speaking of which, the 20th anniversary of Volume 1 releasing in the US is coming up. It would be nice to have something announced for then), maybe we could've gotten a decent port of one of the older ones, or maybe we could've just gotten something cool and new.
But instead, we got Pac-Man Museum.
So since I don't feel like doing a full review, have a Pros and Cons list:
Pros:
+Only way to play Battle Royale without going to an arcade.
+You can play the original version of CE, in case you were ever nostalgic for that version.
+Other Pac-Man arcade/console games if you don't want to emulate them.
+Some other neat little extras (Honestly judging from almost everything after the PS1 titles it's really easy not to expect anything from these games).
Cons:
-The price tag. $20 for 9 games seems like a good deal until you compare it to all of the other Namco Museum games. For example, Namco Museum Virtual Arcade can be found for about $20 nowadays, and it has 34 games on it.
-No option to change window size for games. You know, like the other Namco Museum games have.
-They went the Remix/Megamix route by not bothering to include Ms. Pac-Man. But oh wait, they did eventually include it... As a DLC that costs $5.
So overall, this game was kind of a disappointment. Perhaps I could've given this a positive rating if it costed less and/or had more to it, but there are so many better Namco Museum games out there. I understand that the other retro games may not be as marketable as Pac-Man, but at least give something to the fans. If you want this game I'd recommend waiting for it to go on sale. That's what I did.

Depression Quest manages to convey a believable sense of what one might experience, living through daily life with depression.  While it won't capture everyone's experience with the illness, it can certainly serve to allow players who haven't experienced depression to imagine what others go through better.
On a mechanical level, Depression Quest is also interesting in the realm of interactive fiction in the way it tracks your character's mental health, and presents choices which may be disallowed because of your character's illness.  An interesting study on the power of the *illusion* of choice (or at least, the frustration of missed opportunity, even if certain options are never allowed to be chosen).

First of all, Depression Quest is not a game in any meaningful sense of the word at all. It’s an interactive set of multiple choice questions that lead absolutely nowhere.
What the developers rather optimistically refer to as a “playthrough”, I managed to complete in about ten agonising minutes through severely gritted teeth. And no, it wasn’t long enough to get the point across; it would have needed about another thousand or two hours of teeth pulling for that to happen and still there would have been no point.
The developers have classed this as a game and they call themselves game developers; on both counts they are hopelessly mistaken. A video game has atmosphere, a plot, very often a hero, and generally looks nice and is exciting to play. This is none of those things and one of the many things it lacks is guns, so that we could all blow our brains out by page five.
This is not a game in any sense of the word and it would be more fitting to describe it as cruelty to the depressed and self inflicted punishment.
Games are fun, this is not, so don’t insult us.
It’s so easy to criticise the work of others and let’s face it, critics are just that; they produce very little or nothing at all. In this case, all the criticism Depression Quest has received is entirely justified for the simple reason that it’s a badly executed and irresponsible piece of  self congratulatory narcissism that should never have seen the light of day.

First, let me say that this game isn't for everyone. If you don't like playing games where your fate depends on a roll of the dice, you should probably steer clear.
Having said that, dice-roll battles are classic gameplay, and people who slam this game based on the RNG may just be too young to appreciate it.

Cons:

If it's not the poor clicking its the RNG "combat".
I saw the game and thought I'd give it a shot. The art style didn't bother me in the least, in fact I rather liked it. But that's where my joy and pleasure ended. In the short time I played this game it was clear what it was going to be. About 50% of my clicks didn't register correctly, forcing me to redo certain actions...thus slowing the gameplay down. And when they did work it was pure RNG. There is no actual logic why an attack is a success or failure. What's even more irritating is what could take me 3, 4 or even 5 attacks to take over an enemy tile/space but the computer could do so with single attacks. There are no stats to read. No system of "you have x amount of attack power while this title has x number of defence". There is no strategy to the game. It's just click until you're out of gold. Maybe toss an added tower here and there (which rarely seems to make a difference).
The combat is simply decided with RNG, an RNG system that seems to favour the computer at all times. You have 20 gold to work with? Enjoy those 3 new spaces. Computer only has 10 gold? Well they get to have 5 new spaces (including the 3 you just took). Logically with double the resources I should be the stronger force. But since this game doesn't have logic built into it...it makes no difference. It's pure luck.
Is it free? Sure, which is cool and all. But free doesn't always equal fun.

Overall, this is a nice collection with a large chunk of all the Pac-Man games released. A huge plus is that this is the only way you can play Battle Royale without hunting down the extremely rare arcade version. Leaderboards are nice, and the ability to slowly fill a room with Pac-Man items is a nice touch. Controls are tight as well, which is very important in a Pac-Man title.
The biggest negative is the borders. I think they are done to keep the arcades aspect ratio, but the borders around the game window are massive. I know many of these games used vertical monitors, but even in vertical mode there's still an inch or more of border on both the top and bottom of the screen! At least max out the size vertically for a vertical game.
Also, it was a bummer that Ms. Pac-Man is a DLC extra. This was the most popular game in the entire series, but its considered an extra in this collection. I realize the differences between Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man are small in this day and age, but in the arcades at the time, the addition of new mazes, ghost patterns, and a slight tweak to the controls were pretty big, and Ms. Pac-Man to this day is considered the pinnicle of the series. It's a shame that in a Pac collection, it's not included unless you pay more.
Still, these classics are replicated well in this collection. The big ones are Tournament Edition and Battle Royale, two great additions to Pac-Mans legacy. There's plenty of others to choose from as well.

Tower of Guns is a nice little cross between an Old-School Shooter and a bullet-hell roguelike, with some platforming as well. You run around really fast and shoot things and dodge tons of projectiles and collect power-ups to make yourself better, and when you die you can alter your loadout and start all over again. It's a good formula, and though it has some hiccups, there are a lot of fun elements.
The gameplay feels nice. It's quite floaty and weightless, but that fits with the large, expansive levels and movement required to avoid all the enemy attacks. A lot of the powerups are dedicated to increasing the time the player spends in the air, including speed, jump height, and a seemingly unlimited number of possible midair jumps.
The art style is very hand-drawn-y, which I personally don't like all that much, but not enough to get really annoyed by it.
There're infinite enemies, but you have infinite ammo, so there's no problem.
The game has a very goofy sense of humor, which mostly comes across in the variety of possible randomly selected stories each game can have. They don't really change anything, but they recontextualize the gameplay in funny ways. You can be a young woman trying to claim her inheritance, a goo monster trying to escape a laboratory, a thinly disguised Terminator pastiche, or an old couple with an astonishingly faulty GPS. It's charming, and I'm glad it was implemented.
There's a really pleasant piano soundtrack that escalates with gameplay wonderfully.
The spikey ball launchers can ♥♥♥♥ right off, as can the Egg Scrambler boss.
The game crashed or froze a lot for me, which was goddamn annoying when it interrupted gameplay. I'm not sure if this is an issue for anyone else, though, so take that with a grain of salt.
Overall, Tower of Guns is a lot of fun. The gameplay's engaging, it's charming and funny, and apparently one guy made just about all of it by himself, which is always good to see. I recommend it.

Let's be honest here. This game is super simple. Take a gun and perks into a procedurally generated tower, clear rooms, kill bosses, try to beat the game. There's something like 8-ish guns and a fair share of perks that you unlock through various progressions, letting you try out different difficulties (some definitely seem easier than others, more on that later) or strategies. The short verdict is that this all is done REALLY well, and it's super fun.
For the long winded explanation, here it goes: The game is incredibly fun and has a distinct Quake and/or Doom feel to the gunplay and movement. All the controls feel very tight and responsive, which is crucial given that it's very obviously a bullet-hell game. The progression seems relatively steady, but prepare for the first few deaths in the tower to come quick and unexpectedly. If you stick it out though and find a gun/perk set that suits your fancy, you're gonna have a hell of a fun time progressing through the other unlockables. Please take note, at the time of this review, I'd say I have just over half of the stuff unlocked, with the remaining unlocks being relatively lengthy to acquire. Basically, don't let my game time make you assume you can blaze through this game.
Some of the fun bits: My personal favorite addition to this game are the modifiers you can take with you into a run. I personally like the "Dice Roll" mode, which adds random effects to each room you enter. Obviously, these can sometimes make or break a run, but it keeps it fresh and entertaining. For instance: suddenly fall damage is dramatically increased to where jumping normally chunks your health, or the loot drops are increased to a room-flooding extent, or even EVERY DROP IS A DIFFICULTY UP TOKEN. Things like that make the runs incredibly entertaining, if not a bit silly at times. Things like an Endless Mode and par times for each of the floors also keep the game feeling fresh when you want to mix things up a bit, and the secrets are very fun to find.
Some of the odd bits: I'll preface this with saying that I don't really think any of the things I mention here warrant changing. It basically boils down to broken combinations, but given that this game is in lieu of titles like Binding of Isaac and such, broken runs are just bound to happen from time to time. Some synergies are just undeniably better than others, and some runs just won't go your way. But if you already know the premise of this game and are still interested in it, I would find it shocking if that bothered you.
The final verdict: This is a 3D bullet-hell shooter done REALLY well. It feels great to control, the different playstyles can let anyone hope in and enjoy it, and it's just an all around joy to mess around with. If you think you'll like this game just based on it's premise, you will not be disappointed. I encourage others who just enjoy shooters as well to check it out, as it's certainly a fun thing to hop into every once in a while.

The game is F2P, but it is by no means a "free-to-play, your way" kind of game. The campaigns are nice, if totally blind and very gimmicky. They give enough cards from the set to make a deck with, but it's at the barest level of functionality. To "earn" packs, you either need to play PvP to grind that 400 gold-per-day cap, or non-campaign matches against the AI. The three levels of "difficulty" are actually a lie: easy is the hardest, and hard is the easiest; the AI has been proven to always start with a favorable hand, because they want you to play PvP, and never look into their poor programming. It will hold on to a single card the entire match (40+ rounds) and play it as the, "I won when the game started" card. Easy AI plays strong early game, which often has a good late game, and hard has lots of good stuff, interspersed in the bottom half of the deck. Does shuffling move them? Who knows?
Quests are the worst feature, by far. You can and will cycle and cycle, only to get three PvP quests. If you don't like PvP, because it's stressful, meta'd to hell, slow, and never mind the fact that whoever the hell is in charge REFUSES to ban hackers or exploiters, this is objectively not the game for you. There is no "Clear my quest log" button. You have to log in each day to see if there's one you can do in AI matches. Some of them are ridiculous even there, such as the, "Win two matches in which you generate at least 15 energy." Not only do you have to win, you have to achieve a certain amount of energy, which you should be writing down as you go. This means the match can take twenty minutes to an hour, depending on how controlling either you or the bot is.
Overall, if you like PvP, you might be okay. But if you play against AI for the fun of the actual "Magic: The Gathering" game, this game is strictly worse than Magic 2015, in which they had a clear separation between AI (not really "PvE") and PvP advancement.

For a free-to-play MtG game, this does a pretty good job at delivering.
The game is geared more towards newer players, as evidenced by the most in-depth tutorial I've seen for a TCG/CCG on Steam. It is simpler, yet requires more active attention to the game than paper Magic or MTGO. This is mostly in part to the automatic timer the game forces on you instead of allowing you to set stops in each phase where you may want to respond.
Like:
Entirely free-to-play: You don't need to sink a single dollar into this game to have an enjoyable experience. That being said, get ready to grind hard to get new cards...
Campaign system: Easy way to sample cards from new expansion sets.
Customer Service: While things don't get done in a timely manner, Wizards' customer service team has always been responsive (within 1 business day) and courteous.
Neutral:
Card packs: 150 gold, the equivalent of 5 VS wins or 10 Hard AI wins, for a 6-card pack feels kind of meh, even with 1 guaranteed rare/mythic.
Rarity restrictions: Being able to only play 4/3/2/1 commons/uncommons/rares/mythics is annoying, but helps keep power levels in check.
Formats: Currently only 3 formats: VS 1v1s, VS 2v2s, and AI. All of which are constructed. Would be nice to see some imitation of Sealed, but not necessary.
Dislike:
Auto-pass timers: Makes responding/instant-speed interaction more difficult to time and does not allow bluffing.
Magic: the CCG wannabe: While this would require an overhaul of the card awarding system, I do not like that this is a CCG rather than a TCG. Most importantly, WHERE THE HELL IS THE CRAFTING SYSTEM?! There is no crafting system at all, which is atrocious when compared to Hearthstone, Eternal, and Elder Scrolls: Legends.
Infrequent patches: Most games publish new patches at least weekly to optimize play and address bugs. Duels patches only with each new set, or every 3 months.
Overall, I think Duels was an acceptable digital MtG product. It does not perfectly mimic paper Magic or MTGO, but that's not its purpose. Its purpose, I feel, is to provide a user-friendly entry into Magic and provide some free alternative to playing the game that has captivated millions worldwide.
That said, Wizards has decided to discontinue this rendition of Duels. Their announcement was not completely transparent. There is no article titled "Duels shutting down" or similar. While there is an article announcing the discontinued service of Duels, one must click into that article and read through it to learn of Wizards's decision. There is also NO IN-GAME ANNOUNCEMENT regarding this change of direction. All the pop-up ads I've seen recently have been normal advertising for Magic and other, related Hasbro offerings. With this in mind, I can no longer recommend this Magic: Duels product and strongly discourage people from sinking money into future freemium Wizards offerings.

Roundabout is a frustrating but clever experience.
The core gameplay is very challenging. I had hoped I would improve my revolving limo skills as the game continued, but I found myself struggling throughout to get the timing of each run just right. Part of it is that mastery of each course requires memorization and crashing more than a few times. The game is fairly generous with checkpoints except during the open world segments when traveling from mission to mission - I often found simply getting to my next passenger more challenging than the actual ride.
It's a good thing that the story and presentation is simply not to be missed - it helps ease much of the frustration in the gameplay. The cutscenes harken back to the days of bad FMV games that used to dominate early CD-based platforms like the Sega CD. This means bad acting and cheap production values, but this time it's on purpose and used properly to give breaks from the gameplay (rather than replacing gameplay). It will certainly provide a few laughs to anyone who enjoys campy, "so bad it's good" production styles.
The story itself will only provide two to three hours of gameplay, but there is a good bit of variety in the experience. There is also hours of content to explore and unlock in the game's open world - customizations, mission replay challenges, and so on. Completionists will have a field day.
If the cutscenes presented in the game's trailer seem amusing, it's worth a purchase to experience the lunancy that is the world of Roundabout. Beyond that, this one is really for fans of action-puzzle games and open-world games with lots of unlockables. Players like that will definitely want to give this one a spin.

is an excellent game whose brevity and simplicity belies a profound critique of capitalism. Designed as a "Marxist strategy game",
challenges the player to ruin the world by playing as a member of the bourgeoisie. In that capacity, the player must invest their capital throughout the world to purchase votes, which is then utilized to accumulate more capital. The player wins by possessing the most capital in their Swiss bank account by the end of the twelfth turn, which is achieved by liquidating their assets (namely, purchased votes). At the end of twelve turns (each turn comprising three phases), the world has been ruined, ostensibly due to the consequences that capitalism inexorably produces.
The Marxist influence in
is obvious to anyone familiar with Marxist theory. Capital is dead labor and it is invested in order to generate living labor, which is then transformed into more dead labor and accumulated as such. This process, called capital accumulation, is inherent in capitalism. The state, as an organ of class rule, is used by owners of capital (capitalists) to facilitate their accumulation of capital through corruption. This is an unavoidable consequence of capitalism precisely because capital is what determines economic power and it is the owners of that capital who ultimately own society, including institutions such as the state. This ownership by the bourgeoisie (capitalists as a class) is due to their ownership of the means of production, which forms the productive and economic base for society. The bourgeoisie acts in this way due to their shared class interest, namely the accumulation and utilization of capital to reproduce the material conditions of capitalism and their favorable position therein.
succinctly encapsulates how capitalism as a system compels economic actors to perform according to the rules of that system. As a player, you are compelled by the rules of the game to invest and accumulate capital, despite knowing that the result of playing the game entails everyone losing regardless of who the winner may eventually be. Nevertheless, you compete with other players according to those rules because your success depends on it. This is similar to how capitalists in the real world compete in the global market in accumulating capital and liquidating it into offshore bank accounts, despite how playing by the rules of capitalism entails disastrous results.
For that reason, it makes no sense to blame this or that capitalist, just as it is absurd to blame the politicians they bought, because they are all performing rationally according to the rules of capitalism. The culpability is in the system itself: the consequences of capitalism are caused by the system of rules which govern the actions of its participants, not by the participants who are simply following those rules. Therefore, a rational response to this is to change the system of rules itself, not to simply depose this or that actor.
illustrates this by its very existence: the world is ruined ultimately because of the nature of the game, not simply because one chooses to participate in it. Regardless of whether the player personally participates in the game, others invariably will and they will be compelled by the same rules that any player would face, and it is those very rules which are to blame for the results of playing the game so long as there are players compelled to play it (and unaware of an alternative).
But why is it called
? When the player decides to invest their capital, the most prudent initial investments are those which cost the least capital. The capital cost of a region is principally determined by its economic development and infrastructure. Lesser developed regions will therefore cost less capital to invest. These are the necessary conditions for neocolonialism: capitalists engage in economic imperialism by exploiting less developed regions to maximize profits and use the economic power they accumulate through this exploitation to control the development of those regions, which is done order to guarantee that the conditions in those regions serve their interests. In the game, players demonstrate this by investing in the least developed regions, accumulating capital through those investments, and utilizing the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to either accelerate capital accumulation or impede regional development. In doing so, players essentially simulate Marxian theory of neocolonialism.
I definitely recommend
to anyone interested in Eurogame-style strategy games, especially those familiar with Marxist theory. Although the game design is rather simple, and the game options are very limited,
nevertheless provides an enjoyable and educational experience with an inevitably bittersweet end.
Would I recommend
for its current retail price of $3.99 (USD)? If you have money to spare, you really want the game, and you are aware of its quality, then I don't think you will regret your purchase. If you have reservations, however, or you would prefer to not spend that much money on the game, then maybe you should attempt to acquire
through other means, such as winning it on a giveaway site or purchasing it when it is bundled or on sale. I was given this game by a friend who knew I would like it, and I certainly did. Maybe you will, too.

As a die hard fan of Thief series, I refuse to perceive this latest remake as bad. We've been waiting 10 years for another Thief game, and although this is not the direct continuation of trilogy it is still a very good game.
You can adjust the difficulty level to your liking. Don't like focus? Turn it off. As in other Thief games, you are not forced to kill anyone, you can either sneak past them or knock them out. Some loot can be tricky to find, some are in plain sight but are still out of your reach until you pull the right trigger.
Though this is a remake, it's has nice touch about the original Thief's past: Hammerites cathedral, references to Trickster, cog shaped loot (hint toward the Mechanists), Keeper's Library - it is all sentimental in this new instalment.
Very nice music and graphics, steam punk, dark feel about the story. The story though might be one weaker side of this game. It's not as full and reach as it was in previous trilogy games. Nevertheless I like the game and hopefully we will see Garrett again. Or his apprentice from the end of the trilogy.

As a 'true' stealth game I had great fun in Thief picking locks, disabling traps and finally getting my hands on a fine collectible treasure! Searching around for that one hidden switch that nets you a nice piece is really great fun!
The game has a pure focus on stealth and almost always gives an alternative option (go around instead of fighting) etc.
I played the game on Master difficulty without using the focus ability since that way you really have to look for stuff and figure out the level which for me is the most fun. In total it took my 34 hrs to finish the game including all sidequests (but not all loot), so that's an acceptable amount of gameplay.
While the game mechanics are very nice, sometimes you want to do something (jump of a ledge, go through a specific path etc) which is not possible. So while the game offers many alternatives, it's not totally open. The controls are also somewhat restricted: one button is used for multiple different actions depending on the context. I prefer a single button per action so the player has full control at any time.
The 'City' i.e. the hub between Chapters is very nice. It really adds to the immersion.
The story however is 'meh'. The main idea i.e. the setting, the primal energy etc are very nice and make for a great story potential ... however for some reason it all gets compressed into "save a girl which I as a player don't care about at all". I really fail to see why they centered the whole story about some girl which is just a sidekick to the main character. There are also gaps and holes in the story (you have gone missing for a whole year and not even once wonder where you have been ...) and the ending is total nonsense. The story could have been so much more.
So don't play this game for the story, but play it for having the feeling of a Master Thief skulking through the night and robbing (mostly) innocent victims!

So, I decided to play this game and give it a fair shot despite all the gamergate controversy.
The first thing I want to say, as an aspiring game developer who hopes to one day get a game through greenlight, that if this is the new standard of what constitutes the title "game developer" then 10 year olds everywhere creating their first projects in flash can rejoice with a sense of pride in their new title of professional game developer. What do I mean by this? Well, lets take a look.
The game itself is essentially a wall of text with a couple of highlighted text that links to more walls of text. This "game" is more or less an interactive story that follows the same format as the "choose your own path" Goosebumps books (if anyone remembers those?) After each page of text you are given a few options of how you want to react to certain situations. Each choice will take you to a new wall of text explaining your actions and following the resulting story. Some choices close off other choices later on (I assume, otherwise the crossed out choices presented to the user are arbitrary) giving the user a sense of control over the outcomes. It follows this format until the writers couldn't think of anything else to write and thus they leave it open-ended. They explain this in the game's epilogue where they conclude that the life of a person with depression does not come to a nice and tidy ending, and thus, the game would not have such a conclusion either. This would have been believable if it were not for the games writing.
The writing is horrible. Not only is there missing commas and other punctuation that would help the reader actually understand tone and pacing of sentences, but the writing style is written at a 7th grade level. This is not an insult as many great books and stories are written with this level of vocabulary and sophistication to achieve greater audience appeal. The problem with this is that the writing randomly throws in "big" words and pseudo intellectual vernacular to give the reader the illusion that the writers are actually smart educated people. The writing, however, speaks for itself.
This brings us to the music. I actually quite enjoyed the musical score. As a musician (I think most gamers are to some extent), I can enjoy the mood and atmosphere that the music presented. The music did achieve its goal of gradually gnawing at the player (myself) with a certain sense of beauty and anxiety. Well done!
The layout of the game was very simple. If I want to play a simple game, like cookie clicker for example, I want the user interface to be outstanding. Now, I can appreciate the fact that a game trying to give a non-depressed user a lens to perceive the world through the eyes of those who are depressed, will inevitably be a little bit more bleak and bland. This however, is not the case for Depression Quest. The interface looks like absolutely no thought went into it at all. It looks as though it was designed 100% for utility and no thought went into aesthetics.
Now, for the "vibe" I got from the game. This game dripped with the privileged and shielded eye of a white middle class female who thinks she understands the plight of people suffering depression. It was highly offensive, as someone who has seen, first hand, the affects of depression on family members, this sort of arrogant sense of superior empathy disgusts me. This game is equivelant to a middle class white person making a game about the social-economic struggles of a black person in poverty. It is a level of arrogance that truly warrants a gamergate.

Tower of Guns is a first-person rogue-lite in which you ascend a tower full of guns using- get this -GUNS.
The surprising thing about ToG is how addicting it is once you get into it. The gameplay is fairly simple; shoot enemies, get their loot (money, item-energy, and occasionally upgrades), buy upgrades and new gear, fight a boss, rinse, and repeat.
Many may find an issue with the game's admittedly limited level-generation. After enough attempts each run will quickly blur together, but even after 20 hours I was still finding new and substantial secrets within the game.
ToG also has some of the most insane movement and weapon-capabilites out of any FPS i've played. If you're able to loop enough runs together you'll be able to jump in the air infinitely at insane speeds while destroying whole rooms in seconds with rapid-fire cluster-missiles. Which, lemme tell you: is quite satisfying.
Of course once you've gotten to the point where nothing can touch you the game proceeds to get a tad bit boring and you end up ending runs yourself because there sure as hell ain't anything that can kill you anymore.
PROS:
- Great controls.
- Satisfying gameplay
- Can be beaten entirely with skill.
- Lots of secrets.
- Great for listening to podcasts while playing.
MIDDLE GROUND:
- Art style may turn people off.
- Level design can feel repetitive.
CONS:
- Many weapons and perks are too awkward to be fun.
- Air-jumping becomes too necessary for finding secrets.
- Over-all lack of polish.
- Special-items are borderline useless.
SCORE: 8/10

The other issue, and I can't work this one out, is that the games do not support a NES controller through USB.  Pacman was on the original Nintendo but you can't use that controller here.  I find this a shame because in Pacman CE with the speed you eventually move at, it can be difficult to control with either the XBox controller's analogue stick or 8-way directional pad.
I had Pacman CE on the 360 and it ran in 1080p.  This version will only run in 720p which is a shame.
All in all a great collection of games, incredible value if you get it in a steam sale, and something that will keep you busy.

Okay, let's go with a pro/con style review! ALSO I reccommend this game for NEW PLAYERS to learn the game.
PROS:
Teaches you how to play in the most basic of ways.
Technically F2P (Free to play)
Limits the number of each card according to rarity allowed in decks (4 of any common, 3 of uncommon, 2 rare, and 1 mythic) This means you can put the respective number of any given card for each individual card in the deck which is good for learning the game, limiting those who know how to play from destroying newbies.
CONS
It's a micro transaction  trap. If you pay money to get packs, you are nearly guarunteed to win over someone playing the same total time in the game.
It limits you from making full decks. Since you can only have 2 of each rare you put in your deck, it limits your decks synnergy and ability to test how the deck would run at full capacity.
Only has one years worth of cards out of over 20 years of the game.
Had to replace one of the main staples in Magic Origins because they couldn't get the game to work properly with it (Archangel of Tithes replaced with an M12 Aura called Angelic Destiny, which in most cases is actually better and more powerful)
Time limit on responses make the game incredibly annoying for both new and old players. Miss it, and it might just lose you games.
If you want to learn the basics, play the story lines, open a few packs, construct and play a few basic decks, don't spend money on it, and if you like it enough, find a local card shop and make a real deck with all the cards. Simplist way to do things. Still not the attrocity that MTGO is.

+ Randomly generated dungeon every time with just enough pre-made rooms and events to keep things interesting
+ ^ that and the numerous skills give this game an absurd amount of replay value that goes well beyond an investment of
5 bucks

Cons

Do you know those games that are great ideas that just aren't executed correctly, resulting in a game with a ton of potential but no actual worthwhile content?
Roundabout is not one of those games.
Roundabout is an ingenious game. A game with a clear, well executed theme and a hilarious playthrough. The story is absolutely as silly as the gameplay, too. You play as a limosine driver that revolves, as you pick up a cast of strange characters and drive them throughout the city of Roundabout. The game goes about its goal of creating a 70's B Movie very well, with everything from acting like what you'd exepect from a 70's B Movie to VHS postprocessing effects that really add to the experience. Even little things, such as the HUD and subtitles add to the theme. The characters and story are memorable as well.
My only gripes are of the story length, as I wish it could be longer due to how great everything else is, however there are many challenges and settings that add various other neat things to the gameplay (permadeath mode, limo customizations, various collectables hidden throughout the map) that add some replayablilty.
A great game, I'd give it 9/10

It is really amazing that after all these years Wizards still cannot make a magic game that is not so horribly clunky to play.  Because of the needless timers on rounds this game often makes it so you cannot cast instants when you need to on your oppenents turn, or during combat. The decks you are given to play against the computer are absolutely terrible. Your opponents decks are always good though. Chandra's all red burn deck has almost no one mana spells?  Really? Really? And you are forced to use these garbage decks to complete the single player portion of the game. The single player portion of the game is the only good way to get cards unlocked to create your own decks. So access to cards is locked behind being forced to play completely non-fun matches with joke decks against much better computer controlled decks.
Even the way this game tries to teach new players the game is awkward at best. Rules are often explained out of nowherer in the middle of a game. There you are with your terrible deck trying to luck your way into being able to win when suddenly someone draws an instant card. Now the game will prompt you with a "lesson" to learn how instants work. Guess what, if you click "yes" you are suddenly placed into an entirely different game already in progress. Then that stupid "timer" is running and poof, there went your chance to cast the instant for the win and the oppenent in this other game kills you. You fail, try again. And while you're at it, listen to the game tediously explain to you how instants work. You failed not because you misunderstood this part of the game, but because you are suddenly dropped into a game already in progress with cards on the board. A timer is running and somehow you are expected to look at the cards in your hand, read them, look at the board on both sides of the table, check if you have enough mana, and pick out the correct target, and then cast the spell.
I have also experienced many problems getting the game to start or end correctly. Starting often ends up with nothing happening. Quiting the game sometimes results in my computer getting completely locked up and requiring a reboot. This game is free though. You do get what you pay for in this case.

Here, the poor countries are not working for a bigger one (like "colonies"). Here, there is no debt, nor loans. So, more than a banker, you are a powerful (and corrupted) business magnate, with enough power to buy votes, control the IMF and propose free trade agreements.
So, you may find the name misleading; but don't care, the game shows a very bad side effect of the current system, where people with enough money may get corrupted and decide over what happens in the world, buy politicians, and force the countries to take decisions that are only good for this person business. Even agaisnt the people benefit.
Like I said, I consider it a "Corporativism" simulator.

There is so much going wrong for this game that it would be far quicker to list the good things than the bad.  However, I find it's often best to do things the hard way.
In the opening screen, you are presented with the statement, "This game uses audio as a part of the play experience.  We encourage you to play with the sound on."  This is not a good idea.  The music is very haunting and fairly immersive, but only for the first few bars.  It quickly devolves into a grating noise that is either looping or just played with annoyingly similar chords, throughout the game.  It does not enhance the experience.  If anything, it hurts it.
The story itself is a major problem.  As the game states, people experience depression differently, and the game can only shed light on so much.  However, the game feels lazily put together.   There aren’t many options, just a few blanket ones.  As you plod through, more types of options are locked or unlocked based on your decisions.  But even with the amount of text displayed on each page, the story was very lacking.
The characters felt like two-dimensional effigies.  You could not get attached to, or even empathize with, any of them, because there simply wasn't enough to them.  It was as if each character was their own dating website profile, with only a few words plugged into each text field.
As the protagonist continues to get worse, (or better, as it's hard to tell since it often feels vague) more options are blocked off, leaving the player stranded on a route based on just a few decisions they made early on.  Though this is somewhat accurate to reality–people living with depression find themselves unable to do even simple things like get out of bed or shower, at times–it seems to railroad the player into one of three possible routes:  The good end, the bad end, and the neutral end.
The truth is, these ends come with some loaded messages.  Productive actions will be rewarded, yet by choosing not to make productive choices you will be heavily punished.  This message is incredibly dangerous to spread to those with depression who are playing the game in an effort to feel understood.  It spreads a message of helplessness and worthlessness.  After all, you are made to feel you’ve lost the game, and downright worthless for having done so, if your choices weren’t the “right” choices.
At the end of the game, in the credits, you are pretentiously thanked for "being willing to play games that are meant to be something other than simply 'fun.'"
Even though I have referred to "Depression Quest" as a game throughout this review, it really is not.  This is a "choose your own adventure" book, or an exercise.  There are no real gameplay elements in this thing, save from being able to make choices that have lasting effects.  And yet, it is making itself out to be something better than "fun" games, despite having almost none of the qualities that make a game, period.
In fact, it's barely even a game book.  In "choose your own adventure books," the story is engaging, and what you do matters in the pursuit of your goal.  "Depression Quest" is not engaging, there are no stakes, and it's hard to tell what effect you're having.
Long story short, "Depression Quest" is, at the most, a meretricious, amateur attempt at creating a "choose your own adventure" game book, loaded with text and grammatical errors, being projected as something above and beyond other video games.  This is ironic, seeing it accomplished none of its goals.
It fails as a video game.  It fails as a game book.  It fails as a teaching or therapeutic tool.  It fails at depicting what living with depression is like (especially if you consider the testimonials I've received from friends, family, and online sources).  It even fails at being an expression of the author's personal pain, as it does nothing to instill any sort of empathy in the player.  It's all so tedious, unimaginative and even narcissistic, that it comes off as a whining teenager's journal, destroying any attempt of connecting with the player, even at a superficial level.
Worse still, the game's history renders it even more unenjoyable.  What really did or didn't happen is irrelevant.  Obviously, it doesn't make any sense that the creator would have fraternized with online game journalists for monetary reasons, seeing that the game was always free.  However, after playing the game and seeing what it's all about, it makes perfect sense that they would for pure publicity.  That is quite possibly the only way that this game would have gotten any form of notoriety.  Otherwise, it would have faded into obscurity in less than a week.  And it worked.  The scandal is the biggest reason that anyone knows about it.  It has given its creator more publicity, voice, and money than their talents could have ever brought.
That doesn't mean that the subject of depression is impossible to put into game form.  "Actual Sunlight" is one that better achieves this.  Although, some may think that it's more of a visual novel than a game, it still has more and better gameplay elements than "Depression Quest."  Better writing with a deeper, more meaningful story, and makes no lofty assertions about what it is.  The stakes in the game are clear, and you can empathize with the characters.  Its creators put thought and care into their game, despite it being simple in the game play aspect.
In closing, "Depression Quest" was one of the most poorly made, pointless things I have ever spent time on.  The creator owes $25 to every person who has ever downloaded it.

This was a dark story in terms of how your character deals with depression because most of the choices that were crossed out were choices that had a definite yes or no answer. The choices that were crossed out becomes more frequent, the more depressed you are. You mostly had choices where you would second guess yourself and everything about people's opinion of you.
I never reached the end of the game but it is a game that I would like to finish to see how it ends. I have a lot of positive feedback and constructive critism to put out:
- The idea of an openworld, aimlessly roaming, "screw the laws of physics" skateboarding game is probably the most innovative preposition I've seen on Steam all year.
- Without the presence of quests, it's so easy and comforting for my autistic♥♥♥♥♥to get lost in the game without being conscious of objectives breathing down my neck.
- The whole purgatory realm combined with the hospital atmosphere during loading makes death seem a lot less scary. The inclusion of the programs in the menu give the main character a completely relatable backstory and also sends a message about how you cannot run away from your problems forever.
My constructive critism, while also being aware that programming is difficult and I personally cannot program or mod to save my life:
- The controls and visuals are clunky and could use some work. I spent about five minutes skating around the outside of a tube because I could not figure out how to get onto the ground again; the camera kept shaking so I could not focus on any particular target.
- I found the navigation difficult to get used to, but I also understand that using the mouse would be easier for others. I've never successfully ridden a skateboard so I cannot imagine if the controls in the game are similar to what skateboarding feels like in real life. My suggestion would be to give players the option to use the classic WASD keys to navigate or the mouse, as was the game's initial intention (and the ability to switch between the controls)
- I would definitely donate to the developers of this game so that they can improve our experience (TM). I'd rather give my money to people who work hard on stuff like this!
A personal message to the devs:
PLEASE DO NOT STOP! Creation and innovation is important today in regards to the gaming culture. As someone who needs to relieve a lot of stress all the time forever, this can really help a lot of people cool off and wind down. Thank you!

It's a text adventure game, so there's a lot of reading, which is fine. I'm not entirely sure from where I got in the story before I checked out that the characteristics of your reclusiveness are even depression -- it's more of introversion. I find myself identifying with most of what the character describes feeling, despite being a relatively happy person, so it's hard for me to say that the game does a very good job of actually conveying depression.
Now, every once in a while there are options for paths that are crossed out. I'm not quite sure what's going on there, there are clearly some things happening behind the scenes to determine what you can and can't select, but it doesn't give much agency to the player if they can't really tell, at the very least, if and why their decisions have led to fewer choices. If this formula were visible perhaps there'd be a greater connection that would convey the point more.
Moreover, the effect would perhaps be more dramatic if the very first choice you made didn't involve a crossed-off option, increasing the contrast when you fall deeper into depression. To be fair, the first few choices crossed off were definitely things I myself wouldn't do, and again, I'm a relatively happy person, so there's still the question of if this aided in the conveyence. If a player were able to make these decisions, establishing a character that would normally want to, then removing that option might be more powerful, but removing that option in the first place forces the establishment of a character that doesn't really help one way or the other.

It's also hard to judge whether you're going to be hidden or seen due to the graphics style. Enemy cones of vision might have given the game a wider appeal and a visual aid to show you're actually hidden most helpful.
What's required is learning the layout by trial and error, repeating and perhaps getting lucky. I used an Xbox One pad for aiming which might not be as accurate as mouse but that's what I am used to.

If you've got lots of patience and nerves of steel to keep on trying after so many deaths then you'll probably get lots of satisfaction from the gameplay style. The Pac-Man Musum is a compilation set released by Namco and from its description you would be forgiven for thinking that this game would be a compilation of all the Pac-man games released brought together in one set...this compilation however simply contains Pacman and the half a dozen variations that were released in Arcades following the success of the first, as a result for the money you would pay for this (Currently retailing at £14.99) you effectively get the original Pac-Man, about 4 or 5 table variations and a strange platformer game in which you play as a  side scrolling running Pac-man trying to avoid ghosts by jumping over them (Nowhere near as fun as it sounds)...there is also a tetris variation in which you have to line ghosts up and send pacmans down to take them out (Effectively Dr.Mario meets Bakubaku)
Where it pains me most is that this version not only doesnt include Mrs. Pac-man.. But they instead offer that as a DLC extra you have to pay for...this would be the equivilent of a natural history museum which is already offering limited access  to its exhibits making you pay to see anything about Birds...its simply not on...Add to this that the with a title like Pac-Man Museum you would think they would at least glance on the home console games if even briefly (No Pac-Man 2, Pac in time, Pac man world ect...) just makes for a rather over priced experience that delivers very little content...
If your really desperate to play the original Pac-Man there are hundreds of Flash based versions available online, failing that locating a copy of the original on any home console or even handheld mobile devices these days is almost guarenteed to be possible and for a lot cheaper than you can get it here...
Personally I would only pick this up if you had a nostalgia for one of the more obscure titles included in this package...otherwise I can highly reccommend picking up  Pac Man championship edition DX+  which is also available on Steam, which in my opinion is a vastly superior modernisation of this utter arcade classic. As it stands though for the cost you can definately do better...
