This is, hands-down, the finest first-play experience I have ever had from a casual game.  Mini Metro is an outstanding example of perfection in minimalism, and a resounding lesson that gameplay trumps all.  As of this date, there is no music, and the graphics are simple transit system line art.  In short, you could have knocked this out on a VIC-20 in your basement-- if you'd been this much of a genius.
The concept is brilliant, and the execution is perfect-- but this is still early access at this point, so there's a bit of a level shortage.  That's alleviated somewhat by the several subtly-- but importantly-- different play modes.
Also, there are not a lot of upgrades at this point.  There are only three or four limited, important resources, and they're all really major.  A handful of more subtle, minor-tweak upgrades would make things a bit more visually interesting, as well as giving you a few things to tinker with when you're waiting to see how well a major change plays out.
Nonetheless, this is absolutely the best casual game I've played in years.  Highly recommended, and definitely worth the money.  The only real question is whether you will also want it on your phone or tablet, where I expect touch-and-drag would only add to the fun.

It is really amazing that after all these years Wizards still cannot make a magic game that is not so horribly clunky to play.  Because of the needless timers on rounds this game often makes it so you cannot cast instants when you need to on your oppenents turn, or during combat. The decks you are given to play against the computer are absolutely terrible. Your opponents decks are always good though. Chandra's all red burn deck has almost no one mana spells?  Really? Really? And you are forced to use these garbage decks to complete the single player portion of the game. The single player portion of the game is the only good way to get cards unlocked to create your own decks. So access to cards is locked behind being forced to play completely non-fun matches with joke decks against much better computer controlled decks.
Even the way this game tries to teach new players the game is awkward at best. Rules are often explained out of nowherer in the middle of a game. There you are with your terrible deck trying to luck your way into being able to win when suddenly someone draws an instant card. Now the game will prompt you with a "lesson" to learn how instants work. Guess what, if you click "yes" you are suddenly placed into an entirely different game already in progress. Then that stupid "timer" is running and poof, there went your chance to cast the instant for the win and the oppenent in this other game kills you. You fail, try again. And while you're at it, listen to the game tediously explain to you how instants work. You failed not because you misunderstood this part of the game, but because you are suddenly dropped into a game already in progress with cards on the board. A timer is running and somehow you are expected to look at the cards in your hand, read them, look at the board on both sides of the table, check if you have enough mana, and pick out the correct target, and then cast the spell.
I have also experienced many problems getting the game to start or end correctly. Starting often ends up with nothing happening. Quiting the game sometimes results in my computer getting completely locked up and requiring a reboot. This game is free though. You do get what you pay for in this case.

The Citizen Kane of video games.

So I tells you what you do:
First, take a simple, yet unique gameplay element.  Like, say, a limousine that's constantly spinning.  One that, through a delicate balance of timing and control, you have to guide through a city, weaving through parked cars, buildings, boulders, and whatever else it can throw at you.
Now, polish that one gameplay element.  Take it as far as it'll go.  Be creative.  Have fun with it.  Maybe there's points where spinning *backward* is the key.  Maybe you should spin over water, too.  Can the limousine jump?  Sure, but it'll be spinning the whole time.  Polish the gameplay until it shines.  A built-in speedrun mode that's solid and fun won't hurt.
Then, build your game's world.  A silly, spinning-obsessed city full of pedestrians who don't quite have the right-of-way, cars that park in the most inconvenient of places, construction sites set up so a well-trained limousine driver can spin through them, and a cast of goofy characters all waiting to be chauffeured around town, not a single bit of it being taken seriously.
Finally, sprinkle in actual live-action acting.  The sort where a bunch of people with actual cameras and sets filmed themselves getting into a limousine and acted out the story.  A delightfully cheesy story, no less, one about romance, weddings, civil disobedience, skeletons, murder, and tourism.  All acted out by a cast who were clearly enjoying themselves while they did it.
In short, if you don't at least get a good chuckle out of Roundabout, it's possible you don't have a soul.

This "reboot" of the reknown series replaces Garret w/ a comic book variant that is part Batman and part The Crow.  Picture an Emo Goth Garret, complete w/ eye shadow and dour expressions, who spends his days sulking alone in an abandoned clocktower listening to 'My Chemical Romance' and writing bad poetry:  "The clocktower of bleakness ticks a song for the black sadness of my existence.  I'm so alone and no one gets me." until a crow comes to guide him to do things.  Yup.
Garret is no longer just a Master Thief.  He's also Batman.  Instead of simply running from shadow to shadow, he now "swoops".  Instead of simply knocking some jerks out w/ a blackjack, now Garret beats the living snot out of them in a "takedown".  He can also do beat-downs-from-above ala Batman.   And like Batman he has a code:  No killing.  Well....  sorta.  Not really.  Depends on his mood, apparently.  He even has a "It's not who I am underneath, but what I do that defines me" moment.  They should have just called it:  Batman - The Dark Victorian Knight
We can't talk about Garret without talking about loot.  You'll spend half the game collecting scissors, gears and syringes.  I kid you not.  You'll also find valuables that are "collectable".  These are unique and gaudy (profitable!) items that instead of selling them for a fat payday you'll instead decorate your clocktower with.  Did I mention they destroyed the very heart of Garret's character?  There is actually a moment when he's told by his fence, Basso, that he doesn't have to go risk his neck to break into a  safe that may or may not have something in it, because there's no job and he's not getting paid.  Garret's response:  "It's not about the payment, it's what I do."  *sigh*
The game begins w/ you on a job w/ a reckless young Thief that you taught - a little brat named Erin.  Torturous dialogue whenever she appears in the game.  It's painful.  Fair warning:  The writing is bad and the story is atrocious.  It's like they went to a community college Amateur Writing class and found Stephenie Meyer and James Gunn there and hired them.  Erin is the all-in-one female character:  comrade, emotional foil, damsel-in-distress, antagonist.
Remember all the things you love about the original Thief games:  complex maps w/ multiple routes to success, Garret's snark and sense of humor, overhearing Benny the guard, Pagans and their dialect, Hammerites w/ their inquisition-style religious fanaticism, Mechanists and their lispy leader, Keepers and their Swedish brand of neutrality, Mages and their weird echoey mantras, gas-spewing burricks, undead, bugbeasts, spiders, craymen,  ratmen, exploding frogs, swimming, flooring that gave you away, mission briefings, cutscenes neatly happening before or after a mission, the euphamistic word "Taffer"....  it's all gone!  Garret is now just a humorless prick in a city of humorless♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  The game does, for some reason, retain vestiges of Thief lore that it otherwise doesn't bother with.
Erin has a spiky club she calls "the claw" that she made.  The game goes out of it's way to make a big deal about it.  Garret tells her the claw is holding her back - that it's loud and she doesn't need it.  Pretty soon Garret has possession of it and guess what?  Turns out he loves it!  This despite the fact he has a grappling hook he could use, but for some reason almost never ever does.  And thank goodness that the architects of the city thought to put strategically placed ugly metal grates wherever you need to climb to.  Lucky that!
Wherein the first 3 Thief games you used a blackjack to club people over the head and knockout; now you use it to bash people in the eye during takedowns and as your weapon of choice when going toe-to-toe with sword-weilding guards.  You heard me.
The lightgem was simple and elegant.  So they borked it and added a terrible "shroud" effect to the system, because... well... they hate us, or never played the original games.
This entry sees the return of the rope arrow, but unfortunately you can only use them in predetermined areas.  Also, you can't retrieve them.  That's okay though, because the game is linear and the joy of exploring is absent anyway!  Speaking of arrows:  you get 3 variants of the plain arrow, one water, one fire, one explosive, and one called choke.  Why they felt we needed 3 plain arrows and 2 incendiary, but no moss or gas arrows is puzzling.  Why even bother having the rope arrow when Garret has a grappling hook?  A tool you only see him use in cutscenes and a couple times during the scripted console-boy climbing sequences.  These sequences, btw, are pointless.  There is no gameplay actually happening - you simply follow a series of pipes and grates to your destination.  There are no puzzles or enemies to worry about - it's like they threw them in just to be able to tick off a checklist.
The item system:  new items include wire snippers to disarm traps, a pry bar to open windows, and a wrench to open vents.  Arrows don't have their own world model and instead are represented in game by what looks like a bagged lunch.  You can pick up food, but it also looks like a bagged lunch instead of, ya know, food.  Oh, and Opium.  Garret takes Opium.  It helps him "focus".  That's a great message for the kids, huh?
Items can be found, but they can also be bought.  I thought it funny to find the merchant from Resident Evil 4 moonlighting here as a guy dressed like a flasher eager to show off his goods.  The merchant also lets you upgrade your skills via special items.  Yes, they've RPG-ified a game that in no way needed to be RPG-ified.
You can no longer jump or mantle wherever you'd like, assumingly because the developers are massive d**Kheads.  You're going to hate going through windows by the end of the game.  You pry open a window, climb in, once inside you turn around - window is closed and you have to do it all over again to get out.  Going through vent grates is also annoying.  Opening drawer after drawer in a dwelling may be tedious, but even worse is this new peek mechanic which you will accidentally engage when searching for items in desks and cabinets.  The developers thought Thief gamers had it too good with simple lean keys, so now we have to press a key (the same key used for just about everything else) that causes you to become glued to corners of walls and furniture until you press a separate release button.  Pointless mechanic.  Speaking of pointless:  the game now has quicktime events.  Going through a window, squeezing through a narrow space, and certain sections of game involve a bit of button mashing.  FOR NO REASON.
The graphics are lovely, if you enjoy the black-on-grey Tim Burton motif in EVERY single map.  The sound is abhorrent.  You will hear guys from across a room like they are right next to you, and yes this will drown out some cutscene dialogue.  Forget about the glory days of having to lean against doors to hear what's in the next room - standing in the road a ways down the street is just as good.  My favorite sound issue is when dialogue from an NPC isn't finished before they start talking about something completely different.  The lighting system is also flakey.  I've been spotted in pitch black - and I've seen enemies find bodies hidden away in the shadows like they were clear as day.  The AI is just as broken - sometimes they'll get stuck in place and refuse to do anything more.  I've had numerous "daydreaming" AI encounters that would make ghosting a mission imposssible.  The missions are mostly linear romps with singular paths and they all contain story cutscenes or action sequences, because nothing says "immersion" like having control of the character taken away from the player.  Oh, good luck navigating the City hub - I can't imagine anyone living in such a crazy circuitous mess.
Good Lord, I could go on.  It's just awful.

Roundabout is one of those concepts so out of the box, so unexpected, so quirky, that you can't go into it with a predetermined judgement on it or its genre, because quite frankly, there really isn't anything else like this out there, not in the way that this game works, sure - many games have been quirky, clever, funny, brilliant, and fun all at once, but not in this way. And this is why we're going along for this crazy ride.
Gameplay: 95/100 A
"Roundabout is better with a controller! If you have one, be sure to plug it in and restart for the best experience possible." - The Devs
Yes, take that advice if you're a PC user like I am, playing this game on a keyboard is hell. Not that it is poorly ported, not at all, this game requires precise movements and you can't get that with most keyboards, not like with a thumbstick. Anyways, Roundabout is a fun game, if not frustrating at times as you try and learn the game. It doesn't necessarily drops you in the middle of the game as it shoots you out of a cannon and into a wall and told "Here you go - drive!" But that's all part of the game and the story. Once you get a handle on the mechanics of the car, the game becomes a clever and really enjoyable experience, making the rest of the elements, the sights and sounds, that much better. Going back to the controls, I wasn't able to test the game out with my gamepad as it has up and disappeared and had to play with a keyboard, that said, with some growing pains, the game eventually became tolerable and again, fun, but I agree with the devs, a controller is a must to get the most out of this wonderful game.
Audio: 98/100 A+
Let's get this over with - the music is fantastic. Nothing like 70's disco/funk to get you in the mood for silliness. Okay, now that the soundtrack stuff is out of the way, the sound design is pretty good as well. The voice capture from the FMVs are very well done, and the main character, Georgio, sounds amazing ;). The gameplay effects are well done as well, from the pedestrian screams of anguish and terror, to the explosions, and even the stereotypical 70s/80s video game effects from when you hit something.
Visuals: 91/100 A-
Roundabout looks good, having its own design and style with obvious influences from the decade it is set in. Colorful and playful. The graphics are simple, even abstract at times, and all work together very well. matted neon colors, mixed with blurring effects and that Sims style that appeals to a majority of people, gamers or not, and that could part of the reasoning. Either way, the game is great eye candy even if it isn't the most realistic thing around. Not everything needs realism.
Content: 85/100 B
There's a fair amount of gameplay here and a bit more should you opt for the deluxe edition, as well a good amount of replayability, something many games like this seem to lack. There are also a good amount of visual changes you can make, like big head mode and whatnot, and customizing your ride, changing your special abilities and how you play the game in general, and you'll be left spending a lot of time just messing around with the different combinations you can make, especially in a free ride mode. Yet despite all of this, I feel like there needs to be more, more, more. Maybe I'm just being greedy and I want more reasons to play this game.
Story: 75/100 C
I don't really know what to say about the story. You play as a new limo driver who has a unique way of getting around town and you somehow managed to pass your driving test by sheer amazement. It's a goofy story that doesn't really add much, but it is fun to listen to, especially when the narrator comes in while playing or during the hilarious FMV sequences that are always welcomed and leave me smiling ear to ear. This is one of those cases where the story comes secondary to the game, but just like with Sonic the Hedgehog or Super Mario, did the story really matter in those games?
Design: 96/100 A+
Roundabout is a very well thought out game from the ground up. Yes, it has flaws, but it's fun. Everything from the menu and themes to the city's design, obstacles and courses, mini challenges, hell even the costume designs on the people are all very well done and fit the bill of the period. The characters are all interesting and colorful. Even Georgio's expressions are full of life with each gaze and glare that she gives. Power ups and bonuses litter the roads, just like pedestrians and their bloody remains, and there are plenty of checkpoints as you play for when you crash and die and die you will...over and over again.
Performance: 95/100 A
Overall, Roundabout ran smoothly on my pc with little to no issues in performance. Very odd, very odd indeed. I haven't really enjoyed "playing" the Thief series in general, except for Thief II, as is explained in my other reviews. This game, being a restart of the series, gave me a little hope that I would come in and really enjoy it. My biggest problem with the earlier games was level design, and I expected that to be not as much of a problem, hopefully.
Of course not, though! I am conflicted on this game in that I actually enjoyed it quite a bit for several hours, maybe even the first 10 hours or so, but eventually all of its flaws wore down on me, and I realized that instead of recommending the game, I am going to downvote it because all of those flaws ended up annoying me so much that playing the game lost its fun.
Firstly, the pro's. The game has crisper, cleaner graphics, but it's a very new game, so no big surprise there. Sadly, there isn't any color or "life" to the graphics. Sure, one of the points of the game is the terrible city, but I wish there had been something else. Besides the graphics, the menu design is much better, and Garrett's motion is better than in the original games. But again, it's a big difference in time of development, so no surprise. The gameplay and stealth, as a whole, is still fun to extents, but that's simply because the actual sneaking around and knocking people out (or avoiding them) is fun! Lastly, the Asylum level was the best of the game, not just because it was meant to be scary, but because it was developed and given its own character and history properly.
But there are so many flaws that ruin the fun of the game. Back to level design, which I hated for most of the original games, we are the opposite of the first Thief game. Whereas the first Thief game had wide open expanses of nothingness for levels, this game has very linear hallways and rooms (except for things like the mansion, though that is literally hallways and rooms). In most places, you can only access a handful of rooms in a given area, because you have to go down some hallway and trigger some event.
After you trigger the event, you end up going past a "Point of No Return," as was done in BioShock Infinite. To be honest, these are really annoying. You're not allowed to fully explore a level properly. It is understandable in certain situations, but the game does it every 10-15 minutes essentially.
Motion-wise, you're limited in what you can do. You can't jump freely; you can't lean normally; you can't move objects around. You're limited from what you could do in previous games. Now you have to rely on contextual situations to perform certain motions, which is really annoying, especially because the game is very glitchy in some places. The most common annoyance is constantly having Garrett lean around a desk or chest while trying to get items from it. But I also had the game, several times, make me jump in the wrong direction off a ledge, or not allow me to jump up without me having to move around a lot to get into the "right" spot.
The City map is terrible. The longer I played the game, the more I hated going around the City as a hub. At first, I enjoyed it, but by the end of the game, I hated it. It serves as a nuisance. Firstly, you can't see the whole map at once (which you can't do in levels either!), and you can't get around simply via gates or doorways. Instead, you have random unmarked places to go through like windows, random piles of wood, etc. And the City is split up into a ton of separated areas, making traveling even more annoying. Further, the map doesn't even mark entrances to the other areas.
In the story, when you have to go to Erin's hideout, you have to go through four (4) different sections of the City to reach it. I ended up going through a wood pile, a normal gate (which anybody would use), a window, and then a random door tucked away in a corner above water. Navigating the City is just such a pain. Further, going through windows is a waste of time by having to jimmy the window. The game makes it worse by having you do it twice, as you have to do it again even if you just came through the window. Similar situations occur with vents and having to unscrew the entrance/exit vent, and going through piles of wood wastes your time as well.
Some, not all, controls in the game aren't optimized for PC. The game was designed for console primarily, but some changes were made for PC controls, and the game is playable. But some things are still optimized for controllers, like lockpicking. Lockpicking is annoying both normally and with the upgrade you can buy. In fact, it is more annoying with the Focus upgrade such that I reloaded my save and never used it.
The story of the game is rather poor. I was intrigued at the beginning, then quickly lost interest. As the game went along, it ended up in a convoluted mess which some players heavily defend, but I really didn't enjoy it. Character-wise, nobody was interesting in the story either. I hated Erin; she is probably one of the most annoying characters I have recently seen.
And they ruined Garrett. His development is poor for this game, and he is just a lifeless guy who is pushing along "just because." Despite my problems with the earlier Thief games, I really enjoyed the story and characters in them, even with the simple cutscenes. In this game, the story is a waste. And the random ethereal scenes you kept getting forced into weren't very interesting.
Then, there are a bunch of other random flaws here and there. The audio of the game is badly rendered. I had to jam up the volume of my speakers to hear things, but then turn them back down because the game got too loud, several times, such that I just left the volume down and just watched subtitles. The problem is that the game doesn't properly take distance or direction into account. Many times throughout the game, people who were talking just in front of me either had low volume or were really muffled, whereas sometimes people who were on the other side of a large room would be really loud.
Audio lagged often or would cut off in the middle of whatever was being said. NPCs would start repeating the same thing over and over again. And when it came to NPCs hearing me, the game would be both terrible and magical. I had times where I could make noise right behind an enemy and it wouldn't be noticed. And I also had times where an enemy across the room would alert and run towards me, for no reason. Further, the animals in the levels are annoying; adding the dogs and parrots is an extra hassle to deal with getting around.
Oh, and they took away "Taffer" as a word. I heard one NPC say it once, discussing what it meant. A silly thing to complain about, maybe, but why break the environment of the already-developed world?
In any case, I was interested in this game for a while, but as I played, I realized that all of the bad things ended up overwhelming the good. All in all, I am probably done with the Thief series entirely. The only game that I fully enjoyed (even though it still had flaws) was Thief II, which is also the one that most hardcore fans seem to think is the best.

I was very excited to play Thief, as I love playing sneaky and stealthy characters I was thrilled to find that there´s an entire game devoted to that (as Dragon Age left me more than disappointed when it came to the "rogue" class).
I appreciate that there are moves and actions that are well made and well thought through, but overall there just isn´t enough variation to keep the game interesting past the first 10 hours.
There are pleny of side quests, but they are all the same and the actions you perform are the same, which makes the game monotone to play.
The storyline of a noble thief (whom in the beginning doesn´t want to kill guards) isn´t believable when you later on can kill guards as easily as stepping on ants. That means not playing a character...
Also, the story of saving this girl, who went to an insane asylum and all, it just feels like a cheap Hollywood/Japanese cross over semi-horror story. The story is flat, there isn´t any character development, and the overall genre feels too often used to really become interesting.
It would have been interesting to be able to choose which of the two main characters you wanted to play, and swap their places in the story line, but this game offers no customization or choices in terms of character. Fine, it´s a series of games about this one character, but I still think it would have been more interesting to create ones own character.
The city you have to explore feels tiny, and after a few hours of running around, doing the same check-drawers-swipe-along-picture-frames-loot-loot-and-cut-wires-in-that-box-high-on-the-wall-close-to-the-ceiling-and-loot-some-more motions... it just feels smaller.
Something else that makes the storyline feel lacking and makes the world feel even smaller is the very sparse set of lines NPC´s have to say. It all makes "but then I took an arrow to the knee" sound like the most profound and unique line ever.
It´s like walking in circles.
When playing, something that disrupts the enjoyment of the game is how evident it is that certain actions are trigger points. Person you just snuck by looting their bedroom and disarming traps around sleeping sound... activate the key objective in that house and all of a sudden the character is on high alert and running around looking for you? Yeah, doesn´t feel natural.
Also, everything looks exactly the ♥♥♥♥ing same. No variation in the environment. All furniture, traps, and hidden loot is exactly the same, and after looting about 5 houses I was bored with looting for pens, letter openers, ink bottles, perfume bottles, cutlery, cups, earrings, bracelets, brooches, and candelabras. Would have been more interesting with a greater variation of items, and to have to go somewhere and haggle to get money for the loot, or to trade it for equipment, rather than having it turn to money as soon as you grab it.
I get that the artists wanted THE GLOOM and doom feeling about the whole city, but come on... no colour even inside the houses? Clothing? With everything looking grey, all houses, furniture, and decorations looking very much the same, the game very soon become uninteresting. Audibly, visually, and storyline.
I´m keeping my fingers crossed for another game for us stealthy character players. Yup, I´m imagining a Dragon Age 3 tailored to thieves... or maybe archers. Having archers as their own class is a long lost secrret to game devs... but I am getting side tracked.
Don´t buy THIEF unless it´s for sale. Massively on sale. Like 90% off.

Thief is a first person stealth game and not many like it exists. The series has a legendary heritage and some large shoes to fill. On many levels it succeeds but it's not perfect by any means. I do think it is worth the time and i can recommend it.
A bit of analysis:
Story is there and keeps things moving and into interesting places but hardly is it good. After around 4th chapther i started to hope that my wife who watched from time to time doesn't ask what's going on, because i could not explain. Maybe it runs deep somewhere in the shadows but casual intrest doesn't hold.
Gameplay is solid. Movement feels smooth and there are plenty of options for progress. Doors, wents, roofs or through the middle after taking out the lights are all possible, usually within the same room. Garret can climb on places that are marked so clearly that they are hard to miss but not much elsewhere. Also rope arrows only stick to certain types of wooden poles, but not all wooden surfaces. That makes the game a rather guided experience, but that is common in todays games.

Enemy AI is dumb as is customary in these games. New addition are caged animals that react to movemet. Other than those there are only four diffrent enemy types which gets repetitive at later part of the game. Fortunately there are a lot of combinations of lights, enemy placements, animals and floor types to keep player on his toes.
Sound design is schitsofrenic. Often you hear people talk and it sounds like they are inside your head but looking around you only see  someone a few rooms over. Other times someone standing on the other side of a table sounds like someone on the street. Enemy dialog repeats so much that it's comical. Everyone wants either a drink or a coffee or they are worried about getting sick. Voice actors change, lines do not. There are rooms that are engulfed in flames but you can hear the fire only on one side of the room and silence on the other. Enemies can hear you but they can't haer the sound of a huge wooden gate opening which to the player sounds just like a rusty old gate should - loud.
Graphics are extremely good. The world is so rich with details that you really want to see what is behind the next corner and climb on roofs just to see the view. Light and shadow play on walls and on objects so nicely that it's a shame to put out a candle. Suprisingly the game runs well even with settings on max and there is a plenty of options for customisation.
Difficulty is also handled well. Regular options from easy to hard are avaible but those can be tweaked further for extreme challenge. And i do mean extreme, if every option is used. First playthrough at Master-Custom difficulty that didn't allow any kills (not even bosses) or alerts took about 20 hours. Some side quests and a load of collectables were left untouched so perfectionist can expect more.
I liked it and hope to see more in the future.

I don’t know the first thing about being a mercenary, but it must be pretty hard. You essentially live a kill-or-be-killed lifestyle, always pointing your gun at someone while making sure that no one pointing one at you. Your personality, your hopes, your dreams, and anything of the sort are all but meaningless; as a mercenary the only thing that truly matters is your usefulness as a hired gun, and when that skill set finally becomes unusable for some reason or another, you’re essentially as good as dead. Perhaps worst of all is the fact that, as a mercenary, you’re essentially just a glorified tool. No one really cares about you when you’re alive, and they certainly care even less (if that’s even possible) when you’re dead. Being a mercenary sounds pretty dreadful, and I’m sure most people wouldn’t wish that lifestyle on anyone. There is, however, one place where being a mercenary is acceptable and, if I may say so, even pretty darn cool; the video game world. And, wouldn’t you know it, that’s what 8DAYS is all about!
The story behind 8DAYS is pretty short and sweet. As a member G.O.D. (Gold, Oil, and Diamonds), an elite organization of “peacekeepers”, your job is to use “diplomacy” to “peacefully resolve” problems for your clients… at least, that’s what the media will have people thinking. In all reality, G.O.D. is nothing more than a high-status band of mercenaries, selling their skills to the highest bidder and killing anyone needed in order to make a profit. Though quite a skilled and knowledgeable G.O.D. mercenary yourself, the G.O.D. Chairman one day catches wind that you might be a little too skilled… that you just might know a little too much. And, hey, he can’t have someone like you running around now can he? Things would be a lot easier for him if you were out of the picture. Unfortunately for him, you don’t have any intention of dying or, if you do die, staying dead.
8DAYS is a retro-inspired twin-stick shooter to its very core and mainly focuses on taking down any and all enemies in your path, although it isn’t as mindless as you may think. Many of the areas within the game have stealth-like elements to them, requiring players to plan out their assault as opposed to blindly running into each and every room while firing wildly. Even in the beginning of the game, there are only but a a few areas in which you could get away with that kind of thing. Areas also, more often than not, allows players to play around with hit-and-run tactics. As important as waiting for an enemy to walk into your line of fire is, sometimes you’re going to have to go for them. Of course, being the retro-inspired game that it is, when one enemy in 8DAYS sees you, pretty much every enemy within the entire area will know where you are. If you’re not careful, that can (and most likely will) get you killed. Several times. Fortunately, you can generally use your surroundings to shake enemies off of your trail and take yourself off of “high alert” mode. While it can be a bit difficult here and there to figure out what does and does not exactly work when it comes to employing stealth tactics within 8DAYS, the level layouts are generally fair enough to allow for some sort of out no matter where you are (providing that you’re quick enough).
While stealth segments are relatively commonplace throughout a decent majority of the game the overall tone of 8DAYS changes a bit about 2/3rds of the way through, and the game adopts a style that focuses quite a bit less on hiding and a bit more on getting good at shooting enemies while avoiding being shot. The change itself is a bit unexpected, and occurs after a very strange event that involves a Samurai Ghost (I won’t get any further into that for the sake of spoilers), but it surprisingly doesn’t put a damper on things at all. In fact, as good as the game is in its entirety, I would almost say that the last section of 8DAYS is where the game really shines. Pre-Samurai-Ghost-Event, the game didn’t showcase intense combat a whole lot. Too often I would expect an area to allow for some run ‘n gun gameplay, only to become immediately surrounded by enemies, die, and have to take on a more stealth-based approach. As the game advanced, I found myself wanting more and more to be able to roam around a bit more freely and, for lack of a better term, raise some hell. It kind of felt as though the game developers were saying “oh, okay, I guess you’ve had enough stealth. Here’s what you’re after.” It was a very satisfying change overall.

Short version: imagine if the bloke who made Cave Story got hired to do a Metroidvania remake of Super Castlevania IV. Intriguing, yeah? That's what you're getting here.
Long version: It's a Metroidvania and, genre-wise, tied for second place with Rabi-Ribi under Symphony of the Night in pole position in my opinion. Whereas Rabi-Ribi simply exaggerated everything you love about Metroidvanias (MORE non-linear exploration, MORE hours upon hours upon hours of gameplay, MORE loads of items to find, MORE fantastic music), Momodora does the opposite to equally stunning results. Less is more.
Expect to spend around five hours or so on this one, expect initially punishing platforming (top tip: your healing items get refilled when you save so don't be tight-fisted about using them and don't forget you've got a dodge button) but the atmosphere is unparalleled. Rabi-Ribi is weeaboo heaven/hell, Momodora is much more reserved in that it does a very good job of setting up and maintaining its dark Catholic vibe throughout the whole experience, without ever getting boring. Melancholy permeates every aspect, from the music (no occasionally obnoxious Castlevania bombast for bombast's sake - there's hardly any drums in the soundtrack at all which is simply remarkable in this day and age) to the enemy designs and the gorgeous backgrounds and animation.
Going back to the Rabi-Ribi comparison where that game was stellar in each individual department (design, music, exploration), Momodora seems like a much more cohesive experience, which is very difficult to pull off and for which the designers should be applauded.
In short well worth the tenner spent on this and am looking forward to my second playthrough and trying to beat the bosses without taking any damage for the secret items.

The main stars of the show though are the gameplay and animations (well, the soundtrack too). You can expect tight movement, a simple moveset (which is fine for a 3-5 hour game depending on skill level), and tense boss fights. Plenty of attention was given to the animations. The melee attacks look powerful and can stun most enemies; her movements are accounted for with running, coming to a stop, dodging, idling, and so on; and the enemies were given the same amount of care for their own attacks such as Pardoner Fennel (amazing).
I enjoyed this compact adventure that doesn't waste any time. You'll wring a couple days of high quality fun out of it.

Terrible for this series of reasons:
1. Retro pixel graphics.   But they didn't just leave it at lazy retro pixel graphics, they spent a lot of effort making retro pixel graphics.  This is like demolishing your own house and paying a lot of money for a wrecking crew to come in and demolish it thoroughly for you rather than just taking a sledge hammer to it.  The result, however, is the same... terrible, lazy, retro pixel graphics.
2. Terrible controls.  The game controls are a lot like a terrible console port that never made it to console.  Don't laugh, the controls really are that bad.
3. Fixed resolution.  This is not surprising considering they opted to spend a lot of time, effort, and money on lazy retro pixel graphics that look bad because, well, they're pixel graphics and it's not 1992 anymore.  Regardless, other devs have at least made an effort to scale their terrible pixel graphics so they fit and work well on modern systems.  Not so here.
4. 4:3 aspect ratio.  Developers who design games in 2017 at 4:3 aspect ratio don't deserve access to computers.  Arguably, typewriters are too good for them.  We should question whether they deserve access to pencils.  I'm leaning towards "no".
Overall a huge amount of effort has gone into making a terrible game with a direct and deliberate intention to include as many bad design elements as possible, and equal effort has gone into avoiding, at all costs, making the game look decent and play well on modern PCs.
They want $10 for this pixel nightmare that plays worse than Zelda from the 1990's on a Nintendo emulator.

Pac-Man Museum is a tricky devil to review.  There are some glaring omissions to mention right off the back: lack of customizable controls, lack of graphical settings (including resolution and fullscreen/windowed mode).  At the same time, I got it on sale for $5, so I'm not bitter since I got more than my money's worth in gameplay time.
The games themselves are pretty fun for the most part!  There is a surprising amount of variety, despite the fact that the same structure pops up in almost all of the games.  I found Champsionship Edition to be particularly enjoyable, and I liked revisiting Pac-Man Arrangement (though I think the version on Game Boy Advance from years ago was more polished).
Speaking of polish, some games suffer from horrible control issues.  Delayed response from the keyboard or gamepad make navigating tight corners at high speeds deeply frustrating, let alone trying to time difficult jumps in Pac-Mania (another game I found more polished and response on the GBA).  Regular Pac-Man seems to play just fine, but Super Pac-Man and Pal & Pal are particularly unresponsive.
Finally, some of the requirements to get stickers are outrageous.  If you're the kind of person who will go mental if you cannot 100% a game, I'd advise staying away.
In the end, Pac-Man Museum has some highs and some lows.  The games I was looking forward to playing happen to be the more polished of the bunch, so I'm content with leaving the rest unattended.  For $5, it was a no-brainer, but for the current cost of $20, I would suggest you get your Pac-Man fix elsewhere.

The Gamergater haters are gonna hate this game because reasons. The reality about depression is that many of your options ARE crossed off. That's how debilitating this condition is. If you make different choices, you get different results. I've played this game making different choices and have ended up with completely different endings...you know, just like what happens in real life. Ignore the controversy surrounding the game (which was spawned by an ex-boyfriend's butthurt, BTW) and just try it. You know...because it's free. And also, it's damned good.

This game's purpose was to raise awareness on what depression felt like to those who didn't suffer from it; which it did, but all too well. I personally did not think I was depressed, but after playing this game I had slight hesitations in my head: "Am I actually depressed?"
It delivered it's purpose all too much, with the very detailed information and sound. It felt too real, and really made me think in the character's perspective. At the same time, I was disappointed every time when I couldn't click on the crossed out option, which is obviously the option for those who aren't depressed. It seemed as though although I wanted to take the more cheery option, it was out of my reach and ended up having to take another option which I felt wasn't my first option.
While this game is completely successful in it's purpose, I will not recommend this game even to those who are not depressed just for the fact that it could affect your life negatively, and is not worth any positive points that could be taken from this game.

I think that this game was done very well. Speaking as somebody who has dealt with anxiety and depression, I think that the game embodies what it's really like to have these mental illnesses, and that the feelings this character has are very true to what people who actually have these illnesses feel. Even though the game is extremely sad, I really enjoyed it. I think that it can give people who don't understand mental illnesses a very good idea of what they are like. The game did seem a little boring, but as stated in the introduction, the game was not created to be fun and I think that the goal of this game was to have an accurate portrayal of depression, and it does just that.

This game accomplishes what the goal is supposed to be: highlighting and explaining depression in a realistic way. Thus, it isn't enjoyable or fun in any sense, but it IS interesting. The music choices and visuals offer great atmosphere for the depressing content. Most of all, I like that there are choices listed that someone that isn't depressed would usually make. "Be honest," "Enjoy your night," "get the therapist without prompting," etc. However, for you, being depressed, it is impossible to make those choices. Including them, but making them inaccessible, was an important choice.
I would only recommend playing this game if you understand that not all games are meant to be fun, but can be a social/emotional commentary.

Although the game seems to accomplish what’s it sets out to do to some extent it is all together a very boring game that I don't believe will have a meaningful impact on the people that play this game. It does have a depressing feel to it and your decisions have somewhat of a meaningful impact but in the end there aren't really any consequences for your actions. Sure you can end up losing your girlfriend but even then you have a positive outlook on it. You take away that Alex (girlfriend) will find someone she will be happier with. The decisions made had slight impacts but no real consequences. I went through a second time and attempted to self-sabotage and i was expecting a darker outcome, for instance death of the character, but there was not such outcome. This may be due to the fact that they didn't want this game to be that dark, but depression is that dark. They allow partial reality to the game, not true reality. If they wanted to follow accurately they should have much darker consequences, but also the ability to have lighter outcomes.

To the majority of people, I would not recommend this game. However, to the people who can really understand and relate to the message that this game is trying to get across, I would say it's worth at least playing a few minutes of this game, if only to experience the unique way it portrays depression through the blocked-off options. I definitely feel that this game achieved what it set out to achieve, which is to give people without depression a glimpse into what depression is like, and to give people who have experienced depression a relatable story to play through. Now, whether or not that makes a good game by itself is left open for debate. As a text adventure it feels rather bland and uniteresting, but that is sort of the point it's trying to make. So, while not particularly enjoyable or entertaining to play through, it never set out with the intent to be. It's a game that was created with the intention of bringing to attention a very serious issue, without making any attempt to portray it as any prettier than it is. If that type of game isn't for you, then by all means don't play it.

First you'll cringe at Garrett's new voice. Then you'll wince at the new story. Then you blink, absorbing the visuals and trying to ignore the audio. Then you warm up to the game, starting to appreciate the reboot's new direction. Then you start to enjoy yourself, getting into the meat of the level designs and AI quirks. And then you facepalm, repeatedly, non-stop, forever, as the story erodes every last shred of goodwill, with cheese-bursting cutscenes about ghostly energy and Primals and megalomaniacal siblings unleashing cult members to change the world.
They could have scrapped the hub town, deleted the story, and just made ~10 large intricate sneaking levels, saving production money, and everything would have been fine, even without Garrett's old voice.
As a game, Thief is competent, even beautiful, and its apparent many people worked hard on it. Buy it on sale and get lost for a few weekends.
As a Thief branded game, its a disappointing mess, discarding old characters and methods for misguided AAA marketing ideas and can only be recommended for rubbernecking at the train wreck.
No Hammerites, no Pagans, no taffers. But plenty of expletive-laden spit-shined shlock.

The story of Hammerwatch truly is a modern masterpiece in storytelling. As the campaign begins, the line "The small bridge broke behind you...there is probably no way out!" is displayed.
And that's it. That's the plot.
Hammerwatch isn't the type of game that really needs a plot, however. The fact that the bridge broke and there is probably no way out is actually a decent introduction to the game as a whole: a light-hearted, if not a bit shallow, romp. In addition to the campaign, there is also a wave-based defense mode and the inclusion of a level editor for creating custom levels.
Doing its best to harken back to classic Gauntlet, Hammerwatch is a cooperative hack-and-slash action game. There are four classes to choose from: Paladin, Warlock, Ranger, and Wizard. Each class starts with a regular attack as well as a special attack that drains a certain amount of magic points. More special attacks are eventually unlocked, though it takes a bit too long to actually earn them. In my experience, nothing comes close to the effectiveness of a Ranger since their default attack pierces through enemies -- continuing its trajectory to harm even more enemies -- and their bomb special attack is perfect for kiting and killing large groups of enemies at a time.
It's also possible to strafe while moving, which is perhaps the most important thing to take away from this review if you buy Hammerwatch, as it’s not immediately apparent within the game. Mastering the strafe-and-attack is crucial for any class' survivability, since moving diagonally while attacking is so freaking useful.
There are a handful of secrets, puzzles, and obstacles that don't necessarily require fighting at all. Hidden rooms permeate each floor, and if the player keeps an eye out they should be able to find just about all of them. Puzzles are never too difficult, and in fact sometimes they are insultingly easy. These variants do a good job of breaking up the monotonous wave-clearing gameplay that makes up most of Hammerwatch.
Playing alone feels hollow, since a large part of the difficulty comes in the form of more and more of the same types of enemies being thrown at the player -- a challenge that's far easier to enjoy when in the company of friends. Single-player reveals the game's shallow mechanics; movement and two attacks don't really make for the most compelling gameplay.
Progression comes from a variety of vendors throughout the levels. Early on it is a very linear progression since only certain vendors are available. The first upgrade is the ability to combo, which allows players who kill at least 10 enemies in a row very quickly to gain a temporary boost to their stats. Later upgrades will build off of this, making it easier to combo and giving better benefits for comboing. By the end of the second act, players will finally have access to more special moves as well as having a little more open-endedness to their character's build.
The problem is that the end of the second act is a decent chunk of game away -- especially for players going it alone. While the level design is very open-ended and non-linear, the character progression is the exact opposite and takes way too long to become interesting. It can feel like forever when slogging through the seemingly endless waves of enemies with the basic attacks, waiting for something cool or interesting to happen.
At the gnarled and gore-encrusted heart of Hammerwatch is a combo system of pleasing simplicity. To trigger it, you must kill a bunch of enemies very quickly, and then once it's in motion, you can upgrade it in a number of straightforward ways - to deal 360-degree damage, say, or to heal. You can build it, too, by killing more enemies. It's action game design at its most basic, and it works.
In order to feed the combos, Hammerwatch needs to ensure that you have plenty of enemies to massacre at all times - and this is a favour it's very happy to grant. Grubs, skeletons, wandering eyeballs: these standard fantasy baddies wait for you in packs around every corner, spawning from pits or rotten tree trunks or mysterious fountains. Along with a standard attack, each character has a special that can generally be counted on to do a lot of damage at once, and so, as you move from combo to combo, a pleasant rhythm settles in. Throw yourself into the fray to power yourself up. Get into trouble so you can get out of trouble again.
1
The early levels drag on for a bit too long, and enemy variety is weak throughout. The thrill comes from the sheer numbers.
Around this central relationship is a game of equal simplicity, a straight-up dungeon-crawl in the spirit of Gauntlet. There's a handful of familiar character classes (the paladin's a melee tank with a deadly dash, for example, while the wizard's low on health but just look at the flames he can conjure); there's the lightest trace of a backstory (the bridge has collapsed behind you, so why not keep going, eh?); and the bulk of the game consists of working your way up through a series of stacked dungeons, eviscerating baddies, standing on rune-splattered pressure plates to unlock secret areas or open the path to the boss, grabbing all the gold you can find, and then using your spoils to make you incrementally better at eviscerating baddies.
Like Gauntlet, the whole thing's designed around multiplayer, of course, and you should know in advance that if you're soloing Hammerwatch, it's a bit of a slog. Levels are longer than you might expect and the odds are stacked heavily against you from the off. The perks you buy at vendors scattered about the maps take a little too long to get entertaining, and the bosses present roadblocks that will eat through your remaining lives with astonishing speed. On top of that, Hammerwatch goes against the current trend of procedural generation, so you're going to trudge across identical early levels over and over as you get better.
2
Bonus levels make the homage even clearer. Gauntlet forever!
With friends, of course, none of this matters: you bundle around the corridors and arenas in a bait-ball of chaos, letting rip with melee, ranged and specials at anything that presents itself. You'll stop only to glug a potion or to check the map, and in the midst of the carnage, you'll start to realise that Hammerwatch's simple pieces are surprisingly effective at generating moments of proper panic.
This is the kiting-est game ever made, for example. Most enemy behaviour is tailored to give chase, so foes quickly form huge pursuing crowds - and this might explain why the best levels on offer turn out to be mazes. Dead ends and blind corners present glorious risks when you can't shoot backwards over your shoulder, and they tend to bring out the best in you as a result - they transform you into the frantic, cornered hero, determined to blast a way out of trouble no matter what. At times, Hammerwatch almost feels like a racing game (at least it does if you're using a pad rather than the surprisingly wretched keyboard controls) as you steer through wandering fiends at speed, gathering a pack of nasties in your wake.
Beyond all that? There are wave-based and survival modes and a rather daunting editor, and there's the delightfully grubby pixel art to take in throughout, which offers just the same kind of mead-splattered ambience as the game that so obviously inspired it. There's precious little depth lurking in Hammerwatch, then, but if you've got a few friends handy or are willing to wait around online for the worryingly small community to make itself known, this is genuine old-fashioned skeleton-bashing with a gloriously tidal approach to chucking in the enemies.

Momodora: Reverie Under The Moonlight is a criminally underrated game. I love it.
You play as Kaho, a priestess from the kingdom of Lun on a mission to eradicate a plague that has spread to her home.
This is a 2D pixel graphic metroidvania game akin to cavestory. Many people have drawn similarities to the dark souls series because of its use of refillable health items and spells after resting at a waypoint as well as its dark themes. However, I feel like this game is its own unique entity that deserves its own spot apart from any other games it may borrow elements from because of how well it implements them.
The game's art style is superb. The game is worth the price in that regard alone. You can tell a lot of work was put into making the game an artistic beauty.  The animations are crisp and fluid. You really feel the weight of each attack which works well with the game's great sound design.
Your only weapons are a bow and a leaf. You feel so tiny in such a hostile world but you triumph through each battle. I highly recommend playing on hard in order to better get a sense of how the game is meant to be played. Over time you accumulate upgrades and items that make each battle easier. You become very strong by the end of the game. If you happen to play NG+, it is possible to beat every boss within seconds if you are skilled enough to pull it off. However, in your blind playthrough, you will die a lot - and you will learn the game more and more.
There are some points that the game falls short on. The story leaves much to be desired as not a whole lot is explained or discussed at all. Your interactions with friendly NPCs are rather limited in that you don't really form a personal connection with them at all. They feel very static as characters.
Another thing is that the map isn't so well designed. The map has a solid edge for a room that leads to a dead end, and a small dash for rooms that lead to more rooms - except those dashes blend in and are hard to see. It's a real eye-strain to analyze the map so closely to see where you need to explore. You may become lost often.
Other than those gripes, the game is very solid and the gameplay is a lot of fun. There are many collectibles and secrets to be found. Once you beat the game, there are a lot of items you still haven't found. It leads to replayability in order to get those items and see what you can do differently.
I highly recommend this game. I would give it an 8/10.

A skateboarding game where you see only your skateboard move, and must collect aesthetic cups to achieve enlightenment, is one of the finest examples of what vaporwave and aesthetics are. However, the skateboard is incredibly hard to control, and the camera jerks around a lot due to being able to essentially skate on any surface. And anyways, what is there to really complain about when you have vaporwave playing in the background as you ride a floppy disk ramp to get into a drawing from MS Paint.
10/10.

Okay. You know how you review the game you just played, explain what made it great, how you enjoyed it, etc...
What if I reviewed the developer instead.
There is something, at least to me, more than just this game. It seems silly, but there is an underlying innocence and, honestly for me, jealousy on my end.
Indie Developer, Game Dabbler, Composer, Teenager.
His first game had more structure than this, and was in fact more interesting.
THIS game was for sure an interesting experience, and it was very funny actually.
But I think the story is broader. Steven is an early developer, but the passion and the uniqueness just seeps through his work, its like he's famous yet completely unknown. To be frank, you should be expecting more from him and expecting a journey. This journey is games made by a guy who tries to be himself by expressing himself and finding himself through what seem to be amateur unity games... and yet it is so clear.
I don't even care about the games anymore. This man fascinates me. He intrigues me.
Its almost if a version of myself went off and decided to TRY. That version left my other half, who writes reviews about a reflection in the mirror that I wish I could be. These games invoke a self-journey through someone elses journey.
And since I assume Steven will be reading this, this is a direct message to you:
Don't stop evolving. If someone, anyone, is applauding you, you need to make them throw ♥♥♥♥ing ROSES at you the next time. You are young. You are ambitious. This is the start of something amazing and you know it.
Don't take this opportunity for granted.
I will follow your work. You don't have to care that I care but I will be there at your award ceremony when the world cheers your name and your portfolio is thick, and your changes are made. This is no longer for fun, this is for your humanity. This for others humanities. You have so much power now. You are doing great things. Now slam dunk some more content onto my platter.
Thank you.

This game feels inaccurate in its portrayal of depression. None of the friends save for Amanda seem to be helpful individuals. I would hope that if I had the behavior of our protagonist, someone would try and talk to me or do something. Depression is a legitimate struggle to get out of, but this game makes it feel like a game. By trying to simulate someone’s very personal experience, you make someone with a legitimate medical issue seem whiney. You can’t really relate to the protagonist if you haven’t had depression, and from people who have had depression, it would seem inaccurate. My brother has Bipolar disorder, and has intense periods of depression. He acts completely different from the protagonist in these periods. No one supports the protagonist unlike the girlfriends and family of the real world. While some people don’t get the support they need, I feel someone would at least notice early on. If you wanted to make an impact, make the game from the point of view of someone only slightly depressed, and have game options that can make it better or worse. Starting from the bottom makes it hard for the “typical” person to get into the mindset of the depressed individual.
Aside from the faults in its portrayal of depression, the game feels boring. The red crossed out text is just frustrating in the early game where they are not even a conceivable option. They would be better off when they are something a player could access. The static-text is aesthetically unpleasing as it stands out from the rest of the games aesthetic. The photos on the top often feel like its going for an artsy feel, but overall they feel pointless. This game feels like it’s trying to be artsy, being important. It wants to be profound and interesting, but it comes across is trying too hard to be sad and not capturing what it set out to do. The game only got the attention it had due to scandal, and it shows. The gameplay is boring and the commentary is weak. I would not recommend the game to anyone who wants to understand depression. You are better off with an old textbook or internet entries. The only saving grace is that this game was free, so at least I didn’t lose anything other than a few minutes of time.

As a lifetime Pacman fanatic of 30+ years, I'm disappointed with Pac-Man Museum. My issue is not with the games themselves, but the fact I played them several decades ago and they were basically better on all fronts compared to this version's collection.
First, the good part. This 'museum' contains a lot of the really obscure Pacman titles that were hard to find in the arcades and laundromats back in the 80's. It's a trip down nostalgia lane in that sense. And for those who haven't played those games, you may find it interesting to see what strange variations the Pacman franchise took over the years.
With that out of the way, there's not much this title gets right, performance-wise. The resolution on most of the games is not full screen, but a squashed blurry window that you can't adjust. Why couldn't they update that for computers if they're going to sell these games on a new platform? The controls also kind of, well, suck. I wouldn't say this had I not actually played these games on a native arcade cabinet, but these things are not optimized well for keyboards. Pacman is a game of fast responses. If the game refuses to acknowledge inputs at random times, what's the point even? I noticed this kept happening, regardless of which Pacman title I played. That's flat out unacceptable. If I knew these problems existed and that they had no interest in fixing them, I never would have bought this; on sale or otherwise.
There are also achievements to be had- these translate into the museum section animations, which really are just there to promote Pacman's current cartoon with the characters from the show. That's fine, I guess, but these don't talk about the history of Pacman in any sense of the word and if you don't watch the show, they're largely meaningless repeating animations. The included texts from clicking on them doesn't even say much. So, how is this a museum or an effective advertising piece for the cartoon?
This is simply a lazy quick cash grab title with a small bit of appeal for the obscure games crudely transferred to the PC format. Worse off, Ms Pacman is NOT INCLUDED. You have to pay $5 more for that one title. Wtf?? This game will also remind you EVERY SINGLE TIME that the DLC is available for purchase when you log in to play. Watch how fast that gets old. There's not even steam cards or any visible sign they're paying attention to the forums. That's unacceptable for a large company like Namco. As a Pacman fan, I recommend you stay away unless you've got some change burning a hole in your pocket. And even then, get yourself a sandwich. You'll enjoy it more.

Pros:
It's free. People like free♥♥♥♥♥♥
A good learning game. If you're new to MTG and are looking to play online, use this. The training teaches you keywords and how they work. If you want to move beyond this use Cockatrice.
Easy to understand interface. The game will show you what cards you can play and suggestions on what to play next (not always the best option though, sometimes it's a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). Cards are large and they let you zoom in on them for further explanation.
________________________________________________________________________________
Cons:
The fact that there's a pay to play option. It gives it that feeling of Standard for the IRL card game: the more money you put into it, the better you'll do. Not necessarily the case for this game, as there's been people with fully decked out card sleeves, lands, foils, and they've lost to the nonsense I put together. If you've put as much time into this game as I have, you can get all the good♥♥♥♥♥♥anyway without spending any money.
The AI has no middle ground. I've racked up my 500 solo wins achievement from playing against hard AIs, so I've seen what they can do. Sometimes you'll just rofl-stomp them to oblivion cause your deck worked perfectly or the mulligan'd to 5 or were stuck on 2-3 land. Other times they have answers for LITERALLY ♥♥♥♥ING EVERYTHING ALL THE TIME. This was most relevant when Battle for Zendikar was added and the AI had that weird thing were all the hard decks were identical W/U/X variants. Difficult is supposed to affect how many rares/mythics the AI has but I've played an easy AI back in Origins-only that had 3 of the flipwalkers.
I don't care much for the 4-3-2-1 system for how much of a rarity you can have, but I supposed that would make completing sets take even longer. Also all the sets have missing cards (on purpose), but then you're missing out on some great stuff. Starfield of Nyx from Origins was an enchantment that turns your other enchantments into creatures and lets you reanimate one on your upkeep: not in the set. On that same note, there are some cards that are in the game that shouldn't be. Sphinx's Tutelage: no one likes being the receiving end of this. Mill is a very boring and uninteractive match-up. You just sit there and durdle will your deck gets milled and your creatures get sniped.
The fact that you can foil cards. Despite the fact that I do this every time I get a new rare/mythic, it just seems weird. Here's a shiny version of a theoretical card.
________________________________________________________________________________
There are some other small bugs that don't affect gameplay much, and some incorrect card interactions (Saheeli Rai's ultimate doesn't let you pick what artifacts you want, it just gives you 3 random ones), but still a good game. Yes, I list more cons than pros, but I've got 400+ hours into this♥♥♥♥♥♥so I can see continuous problems.

Is this game grindy? Yes. But magic is one of those games that works well even when it's grindy (if you've ever enjoyed playing control for example).
I do wish the packs were worth less coins (maybe 100 by default, so that it feels a little less grindy) but overall, the game's fun, the meta is interesting with a diverse range of decks, and the special rules on card-counts create a cool format where you can brew just about anything.
And it's free, so what is there to complain about anyway :D

The game gives you the option to buy coins with real money which in turn you use to purchase packs, and other aesthetic upgrades to your deck. However it also allows you to grind for these coins by defeating human opponents, and short stories for each of the sets from Origins upwards. It also allows you to play for coins against AI opponents in varying difficulty for much less than against the aforementioned randomly matched human.
I absolutely would not recommend this game to the Magic beginner as it requires you to build a deck of your own with a very limited and weak pool of cards. Even as a veteran of the game I found it extremely difficult at first to gather enough cards to make successful combos to win against human opponents. Which even then takes much time to gather enough coins in order to purchase a pack of only 6 cards (exculdes basic lands and duplicates above: 4 Common, 3 Uncommon, 2 Rare, 1 Mythic Rare). If you play for 2 hours a day you might get enough coins for 2 packs using decent decks. Also it must be mentioned that not every card in an existing set of the game is available to play with.
For beginners I would highly recommend the previous "Duels" iterations.
For people long familiar with the tabletop game or MTGO I recommend it as a fun way of familiarizing yourself with new sets, mechanics. And a good way of staying in touch with the game without having to spend money, or having an MTG community nearby to play with. The challenge and competitiveness of the game and its community also adds a lot of fun.

I've been with Atu'los on/off for 10 years. The review I can give is mainly based on my own opinion on the game.
Pros:
It's low end based: I started this game on a Windows 2000 in 2006. It still holds a low end based ability to this day.
It's a small download: 40MB's isn't nothing now, but back in 2006; Downloading took forever on dialup/DSL.
Because of these two above pros, the graphics are pretty damn good for it.
Small friendly community, everyone knows everyone. Everyone does their best to help those needing help.
The server has a 99.9% upkeep, even when updating.
It's free to play, simple to play, and can burn hours playing and chatting.
Mixes Single Player and Multiplayer aspects. I personally love the fact that I have my own monsters to fight, while I love to fight other players any given time of the day. It makes leveling up more of a motivation, other than just doing it for nothing. Levels in Atu'los feel more like someones reputation or status. People say "Well Done" or "Congrats", when they see you level. It's a good feeling to know that your levels actually get peoples attention, instead of the hideous popup in most MMO's. "LEVEL UP" and nobody cares.
Cons:
Lack of updates, this is the primary concern and I understand why the lack of updates, because there's only 1 developer trying to run it all while still holding onto a job to pay bills, which is very hard.
Can get boring, repeatitive grinding to level/gold up.
Not rewarding enough, it just feels that when you progress in the story. It just doesn't have any feeling of rewards, not really any loot items, and ALL of our weapons/armor are sold at shops, there's no drops. No special items for obtaining a certain level or defeating a certain boss, our only reward is gold.
The gold is not balanced since the level changes. I've passed Chamber 1 without even needing the Arena Pit armory. (Arena Pit was actually way before the Halls boss, but it's a weapon to get after the Halls equipment.). In the game though, we're short of gold on getting the Halls equipment, but we would be level 25, already able to beat the Halls Boss. So yes, the gold output does not balance with the new level update.
TL;DR. I recommend this game for the Pros, because the Cons can always be fixed.

Momodora: RutM is a game I can gladly recommend. Compared to the last installment "Momodora III" a lot of improvements have been added which make the sequel look and feel far superior.
Beforehand, my verdict for most categories are subjective of course except for
and
where I try to be as objective as possible. If you don't agree in the least, that's too bad.
-----------------------------------
Story: 6/10

From what I can tell the premise of the game sounds promising enough to deliver, although it doesn't sound special in the least.
Sound: 6.5/10
More times good than bad although somewhat boring to listen. The songs give you the feeling of a desperate situation and lonely protagonist which is a plus in combination with that story. I'd recommend the tracks
and my personal favorite
.
Graphics: 7/10
It certainly is no "Owlboy" and it doesn't look as cool as a "Hyper Light Drifter" but it's nonetheless some really fine pixel work. And definitely way more refined than the prequel Momodora III.
Presentation: 5.5/10
The presentation of "Momodora: RutM" felt rather unsatisfactory and might be the weakest point of the game. While the core story gave enough ammunition to shell out some fine world building, the complete work just can't deliver. The characters felt too one dimensional to care for them and in the end the only one I can remember is the man who was looking for his (dead) wife. Same goes for the (true) ending which seemed...okayish. When you want to give some props in that category, then for the castle complex. Be it the sunken corridor, the torture chamber, etc...now THAT really fit the mood
Gameplay: 7.5/10
The gameplay in comparison to Momodora III stayed more or less the same although you can't spam the attack button anymore...which is good. At heart it's a well refined action adventure game with a Metroid-like world you can explore. The combat controls feel tight, the difficulty is super fair and the passages are for the most part tricky when playing the game for the first time.
A let-down is the small weapon arsenal and the rather scarce secrets you can find ingame. But only presumed you compare it with other Metroidvanias. Otherwise it's fine.
Replayability: NORMAL
You might not find everything on your first run.
You need more than one playthrough to get all achievements.
Otherwise there's not much going for the replayability.
---------------------------------
One last tip for beginners and achievement hunters:
Considering you start the journey on "Normal mode", prepare to die . And I mean a lot. Which does not necessarily mean the game is hard, the learning curve is actually really fast after you learn the enemies patterns. Same goes for boss fights which have always a save point right before the battle. Give it some time and you can breeze through the hardest difficulty. Just don't start on easy mode, you can spam-kill all bosses with the amount of health you have and it simply destroys the whole experience.
Additionally save yourself some time and start the game on hard mode if you're in for achievements because you need a finished hard mode-run to unlock the hardest difficulty.

"Delightfully charming" is how I remember Roundabout. The game can be divided into two parts: the gameplay and the full-motion video.
The gimmick of this game is that you are a limousine driver who is constantly rotating. Thankfully, in the town of Roundabout, all roads, cars, and other obstacles are laid out just perfectly for you to snake around to get people to their destinations. The game is as casual or as serious as you want it to be. There are lofty objectives and super-pro highscore boards, but if you explode in a fiery wreck, you'll start back up nearby in a jiffy. Additional mechanics and challenge are layered on slowly, and getting through the game I feel is pretty attainable.
The characters and video are the real delight of this game, though. Taking place in the 1970s, various employees of the developer's company don silly costumes and deliver so-bad-it's-good lines of dialog. Of note is that the player plays Georgio Manos, a silent protagonist whose primary role in the game is turning (with slight variation) from the steering wheel to see who hopped in her car. Yet she is still very compelling!
Hammy? Yep.
Self-aware? Oh yeah.
Hilarious? Georgio gets caught up in dark alleyway billionaire deals, a fierce rotating limo rivalry, budding love, and drug addiction, among many other weird scenarios. That's a yes.
If you're up for a laugh in the B-movie style, I highly recommend Roundabout.

Depression Quest is absolute gobshite. Honestly, as a person who has struggled with depression in the past, I wasn’t expecting much, but this train wreck went far and beyond my expectations. From the outset, it’s obvious the maker has never struggled with depression. The player character has the perfect friends, family and girlfriend. Additionally, the ways in which  this guy gets over his depression are the most by-the-book I’ve ever seen. Get a cat, go to therapy, take medication, talk to someone. Rinse, repeat, rinse, repeat. There were absolutely no creative liberties taken with the story at all. Quinn’s writing was also little more than a dreck slog. There were walls of mind-numbing blather you had to crawl through to get to the next boring text tree, with 4 blocked-off options because you were TOO DEPRESSED. There wasn’t really much to the gameplay, either. You got to select randomly from a bunch of random text lines, and it was outstandingly obvious which ones you were supposed to take. The sole points where the game chucks you a fastball is when Boring McCaricature is moping about a party, and if you choose wrong between going into your girlfriend’s room and nursing a Bud Lite, the game shoves a massive branding iron down your throat, shakes you about and screams “THIS IS DEPRESSION” as loud as it can. After that single incident, after which your girlfriend may or may not get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you for asking if she preferred Friends or Parks & Rec, which sends the player into a spiral of depression so awful they can barely drive themselves to get out of bed in the morning. I am being completely serious. In other cases, the game seems to get Difficulty Whiplash. There are random points at which entire paths are blocked off because your guy is too glum to sit at a desk for a few hours. At other points, the obviously correct answers are right there, displaying none of the difficulty of telling someone about your depression or going to therapy. You just click a button and WHAM, everything’s shiny, cap’n, not to fret.
One of the most common arguments I hear for the validity of the game is that “It’s not supposed to be fun! It’s supposed to send a message!” Yes, but there have been tons of other games that have not been meant to be fun. Thomas Was Alone and the Beginner’s Guide both come to mind. Then what’s the difference between the two games? Both Thomas Was Alone and the Beginner’s Guide were engaging. They had interesting, human characters that players came to care about. Depression Quest had none of that. It was a boring, detached recounting of how depression survivors wish things had gone starring the flattest, least sympathetic characters ever created. Don’t waste your time on this ♥♥♥♥♥how. Go do something more interesting, like licking a horse’s stomach or staring at a wall.
