I just got back from work and, having barely kicked off my shoes, I went to play another round of Mini Metro. Then I noticed I have clocked over 100 hours in the two weeks that I have had this game. It is sucking my soul the way a game hasn't done since I was too young to have anything better to do than play games anyways. Now, admittedly, a portion of those hours are from me passing out with the game open, contemplating the overall efficiency of my entire subway system having been thrown a curve-ball station or two. But the difference between 100 hours total and 80 hours conscious is really not that significant, relative to overwhelming number of 0.6hrs-played games in my library. I don't normally write reviews, but I know there are casual gamers out there with similar disappointments, so this review is for you.

tl:dr : Casual, strategic gamers that like to watch their decisions unfold in as perfect a manner as they can conclude, get this game! Even (especially) in Early Access!
Review:
I forgot this game was Early Access until I came to this page to write the review, and that's a good thing! Most of us have been victimized by vaporware, and I understand your hesitation to trust it (or really anything on steam anymore), such that our reviews are the only information worth sifting through anymore.
Mini Metro is a minimalist game both visually and in its core mechanics. That being said, it does both of these things so well and uniquely, even and its current state, that it seems more polished than a large portion of the released titles that just keep pumping out. And, although I yearn for more maps (when are we ever truly satisfied), the game feels complete enough that if it went full release today, I would clock another 100 hourse easily. The only thing it's missing is sound, but that's on the list to be added and ultimately the silence doesn't really detract from the game, playing my own moodscapes in the background. I'm sure there's more content that they plan to add, but I haven't been following the devs enough to tell you what those are. And honestly, bilissfully ignorant of their promises, I can tell that any new content is just going to be a wonderful surprise as the game progresses out of Early Access, such as the newly added Rush Hour Mode (more on that later). Also what I can't tell you is how fast the game is being updated. I got this game only recently, and in that time they updated with the addition of a whole new mode, but I may have just lucked out on my timing - look to other reviews or follow the devs for this info.
At its heart, Mini Metro is a game where you create a subway (or metro depending on your colloquialism) system that is as efficient as possible at delivering passengers between stations.
I had gotten 1/4 the way into my original review, which was on the way to being pretty fleshed out I thought, but then I learned there is a charlimit when writing reviews. So, it's sorta lost it's cohesion but I hope I got most of my love for this game out.
Stations are also abstract and minmalistic, being represented by bordered geometric shapes. All maps start you with a Circle, Square, and Triangle station, and represent the most common stations you'll see. Having no depth of explanation, it's difficult to call those stations by anything other than their shapes, only learning to conceptualize the different types as things like transfers and major stations once you learn how the stations need to be connected to be efficient later in the game. That being said, you often have to use stations as a matter of efficiency that betrays your concepts of them. This is one of the things I find special about Mini Metro. You can know the rules in and out, but your understanding of their roles changes with every new station that pops up, creating a logic of efficiency that is more conscious and fulfilling than simply figuring out the math.
There is no right or wrong decision (except for Rush Hour mode) as everything you've done on the map so far can be freely and meticulously readjusted instantaneously. The few resources the game limits you with like the number of trains and bridges, when not in use, are returned to your pool of resources with zero loss; you can only get more, and will need more. Even lategame when you're struggling to keep 20-30 stations efficient as a whole, a few clicks and you can wipe the board of your entire subway for a fresh start, but without a restart back to silly ol' 3 stations. Casual, no need to dredge through a game you just played a second time to get to a point where you can use what you learned the first time, you can just continually build on your knowledge.
It's actually those lategame board clears that, personally, are the most fun for me. As you progress on a map, you'll get extra trains. I only ever use one train on a line. This is extremely limiting, but I enjoy the challenge of the game that way, because without a second train to pick up the slack, lines have to be more efficient at interacting with eachother, dropping off passengers in perfect spots, running cross-track or parallel to alleviate congestion, balancing short but heavily loaded lines with long but easily resolved ones. And a board clear of infrastructure allows me to consider an efficient system as a whole instead of one in relation to what I had built already. This is normally where I pass out staring at my screen.
Game Modes, since I'm not sure I've seen a review for since Rush Hour came out:
The game has three modes currently, Commuter (skirmish), Scenic (peaceful), and  new Rush Hour (permabuild).
The difference between Commuter mode and Scenic mode is mosty just that if you aren't being efficient enough on a Commuter map, your passengers pile up and get mad that they're stting in a station too long, you'll fail.
Rush Hour is the bane of my existence. Most of what I have described is in the two modes where you can readjust your lines and resources. In Rush Hour mode, once you connect two stations, you can't unconnect them. You can extend their lines to new stations, but then you're stuck with that order of stations. Trains move down the line from one station to another, and then turn around and do the opposite order (unless you loop them). Because of this, in any game mode, adding a new station to the line affects its overall efficiency by first simply making the people at one end of the line wait longer for the train to get back, secondly because if passengers aren't getting dropped off efficiently, your train gets full and he passes by stations of people already waiting. Even extra trains, when placed, can't be picked back up. The only saving grace to this mode is that while in the other modes, stations just simply appear and you have to deal with them accordingly. In Rush Hour mode, you get to see where and what type the next station will be. I have not spent more than a few minutes in this mode as it requires a completely different mindset than the way I play the other two modes.
For $7 at regularly priced Early Access, probably the most appropriately priced item I've bought on Steam.

Pretty decent Metroidvania style game. If you like that kind of game, it can be a fun way to spend a Sunday.
That said, a lot of the usual things you expect from a Metroidvania is average at best.
Exploration is more up to blindly checking every nook and cranny, as you would expect, but there are only very few of these, and the rewards are mostly just the games currency, which isn't really useful. You also only get a very small amount of "exploration" powers, so the already small amount of areas you originally couldn't explore, isn't getting that much larger.
The monsters are fairly small in variety, and are either of the super easy variant, or the frustrating kind. The overall difficulty is pretty small, as soon as you get your bow a few upgrades, and you basically get the ability to one-shot practically everything in the game.
The bosses are great, however - There are some really good concepts, and most of them are fun and challenging, and well designed. You might feel slightly frustrated at a few certain bosses, but it is never due to broken mechanics or bugs. This is by far the strongest aspect of the game, and does this exceedingly well, even by Metroidvania standards.
The game lacks a proper story, and what it has, it mostly left vague and "up to you", except for the extremely anti-climatic ending, which not only happens extremely abrutly, but also with no real warning. It ends with a very arbitrary "cutscene" ending, with a small dialogue box with 3 lines that barely gives any real idea of what happened, or why. The ending was incredibly unsatisfying, and made the game feel incomplete.
If you care at all about a satisfying story and ending, this game is not for you.

The fourth installment (yet my introduction to the series), Momodora is what is commonly referred to as a "Metroidvania". If you're not familiar with the term, there are a few things the game should feature to be a metroidvania:
Technically another requirement might be that it's 2/2.5d, but there are lots of 3d games that fit the bill (Dark Souls, Metroid Prime) and I wouldn't want developers to limit themselves so strictly to a formula.
Anyway in these regards, Momodora certainly fits the bill and yet I have a feeling fans of the genre would be disappointed with that assessment.
Momodora is a great entry into the genre but it's short. 5-6 hours and you'll have beat the game. Also the attack variation from bosses and how long the 'wind up' is on some of the more difficult foes means combat isn't nearly as hard as in other games of the genre.
But that's a great thing for new players. It's not "baby's first action/adventure" but it's also great training if you wanted to approach some of the more famous games in the genre like Hollow Knight but found the high difficulty to be intimidating.
Beautiful. Animations are stylish and fluid, the various biome regions are detailed and enemies are interesting looking. Sound is great, although the music leaves something to be desired and the story is solid but barebones. The NPCs are memorable, which helps the thin story, but with only a few hours of gameplay there's not that much time to fall in love with the world building.
Graphics options for those who like playing with such things are limited. In this game I don't feel it's a drawback but if you're the sort that MUST play in 4k @ 144hz, you're probably out of luck.
If you're interested in games like Hollow Knight, Castlevania or Metroid but you're intimidated by the difficulty of those games you should play Momodora. If you're looking for a short yet satisfying game, you should play Momodora.
If you're looking for the 'next' Metroidvania fix because you can only play Symphony of the Night so many times or if you're looking for a cutting edge game that will make your hardware bleed, you probably can skip Momodora.

A game hasn't bored me this quickly in a long time. Despite my personal misgivings about the various videos I've seen of this game, I thought I'd give it a try due to the amount of positive reviews it has. I understand this was only made by two people, but to me that isn't a good enough excuse for making such a lazy, uncreative game. Many solo projects have been amazing (Braid, Dust, etc.). The comparisons made to Binding of Isaac and Doom are utterly ridiculous. I haven't played much of Isaac, but it has that undeniable style of Team Meat and a recognisable personality. Doom had incredibly satisfying weapons and varied enemies with cool death animations, as well as a haunting atmosphere (at least for the time). This game has none of that. The guns are♥♥♥♥♥♥poor in terms of 'feel' and lack that punch which can make or break an FPS. Sound design goes a long way in this regard, which this game is also terrible at. The gun sounds are muted and flaccid, and the music goes horribly crackly and distorted at certain times. When enemies die, they all explode in the exact same fashion, regardless of their size, in a shower of stock UDK particle effects and sounds. There is no personality in the game either. The textures are all a horrible poor-man's Borderlandsy style and the 'humour' in the game just falls incredibly flat (HUGBOTS??? LOL LOL THE CAKE IS A LIE). I cannot for the life of me figure out how this got so many positive reviews - perhaps people simply feel the need to support small indie teams? The only other reason I can think of is that the reviewers had been chained in a dark basement for 20 years and this was their first stimulus after emerging.

ZERO configuration options. Volume controls? Nope. Resolution doesn't fit on your laptop screen? TOO BAD. Colorblind? TOO BAD. Want to play a different map? TOO BAD. There's no menu to speak of.
The controls are also buggy. You might have one action selected, and it will deselect randomly. Or not count your clicks randomly.
And it has mistakes in the instructions (what little instructions there even are). "Fleets cost 3 gold" Nope, they cost 4.
AND the poor layout design. The bottom is cut off on laptop screens, so definitely put the DONE bottom there (also on the right hand side, so even on screens where it fits, it is right where the Steam popups are going to cover it).

A short, original video-game-inspired experience. It's free, and your only commitment is time -- an hour or so. I would generally recommend it.
It will give you a view into "depression," but only in an extremely narrow sense. Though the important introduction page explains the premise, it does not do so well enough. It is sure to alienate many people who feel that this story has nothing to do with them or their lives.
Actually, I think this game is valuable exactly because of that.
It's an ethnographic glimpse at the life of an
specific cohort of people: middle-class millennial Americans, most likely white. The issues won't speak to many of us: being invited to college parties, working a 9-to-5 job, trolling Craigslist for new jobs, owning a car, living away from one's parents in one's own apartment, having a girlfriend, watching Netflix, being able to afford and have access to therapy, etc. It's not just an issue of "privilege," as the introduction points out. Some of these culturally specific aspects would actually seem like
, rather than privileges, to many people in the world. Living alone, away from a supportive family? Who would
that? It's amazing that this entire cohort of people doesn't suffer from depression.
But that's where this game seems valuable to me: it's a window into the lives of this strange generation of people, who manifest in their personal, interpersonal, emotional worlds the brunt of capitalist America's crushing isolation.
We all live with capitalism, even if we're not self-centered millennials. We all can sympathize with aspects of the protagonist's life, even when it's unfamiliar (and annoying) to us. It's good to think with.
I do wish the developers put a bit more effort into the presentation: the design is drab, and though the music is fitting, it would have been nice to have some variation. I didn't expect to be entertained, but a sleeker experience could have made this effort more palatable.
A personal message to Zoe Quinn: stay strong and keep doing what you're doing, because even if it's not everybody's cup of tea, it touches many of us and adds something good and useful to the world. "Gamergate" is an embarrassment to any decent human.
Finally, I would like to thank the developers for supporting Linux!
Not about depression and not a game.

I think the most important thing you have to remember is that this game doesn't have "right" or "wrong" answers. This isn't something that you have to try and win, because that's entirely not the point. Some people might hesitate to call this a game, but I think "interactive experience" is a bit less catchy. Nonetheless, it can offer you a bit of insight into depression that simply talking or reading about it won't achieve. Things like being unable to bring yourself to act upon options that seem so obvious or effortless to "regular" people, and how frustrating that is. Being fatigued by repeated interactions with well meaning but oblivious people that offer no solution or resolution. Finding occasional comfort in unexpected places.
For those complaining that this game isn't an accurate representation of depression, I'm not sure if you've actually played it or are able to read, or understand humanity at all, because if you did, you'd have seen on the very first page that it doesn't pretend to represent ALL cases of depression, nor is that even possible since, besides the innumerable different types of mental illnesses out there, everyone with even basic depression experiences it differently, and live with it under unique circumstances. What I got out of it was a familiar retrospection of how my life and experiences had been several years ago, and occasionally (but fortunately rarely) still relapse into every now and then. But it wasn't exactly the same obviously, as I'm not actually dense enough to expect a 30 minute free game to somehow perfectly mirror my whole life experience.
Depression Quest is very honest about merely being an attempt to provide people who know and care about someone who has depression a bit of potential insight into their otherwise private and closed off lives and consider what sort of reactions from loved ones help and what actually makes it worse, despite the best intentions.
If this does not apply to you but you're just curious, it's free!
But for those to whom the events described in the game are familiar, but genuinely struggle to explain what they are going through to loved ones, this could potentially be something valuable.
For me, it illustrated the concept of "I understand what you're going through/went through" so much better than a vague verbal reassurance that, when you're in that situation, often feels ingenuine or meaningless anyways. Just remembering the familiarity of that creeping hopelessness reminds me why the vapid suggestion that people should "just get over it" is so uselessly dismissive, and that dismissiveness comes from the lack of empathy, due to a lack of perspective. If this game can offer people a bit of perspective, that's value.
I'll admit I wasn't overly fond of the music, it was a bit more distracting than probably intended. Here and there were also a few obvious writing mistakes, but other than that, I'd certainly recommend this to people with an attention span.

NOTE: This game is Free To Play, meaning this review and many others do not count. I cannot stress enough that you play it for yourself with an open mind to get an undilluted opinion and ignore this review and any others.
So... I know what Depression is. I've been diagnosed with it for the last 15 years alongside High Anxiety for all that time.
You want to know what Depression is like? Let me tell you instead of you playing this game.
Imagine sadness. Imagine extreme self-disappointment. Imagine self-loathing to as high of a degree as it'll go. It's not always the same, but to my knowledge... Mix them into one emotion and you get Depression.
It is literally the worst emotion on the planet. Mostly all suicides are caused by feelings of Depression. I have no study, no way to prove that, other than just plain logic and understanding.
This game does not convey the feelings of Depression.
It is sad, yes, but Sadness is not Depression. On it's own that is. You need a slew of other different, but similar emotions but also the faint hope that it can get better and mental habits of being pessimistic about your life, you and everything around you.
I've played and read all lines of both endings and choice options. there's multiple choices in most cases, but in most cases the options are locked because the dev most likely didn't program that far in a text-based game. I could also say because of [arbitrary/contrived reason].
Let me be perfectly clear. This game is not depressing, it's not saddening. To me... It's insulting how hyped this game is on the store page.
It's got the pacing of a pop-up book, the writing of an overly-emotional stereotype writing about how awful life is and for a game that boasts "multiple endings" I would have imagined that the developer would've coded in a suicide ending, since I literally did every awful option and nothing really different happened.
The game is as engaging as listenning to someone whine about how awful their life is. I know, it's supposed to convey the feelings of being Depressed, but the thing is... Unless you're a wordsmith (which The Quinnspiracy isn't) then it will never work in text form.
The game would have worked better as a more interactive game that isn't text-based or an auto-biography of part of the dev's life.
While I was playing-no... While I was reading this e-book it felt like I was reading what amounted to angsty, emo fanfiction and not even good fanfiction.
Some options of the game aren't labeled too great, sometimes the result being the opposite of what you thought the option would do (so... control problems in a text-based game?) which basically boils down to those options being improperly labeled.
The soundtrack is... well it's actually just a track, one song looping over and over and not even with a clean loop either, at certain times you'll hear crackling or popping in the audio as it loops.
All in all, this game utterly fails at what it tries to do. Not only that, but it makes Depression laughable, comparable to stupid pre-teens who thinks depression is a cool thing, who we all know are a complete joke, and that's the literal opposite of Depression.
I've seen better pacing in books you can read in any library anywhere, the game wasn't at all uncomfortable for me, it wasn't like an unfiltered mental diary, more like a "pity me, I'm sad right?" type of story written by some spoiled kid who got grounded for the first time.
Just like any poorly-made text-based game, you can look at the first sentence/paragraph, the last one aswell and essentially miss nothing story-wise, ignoring everything inbetween, only with this one, you can look at jsut the last sentence or two and know all you need for the next decision.
The Choice-based content is actually true to a degree, but the multiple endings are comparable to Mass Effect 3's "What color will your ship's explosion be" type of ending, each one summing up all you've done, with ONE sentence of difference ignoring all else (summing up your run doesn't really count) which doesn't matter because this game is extremely far from being long, even if you read it all. I stopped reading all but the last sentence and first one halfway through.
Pros:
- Content based on Choice is true to a degree.
- The "art style" of the game works decently.
Cons:
- Completely makes a joke of Depression.
- Fails to give an understanding view of depression to the player.
- Text drones on about the player's awful life and at times feels like empty complaining and whining.
- There isn't really music, just ambience with awful loop crackles. It loops 3 or 4 times in a 15 minute period.
- You can ignore most of the text without loss of story/choice context.
- Some choices are literally always locked no matter what you do.
- There's a choice or two on the first screen that is locked.
- Due to the third point, the game is dull and couldn't be further from being engaging even if it's in 1st person.
- The wording in some pages are poorly done, or done wierdly to confuse the reader.
- The Endings are technically the same save for one or two lines of text that don't change anything.
This game gets a 1/10. It makes a joke out of Depression by coming off as whiny and complaining about how awful life is, saying how awful everything is rather than using words to imply the feelings so the reader can dig and feel them that way.
If that wasn't a thing and it did what it'd do, it would be a 5/10 simply due to everything else just being passable. It's not well-made GameSpy, it's just passable. I've played many text-based games that are more well executed than this, some of them being Zork, Trials in Tainted Space and Unification Wars. Trials is in beta.
To improve it I would suggest a complete redo of the whole game. It needs or be worded better, don't tell us, make us imagine it so we can be THERE, not watching ourselves like a ghost would. Be less preachy or Emo-y (if that's a word).
I would also suggest the ambience loop be cleaned up and have the crackles removed.
Make the endings ALOT more dramatically different. Not a single sentence of difference, I'm talking the difference between a life that will continue to be happy, or literally suicide (say if you choose all the good options and then all the bad ones in another playthrough).
It doesn't even need to be longer.
Will I give it Forbidden status? Well... based on how it's been released a full year, I'm inclined to say yes, but I will hold off on that as per the usual for my statuses.
I live with depression every day. I know how it feels. This game? Not one single moment did I EVER empathize with the character. It fails at it's intended purpose.

Dungeons of Dredmor - 7/10
Dungeons of Dredmor is a dungeon crawler for Dungeons and Dragons enthusiasts and overall geeks and nerds, using those terms endearingly. Exploring multiple floors (10 to get to Lord Dredmor, 15 if you're using the Realm of the Diggle Gods expansion), your character must grow in strength and loot to take on the challenge of battling Lord Dredmor himself, an evil lich that you have to kill because the game tells you to. That's pretty much all there is to the plot. The formula for a dungeon crawler has been boiled down to it's basic components:  large dungeon full of traps and monsters, the occasional store to sell your stuff (you can even attack the storekeeper and attempt a five-finger discount, though I wouldn't advise this as crime usually ends in death in the Dungeons), and a variety of equipment and items scattered on the floor as if a kleptomaniac had a hole in his bag.
The core of the game lays in the character creation and the random dungeon layout. Notice how I said earlier "your character"? There isn't a named hero or heroine to Dungeons of Dredmor. It's an avatar with massive eyebrows and whatever skill set you want that avatar to have. The game starts immediately by picking out 7 skills from a bank of 35 (+6 if you get the Realm of the Diggle Gods DLC, +4 if you get the You Have to Name The Expansion Pack DLC, and +6 if you get the Conquest of the Wizardlands DLC) either by choice or by random. Then you pick a name and either the massively-eyebrowed male avatar or the massively-eyebrowed female avatar. The process is kept simple, allowing players to spend as little time as possible on rerolling characters once they die. There's even a "Last Choice" option, allowing players to repick the same skills the previous life had. My complaints with this are that (as far as I'm aware), you can't see what the skill trees will look like before or as you choose the skills, which means you can't pre-plan skill progression beyond guesswork from what the name of the skill implies. Also, some skills are rather pointless or even completely weak in my opinion. The loading time between games can also be considered choppy as you have to get past an arbitrary scoreboard before you can get to the new game screen.
The random dungeon layout also adds some uniqueness to Dungeons of Dredmor. No two dungeons are going to be the same. Now, when I started writing that sentence, I was about to type "no two adventures", but then I realized every game of Dungeons goes the same way, which can make the game stale quickly to those not interested in the mandatory grinding it takes to get strong enough to get to Dredmor. The random dungeon layout and room layout can also make some rooms inaccessible because of object placement, such as an impassible candelabra or iron bars. Store placement can make or break a run, as the inventory is cripplingly small. Doing so makes have to prioritize items you want in your inventory for the upcoming battles even though you're only on the first or second floor. Shop items are randomized too, which means you can find expensive, yet powerful, weapons on the first floor or junk for crafting.
The crafting system is meh. In order to craft items, you must a) have the appropriate skill level, b) the appropriate items to craft with, and c) a crafting tool. There are also secret crafting recipes that can be found in bookshelves or dropped from monsters if you have the right skill. However, in order to have a high crafting level, you must have a crafting skill in one of your 7 selected skills. This makes crafting nearly moot, as the more powerful (and more  useful) items require high levels of crafting in order to make. At least the item-upgrade system is easy. Just find an enchanting anvil, pick your item, and bam! It's enchanted! Of course there is a risk of making the item worse, which is always a gamble in any RPG when it comes to item enchanting. The game is secretly turn-based. I say secretly because you don't really notice it until you have a screen full of monsters who are acting at the same time as you. What you may think of as lag is actually the monsters taking their turns in response to your actions, making moving one square at a time feel like a chore, especially if you're attempting to run away.
The game can be, and most of the time is, really frustrating. A lot of grinding is necessary to get past the monsters that lurk in the Dungeons, and traps can be difficult to spot quickly if you're using the WASD controls to move. A really good run can end in moments by stepping on a mine you didn't notice in time or by not paying attention to your health when battling your way through a room. As of writing this review, I still haven't faced Lord Dredmor, even on easy. But even with all this difficulty, I wouldn't quite call it Nintendo-hard. A lot of the deaths I've had have been my own fault, either not paying attention to my health or where I'm going, or just getting so burned out on the run I'm on that I get reckless.
The humor of the game is based entirely on nerdy references. Almost everything has flavor text, and most items and skills make references to nerd culture such as Doctor Who or Supernatural to name a couple. It's cute at first, but grows stale after a while because there really isn't much more in the ways of humor for this game. It's funny the first time you see a little Diggle shouting FUS RO DAH at you as it charges into your sword, but the screen can get littered with corpses, items, monsters, and flavor text quickly. The same can also be said of the soundtrack, which I stopped listening to after about a week of gameplay. The smooth jazz doesn't quite scream adventure or exploration to me, and feels out of place.
Despite of all the complaints I have, I'm still playing. I'm still grinding out achievements and levels, still climbing that mountain of corpses to get to Lord Dredmor. Every time I go in, I say to myself, "Yes, THIS is the run!" only to die ten or twenty minutes later to an Unfriendly AI. It's a game that definitely bites back, and for that I find it somewhat enjoyable. My score for Dungeons of Dredmor is 7/10.

Guns. Guns everywhere. This game is a first person bullet hell, which is a difficult combination to find nowadays. It also incorporates some rouge-like elements, allowing you to collect and purchase loot in the form of upgrades and stat boosts. This in itself is fun, but one of the more enjoyable features of this game is the literal ton of secrets that can be found. Every room has a secret or two to unlock, and because of the randomized nature of the game i'm constantly finding new things on every playthrough. But whats all this mean without the gunplay. Shooting in tower of guns is chaotic and exaggerated. It doesn't take long for your screen to be swamped with bullets, missiles, and bombs. The downside to this is that your first five or so runs are mostly likely going to end in a quick death, as the game doesn't start you with very good weapons. Unlocking new guns should be your first priority, as progression past the first boss is almost impossible without it. The game lets you choose between dashing past enemies to the exit, or fighting it out in the search for power ups and loot. These sort of decisions become very important later in a run, as arming yourself is key to preparing for the next boss fight.
Overall this game has a special charm to it. Being hand crafted as a co-op project between two brothers, you can see the love that has been pored into it. If you are a fan of bullet hell shooters, or simply want to try something different and don't mind a challenge, then you should defiantly check this game out.

-not near the original still entertaining steampunk thieving simulator 7/10-
As I already read several (bad) reviews before buying at a large discount I could keep my disappointment in check. Yes it's not really a successor to the original and acclaimed thief series.
The product is a console-player-streamlined dishonored-like without superpowers.
Movement is restricted: jumping/climbing only where possible and also rope arrows can't be fired in any wood but assigned places (to not make it too difficult for kids). You can't place crates to create shortcuts, reach ledges or hide. You can't throw stuff to distract only the bottles designed for that purpose.
Gareth the cynical thief we loved becomes Gareth the emo dude with a mean GF but it's not that bad as I made it sound. (in fact in reviews the Erin character was usually reviled - she casually murders a guard in the beginning - but I think given her history and everything the character works and as you discover in the game the guards are a bunch of fascists anyway)
Now why the recommendation?
On it's own without the mighty thief series as comparison the game is a quiet good simulation of sneaking, stealing stuff and parcour. Aside from game design, bugs and handling problems the game shows AAA production values. For 10 bucks it's good entertainment.
For all the reasons outlined Dishonored feels like a much better production and was dubbed the spiritual thief successor (has Trickster, more steampunk and style) but Corvo is an overpowered killing machine who always has several ways to easily dispatch stuff while Gareth remains a fragile dude who has to strike from the shadows and he's a much better sneak at it. It's a different approach and also very satisfying to play.
Approaching the last mission now and the game hits the sweet spot between being the badass takedown sneaker and the close combat wimp.
You'll have a lot of exciting moments where you escape detection by a hair.
It's fun to nail an arrow through a guard's eye from the shadows.
Good lot of content with large main missions and several smaller 15 minute side missions.
Bunch of rare collectables and secret treasure hidden in every corner.
Other unsorted impressions and rants
Atmosphere is dark and gothic. I like the visual style and the game characters actually. Voice-acting ranges from poor to good. New Gareth is not old Gareth of legend but an ok dude for a hero.
Mission 5 is the thief-obligatory horror mission.
While the story is usual an excuse to steal stuff and go see places it's especially illogical and obscure here and the ending is just dumb and unrewarding.
There are no hammerites or pagans anymore.
Ambient conversations are projected on your position without any speaker existing - making it appear like you hear ghost voices in your head as noises and conversations from guards are correctly coming from their position.
Oh and often you're supposed to mash some button like to pry a  window. Completely useless feature in a game - should be patched out from ANY game (Batman games come to mind). Ruins your gear so you buy another overpriced controller.
Clumsy "context sensitive controls" - you probably lean on a chest more often than loot it or fumble with controls while avoiding guards in pursuit.

Tower of Guns is a roguelike FPS. You spawn in the first of five levels in the titular Tower of Guns, and must fight your way through it until you reach the top – and victory. Along the way, you will fight numerous automated gun turrets – both fixed and floating – along with various other mechanical enemies which will attack you in hopes of killing you and forcing you to start over. Every level ends with a boss fight in some sort of arena, with a variety of bosses (and indeed, of possible levels) trying to keep things fresh.
That being said, this game is not actually that diverse in terms of gameplay. You only play through five levels (or six, if you go on to fight the optional final boss) in any particular playthrough. The levels are quite short, and can be beaten in just a few minutes, though you might spend 10+ minutes trying to find all the secrets in them (to no success; this is nearly impossible to do). You upgrade yourself by finding various random pickups, as well as collecting coins and using them on random vending machines which contain said pickups. Rarely, you will find a new gun. Enemies drop health (for healing) as well as xp (for levelling up your gun to shoot better shots and deal more damage).
But while all of this is well and good, and you can start the game with your choice of a weapon and a powerup (and unlock more of these by doing various tasks in-game), the sad reality is that there just isn’t that much to this game. The enemies end up being very samey after a while, and the room layouts become very familiar. The secrets are kind of obnoxious to find – some of them can only be found if you have the right items/pickups, which are random, while others are actually hidden behind invisible walls which give no hint to their existence. As the secrets are the primary gameplay extender here, and they’re kind of lame in many cases, this kind of hurts the game’s replayability even more than it already was, and a lot of the time you spend in-game is spent hunting for the secrets rather than fighting. If you just fight your way through the levels, most can be beaten quite easily within five minutes, and indeed, there are unlocks for doing so.
The game isn’t very difficult either; after my first three playthroughs ended at the first boss, I nearly beat the game on my next two playthroughs, and then successfully did so on my sixth, only four hours into the game, at which point the game held little new for me. Sure, there were various secrets that I hadn’t found, but what’s the point in hunting those out when so many of them are arbitrary? Moreover, what’s the point when you have already beaten the game – what challenge is there left for you? Is endless mode really that much of an attraction?
The answer to all this is “not so much”, meaning that this is more or less a game that you’ll play for an afternoon, beat, and unless you’re a hyper completionist, never bother with again. While the alternate text at the start of every level giving a bit of randomized backstory to why you are in the tower is mildly clever, it was simply not amusing enough to make me want to keep playing the game over and over again until I saw them all.
The game isn’t bad, and running through it until you beat it is decent enough, but it is very lightweight and doesn’t really have a whole lot to really recommend it. It is adequate, but is mere adequacy what you really want?

Indie metroidvania game from Japanese indie developper rdein and team.
This game is short (not so much compared to its inspirations) but packed with content: 8 different areas each with its tileset, hazards, monsters and music. Thanks to this each area has its distinct "mood" and feel, which is a must for a metroidvania kind of game.
The combat is good 'though I feel it could have even more depth. Your only two weapons remain nearly the same throughout the whole game. All the same, the dodging mechanics and the platforming work well enough but lack a little bit of renewal - which is compensated by the many boss fights.
Some design decisions (mainly spikes that instantly kill you) imho have a negative impact on the difficulty curve and are borderline questionnable. Hopefully, the game provides just enough checkpoints that it should rarely feel unfair, if at all.
What I think really sets this game apart the most is the extreme care to detail, especially in graphics and sound department. The pixel art backgrounds, characters and animations are gorgeous, lighting and particle effects are used sporadically and well-integrated.
The sound effects are mostly minimalistic (8bit-like). The music and background music is CD quality, the production standards being surprisingly good for "small" scale indie title.
There is a story to the game, but only a few talking characters and they don't have very much to tell you - which is not a bad thing ! In a sense, the places the main character visits and the boss she fights are more telling, 'though some is left to interpretation. Although there exist solid steel weapons and Kaho can use a bow, magic is everywhere in the game. Kaho fights using a maple leaf, saves progress at prayer spots. Most ennemies use magic or *are* made of magic. If you like Japanese stories about mythology or folklore (think Princess Mononoke or Spirited Away) even a little bit, the background should appeal to you - but that shouldn't be a must to enjoy the game.
A must have for metroidvania fans and even others -like myself-.
PS. this is but a detail, but the update history shows the game has had good support over the months, with devs careful to fix bugs or balance gameplay when needed. 'Though not everyone will agree about the difficulty curve, it is a pretty polished game

One things for sure, Ubisoft has found a rhythm for this franchise and they are not budging.
Here’s the thing with this franchise, it’s a love-hate relationship for me. I am a natural completionist and I love collecting. I can't tell you how many hours I have spent collecting♥♥♥♥♥♥even on games that I have completely hated. Far Cry 4 definitely fulfills that desire, but I digress. This franchises problem, and honestly all of Ubisofts games have been suffering from this for years, is that all missions and side missions start to feel like you're just going down the list. There's no real payoff anymore and you are just doing the same things over and over again and expecting things to change. It doesn't help that the challenge is practically stripped away somewhat fairly early on. Strongholds quickly go from "sneak in, stab, kill guy with bow, get seen, and fight off reinforcements" to "let me just pick off every enemy with my silenced sniper rifle." And here's one thing I haven't been able to figure out, what's the point to having an open world when there is really nothing to explore? I mean sure you can find a cave, but what then? It's just a cave with some loot and probably a collectible. What these games need are actual interesting landmarks and bigger cities and villages that consist of more than just a handful of mindless NPC's that give you a random task that has no story or personal connection to either you or the NPC.
In Far Cry 3, the protagonist, Jason Brody, is just a normal guy forced into a life-or-death situation. He is stuck where he is by his need to help his imprisoned friends. Far Cry 4's protagonist, Ajay Ghale, goes into this land to spread his mother’s ashes... and oh wait, what’s that? Now he's invested in the civil war that's happening there. He does whatever he is told without question with no real reason as to why he should care. Jason Brody had character arch, Ajay was as bland as they come.
One thing is sure with this game, death will happen. That is when you have a wingsuit and parachute that kill you at every turn! I got the wingsuit about 20 or so hours in. I immediately hated it. Not because I would start flying and then die from a bird smacking me right in the face (which did happen on a couple of occasions), but because it would constantly deploy on the tiniest jumps and instantly kill me when I would smack in to the wall or mountainside that was previously only 20 feet away. It wasn't until about 15 hours afterwards that I discovered why this kept happening. This game has toggle sprint on at all times. So if you naturally hold down the sprint button at all times in order to sprint, then you are gonna have a bad time. If you continue to hold sprint while jumping the game will think you are wanting your wingsuit to deploy due to them being the same button. It was a very frustrating feature that forced me to consciously change how I have naturally played for years. I know that I am just ranting at this point, but this is on top of the many bugs that were incredibly frustrating. For example, when I pulled out my parachute with absolutely nothing around me only to die instantly for no apparent reason. And that is just one example. Others include a helicopter that was practically scripted to fall and blow up on me and the vehicle that I was trying to protect, getting melee'd to the ground and slowly standing up only to be shot up right as I regain control (not a bug I know but a horribly frustrating feature nonetheless), and having to reattach every sight for every gun on a regular basis. I cannot tell you the amount of times this damn game killed me and how often its bugs made me want to kill myself.
Overall this game is a step down from Far Cry 3. The biggest improvement was the verticality that the landscape had compared to Far Cry 3, but it was practically the same game with slightly better graphics, more bugs, and a crappier story.

1. Your ship propells itself, rather quickly.

3. Use back and forward to go faster or slower, but you'll only ever go slower because if you go faster you'll die.

I normally do not get side scrolling games.  I did that in my youth playing NES games like Contra and Castlvania.  "This War of Mine" catch my eye for its visual artwork and story.  Your characters are placed against nearly impossible odds: survive life as a civilian in a war torn city.  You are given a collection of individuals that have their own distinctive abilities and emotional levels.  Some are the good people, and others just have no emotions (the war removed them?).
Each day is broken into two phrases: Day and Night.  During the day, your chracters try to eat food, drink water, make repairs on the house and other tasks.  At night, one of them goes out to scavange anything you can find.  Danger lurks around every area.  Making the wrong decision can be very costly.  As the game unfolds, you learn more about each character's past and how they came to be in this spot and time.  In all the gloom and dreary, its a fantastic game to play through.  There is even a cooperative board game being produced of this game (for 1-6 players) on Kickstarter.

It took me five separate runs before I even made it to day 20, not to even mention completing a single run.  When I did complete it, I had to resort to murder and theft to survive.  This War of Mine is not a game that gives you a "feel good" ending, but the ending isn't a kick in the balls either.  It doesn't make you feel good, but you certainly feel different after playing it.  Play the game if you want to see what I mean (it's a steal on sale).
My first complaint I have with the game is with the controls.  Combat is very hard relying on only the mouse, so I didn't use it after my first few runs and just used stealth.  You could argue that the developers wanted to reward the patience of stealth over running and gunning, but I feel that it should be easier to kill one person by spraying a Kalashnikov at them than by stabbing them repeatedly.  Still, this is balanced with the enemies who take quite a long time to aim and some survivors (here's looking at you, Pavle) can often run faster than a soldier can aim.
My last complaint is that I feel the game could have a bit more variance.  By the time I finished my first run, I figured out most of the locations and their alternate events and how to effectively manage the shelter.  Different characters change a little bit of the strategy (playing using only Cvete and Anton for example is God awful), but overall I wouldn't change it far too much in subsequent runs (though most of the beauty of each character is in discovering who he was before the war and watching him develop).  I think the game would be better with more locations, more unique shelters and more unique improvements for each.  Overall, however, I think the game is absolutely phenomenal and should definitely be bought on sale.

Not bad, but could have been better. I recommend getting it if/when it goes on sale.
Needs a lot of polish; controls are sometimes awkward and UI needs polish, for example when you bring up your mission list, there's a "show me where" button, but this only highlights the system that the destination is in. You need to then click on that system to zoom into it, so that you can then click on your destination to set it as a waypoint. They really could have had a "add destination as waypoint" button straight from the mission screen. Autopilot also seems to be buggy. You're supposed to be able to press Z to turn on autopilot, but if the autopilot drives near a star, the autopilot "disengages" and there does not seem to be a way to re-engage the autopilot except to quit the game and relaunch it.
The main mission narrative is enjoyable, but there's way too much filler content. The game would have been better if shorter and more focused. Mining is not particularly fun, shooting garbage is not particularly fun, salvaging derelict ships is not particularly fun, taxying and acting as a courier is not particularly fun. Took me about 10 hours to beat the main game, and then another 5 hours to "shoot 1000 garbage", "completel 50 taxi missions", and all the other filler achievements. NPCs also felt shallow. You can do "random chat" with them, or read their biographies, but there's no incentive to care about any of this. Feels like there was a missed opportunity to have them deliver side quests to you.
There's basically 3 classes of ships in this game: traders, fighters, and all-arounders. When you get to the last boss, you can't switch your ship, so I got kind of screwed there because I had to do a massive boss fight in my trader ship. Took several tries and reloads but I eventually got it. Would have been nice if I could have just switched to a fighter ship for that boss fight though -- everywhere else in the game except for the introductory tutorial, you can switch your ships at will as long as you have the money.
The music was both a pro and a con for this game. There's some really nice track that give it that great 80s vibe. The thing is that they chose songs with lyrics, which means the music is very salient to the player, instead of being a background element. This is not necessarily bad, but because there's not that many different tracks in the game, it becomes very obvious very quickly when they start repeating the same tracks over and over. I think if you're going to use tracks with lyrics, you need to "use them once" for a set-piece moment. Take a look at how Saints Row uses the "I Need a Hero" or "Power" songs, for example.

I really enjoyed this game. The FPS and stealth mechanics are top-notch and intuitive, and you face a challenging enemy AI with a gradual ramp-up in the difficulty. The game's core mechanic really shines in the outpost/fortress liberation missions, where you can really savour the non-linear gameplay and test your skills. The variety of weapons is fantastic and they all feel great, as do the vehicles and takedowns. The open-world is bustling with life to the point where random enemy/wildlife attacks will sometime be overwhelming, which can be hilarious or frustrating. In comparison, the campaign missions seem linear and scripted, but there is good variety, pacing and challenge in them. However the storyline "choices" are downright meaningless, frustrating and forced; no effort was made to give the protagonist a sense of purpose, and his allies' characters become gravely insufferable halfway through the campaign. It's unfortunate because the other characters are generally well-written with good voice acting, and NPCs have some hilarious and contextual dialogue. This is complement by a fantastic, immersive soundtrack.
There is a plethora of side quests. Many of them are lots of fun, but they tend to get mundane through repetition and don't offer significant rewards after a while. It's REALLY unfortunate that you can't replay any of those or any of the campaign missions; this capability is what made me enjoy the outposts missions so much. Otherwise, money is ridiculously abundant, hunting is fairly easy, and skill/karma points and signature weapons unlocks (some of which are OP) will saturate quickly if you like doing side missions. Some of the collectibles are interesting, most others are tedious.
I think it's a great improvement over FC3 and I had lots of fun. I think that most of the negatives can be avoided by playing the game in a non completionist fashion, something I'll likely try. The game's graphics and environment is really nice but it ran poorly on my machine, showing some glitchy textures.
Good game.

I played the original Thief games when I was young, and I liked them a lot. Never knew or cared about the plot, but the levels were large and somewhat open, and the player had a freedom to roam the corridors and hallways from loot and secrets. Despite their age, the original games are still good to play and I recommend them a lot.
When the new Thief was announced, I was excited. The trailer gave an expression of Thief being an old school stealthing game executed with a modern graphics engine. Gameplay trailer reinforced my expectation of Thief being something like Dishonored, but infused with the old Thief consept. Large maps open for you to explore and enjoy, search and steal. Awesome picture, right?
Luckily I felt skeptical and decided to wait until the game would get reviewed. When the reviews came out and were talking about Thief being pretty mediocre game, I decided to let the game pass. If Thief would one day come out on Steam sale, I would reconsider.
That sale day was today and I decided to purchase the Thief. Not more than hour to the gameplay, I already see what the most reviews were talking about. My hope was that the Thief would have been a prementioned open level game, a mixture of Dishonored and old Thief games. In reality the Thief seems to be linear in it's plot, level design and game mechanics.
Despite having some small apartments to explore, the levels are basically tortuous tubes, with little choice given to player on how to proceed. The explorable lootable houses are also always on your path, always served right in front of you. This way you never truly feel like tresspassing into an apartment like you would if you would have found it when you would have been exploring a larger map. Talking about exploring, the game always tells you where to go by showing a very clear marker on your screen. And as I already mentioned, there is no reason to try and venture away from the path. You will just find a wall and you're forced to turn around and keep following the waypoints.
Controls seem to have been made with consoles in mind. There is no jump button, protagonist can only climb from predestined and highlighted spots and it is impossible to accidentally fall off plateaus. Even peeking around corners has been rendered almost futile, when you cannot peek to your sides without having to "attach" yourself to a wall first. Instead of peeking (which actually doesn't even work everywhere), I found strafing slightly from the corner to be as effective.
Instead of making the gameplay intuitive, devs decided to add highlights everywhere and give player a focus vision. In crucial or just less obvious place player is prompted to use focus, which will then give away how to proceed. Developers did not want to take a risk that players would get stuck on the most basic level design for even seconds, and added something that will make sure that the player will always advance, will always know where to go. Is this really where gaming today has gone? Are developers underestimating players, or are games designed with keeping the most simplistic players in mind?
Overall, I don't recommend the Thief. Who knows, maybe this is a game that you might like, and if you don't mind it being a generic game despite it's distinguishable game idea, go ahead and purchase it. Just make it sure that you will get it from sale.
TL:DR: Thief pays more homage to modern day generic, linear and dull FPS's than the old school Thief-games that it stole it's name from.

At its core, Thief is a
Hiding behind corners, lurking in the shadows, stealing that shiny jewel and waiting for the perfect moment to vanish unseen works and feels great. Your tools (mainly a bow with different arrow types), your abilities and the environment work together sweetly and create a fluid and very enjoyable stealth experience. Also, replay value is high. I often found myself playing levels multiple times - trying out different paths, trying not to take out anybody, trying to complete all challenges and so on. "The city", the location the game is set in, offers a great atmosphere, with many dark alleys, suffering citizens and a sinister, depressive, somewhat steampunk-ish vibe to it. This is underlined by the great lighting effects, which make the graphics in the game really pleasing. The skill and upgrade system is rewarding - everything you steal (besides collector items) is instantly exchanged to money, that you can spend on all kinds of upgrades, tools and skills - which impact the game noticeably, like simple health upgrades or an amulet that deflects arrows.
I would love to be able to continue the review in such a positive way, but unfortunately the great core gameplay is flawed by
First and foremost there's the story - it is disappointing, told in mediocre cutscenes and dialogues and leaves a lot to be desired. Now that wouldn't be as much of a deal if it would simply stay in the background and do little more than give you a reason to hop from one (mostly excellent) mission to the next. But the scenario, the setting and the small story bits that are there leave you wanting to know more - and the story fails to deliver to that.
Furthermore, the enemy AI isn't always up to the challenge - enemies sometimes get stuck in walls or run into invisible ones, see you through objects, or don't spot you at all, although you're right there. Still, this does not occur often enough for the AI to become a dealbreaker; tension is always high. The city, while having a great atmosphere, has little to offer. While main and side quests impress with a great level design, small puzzles and lots of loot, there's pretty much nothing to do in the streets of the city - no collectibles, no "city events" and exploration is restricted by buildings you often can't enter and short loading screens while moving from one city area to another. Additionally, the included action sequences often feel unneccessary and misplaced. All this leaves the impression of a game concept that is slightly unrefined and not fully thought through.

So this is a good, competent game. But I bought it for the Metroidvania tag, and this is not in any meaningful sense a Metroidvania.
A Metroidvania is built around exploration and rewarding the player with exciting new means of exploration. The world opens up in organic, interesting, unintuitive ways when a boss drops a Samus ball or a double jump macguffen or a cloak that lets you walk through walls. Even if you're not breaking sequence, it *feels* like you're getting away with something.
This game only pays lip-service to that core mechanic. The player unlocks 1 1/2 ways to move around the world, but they don't go anywhere interesting or off the beaten path. The level design actively penalizes exploration with permadeath traps and hidden enemies, so that too often any sense of freedom or wonder is ripped away as you die to a hazard you couldn't have foreseen and run through the same set of rooms again, except this time you know where the spikes are.
Which is fine!
For the kind of game it is, this is fine. The controls are tight enough to be fair. Save points are frequent enough not to be too frustrating, Enemies all have satisfying counters. The cramped, tense feel of the levels works for this game.
But it's not Axiom Verge or Hollow Knight or, I dunno, Unepic. So go in with your eyes open, is all I'm saying.

Honestly, I'm pretty much right on the fence about whether I like SOTS or not. It's probably the roguelike that nails atmosphere the best - the graphics, audio and interface are satisfying, and the game is surprisingly immersive. It has that Die Hard feeling of sneaking around a building and kicking♥♥♥♥♥ The tension hardly ever lets up after the first few floors, which is a good thing and a bad thing. Diablo-style inventory management is cool, and creates near-impossible choices of what to carry around. The classes are interesting and replayable.
The PROBLEMS become apparent when you start trying to actually win - first of all, a playthrough is 40 floors if you have any of the expansions, and it's simply too damn long. Even the original 30 was stretching it. This reflects the designers' brainless "more is more" philosophy, where each expansion keeps piling on more stuff regardless of balance. The item pool is now diluted to the point where you're likely to get♥♥♥♥♥♥like darts instead of ammo you can use, or you'll get three armors in a row that don't apply to your class. Good luck winning in that case, unless you have the TWO crafting recipes that make the game actually reliably winnable (adamantium claws, chitin plate.) These two items are so good that 99% of the other crafting recipes are useless. Incidentally, there's hundreds of them now, so it's less likely you'll unlock those recipes without cheating. Several skills are basically useless and you'd be a fool to level them, unless you happen to get the one decent spear in the game or something. Basically, there's no balance, it doesn't feel like any thought was put into it. They just throw stuff in that there's no reason to use.
Later on, around floor 30 or so, the game gets extremely repetitive. Lategame enemies are just bullet sponges that you nonetheless have to fight because they sense you across the whole level and run directly at you. At some point you have to transition from playing the game to trying to skip the rest of it via wormholes, sprinting or some other cheap method so that you have the hundreds of bullets necessary to beat the boss. The floor 40 boss is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, not fair whatsoever, and easily the worst part of the game. There are only a handful of weapons that can even damage it with its huge armor rating, you have to wade through a bunch of fodder and hope you still have the supplies for it, and most of the time you'll just get screwed out of a 40 hour run. It barely has anything to do with the rest of the game, just a giant "♥♥♥♥ you" because harder means gooder.
I'm gonna go ahead and give it a "no," because the moments of utter BS outweigh the good ones. Now that I've beaten it into submission once, I don't think I'll be playing it again. Still, I'm tempted to give it another go sometimes, maybe because I hate myself. Pick it up on sale for two bucks and try not to take it too seriously.

The Pit is a true roguelike with a few notable features--a greater focus on long range combat, and a unique focus on entropy and attrition similar to many games in the survival genre (but strangely uncommon to purebred roguelikes). In this sense, it blends crafting elements of cousins like Neo Survivor or Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, but in an enclosed environment with random limited resources available.
In other words, your guns will fail, ammo is constantly running low, your armour is held together bu duct tape (literally, at times!), and the hunger clock is ticking away every move. It's an extremely intense and claustrophobic roguelike that's a race to stay on the positive side of the attrition war, as you try to descend 40 levels against tougher and tougher enemies.
Kerberos should be applauded for the love they've put into this game over several years, expanding to 13 playable classes and hundreds of objects. With the exception of a very few skills, the entire skill/stat tree is usable and vastly different kinds of build can succeed--from the oh-so-standard space marine, to the glass-cannon psychic floating dolphin who has to protect its hydration armour from breaking. The flavour text is terrific (as is the background text for the SOTS universe, which this game introduced me to).
If you're looking for an empowerment fantasy, look elsewhere. The Pit is death. If you're from the 'Losing is Fun' crowd though, well, you'll be right @ home.

Sword of the Stars: The Pit is a challenging turn-based roguelike with RPG elements.
You start on the surface of a planet and gradually work your way down through the levels of "The Pit". As you do you gain experience from killing enemies, opening containers, picking locks, and other various tasks. The further you descend the tougher enemies become, so finding useful items and leveling up is important to combat them.
If your skills are at a low level they can progress up to a point, beyond that, you will have to spend points when you level up to improve them. There are both skills and attributes to level up, and each skill has an underlying attribute that affects it. For example, for each five points of strength you have, your mechanical and melee skills are improved by one point. Your character's strengths and weaknesses are dictated by their class, and there are several classes to choose from (especially if you buy the various DLCs).
The characters generally fall into two categories; some are tanky, while others are more of a finesse type character. The tanky classes are better at fighting early in the game, but tend to have poor non-fighting skills, and level up more slowly than the finesse classes, so whatever your play style, you should be able to find a class that works for you.
There is a good bit of DLC available for this game, I think it is all worth getting, but I would definitely recommend the "Mindgames" DLC since it adds psionics (which are essentially the game's version of magic) and several classes.
Since it is a roguelike, permadeath is present, but there is an element of progress even in failed runs. Some loot consists of ingredients that can be used in recipes. These recipes are found encrypted, but once you fully decrypt them all future runs have access to these recipes regardless of their class. There are some messages that don't contain recipes, but are just text that advances the lore of the story.
There are a few parts of the game that are frustrating. The randomness of the game adds replay value, but sometimes you will be given lots of weapons, but no armor, or a lots of ammo, but no weapon that can use it. Since you inventory space is limited, what to carry and what to leave is an important consideration.
I've had several runs that were going well when I triggered a wormhole trap, which teleported me to a much tougher level, and surrounded me with enemies I wasn't ready for.
My biggest gripe with this game, however, is definitely the lack of durability of items. Armor and weapons degrade over time, which I like in principle, but I think there are too many that are just too fragile.
Overall, I like the game quite a bit. Definitely worth a look if you like the idea of a difficult turn-based roguelike/RPG.

Beware, if you aren't used to TRUE roguelike games, you are not ready for this game.  I would recommend anyone who is interested in this to go play Nethack, Binding of Isaac, FTL, and Spelunky.   If you play those games and you like them, welcome to Sword of the Stars.
There's however a reason I recommend those games before playing this.  The sad truth is each of those is a better game than Sword of the Stars: The Pit.   At the same time, those games will prepare you for what you're going to find in Sword of the Stars.
This is a true roguelike, there's only two things that really persists through the game, and that's marginally useful.  The first persistance is messages, as you play the game you can hack computers and read messages, decrypting them.  Often times you'll decrypt more and more as you go, so you might need to decrypt one message multiple times to get the full understanding.
The second, you'll keep recipes around.  That can be a positive or a negative, but personally I don't think it fully violates "Roguelikes" it doesn't make a huge difference if you keep that knowledge in a book next to the computer or in the game.
EVERYTHING ELSE goes away.  Knowledge of items, knowledge of weapons, skills, and more all reset EVERY TIME you die.  There's not even a "not hardcore mode" option.  You play this game one way, and while there's four difficulties, none of them remove the rules of roguelikes.
In fact easy is still pretty difficult after a while, and that's due to my big complaint about Sword of the Stars.  The game really doesn't give you very playable maps.  Now for sure I'm probably playing the levels wrong, or just getting hurt too much, but I feel once the enemies have "Acid" and you meet the big slimes, the game just becomes more annoying than difficult.  Yes there's probably ways around these enemies, but they will eat your weapon durability FAST, and before long, you'll be weaponless.  In fact in my two easy playthroughs, I died once because I didn't know diesease could kill you (and I was knocked unconscious) and the other time I was at level 17, and I had no weapons.  I in fact hadn't seen a new weapon in a few levels.
There's a thin line between brutally hard (nethack, Demon souls, and pretty much all Roguelikes) and unfairly hard (sword of the stars, Teenage mutant Ninja turtles on the NES, Battletoads.)  And yes, I put Sword of the Stars in that later category.
While that's the biggest problem I have with the game (that often the game feels like it's impossible to win), there's another point which just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  When you make a move, you wait for the enemies to move, and often times that means waiting seconds to multiple seconds.   The issue here is that if you walk down a hallway often times you'll know an enemy is nearby just because the game takes a while to process the enemy's move.  Also when you get a nice flow going, the enemy's move tends to take a lot longer than your attacks.   I can't really explain it, but it's VERY frustrating and breaks the immersion.  A shame because I really like this game in a lot of ways, but god that delay on enemy moves is VERY harsh.
On the other hand, I recommend this game with the caveat that this might be too hard to really be fun, and can be quite annoying, but if you really want a roguelike game, neither of those issues might bother you.  While I gave up, I think I can safely say that with some more time and energy, I might have had a better run.  The real problem is I didn't want to spend another 2-3 hours trying to get down to level 15 or level 20 only to have a few moments of bad luck to ruin a run.  While that's true of many Roguelikes, I just feel this one might just be too brutally hard that it wasn't fun for me any more.   A shame because it is nice to see roguelikes are still strong.  It's just not exactly what I want in a roguelike.

Depending on how you feel about FMV, Roundabout will be either one of the best or most cringe worthy games you ever play.
It's a master of the sort of low budget, 70's nonsensical cheese that's so absolutely horrible in every way that it becomes hilarious despite itself, and Roundabout leverages this against a goofy mechanic to keep it from ever becoming too much to handle. As professional limousine chauffeur Georgio Manos, you must navigate the streets of Roundabout City, picking up passengers, battling the bad guys, and taking special unicorn "medicine" to make sure you stay the absolute best driver in the business!
But what sets Georgio apart, you ask? Her constantly revolving limo of course! With it she can traverse the windiest roads, the highest roof tops, and the most populated beaches twisting and turning around obstacles (and only killing a few thousand innocent bystanders in the process).
It's legitimately absurd, yet the act of driving a continually rotating car around these sandbox levels is surprisingly satisfying once you get a hang of the confusion, and provides a level of controlled hilarity as you attempt to navigate some of more maze like environments and inevitably wind up crashing into things along the way. The lack of any penalties for completely wrecking your car keeps the frustration away, and the game simply becomes a lot of goofy fun as you drive/crash your way through the surprisingly large environments collecting all manor of limo swag and miscellaneous stacks of money left lying around as you go from one crazy mission to the next.
What really makes Roundabout so great though is the sheer ridiculous of its FMV cutscenes, which are so incessantly outrageous and over the top that it's hard not to laugh and groan  at them in equal measure. There's a look and feel to them all that's almost like watching your friend's bad homemade movie, laughing at all the wrong places and loving it for the wrong reasons. Only in this instance Roundabout it in on the joke and laughing right along with you.
If there was anything I could say against Roundabout (aside from the disappointing performance issues that will hopefully be fixed in a patch), is that once you get through the FMV in about 3 hours, the novelty of a rotating limo has all but entirely worn off and there's really little more for you to go back to. It's a great ride if you can appreciate it for what it is, but even as someone who greatly enjoyed it the ticket price still seems a tad higher than it maybe ought to be. If by chance you actually have an aversion to FMV and B-movie stupidity, I'd be surprised if you come away from Roudabout with anything but a confused look on your face, wondering what you just witnessed and why I'm raving about it.
To that I say, phooey on you!

Have you ever dreamed of taking a stretch limo, and doing circles until the tires fell off? I sure as hell didn’t but now that’s all I want to do and no thanks to freshman developer No Goblin and their first game, Roundabout. On the surface, Roundabout is kind of easy to explain but the nuances in the game play elevate it above your standard limousine spinning game.
It is 1977 and you take the wheel as silent limo driver, Georgio Manos. I never understood why she never speaks but it does make for some awkwardly funny moments between her and her passengers. Yes, Georgio is a female. A gorgeous one at that, but that’s neither here nor there. Skipping any kind of real introduction, the game starts right off with your driving lesson. I breezed right through the lesson, with a whopping 50% and not meeting any of the objectives. Still passed though. From then on out its nothing but semi-controlled chaos.
Spinning ( and jumping…yes, jumping ) through tight streets and hairpin turns is challenging and you tend to die a lot. And I mean a lot. But the low success rate does not hinder the fun of the game at all. In such an open world game that is driven by streak based scoring and challenges, like trying to bounce a soccer ball on the roof of the limo as many times as you can or staying clear of as many falling cars as possible, its hard to get mad a the constant dying.
You are a limo driver so it should be a no brainer that part of the game is chauffeuring a zany pack of characters around town. These riders are one of the best aspects of the game due to the hilarious live-action cut scenes, filled with actors I assume are No Goblin staff, friends, and family. The kids are my favorite. Not to mention the tender moments between Georgio and a certain female passenger. See, this game even has a love story! The scenes have a very Troma Entertainment feel to them ( given studio head Dan Teasdale’s involvement with Lloyd Kaufman, its no surprise ).
Roundabout is just a ridiculous game. Everything from the funky 70s music to the smooth spinning and fiery explosions. Its rare to see a game be so outlandish but work so well at the same time. I skipped over a lot of the other wacky things this game has to offer in this review but my suggestion is to plop down the $15 ( $12 during the launch week ) and get yourself a copy. Now.
Buy Roundabout
QUICK TIP – If you have a xbox or playstation controller, use it. The game is much easier. You will still probably suck, just a fraction less.
The Breakdown:
Story – 3/5
I only got to 12% but I could feel something developing.
Visuals – 4/5
Its not real life but its a video game through and through.
Gameplay – 4/5
Its fun. And isnt that what video games should be?
Sound – 5/5
The music alone deserves 5 stars. Also, between the pedestrian screams and sweet sound of crashing and exploding, it has top notch sound design
Entertainment – 5/5
I played for hours without any sense of time. Most of the time I was grinning from ear to ear.
Replay – 4/5
Unless you are some spinning badass, it will take a couple replays to complete the game. And I could see this becoming a party game. Easy to challenge your friends.

Dungeons of Dredmor is a roguelike in the traditional sense of the word: a turn-based dungeon crawler with permadeath that is challenging and makes you stop and think tactically and strategically if you want to win. While it certainly doesn't stand up to the big name traditional roguelikes like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup or Tales of Maj'eyal, it's an excellent choice for someone new to the roguelike genre, and can be a good step up for those who want to give true roguelikes a chance.
One of the biggest drawbacks of the game is the animation speed, so it's worth noting that it can be sped up with the + key. The other big problem is inventory management; even with the free DLC, if you take a crafting skill you'll be playing inventory shuffle a lot. That said, the absurd number of skills you can choose from do give you some interesting choices and keep the game interesting for quite a while. For those who are used to the older roguelikes such as DCSS or Nethack this game will come off as a bit easy, but for anyone new to the genre it will give a solid challenge, and is worth at least a few playthroughs trying different builds.
If you're a roguelike fan looking to try something a bit different, or if you're interested in the (real) roguelike genre and you're looking for a good introductory game, I would recommend this highly. On the other hand, if you're already a skilled player of deeper roguelike games such as DCSS or ToME, this game may feel like too much of a step back for you. In any case, it is a well-crafted game, and for its target audience would be a solid buy.
