An adventure game about the life of Susan, a depressed middle aged woman who kills herself and gets cursed with immortality until she cleanses the world of a few serial killers who are comming after her.
I enjoyed the game very much, and played it through in an evening and an afternoon.
The gameplay consists of Susan walking left / right by pressing the left / right key; text pops up when she can interact with an object by pressing the up key, and the inventory is entered by pressing the down key. As the game is essentially one dimensional (walk left or right) there is no pixel hunting, and I felt that the puzzles were always logical.
Much of the dialogue is between Susan and her tenant, Mitzi, and the story of Susan's life is slowly unveiled as they talk with each other in between attacks by killers. The story was interesting and full of exciting plot twists and disturbing scenes and people. I strongly recommend the game if you like a good story and can stand being creeped out and a little bit scared at times.

I know that I get very invested in my games and their characters, but this game "got me." I mean really got me. Towards the end I cried....hunched shoulders, where's my tissue so I can see the monitor again, cried. When I had beat the game, I just sat for a while and watched the credits roll by. I have to admit it was one of the best games I've ever played.
Now this is not to say that I didn't get annoyed at times. The game is not perfect, and keeping track of your saves is a real thing. I'd say number them, as one person suggested. They say the max is about 50 before they start not registering, but I found, even after I'd moved old saves to a folder I created called "old saves," they stopped at about 30. Fair warning. I had to replay one whole chapter because of this. Only keep a max of ten in your active save folder.
Now, why did I like the game? For one, it "felt" as though I had choices, and indeed I did. But sometimes, the choices were merely in what order I'd use my dialogue lines. Even still there was a logic to the way I chose to structure the conversation, that felt as though I had influenced it more than I really did. Sometimes I didn't have to interact with the computer or game at all. I just got to watch as certain sequences unfolded, or parts of the characters' stories were revealed to each other.
The art style is funky, cool. The "path" on what to do next is sometimes obscure. I found a good walk through online, and only used it when I was truly stumped as to what to do  next. I also used it to make sure I didn't miss anything once a chapter, or segment was over. That was helpful more than once.
The sound track and voice acting is fabulous! I grew to love Susan's voice and listening/parroting her actually helped me  work on my own British accent as I'm a DayZ roleplayer.  That practice will come in handy when I want to make a character with a British accent. Just a little side bonus to the game :p
Of course the story is very engrossing. I finished the entire game in a little over 16 hours, spread over the course of about a week. Not bad for an indie game, I got for 3.39 on sale. Not to mention the feels, ah the damned feels. I cared so much more than I realized by the end. This was due to Susan's personality, which is stronger than even she knows.
This game is a metaphor for depression. I mean depression is overtly mentioned, but what you see are all the ingredients that make up the recipe for it. It is persistent, not always understandable to someone who isn't, or hasn't experienced it. Also the game is VERY gory and macabre. Being a die hard horror aficionado, the violence didn't phase me much, but I did enjoy and appreciate the harshness and brutality of it. Be forewarned about that too. It does have trigger inducing sequences, so if you're easily triggered, newly traumatized, etc. probably not a good idea for you to play it right now.
I think many others have set the stage, given a synopsis, etc. So my little two cents is merely my feelings about why I liked it and how it affected me. I truly enjoyed it and was happy with my choices and how things turned out for my Susan. So much so, I don't feel the need to see the other endings, or replay it to get 100% of the achievements. It felt "finished" when I was done.
I'd highly recommend it if you like psychological horror games, that are story driven with very little gameplay. It was more than a walking simulator, but less than an action game. Still, it is compelling, artsy and very engaging. At summer sale prices, might as well give it a try :o)

Bought this game on a whim. Turns out it's actualy really cool. There are a few things that I wish were different, like the fact that you can only use your axe to chop already downed trees which you find scatered around the map, but that's mostly just an inconveinience. I'm assuming the devs made that choice so players would not be able to just farm wood for a few hours and become millionares. You also can not collect water from the rivers on the map and instead are limited to puddles and mostly poisoned wells. Again, minor inconvenience and the scarcity of water adds to the dark feel of the game. By far however, the biggest problem with this game is that it does not have a huge player base. This shouldn't realy be expected though because the game is ambitious and the devs have focused on improving the game rather than marketing. As a gamer I think this is a good move, it means a better experience for me. But a game like this needs to build an audience quickly after release to survive.
Now that that is out of the way I have to say this game is pretty cool already. 100% playable and the last update introduced a cool mechanic which allows you to hire npcs to do work for you around your estate. The game is harsh and has an almost darksouls-y feel to it. You make a new character every time you die. This might sound daunting at first. All in all I'd say that if you enjoy survival games then this is a straight shooter. The setting is perfect for the game. The crafting system is simple if not inovative and the dev team are dedicated. But please do remember this game is in...EARLY ACCESS!!!! So don't go sling poo at the developers because you bought an unfinished product. It is sad and rediculous how many great games die in early access because people jump down the developers throats before giveing them the time they need to develop.

Edit: This title deserves a nomination for the "I'm not crying but" Steam award. Read why below.
To try and put a simply binary good or bad on this game is do do it a great injustice. Simply put, This War of Mine is a poignant, dark, and depressing take on war through the eyes of the victims of war. It's loosely based on the Seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War and subsequent genocide during the unstable period in the Balkans in the 1990's. Echos of this appear throughout the game from military snipers indiscriminately shooting civilians to subtle details like a radio station broadcasting the discovery of a mass grave outside the city. My first thoughts on this had me questioning how tasteful the of the theme of the game was and made me uncomfortable to say the least. However, war child does nothing to glorify anything about this war.
The controls are simple and the mechanics work. Survival is difficult. Winter is cold and wood for burning in the heater of your shelter becomes scarce. If you use all your wood for burning, you might not have enough to forify your shelter which makes you suseptible to looters who can injure the survivors and steal valuable resources. Food is scarce, medicine is even scarcer and the player will have to make some hard decisions regarding their resource management. Do I trade this bottle of antibiotics for these tools or should I hold on to them just in case? Do I help the neighbors with this canned food or do I hang on to it incase we run out of meat? These are the questions you'll have to ask yourself frequently. Conditions aren't just static in the city either. For example, snow or fighting between rebels and government forces can block of previously accessable locations for looting, forcing you to wait until it clears up which can be anywhere from a couple days to a week or two in-game time.
To top it all off, the survivors are all pretty frail compared to their contemporaries in other games. Some more than others. This isn't any old game where you can wrap up a wound in a field dressing and treat a wound imediately. Getting shot two or three times will kill your survivor. If your survivor lucky enough to get away, you'll have to scramble to find enough rare and expensive bandages to dress the wounded for days while they basically take bed rest. You'll be short staffed for awhile while they heal and if it gets cold and they happen to fall ill while recovering it could very well spell the end that person. While falling ill, getting wounded, and starving to death are certainly all risk, the psychological aspect is powerful and emotional in this game. Characters have mental health and are effected by the actions of other survivors, their own actions, their physical state, addictions, and by how safe they feel depending on their individual personality. The stress and sadness of survival is real to them.
These mechanics and a narrative from each survivor that unfolds throughout the conflict really create great atmosphere. Despite almost no background narrative, each character is done so well that you'll find their decisions seperating from yours to an extent. The emotional rollercoaster of this game is watching your characters feel guilt over things that both you and they felt were necessary, but are morally damning. As a player, the attachment you feel to these characters makes them seem so much more than just simple scripts and textures.
The few issues with this game are really just the replay value, which is not as infinite as it seems and the occasionally silly AI movement mechanics. Other than that, This War of Mine takes the often ignored perspective of conflict and creates a stellar, emotional, and difficult survival title out of it. Overall, the game is okay. Not great. I'd recommend only if you have an itch for metroidvania stuff.
Visuals are REALLY beautiful. Excellent pixel art and animations. Sometimes you just want to kill all the enemies on a stage and stick around to inspect the art; it's that good.
Combat feels only decent. Some animations run too long, and some attacks (melee!) make you move forward involuntarily. Some actions cancel charging your ranged attack. When rolling to dodge works, it feels good. When you run into an enemy and suffer contact damage, it gets annoying. Finally, the way you use items is a bit clunky: you have to tab through a list of items and find the one you want. If you value good combat, all of this might irritate you.
Difficulty curve is weird - I'd say the game gets easier as you progress. You gain additional abilities that makes moving more intuitive and responsive. At the beginning, it feels sluggish.
Soundtrack is alright. Nothing too memorable, but each helps set the mood for the environment.
Story is a hit or miss. There is little dialogue, and most of the story is told through visuals and gameplay. Some people like minimalistic storytelling, leaving you to guess/fill in the gaps. Some people really don't like it.
The game is short.
TLDR; Has flaws, but probably worth. Buy on a sale for sure.

Momodora: RUtM is a soulslike metroidvania, with all that implies: pattern-based combat, free exploration, and collecting secret items and upgrades.
The combat is tight and clever. Your character has four main combat actions, being a melee weapon (a magic leaf), a ranged attack (bow 'n' arrow), a dodge roll, and access to items (the main one replenishes health). These are pretty standard and behave as you'd expect, with a quirk that provides some depth. Everything but the dodge roll leaves you vulnerable by forcing you stationary (or in the case of the melee attack, mostly stationary) and unable to do anything else for a split second or two. Because there is no way to dodge attacks, this means the meat of the combat is centered around dodging telegraphed attacks and stunning enemies. Bosses typically follow this pattern as well, although some can't be stunned, and have large attacks and high amounts of health. For the scope of this game, the bosses are epic.
As for the metroidvania part of the game, after the first couple of areas the world opens up and you can complete the rest of the map up to the final area in any order you choose (this totals a little more than half of the game). The areas themselves are filled with branching paths and multiple ways to get to the end. There are plenty of secrets and upgrades scattered around the world. These can be practically useful, such as health increases or new items, or easter egg type collectibles. There's also a decent amount of backtracking and re-exploring areas for new paths and secrets, but never to the point of annoyance or tedium.
Overall the mechanics works very well with a few minor complaints. I played on hard mode, so I can't say whether this holds true for other difficulty levels, but the difficulty curve is more of a line than an actual curve. The challenge stays mostly constant throughout the game, which means the beginning is harder than the end. On the upside, this gives you a good sense of getting more skilled at the game, so it's not all bad. It's also pretty easy to simply bypass all the enemies by spamming dodge or arrows once you know where they are in a room. However, this is also has an upside, as it means the first time exploring an area is challenging, but backtracking is easy and quick.
Despite these minor issues, overall the game is challenging and fun. It aims to scratch the difficult medtroidvania itch, and succeeds at the endeavor with clever soulslike combat.

I will be quite frank when I say that this review is more a rant at Wizard's online practices in general. So, before I do that, let me explain the upvote.
1) This is the Planeswalker's game that I have played with the most content, what with 5 good missions in each set, and 30 in the Basic set. This VASTLY beats out the maybe dozen opponents you had in the other games who you could fight on hard, or easy. Not only that, but they actually have a large collection of each set. 2) I did get this only after Kaladesh, and so far it seems to me like the game runs fine. No bugs or glitches in the matchmaking, or things like that. Not only that, but it looks great, runs about as well as any other Magic game I've played, such like that.
3) This game at least can be completely free to play, and, for me, someone who has been a fan of TCGs for most of my life and dabbled with Magic on and on, I actually found that the packs I could buy, plus the starting cards, could make a decent deck and face off against most other players. My biggest issue is that the randomizer has a tendency to not give lands, but I never know quite what to blame that on.
And my biggest con so far is that it is a GRIND to get packs. Due to my own beliefs, I try to buy 8 packs at a time, and do understand that you need to wait to do things like that. HOWEVER, because I am not interested in playing more than an hour at a time against people, it means that it will take me OVER 8 days to get 8 packs, because the gold system is that cheap. Which, yes, leads to my rant.
Wizards of the Coast... go ♥♥♥♥ yourself with your online content. Despite all the praise I give to this, it's still lackluster. You have a good UI, sure, but no events. You have one game mode for EVERYONE to play in with no great variation. Not only that, but you're so insecure about your paper game that you won't let us access all the cards in each set, despite the fact that I am almost certain it would double each set's amount of cards, and thus make it much harder for people to get all the cards without fessing up the money required.

I have been playing the game of Magic since 1993 when it first came out. IMO this game should have stopped development a LONG time ago. It is simply unrecognizeable from its original format. The color disciplines have all been criss-crossed, the benefit to cost ratio was lost ages ago and in their effort to churn out more and more cards, WotC broke the games integrity. There was only so much you could think up before you broke the games balance and that they did. Between the unbalanced benefit to cost ratio and the broken OP game breaking cards, you would be better off moving on to Hearthstone.
This particular game says "Free to Play" .... don't you believe that for a second. Sure you can do the story line and earn about 1200 or so coin then you can attempt to grind it out for 5 / 10 / 15 coin per match solo vs Bots or try MP and get 30 IF you win but the games drag out for 30 to 45 minutes or more a pop and they are not all wins so when you lose you just wasted a lot of time.
The sheer lack of board wipes in this edition leads to very cluttered battlefields and once cluttered, there is virtually no way to clear the mess out so you sit around and watch 10 minutes of fireworks per turn. The coin earning sytem is geared to be slow and discouraging the hope being people will just say "Screw it" and purchase the cards with cash as opposed to earning the free coin. Of all the video game versions so far to date Duels takes the cake as the biggest TURKEY to date.
It is Pay to Win all the way. If you cannot afford to purchase a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of cards, you will get pummeled over and over as your opponents (who CAN afford to purchase cards) sling around all the OP and broken game unbalancing material that really drains the fun right out of this game. Magic USED to be king of the CCT Games but no longer as it is hopelessly unbalanced and there is no more strategic value to its gameplay. Where once it took timing and strategy to win, it now has become a race to see who gets their broken OP cards out first. It is unfortunate for us veterans of the game to see what has happened to this once great game.
**Update** - My original analysis of the game still stands, it is still a race to see who gets their broken / OP / unbalanced cards first but more board wipes have been added. It is now easier to clear out the clutter.

Despite the controversy surrounding this game, I was very interested in trying it out.
As someone who has had (maybe even still dealing with) depression, I was excited to see its entry into the gaming world.
Unfortunately, I found I was troubled by the image of depression that this game offers, and I have to wonder if this could do more harm than good.
It didn't feel as if the person the player is controlling is even a person. I felt like I was wheeling a wooden plank through a series of rooms, so lacking in personality or any distinguishable features that I found myself bored, and struggling to read the text that was telling me how I was 'feeling'. It worries me that the person this game is portraying is dull, boring, robotic. While some ambiguity and vagueness is needed in order for any player to put themselves in the character's shoes, I felt like that vagueness was taken to a point where we can no longer truly care for the character.
I was also troubled by the lack of options. As someone who has experienced depression, I know that there are times where it feels like options are limited. But people don't express depression in the same way. I have been the person that, despite feeling like death inside, I went out, feigned happiness. I went out and did things, even if I wasn't being honest with people, and that was part of my problem. That was something I had to deal with for years, giving the appearance I was happy and healthy, when I wasn't. I was disappointed to find that so many of the options I'd have chosen, the options that would make sense to not just me, but probably many other people just trying to survive, and maintain the life one has, were just simply crossed out, as if the mere thought of doing such a thing was preposterous.
I couldn't help but feel just a bit insulted by that. That my experience was an impossibility.
So no, I would not recommend this game. Not to my friends, not to people who have never experienced depression,
and most definitely not to others who have gone through what this game tries desperately to depict.
A good way to learn what someone with depression goes through.

It's even hard for people with a mental illness to understand in someone else, due to a large variety of factors, such as severity of symptoms, what those symptoms are, support network, etc. However, I think this game does a really good job of telling you exactly what it can be like. It doesn't let you experience it the same way you would first hand, but it gives you a foundation of what it can be like.
I myself suffer from bipolar disorder. This means I go between depressive states, and manic states. I am of the type that my depressive states are the more problematic. I was able to relate directly to the experiences of the character you are to be portraying as I have been there. This game uses the mechanics as a metaphor well to tell you how sometimes an option is not an option just because you cannot get there.
This is a game everyone can take away something from. I issue anyone reading this a challenge. Playing through this, I want you to stop at each option and ask yourself, "What is the opposite of what I personally would do?" Then I want you to choose that answer.

As a person who suffers from severe depression, and has been for 9 years, I find this game amazing. This game was truly amazing, and I would reccomend it to every single person I know so they know what to do. Thank you, to the creators of this game.

Firstly, the title is a rogue-like, turn-based survival game with a medium-small sized lore where you must advance through floors, levelling and collecting equipment as you do so, to survive and win. The main problem comes with the limited variety of gameplay, and the methods to attempt to make the game more fun and unpredictable. This review is of the base game, without the use of any downloadable content or otherwise.
The game is always biased, giving a painful experience almost every playthrough due to such luck-based gameplay. Skill of the player is judged simply by how much one can utilise poorly thought out and tedious mechanics. The game seems to try to portray an extremely hostile environment with just enough for a competent player to survive but in reality the gameplay is almost completely based on finding overpowered items.
The textures and animations in the game are mediocre at best, usually including painful delays on attack animations and slowing the game down unnecessarily and forcefully without option to remove the feature.
When one modifies their computer, the save data including logs and recipes is completely wiped from the game due to lack of utilising of the steam cloud and inability to find save data on the computer's memory, despite such data being automatically recognised on most other games, wasting countless hours of gameplay.
To conclude, the game is unique in it's role as a turn-based rogue-like, but lacks any decent amount of strategy for serious gaming, and since most fun is taken from collecting new logs and equipment, it is hopeless to think many who would enjoy the casual uncontrollability would enjoy the slow-paced, turn-based gameplay for a prolonged time unless they enjoyed obtaining collectables.

Cautions
*The learning curve can be steep.
*You must manage a lot of resources.
*If you want to do well, you must play actively.
*Lots of death.
Benefits
+If you legitimately enjoy the game system, this game can challenge you for days upon days (if only most of my play-time wasn't done in offline mode!).
+If you're running an older rig or a laptop that's not meant for gaming, this is a solid purchase.
That being said, this game definitely falls under the category of roguelike.  You'll need to play to your character strengths, learn to minimize or bypass your character weaknesses, and learn to adapt your plan to what the game hands you.  There's lots of inventory management (until you learn what's important and to whom it's valuable) and lots of ways to die.  Fortunately, there are (optional) mechanics that let you store up game-progress and/or items to future characters.
If you're expecting an average dungeon-crawler or rogue-lite, this game may not be what you're looking for.  It's a game for those who enjoy thinking and planning AS A LEISURE.  Especially if you buy the DLC, there are plenty of character concepts to choose from and they all play differently.  I'd say the key play-affecting aspects in this game are resource management, risk-vs-reward, understanding probability, and tactical combat in a turn-based system.

What I like:
-The UI is very clean, though it lacks some key features, like recording discovered recipes.
What I dislike:
-The first 8 floors (I stopped playing 8 floors in) involved no tactics whatsoever. I had to keep a mental list of "this monster is scary enough to donate some bullets to it's face" and that was it. No positioning, no abilities, few combat consumables.
-The game felt like a total grind. Every door can be picked for exp, every crate jimmied open, every station hacked. There are a large number of such objects.
-Character customization felt... lacking. You can put points into various skills on level up, but I did not notice a significant impact, particularly for combat skills. It seems equipment is far more important for what form your character takes, and as that is pretty much totally random, it can hardly be called customization.
-The crafting is awful. Even Morrowind stored past recipes for you. SotS? Better keep a notebook of what strange combinations of bindings, cloth, and animal detritus obtain you useful equipment.  Sure, you can find hints to recipes in-game, but cross-referencing the ingredients listed in hints. (Note that crafting or absurd luck seems to be necessary to get decent equipment)
-Hoarding ingredients for crafting is awful. You can't craft just anywhere, you need to find a specific bench to craft each variety of item. You can either horde every ingredient (bad idea, inventory space is valuable) or track what ingredients are needed to make the thing you want.
I'm sure it's possible to derive enjoyment from this game, but to me it felt like a slog.

This game is a mixed bag of quality; on the one hand, the main storyline is plagued by under-developed characters and an overall forgettable narrative (not to mention the presence of Erin, the most annoyingly pretentious character to ever grace a Thief game). In fact the only character that I personally remember from the main storyline is a corrupt Watch officer named the Thief-Taker General, mainly because he was just so much fun to watch in the cutscenes (everyone else is either mopey or bland). Furthermore, certain levels in the main storyline feel annoyingly streamlined and linear, which hurts the overall experience greatly (at least for this player).
On the other hand, the gameplay itself is solid and the visuals are stunning. While certain levels do follow a specific path, others allow you to approach them in your own way. And some of them are even memorable, like the "Dirty Secrets" mission where Garrett infiltrates a brothel. I especially like how immersive Thief feels; the way Garrett interacts with the environment really feels natural, as if we're really seeing through his eyes. The game's setting, simply dubbed "The City", is a joy to explore -- especially with the new gadgets introduced in the game, which allow you to access places and trinkets that are otherwise unreachable. The atmosphere in The City is thick and gloomy, with sickness and doom as far as the eye can see. And for this reviewer, it was downright beautiful in its own twisted way.
Furthermore, the "custom difficulty" options are superb and really let the player customize his or her gameplay experience as desired. This was a spectacular idea by Eidos-Montreal, and is something we could stand to see more of in future triple-A titles. However, the difficulty interface is also hindered by Eidos-Montreal's bizarre decision to prevent the player from changing the difficulty mid-game, instead forcing players to start a whole new save file to experience higher or lower difficulty.
Overall, the matter of whether you'll like this game or not really depends on what you want from it; if you want a good story with interesting characters and a satisfying conclusion, don't bother. But if you want an immersive and atmospheric addition to your gaming library, or if you're just curious about Thief 2014 in general, I'd say give this one a go at least once (but it's not likely you'll care to go through the main storyline again). For a better overall experience, though, check out the original Thief trilogy -- all three games are dirt-cheap here on Steam, and this humble gamer recommends each and every one of them.

To begin, I want to establish that I haven't played any of the prior Thief games, so I'm not colored by the previous entries. However, that is not why I still can't bring myself to recommend this game. Overall, this feels like a game that has a lot of promise in theory, but it ultimately lacks the polish it needs to make it a truly good game that stands on its own merits.
Anyone expecting a game that combines stealth elements with combat will be disappointed, and rightly so. The focus in this game is on stealth and not getting caught doing what you're trying to do... It's up to you whether you slip past everyone without leaving a trace you were there (save for some pilfered items of value), or if you silently knock out guards one at a time to clear the room and loot at your leisure. But once you're sighted, get ready to have your health bar hammered. Normally, this would make for a very thought intensive game where you have to plan and time your movements to achieve your goals, but what gets in the way are controls that, to me, were less than intuitive. I spent half my time thinking of my route, then the other half trying to remember how to control the character. Frequently, I found myself trying to navigate some elevated platforms and support beams in order to avoid confrontation, only to be forced into it because my character didn't move just right and I'm suddenly plopped right in front of the city watch with a drastically reduced health bar.
Another jarring aspect for me was how difficult it was to gauge the 'awareness range' of the guards. In a lot of the current stealth games in the market, there's not much difficulty to learning when you're getting too close to the enemy, and when you're safe, but Thief almost seems to be set on a random number generator when it comes to enemy awareness. Sometimes, I'd be standing in the shadows not ten feet in front of them, and the guard just keeps moving as if I'm invisible. Other times, I'd be that close and suddenly the guards notice I'm there. While it upped the adrenaline of gameplay to constantly be 'on alert', it still made it even MORE difficult to plan my moves and make it through the area alive. On top of deadly combat, and a clunky movement system, it just serves to make the game that much more of a chore.
The world itself also shows a lot of talent, as there's a huge amount of visual detail in the graphics, and there's a number of things that serve to bring the game to life, but it all falls flat. There's only a few conversational tidbits that quickly get repeated in the game 2-hour gaming session, and while there's some unique conversations that serve to give you some useful info, I frequently disregarded them as 'background chatter'. There are unique items you can hunt for across the world, but mostly I came across these various and sundry items purely by accident, further pushing the immersive qualities of the game to background noise. I'll also confess that I can only name two characters, Garrett and The Thief-Taker General. One because his name was repeated in a review I saw on You-Tube for the game, the other because of the rather absurd title to start with. If I'm having trouble explaining the story and I can't even name characters after playing for a couple hours.... Well, it's not a good sign for me.
TL;DR summary: The game has a lot of promise, there's a lot of mechanics that make for some dynamic gameplay, and there's a rich world to place some very interesting stories and missions, but it simply is just too conflicted, unpolished, and frustrating to really make this more than a Steam Sale buy for people who are determined to play it. It honestly feels like a game that is still in Beta to me.

What should I say. This game is not like the other spinoffs of the Neptunia series. It's a JRPG with Visual Novel style story telling - just like the main series games.
The most obvious one is that all the characters not related to Planeptune are absent - this means no Noire, no Vert, no Blanc.
However seeing that the game includes the SEGA Hard Girls who represent the SEGA consoles it makes sense in a way.
As a player you move through multiple eras of the SEGA console history - each era having one goddess from the Neptunia series and one SEGA Hard Girl. In my opinion this way of telling the story works great.
And well: IF as a main character works perfectly well. She got a new sidekick for this game with Segami who's supposed to kind of represent SEGA as a whole. Both Segami and IF harmonise perfectly with each other character wise.
The basic gameplay is as you expect by Neptunia games. The battle system has been slightly adapted and allows for more variety of battle styles. Other things have been simplified.
A negative aspect about the game: the difficulty can be all over the place. The game seems to have a quest order in mind but as you can choose quests in a random order you might accidentally choose far too difficult quests for your level which would either require extreme grinding or retreat. Your choice.
The game uses those missions to tell its story. A short non spoiler idea: the history is disappearing. Goddesses and SEGA Hard Girls across all eras are fighting each other destroying everything. You have to return time to its original state - fix it and find out why it has changed.
Last but not least: graphics wise this isn't a cutting edge game. It's a Vita port. However, I like it. I grew up with SEGA consoles and the hints to my personal past were a lovely experience. If you love Neptunia, get it. If you love Neptunia and grew up with all those old consoles - get it, it's urgent.
Don't get it if you don't like the Neptunia style of story telling or RPGs with unbalanced difficulty spikes.

Anyway, i think that this is a good game that deserves a chance.

To try and put a simply binary good or bad on this game is do do it a great injustice. Simply put, This War of Mine is a poignant, dark, and depressing take on war through the eyes of the victims of war. It's loosely based on the Seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War and subsequent genocide during the unstable period in the Balkans in the 1990's. Echos of this appear throughout the game from military snipers indiscriminately shooting civilians to subtle details like a radio station broadcasting the discovery of a mass grave outside the city. My first thoughts on this had me questioning how tasteful the of the theme of the game was and made me uncomfortable to say the least. However, war child does nothing to glorify anything about this war.
The controls are simple and the mechanics work. Survival is difficult. Winter is cold and wood for burning in the heater of your shelter becomes scarce. If you use all your wood for burning, you might not have enough to forify your shelter which makes you suseptible to looters who can injure the survivors and steal valuable resources. Food is scarce, medicine is even scarcer and the player will have to make some hard decisions regarding their resource management. Do I trade this bottle of antibiotics for these tools or should I hold on to them just in case? Do I help the neighbors with this canned food or do I hang on to it incase we run out of meat? These are the questions you'll have to ask yourself frequently. Conditions aren't just static in the city either. For example, snow or fighting between rebels and government forces can block of previously accessable locations for looting, forcing you to wait until it clears up which can be anywhere from a couple days to a week or two in-game time.
To top it all off, the survivors are all pretty frail compared to their contemporaries in other games. Some more than others. This isn't any old game where you can wrap up a wound in a field dressing and treat a wound imediately. Getting shot two or three times will kill your survivor. If your survivor lucky enough to get away, you'll have to scramble to find enough rare and expensive bandages to dress the wounded for days while they basically take bed rest. You'll be short staffed for awhile while they heal and if it gets cold and they happen to fall ill while recovering it could very well spell the end that person. While falling ill, getting wounded, and starving to death are certainly all risk, the psychological aspect is powerful and emotional in this game. Characters have mental health and are effected by the actions of other survivors, their own actions, their physical state, addictions, and by how safe they feel depending on their individual personality. The stress and sadness of survival is real to them.
These mechanics and a narrative from each survivor that unfolds throughout the conflict really create great atmosphere. Despite almost no background narrative, each character is done so well that you'll find their decisions seperating from yours to an extent. The emotional rollercoaster of this game is watching your characters feel guilt over things that both you and they felt were necessary, but are morally damning. As a player, the attachment you feel to these characters makes them seem so much more than just simple scripts and textures.
The few issues with this game are really just the replay value, which is not as infinite as it seems and the occasionally silly AI movement mechanics. Other than that, This War of Mine takes the often ignored perspective of conflict and creates a stellar, emotional, and difficult survival title out of it. If War Child suceeded in one thing it is creating the theme and atmosphere that there is no black and white, but only progressively murkier and questionable shades of grey.
In war, everyone is a victim.

Well after playing the game for a bit and getting a hang of it, I think I can make a decent review on the game. Do keep in mind it's in Early Access, so many things are subject to change. I will include suggestions that can be added to the game later.
So Pros
-It's a fairly easy game to run, getting 70+ fps on native resolution with medium graphics.
-Has a customization system sort of like Blacklight Retribution, now there's not many customizations, but that'll probably change
-A firing range to test customizations before I buy them
-Small group of developers. I think because Blackspot Entertainment is a small company, they can focus more on the players and have better communication with the community unlike big companies like Nexon.
-Nice community
-A variety of guns, (not yet) but it'll definitely come.
Now to the Cons/ Suggestions
-Add player limiting, maybe I want to 1v1 my friend without locking the room. Or have a simple team based 5v5 classic search and destroy without locking the room
-I don't know how spread is calculated in the game, I primarily use the AK-74 and sometimes my bullets are not first shot accurate. Maybe have a set spread like CS:GO? Or at least have first shot accuracy.
-More servers. I believe the servers are located in California, I'm in NY and I get red 3 bar ping. Which isn't terrible, but I sometimes get lag spikes middle combat.
-The movement feels clunky, I don't know how to describe it but things feel slow. Also when I quickswitch with the L11 after I shoot, the scope zooms out very slowly and sort of glitches out
-Weapons are too expensive and GP is hard to earn. Daily missions give 1k GP per mission, but weapons costs 200k plus. Ranking up gives me 2k GP, which is barely anything. Customization is an average of 4k GP per item.
-I think there should be a different set of customization for secondary weapons. When I have the largest silencer on my M92SF, it actually covers my iron sights. Also a sniper scope on a M92SF is ridiculous.
-Nade throws should be affected more by movement. If im running and jumping my nade should go farther, also the standard distance for nade throws is kind of short, realistically soldiers should throw nades much farther.
-Better lighting, enemies blend in with dark rooms
I'm not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the game, there's much to be worked on and there's so much potential to the game.

People really over hype how bad this game is, but honestly, its no where near as bad as its made out to be. Line of Sight is a game along the lines of Combat Arms, A.V.A, and other early F2P FPS games from the past. Its fast paced, its frantic, and once you understand that, its a hell of a lot of fun. However, most people either don't understand this, or come in expecting other things. If you want a slow, methodical game, you might have come to the wrong place. Another thing to bring up is the netcode, hit registration, and other factors.
First off, I must point out that this is an Early Access. Despite clearly saying that, everyone refuses to understand what that entails. This is NOT a finished product. A lot of content from the other territories is left out along side unfinished networking, hit reg, and hitboxes. Buying this is buying into an Beta. Another thing is that this is made by a indie studio. The only way to launch the game was in Early Access. Some people have complained the game was listed under Free To Play when it was Buy To Play in the beta period. That is a mistake by the devs, but with a message or post on the community hub, that could be fixed easily. These are some of the most dedicated and friendly devs I've seen. Even before release, I have messaged them about grammatical errors on their steam page and they responed in an hour and fixed it in less than a day. They then proceeded to let the fans be proof readers for the game by recruiting on a Facebook post. If that isn't any indication that they care about this game a whole lot, then just look at their announcements. Already they are tackling the biggest issues and complains about the games in game money, graphics, and weapon balance.
All in all, the game isn't done. Thats what should be said first and foremost. Is it bad though? Not at all. I played the game prerelease on Brazilian servers, and I can say that the game is exactly what I anticipated and lived up to my hype. Line of Sight is a love letter and call back to the F2P FPS games of the late 2000s and early 2010s, and I hope it catches its niche and stays alive for a good long while.

After sinking 15h in this game I must say first that most if not all the negative reviews are from last year where the game went to sale prematurely, however the game grew A LOT from that time and really improved itself in all aspects.
But what its The Black Death? Its a gloomy survival game set in probably one of the most hopeless times in the history of humanity, where you will have to scavenge, trade, craft, farm, kill, hunt and steal to survive. If this concept is exciting for you, please support the game.
On to the specifics:
PROS:
- The class system. Not everyone is a fighter each class is good at something and players need to interact with one another to grow, for example: If you play a merchant, you can fight but you wont be very good at it, so if you need to go to a dangerous area, your best bet is hiring another knight or militia player to escort or go for you, so on and so forth. The game has those kind of interactions as objectives, and is growing really fast towards it. Just the other day I bought some stuff iron ores from a player smith!
- Resource gathering. Resources vary gratly from area to area, so you are always encouraged to explore to find the materials you need and in the best quality possible.
- Crafting. It is not cryptic as in other games, you unlock recipes with skill points and those will tell you what materials you need for it, the quality of those materials determine the chance you have to succesfully crafting the item and its durability.
-The community. When you are able to talk with other players, in my whole experience, everyone has been extremely nice and helpfull.
- The disease system. You can get ill in a lot of different ways, it brings a nice challenge.
THE CONS
- Low average player count. This game had a lot of bad reviews at launch and its still in early access so its understandable, but having more people to interact with always enhances the experience. You will be able to do so at times, but expect to sometimes have a more solo experience.
- Combat. The combat isnt bad itself, the concept is decent enough and it actually works but it has to be ironed out BIG time, the animations are and buggy and clunky specially on animals.
-Class change. To change classes you need in the current version to commit suicide, loosing you night survival progress (you keep the unlocked skills), it sucks I know, but there are ways to make it just a minor annoyance, such as having a house with storage or simply stashing your things in a world container while you change. I think this is just temporary though.
My overall opinion
The Black Death is a surprisingly fun game, especially considering the state its in. The devs are really passionate about the project and are always looking for ways to improve the game. At first I bought it just for the concept, not expecting anything, and now I play it every day, and if it is this entertaining at this point in dev I cant wait to see how will the final product turn out. The price may be slightly above the ideal, but please go support this game, if you are looking for a world to immerse yourself and survive in medieval times, you will not be disappointed. And if you are ever in the Chicago server, shoot me an inbox!

SO, When I initially downloaded this game a few days ago, I couldn't get it to load. Every time I would click play from Steam, it would tell me that a fatal error had occurred, and that it couldn't passthrough C:\blahblahblah... I thought that this was because I was having Administrator Issues with my computer, so I restarted but it never worked. Today I was so frustrated that it wasn't working, I went into the Program Files and under Steam\SteamApps\common\Thief I had 2 binaries folders. You should only have one folder called "Binaries", but I had that one and one that was called Binaries2. Apparently everytime I pushed play, it would try to go to binaries, and open the 64 bit exe, but the binaries folder said to go to binaries2 to launch the exe. Well Steam basically didn't know how to do that, so it just failed. THIS IS HOW TO FIX IT. Which ever binaries folder you have that has the .dlls and the exe that is 30 or so MB, keep that binaries folder and delete the other one. Rename the folder "Binaries" and then try to launch from Steam again. Very very weird, but somehow it installed incorrectly. But when I was troubleshooting before and verified the game files from Steam, it said they were all ok, so I feel like there are probably a lot of people that will have this same problem. Hope this helps :)
Just to clarify, you should have a folder in Thief called "Binaries", and this folder should contain 2 folders, "Win32" and "Win64". Both of those win folders should have a few .dll files, and the .exe that is about 30ish MB. If you have 2 binaries folders, delete the one that doesn't have these files and rename the other so it is just "Binaries".

I recently played Watson's Watch on my stream at the request of a friend, who gifted me the game (so it was free, but not from the developer.) This isn't my cup of tea, so to speak, but I'm reviewing the game, not the genre.
Watson's Watch is a JRPG-styled indie game. It is short (I started and finished it in the same stream, and the always-onscreen clock in the corner showed me that it took 75 minutes.) Contributing to the shortness is that the game is very linear. There's really only one straight-path like route through the game... in that sense, it's really more of an interactive fiction than a traditional game; while it's true you can go where you please (among possible destinations), the story only unlocks in a "follow the bread crumbs" manner. This is where it becomes not my cup of tea... I am much more into games with a modicum of freedom. However, some people just want a good story, and that's the strength of Watson's Watch.
The player character is a detective staying at a hotel in town. A mystery is soon presented, and the first episode is about putting that puzzle together. For what it is, it's a good game. If a story is what you're after, and you're a fan of JRPGs, then Watson's Watch just may be for you. At the very least, with its price point, you could do far worse. I will amend this review when Episode 2 comes out, and I have seen more of the story.
PROS:
Strong story, with a number of plot twists.
Simple and easy to run (if your computer is reading this, it can run it.)
CONS:
Very linear.
No options at all (the ability to change the volume level of the music would be nice, although I suspect that lack of that is to set the mood and tone. However, the ability to change the game resolution would have been very welcome.)
Ultimately, the downsides of this game are not enough to outweigh the benefits, which is why I recommend this if the genre appeals to you. Enjoy your stay in Watson's Watch!

So here I am, writing my first early access review. I'm trying to balance out the fact that there is a lot of progress to be made while still providing constructive criticism. To sum up my thoughts in one sentence: Watson's Watch needs work, but it has several promising elements that make me want to see more. For further details, please keep reading!
I had never heard of Watson's Watch until I saw it in an IndieGala bundle. Being the sucker I am for RPGMaker games, I happily kept it. At the time of purchasing it, Watson's Watch had no reviews. Thus, I put it high on my priority list of games to play so I could help people decide whether it is worth picking up or not. It only has one episode released so far out of three, so everything I write here is based on this first episode.
Watson's Watch is a mystery game that focuses on storytelling. There is no combat, nor does your character have stats at all. I didn't go in expecting any, and it suits me just fine. If you want a "typical" RPG with turn-based battles and such, you're in the wrong place. If you're interested in a fairly good story with some intriguing elements, it ought to suit you well.
To avoid spoilers, here's a bare-bones summary. You play as a detective (who you get to name) that is on vacation in a town called Watson's Watch. Except work never takes a break, because while he's staying in a hotel, he learns people in Watson's Watch have gone missing. Suspecting foul play, he takes on the case, and it's your job to lead him in the right direction.
The mystery elements are good. It kept me wanting to know what twists and turns would occur. Watson's Watch is a strange town that serves as an effective setting. The answers that come forth are not as clear-cut as one might first believe. The story leaves off in episode one at an effective cliffhanger point. I am a bit puzzled as to why some of the bigger plot twists were revealed in episode one, but I trust that they are needed for the remaining two episodes.
One thing that bugs me, though, is that you don't do a lot of detective work. Let me compare this to the Ace Attorney series for a better example. In Ace Attorney games, you can go to multiple scenes and interact with people in different orders, find clues at your own pace, and take different routes to the same outcome. In Watson's Watch, you have a linear path that can only be deviated from a limited amount of times. I don't mind a railroaded plot if it makes sense. However, you are working as a sleuth. It was weird to me that there really wasn't much exploring, especially with so few places to visit. Honestly, this might be one of the biggest flaws for this game to have, given what type it is.
On a higher note, the characters are done well overall. The protagonist has more to him than meets the eye. There are different traits to each person that define them for who they are. Even the cab driver has his own quirks. Yet some of the actions these characters take are a bit strange. I can't go into much further detail without spoiling it, but there is one especially odd choice at the end of the game that left me scratching my head. Luckily, that's what early access is for. I plan to bring some of these concerns up in the forums with a proper spoiler-warning title.
The dialogue could use some work. Some of it feels a bit disjointed. There are spelling and grammar errors all over the place, but I still understood everything. I would normally be a lot harder on those kinds of errors, especially in a story-driven game, but the developers have said they are working on fixing these. Since they have said that and it is an early access game, I'm more understanding of it in this circumstance.
Speaking of the developers, they are friendly and responsive. I reported a bug and they fixed it swiftly. They seem dedicated to the project and eager to hear player feedback. That goes a long way in my mind. I appreciate developers that seek constructive criticism and that pour their hearts into their works. That kind of passion is in Watson's Watch, which is one reason I am enthusiastic about where this game will go.
All that being said, the cost of the game is still pretty high. It took me two hours or so to beat the first chapter of Watson's Watch. If all the other chapters are going to be that length, we're looking at about six hours total. A two-hour RPGMaker game would have to have something truly spectacular to warrant a $7.99 price tag. When the entire thing is released, I'd say that it's still a tad bit high, but more acceptable. I was quite pleased with it as a bundle purchase, but I would have felt ripped off if I poured the full price into it. At least, I would have felt ripped off at this stage of the game. It will supposedly cost the same amount when the final version is out, so that might be justified.
Graphics-wise, everything looked fine to me. I don't know much about common RPGMaker assets so I can't say if they're overused or not. It ran smoothly beyond that bug I mentioned, which has already been fixed. The controls are simple. However, you can't sprint. That really, really bugged me. A lot of RPGMaker games let you run, and that would have made it less tedious to check some areas for further clues. There were some oddities (apparenlty you can walk on water!), but nothing that got more than a shrug from me.
Other than an items list, you also have a journal. That's useful for keeping tabs on where you need to go and getting some insight in what the protagonist is thinking. It's a good combination for a game like this. The journal does assist a bit in the railroading, though, so I'm torn on whether I think it's good in its current state or could use some alterations.
There are four achievements present, with two being automatic to find and two being more out of the way. I like that ratio, and they were a nice touch. Apparently there will be trading cards added at some point. It would be nice, but it's not necessary by any means.
In conclusion, I like a lot of what Watson's Watch does. If this version was the final product and was selling on Steam for this price, I would probably not recommend it, much as I enjoyed playing it. However, for an early access version with promised improvements and two more chapters coming, I encourage those interested in the game to pick it up, play it, and weigh in your recommendations to the developers. The complete package should definitely be worth it!

While it came out years before the show, this is probably the closest any game has come to capturing the spirit of
.
This is simply the best space-pirate game ever made.  It does an amazing job combining a tactile sense of realism - freighters you're stealing from ejecting their supply-boxes into space so your support can tractor-beam them in and take them back to your base - with simplicity and smooth, easy-to-use controls.  The game is at it's best when you're just lazily shooting around the galaxy looking for possible heists.  The entire universe is dynamic and feels alive, allowing you to predict what sorts of shipments will pass through which gates or arrive at which stations - a mining station, for example, would import supplies and export ore.
And, smartly, the game makes almost all the new technology you unlock for your ships and wingmen be "sidegrades", ways of customizing them for specific missions rather than just numerical increases, so it feels like your capabilities are expanding rather than just keeping up with higher-numbered enemies.
The game isn't completely perfect.  Inexplicably, you have to fiddle with a config file to get mouse controls working (you can find a premade one if you search online; for some reason it was included with the GOG release and not this one.)  Additionally, the difficulty of missions is all over the place, sometimes spiking dramatically with no warning, sometimes throwing you softball after softball.  Finally, it's possible to accidentally bypass a huge chunk of the main quest by accident (if you find yourself in the second part of the galaxy without having really explored the first, you screwed up.)  Still, given the low asking price today, these are minor issues for a game that captures the core essence of "be a space pirate rebel" so perfectly.

Even before you hit the menu screen, you've seen that same Hemingway quote so often trotted out by the Call of Duty series: "In modern war you die like a dog for no good reason." Except in This War of Mine, that quote really is a guiding principle. As you try to lead a group of survivors during an unnamed conflict, by scavenging for items, jury-rigging survival aids like heaters and vegetable gardens, and bartering with other survivors for goods, you might occasionally feel like you're getting the hang of wartime survival. But then This War of Mine reminds you, in shockingly effective and heartbreaking fashion, that war doesn't follow predictable rules. Sometimes everyone just dies, with no rhyme or reason.
One of my first games of This War of Mine turned out to be one my easiest, but I had no idea how well I was doing until later runs, when I struggled to regain the same ground. This time, my three survivors — Bruno, Pavle, and Marko — had almost everything they needed. I watched over them from the 2D, cutaway view of their shelter as fresh water came via a rain trap I'd built from assembled raw materials, and fresh meat came in from the homemade animal trap in the basement. They had a series of small workshops where they could build new furniture and appliances, plus an herbal workshop where they could create fresh bandages and homemade medicine.
By night, Bruno usually slept in one of the homemade beds while Pavle stood watch over the apartment with a knife, protecting it from looters, and Marko went scavenging in the city. Every morning my game auto-saved, ensuring that I couldn't undo any nighttime disasters.
The scavenging phase plays out as a tense, atmospheric 2D stealth game. While some abandoned locations are looters' playgrounds, the war-torn city features a lot of other unsavory types. Soldiers and militia might be willing to trade with you or simply ignore you, but they can turn on you in a heartbeat. Other survivors might shoot you on sight. Rummaging through a pile of rubble sends sound waves far into the distance, alerting people to your presence. Get spotted in a place where you shouldn't be, and you'll have a choice: run, hide, fight, or die.

Alright. So... how do you describe Dungeons of Dreadmore?
- - - - -
Imagine, if you will: You are in a room. There is a pair of pants on the floor, a hunk of cheese, and a door in the far wall. There are vending machines to your right and left, and you have a sword in your hand.
These are your first moments in the dungeon.
You grab the pants and cheese, walk over to the door, and push it. Its locked. So you kick it untill it finaly splinters and falls down. Inside the room, wall to wall, floor to celling, packed with monsters.
And they all turn and stare at you.
These are your last moments in the dungeon.
- - - - - -
So, overall? This game will beat you over the head with a rusty pipe, mug you, and then call the police and tell them you called thier mothers fat.
Yet, you will grit your teeth in frusration, slam the reload button, and take another shot at the Monster Zoo that turned you into a pile of mewling organs.
Why?
'Cause loosing is fun.
10/10. If you can get it on sale, do it, but totaly worth buying at full price. DLC is totaly worth it, ands a bunch of additonal content, plus five more levels of ball-busting dificulty. The modding community is still active, and has a wiki dedicated to helping mod the game. Very fun.

This game... oh, this game.
Very rarely do I find a game that I consider I might actually play -Forever- (or at least until I am no longer able to).  This is one of those games.  I will play it, revisit it, time and time again, until I can't anymore.  It's that epic.
True to it's rogue-like nature, there is very little hand-holding in this game.  There isn't -too- much to figure out for yourself, but there is definitely enough to keep things interesting.  The turn-based combat is refreshing, as is the way you can use items (clicking on an enemy while holding a bolt from your inventory will shoot them with said bolt).
The base stats are a a refreshing new twist, with stats not seen in any other games.  Of course, you've got about a million ways to start your character depending on what type of play-style you're going through.  Base stats serve only to enhance secondary stats, which are used throughout most of the game.  Nothing big to figure out, but you could definitely be a min/maxer if you wanted to be.  I prefer the role-play / lore route.
Perma-death mode is the only mode I'll ever play.  As your characters die, your name, level, and score all get added to a giant headstone which shows all of your previous deaths as well.  Making it exceedingly interesting to see just how much farther you can push into the dreaded Dungeons of Dredmor.
Over all, I HIGHLY recommend this game.  I feel like it is one out of over 150 titles that I own that I got much, much more than I paid for.  If you pass this one up, you're missing out.  Buy it.  Buy it now.

Really good fun. Takes a little while to learn all the things that are possible, but once you learn the game mechanics, you're on your way!
Totally recommend.

Positives:
Though still in need of some refinement and balancing—and possibly some additional features—the core gameplay of Mini Metro scratches that city-building itch without requiring a major investment of time. You can play this on a break without worrying you'll be sucked in for hours (though you won't get bored if you did waste a day on it).
The interface is a case study in complex, context-sensitive functionality from simple interactions. Click, hover, drag and drag paths all combine to do just what you want without requiring a tutorial. Though you might spend your first game puzzling it out, it all just works how you'd expect on the first or second try. Pure, blissful affordance. If only more games thought out their interface so elegantly.
Negatives:
There is a well-known "cheat" that isn't really a cheat (it's inherent in the game rules) but that renders the leaderboards meaningless. The devs are still struggling with this issue, and I think it's resolution must lie in clarifying the game's biggest ambiguity: am I running a simulation of a real subway network (in which case, shouldn't it cost me something to re-route lines) or am I stress-testing a subway plan by iterative design under increasing load (in which case, shouldn't I have some prior information about where additional stations will appear). This ambiguity is at the heart of the game's ultimate success or failure, and the devs need to do more than apply band-aid solutions and ad hoc rule tweaks. I feel like the solution is to split the game into entirely different game modes which rest on different existential assumptions about what the game really is.
A little more information and clarity, compactly presented, would reduce some of the minor frustrations and provide greater insight into the network you've built. How many trains do I have on a given subway line? Can I see some meaningful data on throughput or efficiency? I have trouble believing the devs haven't read any of Edward Tufte's masterful works on data presentation. They'd do well to revisit his books for ideas.
[REVISED] The passenger AI is improving. Rather than being deterministically stubborn, passengers have acquired a variability that sometimes even includes whimsical train hopping in the wrong direction and then back again. This is an improvement. There's often more than one way from A to B, not to mention that sometimes B2 or B3 offer variety. It's slightly mad, but it's better than robots.
Some other minor complaints:
- why am I limited to 4 trains per line? Couldn't that limit be a function of the line's length and/or the number of stations?
- why can't a line go around a river bend rather than cutting the corner and requiring a tunnel?
- why no save feature? sometimes I'm having a very successful game, but I have to get back to work, or join friends in another game
TL;DR:
Enjoyable game. Can be played casually or obsessively. Brilliant with the potential to be an all-time classic. Well worth full price. It would be criminal to wait for a sale price.

Let me start by saying this is quite a good game, but you have to persevere with it because it takes time to get used to the controls. Making use of the map is to be advised, because memorising the layout of the city is pretty hard, particularly when you often travel through peoples' homes, over roof-tops and through service tunnels. The first few levels are a bit lacking in interest and you need to find Basso, who gives Garrett - the thief - underworld jobs to do. The main story leads to set-piece missions, which reveal the mysterious and supernatural details of Garrett's quest.
The graphics and sound are really very good, although there are one or two places that are a bit rough around the edges. Before I played it, I wasn't sure about the historically mixed-up environment. After playing the game though, I realised the other-worldliness suited it, like Bioshock Infinite, which is very similar both in the game-world and the story. I will say, though, that the story is not fleshed out very well and you encounter interesting characters who go on to play little further part.
The game pushes you towards stealth and away from combat. When the watch-men are alerted, you can either hide, run away, or club them in the face until they are unconscious or dead. Other opponents require different strategies. The combat frequently involves using the environment to enhance your bow attacks. Garrett is quite weak, which encourages sneakiness over brute force, particulalry beyond level 4 (by which stage the controls should be mastered). One-on-one, Garrett can stand his ground, but oponents usually start a 'hue and cry'. There's actually an imperative from the very beginning to kill as few people as possible, preferably none. You can also earn greater rewards for specialising in thief-like characteristics, rather than murdering people with your bow and club.
Thief won't necessarily please someone who wants a straightforward FPS, but if skulking in the shadows, crawling through ducts, pick-pocketing, and looting are your thing, then I'm confident that you will enjoy this game. I would say though, that you have to be really keen to get the most out of it. If you try to play the game almost entirely without being spotted, then you will find it virtually impossible first time around. You could replay it using a different approach to brute force, but life is too short to waste time on such a difficult task.

The platforming aspect isn't for everyone but it's not unfair as other reviews have said. There aren't any blind jumps in a pitch black evironment save for a moment after beating a boss near the end of chapter 2, but I didn't die from it at all. The Cat Lady is a story heavy horror game with very simple mechanics and puzzles but one of the darkest and best-told stories I've seen in a video game. No doubt it requires great game design skills to make the average player feel some empathy for a suicidal protagonist who at first does nothing but complain about how useless and awful life is, and the fact that The Cat Lady manages to do so in such an artistic way is what makes it one of my favorite games of all time. Susan Ashworth is not only brought to life by incredible voice acting, but also she is so smart and skeptic and has such a strong personality, it doesn't take long for you to stop being annoyed by her "emo-ness" and get really interested in knowing why she is so tired of living. Simple art and simple mechanics, original storyline, great character development and over the top voice acting. Any psychological horror fan should play this... probably more than once.

I can recommend this game, but only as long as you get it on sale, or if you manage to pick it up off the Humble Bundle like I did weeks ago.
Tower of Guns is a simple game where you pick yourself a gun, pick yourself a perk, and then go into the titular Tower of Guns to destroy robots. If you wish, you can enable to "silly story" mode that gives you a randomized story each time you play the game, but that's just left to dialogue at the start of a level and sometimes at the end. Story is put on the backseat for the gameplay, so the gameplay must be good, right?
Well, I would say the gameplay is polished, but not good. If you played something like an arena shooter or touhou before, you'll do fine. Only a few enemies actually move, and the rest just stand still and shoot at you, which makes it easy to destroy them. The "challenge" comes from an overspawn of enemies, sometimes right on top of you when you enter a new room (literally, they appear right on top of you, this is not an exaggeration). Well, that's one of the games selling points. Jump around, roll around at the speed of sound, and shoot stuff. So the game is polished, you shouldn't have FPS issues, but the problem is. It's boring. The guns themselves don't really offer much of a difference in a "kick". They are feel the same when you fire them, there is no "weight" shown to the guns, no real recoil. The only difference between a gun is how fast it shoots, how big the bullet is, and how much damage it does. When you realize that, then its just plain smarter to pick up one of the "rocket" guns, pick the perk that makes you immune to self-damage, and jump-n-shoot.
Levels are short. Very short. Before you enter each new level, you're given a PAR time, which can go from two minutes to five minutes, and you don't need to kill all the enemies you see. You could jump-n-shoot from door to door until you get to the boss of the level, kill it, and move on. The levels also lack variation. If you've been to the "Warehouse" level at least three times, then you've seen everything the Warehouse will ever offer you. You'll be able to move through it like it was nothing, you'll be able to know where the power-ups are probably hiding, you can take a detour to the secret rooms, then head for the doors.
Perks seem to have minor differences that don't make much of a difference in the long-run. The starting perk lets you have three jumps, but you can aquire items that give you three jumps anyway. Some perks increase armor or speed, but again, you can just find items. Speaking of items, they are very ehh. You got stat items, and usable items. Stat items are just increases or decreases in things like HP, difficulty, armor, etc. As for the usable items, well, this will make me sound dumb, but I wasn't sure what some of them did. One item I used kept me from moving for a bit, and I decided to not use that anymore, another item regenerated my HP as long as I was standing in a green pool, and another gave me a pea-shooter (PEW PEW) that could be fired along with my normal gun. The usable items are also given dumb, "silly" names that just... why? Really, why? If I pick up a usable, I want to know, from the start, what it does, and only like three items gave me a clue of what they did.
But it can be a decent time waster if you only got an hour or two to play a game. Don't buy it at the full price, however. Wait for a sale or for it to go on a humble bundle again.

10 hours in now and I'm still learning.
Tower of Guns is great some of the best Run 'n' Gun Fun available.
The game mechanics aren't too punishing or lazy, things are simple and work well, when you are fighting through a horde of spikes are shooting a wall of spikes you don't need clutter and there isn't.
The gameplay is fast and keeps you on your toes even with a high level gun with a powerful mod to boot, level design is great fun and beautifully imagined. The secrets idea is great fun as you'll never know when you'll find one or see a platform above you and wonder whats up there and you may well spend minutes scouring a level for fake walls and platforms long after the enemies are gone.
The silly stories are good for a chuckle and when you're tired of them or you've seen them all it allows you to turn them off which is good of the devs to make things like that toggleable.
The Guns are all good in their own way (except perhaps the basic pistol and the pizza cutter early on) and even the ones which aren't particularly great it is fun to see how powerful you can get them with the available weapon mods. You can turn your Dakka weapon into an uber firing, minelaying, level 6 dealer of death or your rocket launcher into a enemy seeking, rapid fire rocket cannon, the mix and match opportunities available are excellent as it will keep you hunting for different mods.
The perk system is well thought out, you have ones which soften the game for you, increase difficulty and ones which can help you in certain ways or allow certain playstyles but I won't spoil anything. Some make a few achievements slightly easier for you to get too but of course you must unlock them first by completing the challenges set to you. The game progression is geared around getting you to play more but it doesn't force you to grind anything as you'll be doing it anyway.
The items are funny and effective, some seem almost benign whilst others you are scared to activate and some you don't want to waste just now...or now....not yet.....not ju-- damn, another death.
Endless mode is excellent fun too, the more you go on the more upgrades you can find and end up like myself did on endless level 38 with 35 jumps available, a rapid firing with an insta crit mod, max health & armour so tough I was nigh invincible or so I thought but at the end of it I'd discovered all sorts of goodies and upgrades which you are allowed to see at the end of your gunning and in the collection menu.
The enemy types are great and varied, I probably haven't discovered them all yet hopefully. Some are utter fodder for you whilst others are an absolute bane and must be prioritised above the others. Some combinations of enemies compliment each other well whcih adds an added threat for you to overcome. The look of the turrets and other mobs is wonderful. The art style they've employed for them is great, it's not graphically intensive and it doesn't need to be as they are often dead by the time you've got close enough to look at the paintwork and sometimes it gets so overwhelmingly full of things trying to kill you that lag spikes can occur if you really are dishing out the punishment.
The loot drops are good and gives you something to look forward to at the end of the level whilst also making destroying enemies a neccessity to advancement, of course once your all sorted you can just bounce through levels completely disregarding all foes but the boss, you might even grab an achievement for that.
The shop system is good and doesn't pressure you into using it as the item is almost always visible so there are no let downs unless you let yourself in for it.
Also I want a Hugbot Plushie, Velcro hands to pose in a huggy manner.
Get Tower of Guns, you can pick it up and put it down whenever you want and it's just damn good fun.

Visual: Great for what it is and what was to be expected. Has atmosphere. Has nice touches to make the places feel different and unique for the most part. Characters and monsters despite their small numbers were nicely designed. 8.76/10.
Audio: Music fits the visuals and atmosphere. Sound effects are well-suited for the actions taken. 8.25/10

The boss battles were also just a series of patterns that you dodge and counter. Nothing complex, but still a challenge the first few times around.
The real challenge of this game would be beating all these bosses without getting hit a single time. Along with other achievements that I think would really be achievements should people manage to do them. The few secrets in the game were interesting finds. Items don't offer many choices, and overall not really necessary to the game, though they were nice touches. 8.37/10
Story: No story really. There's just enough story to justify why and what your character is doing. No explanation about why the antagonist is doing what she's doing, other than maybe that she suddenly became crazy or possessed. Still, doesn't explain how she got possessed or why the demon or ghost chose to possess her. Nothing is known about the protagonist other than that she is a priestess from a village. No background story offered to any character. Dialogue in games are short as they are sparse (not necessarily a bad thing, but I did want just a little more than what was offered). Overall, since this isn't really a story-oriented game, and I didn't particularly expect it to be, along with the relative standard of the game's expectation, I waive giving the story any score.
Overall, buy it and enjoy, especially on sale.
