Momodora: RUtM is a metroidvania platformer that I've come to enjoy. At the time of writing this, I've only put an hour and a half into the game thusfar, but I would have to say that it has been a pleasant experience thusfar!
Graphics: 8/10 -- It goes for the retro style, harkening back to the old 8-bit style of NES platformers, and I feel that it achieves this very well. It isn't a lazy sort of retro 8-bit that we've seen in many other games; the spritework and the environment art show attention to detail while maintaining that 8-bit retro feel. Even things such as detailed idle animations if you let your character stand still for a second are here.
Sound: 8/10 -- This game is called "Reverie Under the Moonlight" and the background music very much fits the theme of the game. It's a dark and depressing world, and the themes I've encountered thusfar are good, while the boss battles are good for getting you psyched and pumped up for a fight. The sound effects are also pleasant -- not too overbearing but yet exactly what they need to be. My only nitpick here is the character's death scream; not really a complaint but a personal preference is that it is a bit... unsettling. Fitting, but unsettling. Personal opinion.
Controls: 7/10 -- The game's movement is nice and snappy. Your character does exactly what you tell her to do, and the game's physics are very solid and fluid, and consistent. The double-jump mechanic takes a little to get used to, but once you do everything feels nice. I subtracted one point for lack of legacy controller support, though. I don't like using xpadder to use non-360 controllers. Platformers REALLY need to support non-360 controllers, because I am not going to want to play a 2d sidescroller with an analog stick, so I use a Playstation2 controller hooked up via a USB adapter so I can get a nice solid D-pad. So, please consider adding this in either a patch, or any future Momodora games. People like me would thank you kindly for it.
Gameplay: 9/10 -- The game is very basic (in a good way!). You have your short-range melee, a ranged, a dodge, a double-jump and an active item. That's it. That's all you should ever need in a metroidvania IMO. This game does it quite well.
Challenge: 9/10 -- Selectable challenge difficulties FTW! The fastest way to make me happy. I started the game on Normal (there's an Easy) and the challenge feels about right. At first the game felt a little cheap becuase it is so easy to die, but restarting from last save is fast and easy, no loading screens or anything and save points are dispersed around and it isn't too hard to get back to where you died for another try. Boss fights seem a little long, though but I bet later on, after a few health pool upgrades and healing items, it won't be so bad. The first boss or two, though? You might need a few retries but they have predictable patterns and don't feel TOO cheap. I think they did rather well here.
Overall: 8/10. Very solid game, and well worth the price point. The only cons I can think of, is the lack of legacy controller support and I put 75 minutes into the game and already have 40% of the map explored so the game seems a little short. But I don't mind that so much, for such a pleasant experience.

I played through this game twice, and I can honestly say that I recommend it. However, there are a few things you should know before you get into it.
It is exactly what it says on the tin: an interactive (non)fiction game. "Interactive fiction" fits better than "visual novel" because it's almost entirely text-based. Sure, there are some accompanying pictures, but the text is the main focus. The "(non)fiction" label fits well because while the scenarios and characters are entirely made up, the underlying premises are very real. The descriptions of how the main character feels and what they're thinking are scarily accurate for someone suffering from depression. You can tell that the people who wrote this have firsthand experience with it.
Playing this made me anxious, not gonna lie. The breezy writing style lets you immerse yourself in the main character's persona, and I had some heart-poundingly anxious moments while playing this. The scene where you talk to Attic about what's going on damn near made me cry, because he said exactly what I needed to hear in that moment.
My only complaint about this game is how easy it is to railroad yourself onto the worst possible path, and end up with the "bad ending." The choices you make at the beginning of the game have much more of an effect on the outcome than your later choices. The degree to which your options are limited in the last half of the game is a tad unrealistic; having been in the depths of this debilitating condition myself, I can say that even at my worst, I could still at least attempt to bring myself to do things that were blocked in the game. I found this unneccesarily restrictive. I understand that it's meant to illustrate the hopelessness that one often feels when deeply depressed, but it still felt unrealistic.
Bottom line: this game is not "fun." It's not meant to be "fun." It's meant to illustrate the struggles that depressed people go through every day of their lives, and I think it gets the point across really well. I enjoyed playing it; the first time through, I answered the way I felt like I would probably answer if it were actually me in these situations, and got completely ♥♥♥♥ed in the end. The second time, I was actually invested in the characters as third parties rather than actors in my own life, and tried my hardest to make things work within the context of the story, and ended up with a satisfying enough ending.
Give it a try; it's free, you have nothing to lose other than maybe half an hour of your life, and let's be honest, you'd probably squander it by watching something stupid on Youtube anyway, so why not give this a try? Try to ignore for a moment who it was that made this game, and focus on the game itself; you might be a little shaken up, but you won't be disappointed.

Positives:
Though still in need of some refinement and balancing—and possibly some additional features—the core gameplay of Mini Metro scratches that city-building itch without requiring a major investment of time. You can play this on a break without worrying you'll be sucked in for hours (though you won't get bored if you did waste a day on it).
The interface is a case study in complex, context-sensitive functionality from simple interactions. Click, hover, drag and drag paths all combine to do just what you want without requiring a tutorial. Though you might spend your first game puzzling it out, it all just works how you'd expect on the first or second try. Pure, blissful affordance. If only more games thought out their interface so elegantly.
Negatives:
There is a well-known "cheat" that isn't really a cheat (it's inherent in the game rules) but that renders the leaderboards meaningless. The devs are still struggling with this issue, and I think it's resolution must lie in clarifying the game's biggest ambiguity: am I running a simulation of a real subway network (in which case, shouldn't it cost me something to re-route lines) or am I stress-testing a subway plan by iterative design under increasing load (in which case, shouldn't I have some prior information about where additional stations will appear). This ambiguity is at the heart of the game's ultimate success or failure, and the devs need to do more than apply band-aid solutions and ad hoc rule tweaks. I feel like the solution is to split the game into entirely different game modes which rest on different existential assumptions about what the game really is.
A little more information and clarity, compactly presented, would reduce some of the minor frustrations and provide greater insight into the network you've built. How many trains do I have on a given subway line? Can I see some meaningful data on throughput or efficiency? I have trouble believing the devs haven't read any of Edward Tufte's masterful works on data presentation. They'd do well to revisit his books for ideas.
[REVISED] The passenger AI is improving. Rather than being deterministically stubborn, passengers have acquired a variability that sometimes even includes whimsical train hopping in the wrong direction and then back again. This is an improvement. There's often more than one way from A to B, not to mention that sometimes B2 or B3 offer variety. It's slightly mad, but it's better than robots.
Some other minor complaints:
- why am I limited to 4 trains per line? Couldn't that limit be a function of the line's length and/or the number of stations?
- why can't a line go around a river bend rather than cutting the corner and requiring a tunnel?
- why no save feature? sometimes I'm having a very successful game, but I have to get back to work, or join friends in another game
TL;DR:
Enjoyable game. Can be played casually or obsessively. Brilliant with the potential to be an all-time classic. Well worth full price. It would be criminal to wait for a sale price.

Dungeons of Dredmor is a rogue-like dungeon crawler. On first glance, it seems pretty basic and generic as there are so many games with the same genre. However, Dungeons of Dredmor manages to stand out from the rest with it's wide array of skills, items, floors and monsters, it's humor, and how much fun you have playing it.
Dungeons of Dredmor has you as a hero to defeat Dark Lord Dredmor. On you quest to defeat Dredmor, you will need weapons, armor and a brain to slaughter monsters across the 10 dungeon floors.
DoD has you start off with you picking from about 30 skills (Excluding Deadshot which was removed) and you have the freedom to choose whatever you like. It's a great sense of replayability that is added this way. You can mix and match different skills to see what you like as a player and various skills change your playstyle.. If you happen to mix to certain skills together, you may come up with an amazing combination to destroy some enemies. When you've picked your skills, you get spawned on the first floor. It's good to note that every floor is randomly generated and that the game is turn-based, allowing you to strategize your next move.
Now as you progress through the game, different items will be there to enhance your character through different stats, I won't go into detail though. While the same items do pop up on occasion, they feel different because the stats and it's name is always different. Killing enemies will give you XP and will eventually get you to LVL up, therefore giving you one skill point to give you a passive or active skill. As I've said before, the game's large variety increases how much you play. DoD also has a surprising in-depth crafting system that will let you make better weapons, armor and various items like food and potions.
DoD also has DLC, which is a must buy. It only enhances the game that's already worth your money.The DLC's add more skills, items, floors and balances the game in general. There is also a decent sized workshop community, constantly added mods to make the game better.
Overall, Dungeons of Dredmor is an amazing buy. It's challenging with the option of Permadeath and it really makes you think in a lot of situations. For anyone who loves rouge-likes, you must check this game out.
PROS:
+Fun and Addicting
+Charming
+Humorous
+Wide Array of Skills
+Hundreds of Items
+Challenging
+Excellent Soundtrack
+Permadeath Option
+Deep Crafting System
+DLC enhances and balances the Base Game
+100+ Achievements
+Steam Workshop
+Bang for Your Buck
CONS:
-Graphical Style may not be your taste (Grew on me)
-Other players have been known to lose their progress
-Items don't change character appearance.
DUNGEONS OF DREDMOR: 9.5/10

Read a lot of reviews and finally decided to jot a few lines. I understand that many are frustrated because this game was listed under survival and I can see why. Yet if you think about it, anything where you would have to try and not get killed can be classified as such (I personally would classify Prelude as more of a stealth game... but then again, not exactly).
For those who gave it a thumbs down simply because "it wasn't scary enough" remember - just because it didn't scare you, does not mean it didn't scare anyone else. What DO you find scary? Seeing someone being sliced in half with their guts all over the place? Stupid in my opinion. Or having to check yourself every once and again because you feel like someone's following you? Because that's what Prelude (or any Doorways game) is in essence.
I felt so immersed in the atmosphere and the score that I had to turn around to see if anyone was behind me. Sometimes I would simply walk around just to LOOK around because everything is so beautifully made (also applies to Holy Mountains). The game knows exactly when to slow you down or speed you up and there's nothing you can do about it no matter how uncomfortable you get. Smooth movement and very effective narration.
I play a lot of horror and I must admit that a certain chapter of this game made me truly physically ill (in a good way!) and I will never look at sculptures the same way again :)
Personally, Prelude is my favorite in the series (although... Holy Mountains is so beautifully done!).
And please turn up your brightness before you complain.

I also really enjoy that the game can be enjoyed in multiple ways.  I'll never be able to speed run this game, but I like ocasionally going back to levels to see if I can figure out how to complete them with the least amount of jump/rotates.  I also enjoy trying to get the collectables, but just note that not every stage will have them.  Respawn times are nice and quick, which always leaves a feeling of: I'll get it this time.  I also like that, for those who do like to perfect their runs, it even has a "loop mode" by pressing UP before selecting a stage to respawn at the start of the level when you finish it.  I like the thought put in to that.
And most importantly, color switching while wall jumping and bouncing on enemies FEELS SO GOOD when it all flows togeather, like it's tickling a part of your brain you don't usually use when playing a platformer.

Color Jumper blends the puzzle and platformer genres in a perfect way. You can’t simply button mash your way through a level, and you also can’t just plot out everything without the having the dexterity to pull it off. You have to be good at both of those aspects to succeed.
In the beginning the controls can be a bit frustrating, but you get over that pretty quickly. At first I didn’t like that the jump and rotation are the same button, but it quickly becomes clear that the entire game was designed with that mechanic in mind. If those actions were placed on separate buttons, many of the puzzles would lose their challenge entirely. The player really has to think about how to order their jumps to get past certain points in the level.
The one boss level I’ve played so far was very well designed. Although I died repeatedly, I continually learned the aspects and timings of the fight, so I did a little better each attempt. Beating the boss, or any level of the game for that matter, gives you a super gratifying feeling that you’ve really overcome something.
The visuals are simplistic, yet engaging. There’s not a ton of flash, but that’s a good thing. I wouldn’t want a bunch of over-the-top visuals getting in my way when I’m trying to see the puzzles. The music and sound effects match the game very well.
The content is definitely worth the $8 price tag, even for someone who is absolutely terrible at platformers like me. If you’re a hardcore platformer junkie, I’d say Color Jumper is a steal. After you've beaten the 100+ there are additional time and rotation challenges to dive into. Ghost mode is great, too.
My only real complaint about the game is the lack of tooltips for explaining menu items. I’m still not sure what changing the rotation setting does, and I’m not super clear on how the time and rotation challenges for each level work.
All-in-all Color Jumper is a fun, engaging, and at times enraging platformer that sucked me in even though I am traditionally very VERY bad at the genre. I would certainly recommend it, and I’d consider it a must-have for any speedrunners.

Color Jumper is a fun and challenging experience and I'd strongly recommend it to any fan of platform and puzzle games.
It's difficulty ranges on how much of a perfectionist you are.  Levels become harder to clear while you also try and focus on time, rotations and secrets hidden in the level.
Overall it's a great game that can be cleared in a few hours with dedication but will take days to get everything.

Challenging, clever, hard af, with responsive and pretty spot-on controls.
The first few levels introduce you to the mechanics, but also to another subtle concept which I loved: this is not just a platform; it's also a dynamic, savage puzzle game. Each level is built around your starting color, hinting at the sequence required to complete it as fast as possible. Once you get it, it becomes a crazy ballet of both skills and logic. Great!

Let me start out by saying Color Jumper is only for fans of hardcore platformers. I'm on level 34 at the time of writing this, 1/3 of the way through the game and I'm already having flashbacks to Cuphead and Super Meatboy. If you are not a fan of retrying levels over and over again, then this game isn't for you. That being said, there is a lot to like about Color Jumper and enough to set it apart from its forefathers to make it worth picking up.
A great deal of the difficulty comes from managing your rotation, as certain objects in the level require you to interact with them with the side of your square of the corresponding color. Every time you jump, or press the jump button while in the air, your square rotates 90 degrees. This allows for really cool and unique gameplay that I have not experienced before. The levels are well designed, with a nice difficulty curve to help ease you into this new mechanic. Platforming fans will feel right at home here and if you get stuck on a level, you have the option to skip it and come back to it later.
Another huge positive in this game is the soundtrack. Levels vary in their background music and I haven't come across one I didn't like yet. I might even go back and buy the soundtrack after I finish the game.
Visually, the game is very simple with just about everything consisting of simple geometric shapes. They aren't anything to write home about, but they get the job done and most importantly are very readable to facilitate the fast paced gameplay. The large portions of the standard gray wall in particular could have done with some more visual vareity. However, there is a fair amount of particle effects that help make things much more pleasant to look at.
Overall, this is easy to recommend to fans of Super Meatboy and other hardcore platformers. Completing the 100 levels in the main game unlocks additional challenge levels, and there is a speedrun mode built in. In my opinion there is easily enough content to justify the $8 price tag.

Color Jumper is a fun, challenging, and fast-paced 2D platformer. A truly exceptional first game from an awesome indie developer!
The simple controls are responsive, and produce quick fluid movements using either keyboard or controller. Gameplay mechanics are gently introduced through the first two-thirds of the main 100 levels. There is increasing complexity and some challenges sprinkled throughout, so don't be alarmed if even some of the early levels seem difficult. If you get stuck and want to try another level, you get 5 tokens that let you skip a level (and beat it later to regain the token).
Levels closer to the end of the game are generally longer and more difficult, combining all previous gameplay elements in new variations. Additional bonus levels after the main game contain even more unique twists. Beating the harder levels after many attempts is extremely satisfying - like finally solving a tough puzzle. When you play a level enough, muscle memory builds up, and areas that initially feel intimidating turn into smooth and precise platforming. After completing a level you can replay it to optimize your path, and shorten the time or reduce the number of rotations to beat the goal.
The graphics may appear somewhat simplistic and possibly dull at first. This is deliberate and actually helps focus your attention on precise movement rather than get distracted by unnecessary details and special effects. The choice of colors and shapes creates a nice and coherent atmosphere for the game. Audio complements the visuals - satisfying melodic sound effects provide feedback for each action, while a mix of chill and upbeat music adapts to the intensity of your playthrough.
After many days of playing Color Jumper, I still enjoy coming back trying to fully complete all the levels, and replay those I've already beaten. I first played the demo in late 2016, and participated in the beta testing for the full game. It's great to see the final result with some improvements based on feedback from myself and others.

My first thought after seeing "Tower of Guns" pop up on my featured games list was "3D FPS bullet hell? What a pathetically stupid idea"
After acing the campaign and playing around a bit I have to admit... I was wrong. This game is amazing.
This game is an FPS rogue-like, first and foremost. The genre tends to be quite stagnant; I would argue that noone really knows how to do them well yet. ToG gets super, SUPER close to hitting the nail on the head. The unreal engine allows for beautiful controls and rewarding gunplay, the levels are nicely randomized through each playthrough with some hellishly deviant secret areas hidden in practically every room. There are guns and power-ups aplenty. Enemies tend to be lacking somewhat in creativity, but the BOSSES. Oh man. I haven't said "Holy Sh*t" out loud so many times in my life.
The secret areas deserve special mention. Some secrets are easy to come by. Some secrets require specific power-ups to obtain, mixing up playthroughs even more. Some secrets require real, legit hard work. These secrets are the epitome of rewarding gameplay. A player knows he doesnt NEED to do these things, but he puts in the effort and gets it done... and he gets to reap the rewards.
The guns are all brilliant. They all do something different and they all feel interesting and unique to play with. There's no damn ammo capacity, just shoot and shoot and shoot some more. You start with a gun of your choice and have the chance of picking up a second or third as you play, which all level up as you progress. One unfortunate thing is that levelling the weapons never does anything interesting. For me it only ever gave me Damage+ and particle effect+. I feel the final level of each weapon could have been made special... make the shotgun fire grenade flak or the pistol turn into a laser, that sort of thing. Feels like a missed opportinity.
EDIT: Turns out that most of the secret weapons do have special abilities at level 5. The blunderbus' flack explodes midair into more flak, the motivator creates speed-boost jelly upon firing, the noisy cricket turns into something that'd make Will Smith himself crap his pants. There are a few other examples. It is only the base weapons that tend to keep it simple.
ToG really feels like it came right out of the 90's era of shooters with his secrets and gun selection, only with better graphics and infinite levels. The story is 90's as hell aswell. The game picks from an assortment of different story scripts before you start your game, and gives you one at random. In one run, you're a brave warrior looking to take down the tower to save his city, and the next, you're an old granny who gets herself lost on the way to the recycling depot. The story is completely aesthetic and nothing else, but in this sort of game I would expect nothing less. It's a game where you ascend a randomised tower and shoot stuff. Get your story out of my peanut butter! The dev did a great job here, honestly.
I still can't say that 3D bullet hell works flawlessly, since at times it's impossible to dodge everything being thrown at you most of the time. One could argue that it's a sign of a bad game if a player is penalized for something outside of their control, but then again... I cant remember a single point of playing this where I really cared. In this game, you're either f*cked or you aren't. A single hit isn't going to effect the state of how f*cked you are.
Tower of Guns is an INCREDIBLY well-polished roguelike with some phoenominal gameplay innovations. and I suggest you go and buy it right now.

While you don't need to play the previous games at all to enjoy the story (mostly unrelated to the prequels), I recommend all the games. They are space simulators packed with action and adventure. The game may also have some bugs if you play it on later systems than XP, but these can also be solved.

Very deep and engrossing. The Cat Lady is a dark and twisted story about a lonely middle aged woman, Susan Ashworth, who commits suicide at the start, only to find herself in the realm of the dead where she is granted another chance at life by a mysterious old woman, but in return she must seek out and kill 5 terrible people, termed the Parasites. Along the way, Susan will have to come across some very difficult situations, witness horrific things, but also learn some lessons for herself and even make a friend.
I enjoyed this game very much for its dark atmosphere and completely uncensored themes. I warn you, this game is not for those with a faint heart. It has some very sickening and twisted moments, but that's what makes it so immersive. It delves into the dark corners of human existence and shows the horrible things humans can be capable of. It especially deals with themes such as death, suicide, and depression. Most of the characters were pretty well-developed, even the episodic ones who appeared in a single chapter.
Most of the gameplay is similar to standard point & click games, with basic puzzles that require you to do something to make progress. I normally dislike point & click games since most of them have very illogical puzzles, but this one's are pretty straightforward and almost always make sense. There were maybe only 2-3 times I had to peek into the walkthrough, but otherwise there's nothing that will keep you stuck for hours. I did enjoy the fact that it was all on a 2D plane, which made it easier to interact with the environment. No more having to go and press 'action' button on everything as other point & click games make you do. Everything that can be interacted with gets highlighted here.
Voice acting is all pretty superb, the music is also great and in some scenes is very well-fitting. The dark art style is also awesome and very nostalgic. Reminds me of the older games that had a bit of that alluring stiffness in the animations, which in this game also made some things appear scarier than they would normally be. Something about an erratic, jerky movement makes some things appear very disturbing.
Overall a great game and surprisingly immersive. Anyone who's fond of dark, disturbing stories should check it out.

Momodora IV is an adorably dark metroidvania game.
If you're going to play any Momodora game, make it this one.  The controls are tight, the level design is challenging but fair, and it has plenty of secrets and unlockables for the player to find.
The controls in this game are really fun. The combat is a simple 3-hit melee combo and light ranged attack, but the enemy patterns and movement system (dodge roll!) really make the system shine.  The platforming is tight enough that you can do really precision stuff without sliding off of small platforms, and certain unlockables only add more stuff to your combat and movement repetoire.
The world itself is fun to explore.  It's organized much like your typical metroidvania game; you explore various areas of a large city. There are plenty of hidden areas and items that encourage backtracking.  The game itself is nonlinear; there are only a few segments that require you to complete something else first for obvious reasons.
The aesthetic itself is beautiful. This is the most aesthetically pleasing entry in the Momodora series, and the style really pulls the sparse story together; adorable characters and enemies blend seamlessly with the bleak and dark Karst City, with plenty of environmental storytelling to go around.
I highly recommend this game, although I'm not sure if I'd pay full price for it if you aren't into unlocking hidden things. I easily dumped 11 hours or so into this game finding all the collectibles and beating every boss without getting hit (for special items!), but a straight run of this game probably lasts about 3 hours, even if you're bad at video games like I am.  If you aren't too keen on unlocking everything, I'd recommend you wait for a sale.
Some of the collectibles and interactions also feel kinda useless. For me, it was fine, since they usually made up for it in some form of sentimental value, but I know not everyone is a sucker for that stuff like I am.
Other than those minor gripes, though, I'd recommend picking up this game!

Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is a 2D platformer so solid and lovely to control i wanna kiss it.
like, imagine Dark Souls and Metroid had a little 16-bit baby, and then that baby made a game called Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight for his preschool project. thats this game.
Momo borrows its core mechanics from games like Metroid and Dark Souls, which i heard are pretty good. main gameplay really only includes jumping on platforms and slashing/shooting bad dudes, but Momodora likes to get a little deeper than that. your main weapon is a leaf, which attacks slowly and leaves you vulnerable between slashes, but you have a roll that gives you invincibility frames if things are dicey. your other weapon is a bow that's pretty quick but forces you to stand still, again leaving you vulnerable. this means you cant be strolling along willy nilly and you gotta take each group of enemies on with care and strategy. as a result you get combat that's pretty gosh darn fun and challenging (hey this kinda reminds me of Dark Souls).
the map that you explore is linear for about 2 seconds while the game teaches you how to play it, and then immedietely opens up, branhing into paths leading to the game's several areas (which all look damn beautiful btw) that you can explore. along the way you can buy/find abilities and upgrades that help you kill baddies faster or move around faster or use the power of wind or whatever, and its real neato (huh kinda like that Metroid game hmm). the map is also sprinkled with a lot of hidden goodies, hints toward lore, easter eggs, and a secret boss if any of that scratches your itch. overall its a treat to explore and discover.
speaking of bosses, the few that pop in during the game are pretty good. the average boss battle is a lot like Dark Souls, bosses hit hard, but their attacks are predictable and telepathed, and leave them vulnerable to a few swings from your leaf if you execute correctly. each boss looks, plays and acts different from the others, adding to the world experience as you come across them. their rarity, combined witht the bangin' soundtrack, makes each boss intense to fight.
the death system in this game is also a lot like Dank Souls, in that you have several bells (bonfires) sprinkled about the map that serve as save points. hitting the bell (resting at the bonfire) heals the player, refills active item charges, and sets that location to be the respawn point, yadda yadda classic game stuff with a sprinkle of fun new bits. what im getting at is the game is neat
presentation-wise, this thing is so damn delicious to experience. animations feel like they have some weight, and scenery looks pretty dang pretty on this one. im no artist, though, so i cant say much else. also the soundtrack gets soooooo good at times. my favorite track is "Pardoner's Dance", which plays when you fight Fennel (that hot gal in the white dress and the red sword).
uh, story, right. you get a vague idea of what's going on via talking to npc's or pre-boss banter, but i had a lot of trouble putting together the whole pie, and there's a lot of reading between the lines on this one. i ended up filling some info with my imagination, which was okay, but left something to be desired. maybe it's cause i haven't played the other 3 Momo games, but i dont know. you should ask someone else about this to be honest.

This "game" felt real to me. Depression Quest is very upfront about its intentions and what it is. This collection of choose your own story narratives is the result of a few people and their friends/family who experienced depression using their collective experience to tell a story. It isn't the story of every depressed person at all, no matter how many variations you try to go through, but from what is there, you can get an idea of what it is like for some people.
They clearly say this and I'll repeat it. This is not meant to be fun. This isn't an enjoyable game. If you yourself are or have been depressed then you may not want to play this. It gives you a vague idea of how someone suffering might not be able to act in certain ways, and the resulting feelings they are experiencing when they make a choice.
Going through this, making choices that I would see myself making years ago, I could relate to the narrative that was told as a result. For this reason I think this is an alright way to try to vaguely understand how someone with depression might be feeling.
This is just my advice. I do not recommend choosing the "right" responses based on what you know to be the best course of action. Try choosing options that are maybe a little isolated from people. Avoid what might be considered uncomfortable for an introverted person. Don't try to act like a healthy person if you're playing it to try to understand someone who isn't.
And don't play this for fun. It's hardly a "game". It's an interactive story.

I think this game does what it aims to do quite well. It makes it clear that, when depressed, there are some things you just can't do, even if it would seem like a logical course of action.
Another thing that really captures the feeling of powerlessness associated with depression is that, since it's presented as a choice-based game, the player instinctively feels like they can make good choices and somehow "win" this game... which, in the end, is just an illusion.
This game is by no means "fun", and it's very likely to be triggering for people with current or past experience with depression, but that's explicitly stated at the beginning. I think it succeeds at being a poignant representation of what depression can be that is easily understandable by those who have no experience with it.

Before the review, please see my short list of things you can do to improve your gameplay experience:
1)	Adjust the FOV and Weapon FOV in settings
2)	Add a scope to your weapon rather than ADS
3)	Don’t be afraid to play the Psionic / ESP modes, they are genuinely fun and quite balanced
Line of Sight is a very good UE3 FPS game. It’s not perfect, but the developers have proven their commitment to making changes.
PROS:
-	Great graphics – made even better by adding Anti Aliasing via your graphics card settings
-	Intricate detail – the ‘hideout’ page will give you detailed stats about your performance, there are daily-weekly-monthly missions and well over 400 Steam (& in-game) achievements
-	Not Pay2Win – the developers have made adjustments to suit the Global market that prefers a fair game, and more adjustment is coming
-	Ability to test any weapon or attachment with the Firing Range feature
-	Fun ways to mix up the game with Psionic and ESP abilities – completely optional, but worth playing
-	Fantastic community engagement from the developers
OTHER COMMENTS:
-	The menu system is a bit confusing and changes can definitely be made to simplify it
-	More environmental sounds could be added to make the gameplay feel more immersive
-	Adjustments should be made to aiming accuracy and player movement
-	Players should be able to access more parts of the maps, so there should be less invisible walls
I am rating this game ‘positive’ for the following reasons:
-	It’s a $10 early access that gives you some decent items including 2 permanent weapons with animated skins. Good value.
-	The development team are committed to making improvements to the game.
-	There is a lot of content that has already been developed for the game that will be coming soon.
I urge people to try out the game properly and if they don’t like it, to leave a critical review explaining why. It’s just $10, needed to support this lone development team that have created a great game with decent foundations, and you could always refund it if you don’t like it. Give it a go!

I'm not really sure what it is about this little indie game, but seriously, if the subject matter interests you at all, then I recommend you pick it up.
It is, by far, one of the most compulsively playable titles I have set my hands on in quite some time. Even though it resides in the early access areas of Steam, it can comfortably sit beside others that are deemed to be finished. The only thing missing from this game is sound. That being said, the sound is something I couldn't care less about. It is the least of my concern as I continue to further the efficiency and optimal layout of my subway lines.
The game itself is played through various stages, in this case, cities of the world. Each stage provides you with a basic layout map and routes or "lines" to place between stations. The stations are represented as shapes on the map that you must connect using your lines. As you do so additional symbols are shown on the map to represent the passengers.   Your locomotives move around the map autonomously along your set routes picking up and dropping off passengers as they go. This would present itself as an easy puzzle to solve, however, as the days and weeks go by in game, that couldn't be farther from the truth. It becomes a complex balancing act to try to get passengers to and fro as quickly as possible without allowing them to build up at an individual stations. This, as far as I can tell, is the only end game state. If a station has too many passengers, the countdown begins until finally the game notifies you of your defeat.
The game is so simple and elegant, yet complex and harsh, all at the same time. I haven't played anything like it before. Friend suggested this to me for a variation on our Co-op playing, and well worth it.  The game's retro art style may be a bit pixelated, but it's clean, crisp, artistic pixels.  Gameplay is solid top down hack and slash and every character class feels different with it's own play styles.
There does feel to be some balance issues with the classes, at least in solo play, as some classes are decidedly stronger in different stages of the game, but in a team you can balance that out against each other.  For instance, Ranger's abbility to snipe at a large distance is very useful early on, while Warlock in the early game just has a basic dagger and a spell that, while powerful, recharges slowly.   But by endgame the ranger has to pick it's fights more carefully while the Warlock can use it's third spell and run through multiple monster spawners, regaining HP from hits and mana to recast the spell infinitely.
The music is solid, though a bit more variation could be nice, the main Hammerwatch Campaign uses one song for each set of 3 floors within a Act, plus a boss theme, and a Retro theme for the Secret levels.   And since each act can take about 2 hours, you'll hear that same song a long time.   It's good but a variation wouldn't hurt.
The main campaign is worth revisiting a time or two, but nothing changes aside from difficulty and which character you use, while there's also Temple of the Sun with some differences to the formula.  But it need not end there, as Workshop lets players create their own maps, so the game should continue on for a while.   Only downside is, there's no way to create custom bosses or characters so unless the game gets a update on those, the challenge will come from floor design.
All in all a 8/10 experience, and that's only because I'm late to the party.   With maybe some character tweaks or even additional classes, and bosses, this could be a even better game, and since it's already recieved one major patch, I wouldn't rule anything out at any time.

The basic idea is great: a simple roguelike FPS that you can finish in an hour or so. But it just isn't worth the money. There are just so many things lacking.
For example, there is no sprint button. And you can have one, and only one, weapon per run - and they are not exactly the most exciting wepons to have been seen in a video game.

But the worst thing is that all difficulty in the game comes from just throwing out heaps and heaps of enemies and bullets at you, there is no AI to outsmart or anything, just gazillions of small flying enemies that shoot at you and who are difficult to hit since your own bullets are just as slow as the enemy bullets - which means that I'm pretty sure it is actually possible to run into your own bullets, with some of the slower weapons and with a speed-up powerup.
It's not a horrible game, it just feels kind of cheap. If you get it really cheap in a humble bundle or something, give it a shot and see what you think. Me, I hope there is a sequel that feels a little more worked through.

Tower of Guns is a fast-paced FPS rogue-lite featuring procedural levels; random bosses; a random, silly story per playthrough; a bunch of items and weapons mods to discover; very angry robots; the ability to choose a starting perk; and satisfying movement.
Tower of Guns' has variety. In regard to the level design, there are some set pieces like starting rooms, boss rooms, (which boss you encounter is random), and certain paths, but you can expect to see a bunch of different rooms that follow a theme for each stage. All those stages randomize those rooms to keep the game interesting. What also keeps the game from becoming stale are the random enemy spawns ; so even if you come to a similar section, you'll need to change your tactics according to whatever foe the game throws at you next. Useable items with a multitude of different effects are present in ToG; some of them summon movement altering jellies, fire a barrage of rockets, or make your weapon even more powerful for a limited time so long as they're fully charged.
Continuing on the topic of variety, you start off the game with two available weapons and one perk. As you play, you can unlock up to eight more weapons and ten more perks more to choose from (only one weapon and perk per session). You can then further modify your weapon in-game via the various weapon mods that drop that can simply increase fire speed, give your gun spread, or even turn each projectile into an aoe fire mine when they hit a surface (great with a shotgun). You can then modify your character through the plentiful power-ups you find from your defeated enemies or secret rooms. There are plenty of secret rooms waiting to be found, unfortunately a good chunk of them revolve around having plenty of jump power-ups on your character, which is not a guarantee. The power-ups that you can find include how high you jump, how many jumps you have (I've experienced a thirty plus jump), your weapon experience rate, and even the difficulty.
This game is not easy. It's a fast-paced shooter involving dozens of enemies and even more bullets, spikes, bombs, etc. If you play Endless Mode, you can expect to run into bullet hell scenarios once you're far enough. What's nice though is that you can modify the difficulty by picking up a (RIP--) power-up or a (RIP++) power-up that decrease and increase the difficulty of the enemies respectively. It's a great way for players to manage the difficulty as they see fit because one too many damage and armor power-ups can make you too powerful which is boring. If that's the case, grab a (RIP++) and restore the challenge. And if the game is too tough, there is a Too Young To Die perk that will start off the game with weaker enemies while buffing the player at the same time, just pick up some (RIP++)'s when you're ready to go fast.
Tower of Guns lets the player move really, really fast. It's quite the experience to circle-strafe an enemy with a sixtuple jump or smacking the roof of the game world with a forty jump (you can ignore the ground at this point except to recharge jump). Some of the enemies will start to keep up with you as your progress through the game so expect to run around and engage in a most elegant gun ballet on the ground and in the air.
All of the above help to contribute to the replayability of this game, but the developer also programmed incentives into the game to keep you playing. Each weapon and perk in the game can be starred upon beating the boss. Ten weapons and eleven perks means perfectionists will have something to chew on while they also chase the achievements. The achievements for this game are well done too. Instead of being just milestones, there are some funny and challenging ones available like
.
In conclusion, Tower of Guns provides a really fun experience and will entertain for awhile since it's designed well for multiple playthroughs.

The resolution is terrible. For starters, the game is stuck in windowed mode and there's no way to change the resolution or even maximize the window to fit the screen. Which means on my monitor, I couldn't see all of the game window, thereby making the game impossible to play properly. All I could do was spin the spinner. The different cards I had to play against the AI player(s) were inaccessible, and using them can often tip a game in your favour.
: The camera is terrible. It starts out with an overhead view of the spinner, then moves to a behind view when your token (car) starts moving. That would be OK, but it then twists and turns around the car whenever it moves around corners or stops. It's kind of motion sickness inducing, to be honest.
------

I adored this game. It's a 2D Metroidvania style action game that also borrows heavily from the Dark Souls series, particularly Bloodborne. Combat is fluid and challenging, utilising physical attacks, dodge-rolls, a bow, and a range of collectible active and passive items collected throughout the game. You can't block, meaning you have to rely on rolling to dodge, i-frames, stunlocks, etc. in much the same way that you might in the Souls games. It's challenging but deeply satisfying. The story is presented in a minimalistic way: the basic thrust of the narrative is easy to understand, but it's the mysterious yet endearing roaming cast of characters and fellow adventurers that helps make this game memorable. Ultimately, you can't save everyone, and you have to live with that fact. The whole game is steeped in gothic darkness, and you can really feel the sense of corruption and decay everywhere. I loved the sense of exploration and freedom, the really engaging and rewarding combat system, the diverse cast of characters, the boss designs and battles, and the tasteful, minimalist gothic plot. Highly recommended.

I don't get all the hate for this game. There are some misspellings and grammar errors but they are fairly minor. It's not particularly fantastic storywriting, but it's not supposed to be. It's supposed to be as accurate of a representation of depression as possible. Depression isn't romantic.
I also don't feel like it portrays depression as being "whiny" as some people say, however it may seem that way because the person's feelings are unwarranted. This is actually a huge part of the problem of our societies' attitude toward depression - that it has to have a reason, that the person's feelings are invalid if they don't have a reason. This only makes people suffering with it feel worse.
I feel like despite the fact that this plainly says it is not a "game", people still expect it to be. It's not, it's more like a visual novel. The reason choices are crossed out is to portray the idea that people with depression feel like some choices are IMPOSSIBLE. Whether they are or not, the person feels trapped by their own mind. If you go back and make different choices, you would find that choosing to open up, see a therapist, take antidepressants, etc. opens up more options.
I DO wish it didn't end so abruptly - In particular, if you choose the options to not get better. This sounds really messed up, but I think the story could make more of an impact if it led to the character's suicide or self harm or something. As it is written, while the indicator at the bottom shows that you are getting worse, the story doesn't really describe it. It should delve deeper into the thoughts and feelings of the character, rather than just describing it as exhaustion, anxiety, etc. It doesn't describe the self-hatred, etc. of someone with severe depression. I think that's part of the reason people think the character seems "whiny".
Is this game a perfect representation of depression? No. But it IS eye opening and perhaps could help some people relate to a person in their life that may be struggling with it. Depression is something that needs to stop being treated with a stigma, and it needs to be talked about more openly. Hopefully stuff like this can help with that.
Finally, to anyone struggling with depression - You can make it through this. You're not worthless. Even the smallest gestures you do can make an impact to someone else. Don't try to go through it alone, there are people that care and will help.

For someone who is constantly battling with sever depression/bi-polar disorder for many years. This is a definitely hard game to play through. But an enlightening and educational one.
The actions that your character does is so synonymous to the actions I exibit ... to the point that it is hard to deal with. Break up from relationships, having the sense of crushing dread and being unable or incredibly hard to talk to people or anyone (including family members and close friends) about how I feel on a day to day basis, being agitated and frustrated by general minutiae, finding studies and focusing on projects so difficult to focus on (even when there is impending deadlines) the self-worthlessness, lack of confidence, and inability on dealing with peers & lecturers. It's all covered in this, and more.
I couldn't say how someone would react to playing this game for someone who doesn't suffer from depression, but I could imagine it would be a frustrating experience for them. I guess that is the point ... to show how difficult it can be. When you know the actions you should take, but you can't.
As you read through, having the options that you want to be able to take being locked out, or even choosing the wrong ones (there is no right or wrong choice in this game, neither do you have in real life) and seeing how this effects you. it's an eye opening experience even for myself. Seeing habits and traits. I have to admit it was hard to start composed, and I wept alot, especially when things where resonating with me.
I don't want to spoil it for anyone, but if you want to gain a better understanding on how depression effects you friend, loved one, co-worker etc ... this is a good game for them to play.
Depression is not an easy condition to live with, nor is it easy on people around you. All I can suggest is to try and talk to someone there are plenty of support available ...
NHS -
MIND -
SANE -
Samaritans -
It is hard, especially making that first step. As long as you know you will never be alone with this, even if you feel like you are all alone.
Take care, and thanks for reading :)

Right away, I liked the way the game gives you information. I like that it gave you the option of getting more exposition/background details or just moving on with the story. After the gray boxes under the options started changing, I felt like I was helping my character and that the options I chose could really influence the story. I like that they show options you can't pick because of stress or exhaustion, which implies that, if you make good decisions, some of those choices may open up, and also shows how depression can make it harder to communicate with people.
I was skeptical when I first opened up this game, since, with the title "Depression Quest," it doesn't sound all that engaging. However, a few minutes into playing, I found that I was really invested in my character and wanted to help them.  I don't have depression, but I can empathise with my character with so many more things than I though I would. I have felt the "end of the week, I don't want to do anything" feeling, I know what it's like when you feel like you can communicate better through writing than speech, and the procrastination is very similar to how I deal with almost all of my work. It felt to me like my character's successes were my successes, and the character's pitfalls were my own. I felt a real sense of accomplishment and happiness when my character felt better and felt sad when they were having a bad day.
What matters in a game is the experience. It might not be for everyone, especially if you're someone who can't get into text adventures, but this game made me feel for my character. Even though they're just a cluster of words in a simple text-based game, I genuinely wanted them to succeed. I felt accomplished, like I'd done something really good, by the end of it. If that isn't the mark of a good game, I don't know what is.

This game has hit close to home for me, I sympathize with the main protagonist on some levels. I have suffered from depression before and continue to face obstacles because of it. Before writing this review, I've noticed how people say "this doesn't accurately represent what depression is like." Everyone is different. People go through depression differently be it extreme or mild. Besides this game is only giving us a basic idea of what it's like for someone to experience depression in their daily life. It may not have been how YOU experience it but that doesn't make the game completely inaccurate.
Now about the game itself, since you have to make choices in this game I actually appreciate having a "back" option to change your decision. Although there's no button on screen, you simply click the backspace button on your keyboard to go to the previous pages. I enjoyed reading the different outcomes and it helped to decide which route I'd rather take.
Depending on the decisions you make, later in the game some of your choices will be scratched out. Often they are choices that may seem simple and the logical thing to do, but it's not that easy for your character who's having neverending battles with his/herself. More choices will be available to you, the player, when you make the right decisions and help your character fight against the depression.
I must note that the audio caught my attention. The somber piano music is very mellow and slow. It is played on a loop but it honestly didn't seem repetitive to me. Each page or section in the game has more sound going on depending on the setting. There's a scene where your character is at a party and you can hear jibber jabber and party music all while the piano still plays. I think that's rather clever to keep the piano music. In my opinion it symbolizes the character's depression. The piano music follows the character wherever they go, even in a happy setting, it's always there.
After completing this game, I actually do recommend it to others. Anyone who can be triggered easily, play with caution. If you're curious to see what it's like have a go at it. Keep in mind the experience with the protagonists' depression may not be 100% accurate, but it does offer an idea to those who want to understand what it may feel like to be suffering from depression.
Don't forget this game can and will make you feel down, so go play some Katamari Damacy or watch cat videos afterwards. =)

This is definitely a good horror game. It has good atmosphere and antagonists which will make you cower in fear and want to hide in a corner. The difficulty is not overwhelmingly ridiculous, while not being too easy. It will keep you on your toes and perhaps make you cry a bit.
One of the things I really liked was the huge variety of gameplay environments. You go through dark forests, a castle, and more.
Some other reviewers complained about it being too dark. I'm guessing most of them didn't go into the game's video settings, where the brightness can be turned up (it's set to minimum by default). I never had a problem with it being too dark.
The only thing I did not like about this game was its inventory mechanics. At times, you need to hurry and grab something out of your inventory (and I mean, really quickly), but it takes a good few seconds to pull up the inventory and take something out. That's just enough time for one of the antagonists to murder you.
Overall, though, I strongly recommend this game.

The story: Prelude is Chapter 1 and Chapter 2. You are a kind of agent who is tracking down some psychopaths in a very surreal environment and at the same time trying to sort out his emotions about the things he is experiencing through his search.
Have you ever watched the movie "The Cell"? Yeah, 2000 with Jennifer Lopez.... this game is very much comparable to that. And maybe that's why I enjoyed this game, because it felt like I was physically exploring the twisted minds of these psychopaths.
Visually, this game was kind of nice. Not always. Not spectacular, but most of the time just nice. The different environments were great (except for spikey forest... that was kind of lame).
Some points during the game, it was just too damn dark to see anything at all... which has been mentioned in previous reviews...all points are true. It was bloody difficult to comlete some puzzles in the dark. WOW. Pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
The puzzles/scavenger hunts were neat. Easy enough though... maybe a bit too easy. I'm hoping for more puzzle challenge in chapter 3.
Chapter 2 was great! Spooked the hell out of me at one point, so that was nice.
Overall scary? Meh... sometimes... no real threat, but there were a couple scares a long the way. Especially in some of the halls in Chapter 2. Not Amnesia scary. Not Outlast scary. More like Anna scary.
I'm really looking forward to the direction the story is heading and looking forward to the next Chapter. I already have a theory................ but I won't spoil it for you.
Do I recommend this? If you don't mind a really short game, sure. The price was a little steep for the short game, maybe try for it on sale. But overall, I recommend it.

This is a fine expansion to
.
It adds about half an hour of content (myself I beat all new levels in 25 minutes). Currently, there's not much new story, the only story piece being the ending text. Strangely, there's not even an introduction. To be generous, I would say the new story is
.
However, the main content is in the levels anyway. I think the new levels are alright.
The new levels introduce a couple of new variants of the earlier traps. There are sound detectors that encompass almost the whole level but usually go off at longer intervals. There are also "two-ended" lasers, with a generating device at both ends, so you'll need two boxes to get through it.
In difficulty the new levels range from slightly challenging to fairly difficult. I think the bonus levels from Episode 1 were more difficult than any of the levels in Episode 2. The difficulty of the new levels is more on par with the last regular levels of Episode 1.
So if you enjoyed the base game, you'll probably like the Episode 2 as well. Mind that if you played this game previously, that there are no longer limited lives in Episode 2, and that this change was done to Episode 1 as well. Since it's a casual game, I find it's a good change.
EDIT: Many things have changed since the DLC was published. For instance, it used to cost money - it's Free-LC now. Initially there were no achievements with the DLC, because the developer felt that would have been forcing people to buy the DLC for a 100% game. I think this is an admirable stance. Then achievements were added anyway, and as the latest development, the DLC became free.

Far Cry 4 supprised me. I came into this game having not played the other games in the series. I was instantly blown away by the great looking world. The  combat was very fun, and the variety of weapons made it fun to find different ways to kill people. The controls were fluid and I never once felt like I died from bad control. What I don't like is the healing system. Having to hit ctrl to heal was monotonous. If I didn't have a healing syringe i was stuck waiting behind a wall waiting for the slow healing animation to finish. After running out and killing a few enemys I was stuck behind a wall again healing. Driving cars around Kyrat is fun and its fun to listen to the radio and hear what they say. The stealth parts were the worst as you had to very slowly crouch evrywhere and stop for a minute to wait for a guy to turn around and kill him. It slows the game down so much that it makes me not want to play. On the otherhand, parts where you and the golden path charge bases is always fun and gets your adrenaline going. Pagen Min is a great antagonist as he's fun to watch/listen to when he's there, I wish he talked more in the story than he did. Amita and Sabal are forgetable characters and I personally didn't like either of them. There are many missions that are available like yogi and reggie were you get high and run for a few minutes then it's done or Hurk where you have to collect these monkey statues (my favorite) and Willis which is are the worst missions. The most dislikable character and some of the hardest and unfair missions in the game. The Golden path missions are very fun and had the most action. Whether your in Kyrat, Shangri La, or the Himalayas it looks amazing!!! The ending was a little dissapointing but the atmosphere of the game was great. The crafting system worked well, even though I didn't use it much it was very useful when I did. The different skills you can learn add to the experience (The extra Health bar is the best in my opinion). Overall Far Cry 4 is a great experience, is it the best game of 2014? No, but it is a great game to the Far Cry franchise and made me want a Far Cry 5. Anyone can have fun with this game as there is something for everyone. Far Cry 4 receives a 8.2/10.

At first, I expected this game to be different than the other games that I used to play, but I thought I was'nt supposed to be really effective in scaring me to death.
Well, I was wrong.
Yes, it does sound cliche but I never thought this games would really pierce in to the heart and mind and make you question of the foundations and fundamentals of humanity. The dark atmosphere, the feeling of despair, hopelessnss, misery and the core entity of this game, death. From the perspective of Susan Ashworth, this game shows you on how demented a depressed and deranged a depressed person's mind can be. Many times, the general public would not want to associate themselves with patients that are suffering from mental illness and would exclude them from the community. This game shows us, the general public that people with mental illnesses are people who need special care and love and because of this, they must not be exiled but be brought in and showered with love and affection.
Thanks to this game that my Sister recommended to me, I also got to learn more on how I can attend to the people who are in the midst of having a hard time overcoming mental illnesses. Again and again, I used to ponder on how I can really help them to feel better and not dip themeselves in immense guilt and anguish. Even though this game does not have what it takes to give me a PhD in Psycology, but it does give me insight on what goes on in a patient's mind and helps me to choose my words and actions wisely.
So, now. The main point. Should you buy this game?
In my opinion, by all means, buy it. It's educating, offers the player a gripping experience in the mind of a patient who suffers from depression and suicide and from time to time, it does give you the shambles, but for a good cause. I must say this, if you're looking for a horror game, I really must apologise, The Cat Lady isn't the game you're looking for. Remember, The Cat Lady emphasizes on depressive and suicidal themes. This game is not for the weak of heart. The plot is alright but do make sure you're ready for the sudden chord scares and atmosphere change from time to time.
So...yeah. Do buy The Cat Lady. It surely is a game worthy of someone's attention and time.

I can honestly say that this game has made a huge impact on my life. I played it when I was going through a very dark time in my life and I felt understood and not so alone. This game is powerful, especially if you are dealing with suicidal ideations. It will always be one of my favorite games.. The artwork is quirky, dark and represents the story in ways that couldn't be expressed in words. It feels lonely, hurt and damaged and as you play you can either see it become something of closure in a positive way, or closure in a way you might not want to see.. That being said, I got the sad ending initially but I played the ending again because I didn't want it to end on a negative note for me. And then I started it over again because I wasn't ready to let go. Again, this game is powerful. It's depression expressed in pixels and you decide how it ends.

The Cat Lady is an insanely amazing game, but it isn't the type of game you really want to play with friends and kick back on a Friday night. I would recommend playing The Cat Lady alone and just letting yourself be enveloped by the atmosphere of it. The Cat Lady's main character has struggled through depression and is saved from the brink of death. However, she is still very depressed and because of this, The Cat Lady might not be "fun" like Mortal Kombat, but it is incredibly interesting in how it portrays other humans' emotions. The game is largely puzzles and working your way around to the next scene, but they aren't too difficult, and that's how I would keep it. The story keeps going that way and keeps the player from becoming frustrated. Finally, you might not think that a sidescroller can be too scary, but there are scenes that are pretty disturbing. This might be a turn off for some people, but I love that The Cat Lady both has incredible imagination behind it, and that it isn't afraid to show a gruesome side of life.

Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is a Metroidvania action platformer. What makes this game great is not only its fluid gameplay but its story and setting.
You play as a priestess named Kaho who wishes to talk to the Queen of Karst because a plague of demons has invaded originating from Karst has invaded her home. Upon arrival in Karst you find that the population has become insane from all the demons. After the forest level the game has a dark and foreboding atmosphere which really captivates you in the story.
Gameplay is simple. You move with the arrow keys and can do the following, jump, roll, perform a melee attack, cast magic, and shoot arrows. You refill your magic items and health at checkpoints. You have two types of magic items: active and passive. Active items work upon activation and you get a certain number of each item before you have to refill it. Some active items include healing items, attack up items, and attack items. Passive items affect your stats or ability. One can increase your resistance to status ailments, another can increase the speed of your arrows, and another can give your attacks flame damage. It is not overwhelming unlike other games where you get so many abilities so that the game has a steep learning curve.
As I said before this is a Metroidvania style game so you can go back to previous areas and unlock new passages. Karst city acts like a central hub for this game and later in the game you get the ability to teleport between certain checkpoints. There is also a side quest where you can find 20 bugs in the game and you get items for each five bugs you find (maybe it's five).
The simple and fluid controls, customizable playstyles, and an exportable world make this game a must buy.

Surprise! A positive review!
Depression Quest was a very interesting game to play. I do not suffer from depression myself but I do have a few close friends who do. The actions that go on in the game are accurate to what my friends care to share about their situations. I like how the game brought me to the lowest place I could (it made me tear up at points) and I actually felt like what happened to the protagonist was happening to me. So, when a happy or improving moment came up, I felt like I was actually getting better. I know depression cannot be cured or solved, same as was addressed at the beginning and end of the game, but getting better is possible.
The game's physical qualities were also very cool. I really liked the static-looking effect applied to the "status" updates at the bottom of the pages. The sound effects were a really nice touch; they fit the scenes nicely enough where they did not distract me from the game's happenings. They provided good background noise so that each scene was not defeningly silent. I know that's a weird prase to say but, I often find it hrd to concentrate on reading something if there are no other sounds or noises happening and the silence itself is bothersome.
There were one or two spelling/grammar mistakes, but so little to the point where it does not take meaning away from the game's message. I really liked how Attic asked the protagonist for help for his personal issue; I felt good that I had the option to help him fter he helped so much before, I felt like I actually helped someone.
Overall, a really good game. A great experience for someone without depression to get a glimpse of what someone with it experiences everyday. I wish more people could have apprecated it like I did.
--Drew

If you're looking for a fairly well made FPS for a cheap price, then I can recommend giving it a shot. Buying the game now also gives you the founders pack which gives you a bunch of stuff that's worth well over the price of the pack it self, you also get what I think is basically the best sniper that basically 1 shots everything unless they're at the other side of the map.
One of the complaints I've seen is that it's "obvious p2w" in which I fully disagree, pay to progress quicker perhaps, but by no means pay2win because every single weapon and attachment is earnable with ingame credits, within my first few games I was able to upgrade the terrible first gun you get into a a completely different beast, due to the fact that the default scope on it is horrible due to how "blind" you feel and the muzzle flash being insane, I stuck a low range scope on it and a silencer that I earned enough cash for within about 4 games? which made my ability to aim so much more incredibly easier, also with the ability to stay off the radar which is always nice.
The game has a fairly low population atm, though finding games hasn't been too hard to get into, I think my only complaint would be going up against snipers on the larger maps while they have the heat-vision scope on, it can be quite a nuisance to play against lol
I think one of my only complaints on the gun-play is how when you're using an assault rifle with trying to kill someone at long range, your damage drop off is actually huge, at one point I think I shot someone about 6-8 times and took about 30% of their health, in which they then proceeded to 1 shot me with a sniper, wasn't really too sure what to make of that, the AR drop-off is huge while snipers seem to virtually get none.
Graphics are solid though, I have no idea what some of the complaining people with negative reviews are whinging about, apart from complaining for the sake of complaining, I also get absolutally no lag on max settings with my 2-3 year old PC, so overall it's a good game, I would just like to see the population increase.

Choices with pernicious consequences call for sacrifices to be made from the very start of
. It is a rich blend of HnS and RPG. Superbly it preserves the riot of strategic elements within role playing games while maintaining non-complex arcade-like features of any good hack and slash through making use of basic skill upgrades and combat, loot usage and simple story progression alike (the patch expansion,
is a bit more story orientated).
An openly avid indie game collector and player, my dirty little secret is an obsession with enjoying indie co-op and multiplayer games (online and local). It's dirty and a secret (well, up till now) because I'm a sporadic multiplayer and don't consistently play with other people.
is of a select few which lure me out of the mole hole, blinking against the raging sun. And this is one furious Sol as people will curse you for your mistakes if not careful. Like I have mentioned, sacrifices and choices must be made and other than a secret puzzle in the game,
should not be played reliant on chance (unless you want a quick but painful death). Nothing here is eternal (unless you cheese or cheat for some wild reason). Though
has solid single player, and campaigns can be beaten at a similar difficulty level to that with any number of players in a team (2-4), it's a game which shines when you're fighting off the baddies together. It will also feel less tedious as being all alone in a dungeon can get mighty lonely, long and arduous. Co-op forces you to make choices that directly affect your teammates and may free or crush them. This makes it crucial to comprehend early on the definition of teamwork as you cannot just play as you please with friends and hope they'll clean up after you or that it won't matter as long as you keep eating fruit and meat and hoard lots of gold by cheesing between dungeon entrances (nooooo). You will literally get into altercations with friends if you do not pay attention to what you're doing and why. Gold is divided equally between each player but lives are pooled together. If you waste your lives or gold for selfish reasons your team will die. On the bright side, for such games reliant on skill, efficiency and the cost of your actions,
is relatively forgiving. Had it not been made so forgiving and added procedural level generation and perma death* it undoubtedly would have made a flawless roguelike.
*Note: You can add challenges through the modifiers menu to make it seem similar to a roguelike with perma death at least. Crutches on the other hand aren't needed.

Although my SO is rarely sold on any game I bring up (I play some odd indie games...), the moment I described

On the subject of balmy levels, the uniformity of blazing energy balls, poisonous spit, spike traps beneath your feet and arrows whizzing past your head every second as well as ever spawning ticks nipping at your ankles and minibosses that don't seem so mini when clumped to excess will frequently lead you to reminisce the non-stop craziness of shoot 'em up games with lasers blazing in all directions trying to kill you. Oh yes, the shooters we'd mastered so cleverly only for being an eight year old too poor to play much else at the arcade... ah no... wait, so deprived of pocket money (from spending it all on crisps?) that we'd honed our own expertise by ever watching the screen of the older children bashing the keys like maniacs with little skill. if your mind ever drifts and you will be mauled to death and ripped to shreds in the manner of season 5, episode 14 of

- Rangers are great to start off and the most versatile against enemies and traps for beginners. Personally I like warlocks as their power increase is much more intense further on, helping make swifter and heavier attacks for large mobs and swarms which more combat based classes just cannot pull off. Obviously this depends on your style of play so test everything in single player. It is also fun to try many different combinations with friends as it will change gameplay extensively.

Even though this was more an educational thing than an actual "game" for fun, I actually would've enjoyed something like this. I like the wilderness, and survival games, and I find animals fascinating. There's not nearly enough games out there that let you play as wildlife with a survival theme. The game 'Shelter' was a disappointment in the same regard; I don't want silly or crappy graphics, or dumbed down with no real conflict or survival. I would prefer at least Skyrim-level graphics (and that game's rather old by now.)
My biggest problem with WolfQuest was the low-quality feel, which is understandable for their budget, but I simply couldn't tolerate it. The textures, the barren landscape, the clunky controls and camera, the lack of any serious customization... and also the lack of decent combat, with graphic content like blood. Even keeping it utterly realistic, such a game should accurately portray hunting and eating to survive. The graphics for detecting scents and such was also very unappealing to look at, and could've been represented better.
There's actually a large market for a simulation game like this, it's just that nobody has ever done it right or with enough quality. That's actually why I also own 'The Isle' (and have been considering 'Saurian'), because dinosaur survival was intriguing too.
Perhaps someday they'll do a WolfQuest 2 with proper funding, or someone else will take up the mantle.
On a final note, the fact that they offer a limited free demo and make you pay to access features when the game already offers so little... was highly annoying.
