After finishing this game three times (and doing the side quests and what not), I have decided that I like this game. I like the fact  that you can choose sides in order for the story progression, even a quick ending to the game if you keep your ears open and have the tolerance to wait, there are some new and different side quests, new vehicle; buzzer to navigate the nice scenery of Kyrat, riding elephants are pretty fun too. You can also autodrive vehicles if it's on a road and shoot, which is pretty neat.
You can now tackle outposts by throwing bait to attract predators, which is a nice new way to help capture an outpost without raising alarms. Also, new animals that don't like you are Rhinos and Eagles. Rhinos like to charge into cars, so if you see a rhino, don't slow down, keep that accelerator slammed down and make sure they aren't close to wherever you're driving. Eagles make some weird noise before they swoop, so aim a nice gun at it's face and shoot that off. I like the idea of having to look in the sky every now and then.
Other than that, it was pretty similar to Far Cry 3. I liked the idea of the tatau in FC3, except I hated those Rakyat scrubs; when you caught an outpost and they say, "We have the outpost, but your work isn't done!" in some smartass tone. I remember I lost it once cause I thought I've done enough work and shot that guy in the head, but anyway, thank God there's none of those slackos in this one with that kind of tone.
So basically you mainly follow the main missions with The Golden Path, and it's up to you whether you want to follow this conservative guy's thoughts or this open minded lady's thoughts and ideas - both used to progress the story, which will lead to a slightly different ending to who will end up leading The Golden Path. Other quests include helping out this priest who deals with arms, two drug dealers, plenty of new sidequests (which I recommend you doing - especially hunting for the fashion week). Karma events happen close to an outpost to where you fast travel to, or randomly while driving. They are small optional missions. There's different types of missions like playing as this guy called Kalinag that was to do with something in the Kyrati history, and can summon this tiger guy who is your best friend.
If you buy the Gold pack, you get access to Hurk's missions and the extra missions in the Himalayas. Sure, they're fun and all, but at this kind of price, it's really important to consider the fact that it may not be worth it at this stage. Probably getting it while it's cheaper or comes on sale might be a better idea.

This must be the best rogue like game I have played thus far, it lets you dwell into the futuristic theme without being too punishing early on, but it soon catches up. There are plenty of ways to tackle this game and each character available has different options available for you depending on their stats, there are a lot of numbers to choose from when you level up.
You start as a footsoldier equipped with the essentials for your chosen character, a few weapons, food and and medikits to help you started. You can choose to melee, shoot, run or a bit of everything in order to stay alife and keep your equipement in decent shape.
As you progress you will learn to craft from recipes found in the game which will help your endevour a great deal, you will learn to adapt to new challenging foes and find new strategies. This is also a game which easily fits into a 10 minute break of your busy schedule, save and quit at any time and return when you wish for more monster slaying.
The graphics are perfectly suitable for this sort of title and everything looks and feels polished. Nothing is perfect however, there is room for improvement.
I can warmly recommend this game to any adventurer outthere looking for a rogue like game and remember ... KILL THE RABBITS ... they may be furry and cute .... BUT KILL THEM.

This was the first game that I paid full price for that was not on any steam sale and I was pretty dissapointed. The game has stunning enviourments and beautiful phisics but it lacks and intriuging storyline. I can tell that when this game was developed, that they were banking off the siccess of Dishonored but where Dishonored had succeeded, Theif had failed. The enviourements load in sections which should allow more fluid movement and a better physics but it is just as glitchy as rendering the entire map and when you are constantly trying to load from room to room or map to map, It gets very frustrating and boring because you spend more time loading then playing. The game tries to introduce more of a dark paranormal presence but it is introduced so randomly that it offsets the the standard gameplay, which is overwhelmingly predictable. The use of combat and weapons is almost pointless as the game tries to enforce that you are a shadow dweller and when you do fight agianst the NPC's, Its regarded as negative which is annoying as they allow you a selection of fatal weapons.
Its my recommendation that if you are looking for a game along these lines, Buy Dishonored, It has a better storyline, Physics, Enviourments, and the game allows you to dictate the outcome. Its a linear based game with a non-linear based feel that allows you make the choices that define the game.

I just can't like this game. Aside the fact this is not a title for legacy Thief fans, its just a poorly executed in itself.
Beautiful level design and detail, but feels like a benchmark program that you have been dropped into and can walk about in. You can't actually do that much with the environments around you that are 'thief like' - the open world-ish side to the game that it tries to pull off is a lie.
Stealth and AI is acceptible but again you are confined by the level design; for example, In the open city Stonemarket, there is a side mission to steal something from a local doctors. To get in you must open a window, inside there are 2 guards, 1 civilian NPC but you are tied into 2 rooms and one corridor... if you are seen and need to hide... where do you go? You can't dash out the window... you are running into room 1, then chased into room 2, then into the corridor, dodge, back to room 2, back to room 1... your ♥♥♥♥ed basically. To open the window you have to mash the use key, which you can't do in (shudder) 'combat mode' anyway... Who thought this was a good idea? Garrett, the master thief, trapped by a window he just opened two minutes earlier... Really?
Every action is a cumbersome longwinded animation of Garretts busy hands, rummaging through drawers, opening doors, peeping round corners, lunging up rooftops, opening randomly placed wardrobes and cupboards to save the game.... on top of not being able to quickly open anything like a total tard, actually makes you feel like a bumbling gimp in a tight leather suit, not some master thief.
I tried to like it, I started the game again and again and I just can't bring myself like it... Other than the impressive visuals, the gameplay, well its just a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't find any fun or satisfaction in sneaking about or climbing up the clearly marked white bits of the city.
Developers should have kept it simple, stuck to the roots of Thief 1,2 and even 3 a bit more. Made it a quicker, more punchy and fast paced sneak in, sneak out. Risk vs equipment vs partolling guards.
Thief fans of old, definitely avoid. New thief players - Honestly? Buy the Dishonored collection, despite being a different game it does the whole thiefy thang a lot better than this.

Well, I read so many reviews and was stunned by the positivity and at the same time reading so much about bugs. Which is the main reason why I do not recommend this game.
The first simple thing is, if you can't even alt + tab a game without crashing it, then I cannot recommend it. I don't know a single gamer who doesn't have to do that once in a while. The second thing (also connected to the bugs) is the saving system. If the game crashes or you leave after a day (day and night are played one after another), you cannot continue at night, no, you have to start during day again.
I could go on as there are MANY things like that that got me to this opinion. Don't get me wrong: the idea of this game is nice. The graphics are decent. But if bugs ruin your game experience so much as they did for me (within the 1st two days of playing), then I have to say that it is poorly programmed and needs a lot of bug patches. A lot... browse the forums if you do not believe me.
As soon as they got rid of the bugs, I can recommend this game, but not before that. Clearly not.

There was a moment the first or second time I tried this game where I actually felt breathless after going through a room.  The sheer frantic level of action needed by this game is amazing, and the fact that the levels are semi-random and every playthrough is different just makes this one of the most fun first person shooters I've ever played.  The humor is very off-kilter (I love that the 'story' behind the tower is as randomized as the levels, including a version where the story is actually the randomized story of the levels), the action starts out at intense and ratchets up - the weapons are fun, the items are crazy; in a lot of ways it's reminiscent of MDK, but amped up even more.  It's as much a platformer as a FPS, which is in its favor.  It's like FPS meets Binding of Isaac, in the best possible sense.  I absolutely love it.  I've only chalked up one win (and that wasn't even a full win, just the easy way out), but this is one I'll come back to over and over again.

While I haven't finished this game yet, I noticed that there were a lot of negative reviews. I noticed that a lot of them didn't like depression being defined for them by someone else, but they were more than willing to provide their own definition. I find that to be weird, because in my experience depression takes on many forms.
The game even tells you that this isn't meant to definitely define what it means to be depressed. There are just too many types of depression and people in order to have one set definition.
I do have a bit of a theory that some of these negative reviews might be a knee-jerk reaction of shame. Such as us saying "No, I'm not that PATHETIC." or it could even be that you think you are far more pathetic than this. It depends on your depression I guess.
There were some statements I agreed with a lot. I have seen a therapist recently and have been doing better. I'm not sure there's anything like a cure out there for depression, but I do think there's a possiblity of living life fully without it fully controlling you. I don't think it's easy to get there and it depends on each individual if we can make it to that point. I hope I continue down the road where I am relatively happy instead of how it has been, but I don't know for sure.

I've been pushing a lot in favor of this game and did an inane amount of testing and community work, including answering questions and even moderating at some point, but with the last update, I must update review to a negative one
Refined design efforts
Multiple new gameplay mechanics
Work on the game world++
This game doesn't know what it is. It set out to be a sandbox, and now they're slapping in themepark features and questlines and minigames. They are unable to provide a consistent playing experience and they don't seem to know (and/or share with us) the direction they're trying to take this game in.
Despite repeated asks from the community since it's launch 18 months ago, the developer has yet to add in much requested social features like a proper chat channel, sharing of things and in-game guild-like structures.
They've also recently decided to take a stance where they interact less with the community. They've shut the official Discord, reduced forum interactions and abandoned a "champions" program without ever saying a word about it all. This was all very disappointing for those of us who invested north of a thousand hours helping them build and test, etc.
They're also unable to properly moderate their own community or interact in an adult way with their supporters and fans in a way that they can work collaboratively. It's a tough thing to do, but it can pay off. Not for this team, though.
After a long time of being told how much it aggravates the community and make for bad play experience, they've YET AGAIN released an update with tons of half-baked, half-done, low-quality and buggy features.
Agile development and rapid iterations should be accompanied with quality releases of a smaller subset of features. More traditional waterfall model aims at more well-rounded, feature-heavy releases. This team's development cycle is neither because of the way that they have of releasing very large, chaotic and unpolished versions of the game.
While I had a lot of fun in this game, and playing the meta and testing, etc. over the last 2 years, I think this is headed the wrong way. I'm sorry, but I cannot condone that type of development strategy anymore.

I really thought I would enjoy this game, but it seems to need a lot of work.  Even for a game thats not released officially yet its way too soon to have put it out to customers.   I really do hope this game gets up and running eventually with better quality.  Here are some things I noticed while playing or experienced that I found negative.
The Lag   - I have great internet and a high end computer system, yet I am getting lag just walking around a city or town.  Combat, forget it.
Combat - Ridiculous, A peasent will approach me and start swinging away, I cant tell if I am hitting him or not, and even though it looks like I am making contact the game says nope.  I had a really nice sword but its taking me forever to kill a guy thats attacking me with a bone, since I am playing move forward and backwards a lot since I cant tell if I'll get hit, I just stay away from combat entirely and run away as I will mainly die due to lagging.   Why do they swing so slowly in combat?
Minimal Npcs - Where is everyone?  I get it, the devs thought a lot of people would be playing and that would make up the worlds but I only ever see one other person on at a time.... So in the Queens city for example you have a few guards by the front gates, one guy tilling.  I found a few people inside a tavern? that was it.   The entire city is barren.  Would be nice to see a lot more npcs walking around.
Online only - will there ever be a single player experience with this game?  Seems this game could have a lot of potential with a few quests and Npcs implemented.  Playing online just stinks as theres nobody playing.
Servers - 50 per server and servers are around the U.S., I play on N.Y. server and I live in Boston, think it would be pretty good but laggy.
Perma Death - I understand that in the future this may not be, but for right now if you die you loose yoru character and all your items unless you put them into a house you bought for 3k gold, which takes quite awhile to get.
Food - it rots way to quickly.  I find myself most of the time scrambling for something to eat in boxes or the occasional garden i find somewhere.  Honestly would be nice if it lasted a lot longer.
Character creation - there is none?
This has just been my experience anyhow.  I will look into this game from time to time hoping for more frequent updates.    Seems a long way to go though.  Good luck Devs!

Not good enough to keep me going. I stopped early in chapter 1 and uninstalled.
The first hour or two of the game consist of trudging through an unexplained strange terrain, with "spooky" music and sound effects, while occasionally picking up extremely vague and disjointed notes that appear to have no connection at all. Deadly ghosts may appear, apparently only to serve as a very startling "try again". The only "challenges" consisted of dragging something in order to jump from it, a "move between checkpoints before your torch is extinguished" puzzle (otherwise something goes "boo" and kills you), and very simple "jumping over a chasm" puzzles.
There is no explanation of who you are, why you are there, why you are seeing ghosts and hearing spooky noises. Basically, the first hour is walking in a straight line while things go "boo" at you, which after the initial heart-pounding is just plain annoying. The only challenge is to endure this linearity while things try to startle you.
Now, compare this to other games.
In Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you don't know who you are or where you are *as part of the plot* and that is made *immediately* known to you. Which is an awesome hook. Also the puzzles are rather clever, progress is often not linear, and you actually have some action - albeit you can only run & hide rather than any fighting. But, hiding someplace dark with your head down while *something* seems to be shuffling its (feet? tentacles? body?) outside provides a true atmosphere of genuine horror. Being startled is a less-used aspect of the game, whereas finding tinder for your lamp so your character doesn't go insane from the horror of being in the dark too long is much more satisfying and works a whole lot better. If you want a real "horror" experience, that's the one for you.
In Deadspace, they rely on startling you quite a bit, so if that's what you like, head on there. But, over there you know who you are and why you're there, and while some aspects of what occurred where you are remain unknown for a good while, hints are everywhere and it's very clear the place had a clear function that has turned into a horror scene. While the ultimate causes remain mysterious, the actual occurrences are not and are merely a sign of how screwed up an otherwise ordinary place has become. So again that works much better. Also, you get to actually fight whatever jumps at you rather than a bland "try again", and other action (e.g. zero gravity, zero pressure environments) is very fun and very satisfying.
Now, you may think I just have a short attention span, and maybe I do and this game deserves a more thorough examination - but I don't think so. Both of the games I mentioned gave me much more entertainment in the first 5 minutes than this was able to deliver in an hour. There I cared about the characters, here I suddenly realized that I don't give a damn what happens to this nameless character with no motivation in a place we don't know how or why the character got to and no attempt is made to explore this or even acknowledge it.
Bottom line: Not worth your time.

Insanely, stupidly difficult, even on the lowest difficulty setting.
And this is coming from a guy who often beats difficult games on the hardest difficulty setting. I consider myself very good at roguelikes, and incredibly good at rpgs.
And I really love a challenge too, but this game just doesn't offer any reasonable challenge. It calls the lowest mode "easy", but thats so far off the mark it's rediculess.
Yes the first ~10 floors are quite easy, on easy mode.. But it quickly ramps up and becomes incredibly hard.
Normal mode is more like most games "Very hard"
And the game has freaking two more modes: Insane and Seriously? . Insane is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you 100% can't win most games even if you play perfect and spend insane amounts of time strategizing every agonizing move (in a game that will take 10s of a thousands of moves to complete). And seriously? I don't believe anyone has ever completed it without cheating. Hell even getting past the first few floors on that mode is insanely frusterating.
I beat easy mode, after some ~15+ frusterating hours of attempting normal. I usually hate playing lengthy games on easy, as I want the victory to be meaningful. But in this games case.. Meh it should just be called Normal for easy. Theres nothing easy about it.
The final floor alone took me some 4+ hours to beat, and had to use an insane stockpile of crazy rare items and cheesy strategies im really not proud of.
Plus the game has no real progression system like some ohter rogue likes to give you advantages on later play thrus really. After you die, your dead and thats it. Sure there are recipes you can learn, but the crafting in this game is painfully difficult, insanely random and unrewarding.... And after 15+ hours I had no real good recipes learn anyways. So I just did what had to be done to have ANY chance at beating this game in less then 100+ hours: Checked the wiki - yea nearly all the recipes are there, and you dont actally have to unlock them to craft anyways.
Protip: The most important/useful item to craft is the Quantum Scan Helmet. It lets you see thru walls and behind you, which is damn near neccesary on the lower lvls to conserve amunition/durability. But like all things in this game - its very hard to craft, requires 4 very rare drops. I managed only to make 2 near the last few levels, and the durability on them suck, so they both broke too.
I think a major part of the reason for the unbalanced unfun difficulty is the dlc - I bought only the bare minimum version you can buy here on steam, which included base + gold + mind games.
These dlcs do add cool stuff to the game, but the developers seem to think the main purpose of DLC is to increase difficulty.. Because nearly all of the enemies added in these, are vastly harder then the base games enemies, that and each introduces more ingredients - which you can only carry a very small amount on most classes, and more is not better, as it reduces the chances of you finding the exact ones you need for a given recipe, and makes managing your inventory more frusterating.
So yea the original vanilla version may well have been balanced better. Wish I could tell, but far as I could tell sadly there is no way to disable the DLCs, nor does steam offer the game without them.
Glad I didnt buy the other 2, as they seem to even further increase the difficulty of the game.
So yea, what could of been a very great game I just cant recommend due to the fact its just unreasonable difficult to beat, even on the lowest settings.
I see the devs are stll active ont he game tho, so I'll offer some simple tweaks that may aleviate this:
1. Add options in the game to disable the DLCs. Add a notification to the game explaining they may increase difficulty.
2. Rename Easy to Hard, Hard to Insane, Insane to Impossible. first 39 floors are ok but please make the final floor less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly insanely hard.
3. Add a new easier difficulty called Normal - recommended. Reduces total number of enemies by -10% (-50% on the final floor). Reduces chances of equipment damage. Increase all items durability +50%.

The Good:
Interesting start; generally thiefy feel.
The Bad:
Light and sounds are NOT gameplay elements; linear levels; bow and RPG system are pointless; non-ending; no challenge for experienced Thief series players.
Rating: 6/10
Thief lite, fun but not filling.  May be good to ease someone into the true stealth gameplay of the rest of the series.
Details:
Full disclosure, I have played and enjoyed the first three games in the Thief series.  I'm sure there are more hardcore Taffers out there than myself, but I enjoyed the original trilogy immensely.  With that bias in mind, how does the Thief reboot fare in and of itself and against its lineage?
In Thief you take on the role of Garrett, the master thief.  Garrett just wants to make a dishonest living stealing the treasures of The City, the hub of all action in the game.  As happens to characters who just want to mind their own business, Garrett gets swept up into larger events.
The game opens with an interactive prologue that serves as a tutorial for the gameplay.  As a thief, you need to stick to the shadows and remain silent to avoid detection form the guards.  At least, you did in the original trilogy.  The first three games made light and sound integral gameplay mechanics.  You could be fully illuminated, completely in shadow, or somewhere in between.  You could make a lot of noise running over tile floors and not a sound stepping on moss.  The use of sound was especially lauded when the original Thief game came out.  In this new Thief, you are either completely visible or completely hidden, no middle ground.  And sound plays no factor in the game at all.  If you are standing still you make no sound (although you may hear sound yourself as Garrett shuffles his feet), if you are walking you make almost no sound, if you are running the entire world can hear you.
The failure of the sound model also extends to the NPCs in the game.  In the original trilogy, you litsened carefully for approaching guards and could gauge where they were and how interested in finding you they might be.  Here, if you step behind a chair, the sound from guards may be completely cut off.  Or maybe not.  There were times where I was creeping through a sealed building and guards were on patrol chatting outside and yet they sounded like they were standing right on top of me.
Garrett's stealth abilities are supplemented in this game by the bow and arrows he carries.  In the original trilogy, these were essential tools.  You could dowse torches with water arrows, silence floors with moss arrows, reach inaccessible places with rope arrows, and so on.  In the first two games, you had a limited number of arrows per mission, which meant that you had to conserve your arrows for the appropriate time.  The number of arrows you can carry in this new Thief game is also limited.  However, except for still using rope arrows to reach inaccessible places, I found I used maybe four or five other arrows total through the entire game.  The bow has really been nerfed here.  As the game doesn't expect players to use the bow in clever ways, much of the challenge of the earlier games is gone, which may appeal to players just easing into stealth games.
Another aspect of this game that makes it "new player" friendly is the level design.  In the earlier games, the levels were varied and complex.  You had many ways to tackle a level and many different avenues to success.  In this new Thief game, the level design has been stripped down to the bare essentials.  With the exception of the open hub area between levels that is The City, all of the levels are extremely linear.  Rarely will you find yourself wondering where to go or how to reach your objective.  For new players, this will allow you to get a small taste of the thief experience without fear of getting stuck.  Experienced Thief series players will find little in the way of challenge here.
Not content to simply emulate the gameplay of the earlier series, the designers of this Thief game chose to add a few new mechanics into the game.  One of the key ones is the "swoop".  Hit a key and Garrett will quickly dash a short distance.  This usually allows you to cross patches of light without alerting the guards.  It also allows you to move silently while moving quickly.
Garrett also has a new "focus" ability, which he gains early on in the game.  Going into "focus" mode allows Garrett to remain hidden longer, to move faster, and to have hotspots highlighted in the environment.  I really only found focus to be useful for hotspot highlighting when I was too lazy to search an area myself.  The rest of the game, at least on normal difficulty, is too easy to require focus for much of anything else.
The designers also added a lite RPG system, which you can use to improve Garrett's abilities.  It's an odd inclusion as the majority of abilities you can improve are related to your combat capabilities or to your "focus" power.  One of the key points of a stealth game is to avoid combat, so improving combat abilities is a bit pointless.  As for improving the focus ability, since it's not needed to progress through the game it ends up being an odd choice to get the RPG treatment.  Still, for those who like character stats, that element is here.
As the game starts, Garrett is working with a partner/protege, a young woman named Erin.  Garrett tries to impress on her not to use lethal tactics in dealing with guards as it will cause trouble later.  Erin is more devil-may-care than the reserved Garrett.  The differences in the characters' approaches works really well and I enjoyed the chemistry they had together.  I thought it would be an interesting change to the Thief series to have a companion along on jobs.  Unfortunately, that was not to be.  Garrett and Erin are separated after the prologue and Garrett spends most of the game trying to be reunited with Erin.
The character of Erin was the most memorable part of the game for me.  I found myself wanting to discover more about her and where she had gone following the prologue.  That alone carried me through the game.  There is some political intrigue in the story, but really it's pretty bland and generic and I found myself forgetting much of the story even before I reached the end of the game.  Contrast this with the the much more individualistic factions of the earlier games and this new Thief game really pales in comparison.  Through your journey to find Erin, you meet an assortment of different characters.  To prove how "adult and mature" the game is, nearly every character you meet, with the exception of Garrett himself, spews expletives.  For myself, this is a turn off as it makes the characters and the general quality of writing feel much more immature and amateurish.
Mild spoiler alert: As mentioned, the search for Erin is what drove me through the game.  And Garrett and Erin do meet up again at the climax of the story.  And then...the game just sort of stops.  There is a denoument to the Erin storyline, although one other major storyline involving The City's Thief Taker General is left dangling.  I really found the denoument to be artificial and pretentious (which is a pretentious saying in and of itself, I know) and really not satisfying.  To me, it felt like the designers had exhausted their budget before they could complete the game.
So, at the end of the day, how is Thief?  Despite it being a pale imitation of its predecessors, despite its simplicity, despite its poor climax, I actually did have fun playing this game.  It makes for a nice, light distraction from heavier fare.  It's really kind of a one play game for me, I don't have any compelling urge to go back to it.  If they were to make a sequel to this, I'd pick it up if it continued Garrett and Erin's story together.  If you're looking for a full stealth experience, pick up the earlier games in the series instead.  As for this game, wait for a Steam sale.

A rogue-like for newbies of the genre! Dungeons of Dredmor is a fantastic starting point for people who wish to play an often unforgiving and visually lacking genre. So let's start at price, Dredmor is dirt cheap. At £3.49 for the base game, it's a steal that will offer countless hours of adventuring fun, and this is helped by the fact that no dungeon is ever the same, thanks to procedurally generated dungeons! The story is the Evil Lord Dredmor is here to do bad things and you are a hero who has to kill monsters, pretty generic... However, the game is packed with humour, which is super pleasant and the game doesn't take it's self serious! Gameplay revolves around stat-checking, crafting, combat and cleverely disguised turn-based mechanics. The game is surprisingly tactical and you can often mess up if you don't think about your character's positioning! And that leads me to my final point: Permadeath and replayability! You can pick 7 base 'Perks' in character creation (which can be randomised). As you level up you can evolve these Perks. However, should your character get killed (and they will), you stay dead and start fresh! This is optional for the less hardcore rogue-like players. In conclusion I say if you like role-playing games you should give Dungeons of Dredmor a shot. It's fun, simple and hilarious.

Your enjoyment of Magic Duels will depend on your expectations. If you want a collectible competitive game like paper Magic or Heartstone you’re better off looking elsewhere.
What Duels offers is a way to play with some of the newest Magic cards without the expensive price tag of paper Magic.
This the most generous free to play game I’ve seen. You can easily get grind the whole collection in a couple of months playing a couple of matches a day. There are no repeats so every booster contributes 100% to your collection.
Obviously if you feel like paying real money you can have the entire collection in one day, though I’d recommend waiting for sales just as a new set is due to arrive.
The game itself is different from regular Magic, for example, there are no set rotations, no upkeep, and individual cards quantity per deck is restricted by rarity. Wizards further limits the game by only including about half of a given set’s card pool.
What shines is Wizard’s support, every time I’ve had an issue they have been quick to resolve it.
As long as you treat it as what it is, a casual experience with some bugs, you’ll probably enjoy it.

First of all, although Dungeons of Dredmor is a very fun roguelike, it's also incredibly unforgiving - which is what I feel some players may be put off by, when starting the game. But don't stop there! Once you've died a horrible death or five, (heh, don't worry, it'll likely be a quick demise!) you'll start to get the hang of it, and be able to delve deeper into Dredmor's residence; killing off his foul minions and living vegetables with ease.
There is also a lot of humour and references to be had in this game too, which is certainly one of its strong suits; whether it's finding a Holy Hand Grenade from Quest for the Holy Grail, or having the option to purchase incredibly expensive (and pointless!) horse armour from Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. Another one of the pros of DoD is that it's a completely new experience every time you play it, as the floor layouts differ between playthroughs, as do the items you find.
So yeah, at the price it's at, I'd definitely recommend buying it if you're interested in a very challenging and rewarding experience, provided you're prepared to potentially suffer for an hour or two, before you get the hang of it.

After playing this game for far longer than I'd ever want to admit, I think it is time to write a review.
There are two things that are very good about this game. First, it is free to play. For anyone who has played the physical game, you know it can be quite expensive. This game is a good stepping stone to learn the game and to get a good taste of the sets. Second, they have updated the game with the new sets as they come out. This is something I had been wanting since I started playing the MTG games on Steam, so I am glad it finally happened.
Now, the bad...
Unlocking cards is very tiresome. You need 150 in game gold to purchase a booster pack, which unlike their real life counterparts, has only 6 cards. The main way to earn coins is by playing multiplayer matches and getting the daily achievements. As a person who doesn't particularly enjoy playing multiplayer, I usually did the latter. The daily quests can score anywhere between 40-120 gold, so even with those, it can still take a while. Playing a match vs an AI can net 5-15 coins based on difficulty. The matches can take a long time, the AI can be cheap, or you can just get bad hands so it can be quite painful sometimes.
After 469 hours of playing, completing all the story mode missions, I have only fully unlocked the first three sets out of the now six sets. Of course, if you are impatient and/or have money to burn, you can buy them with real money but if I were to spend the money, it would be on real cards. They have also added on extra stuff you can buy as well, like sleeves.
Multiplayer can be frustrating, the matching can be off and people can be generally annoying. For example, some people will simply wait until the last few seconds to make a move in hopes you will forfeit. It is also can be hard to compete against the people who have bought all the cards with real money, as with other games with micro-transactions.
Pros:
+Free to play
+Great way to learn how to play
+Allows you to test out a new set before actually investing in the real cards
+Allows total control in deck building
+/- Daily quests revolve more around multiplayer now after Kaladesh, which for me personally, was a huge turn off as I rarely played online. However, for most people this probably isn’t an issue.
Cons:
-Obviously not all cards are included, they want to try to sell the real thing too
-Matches can be painfully slow
-AI tends to be cheap
-Grinding for cards is extremely tiresome
This game is great for those who want to learn how to play but other than a time waster, it doesn’t go much further than that. While I used to play it a lot when I had short spans of free time, my interest has waned greatly and aside from seeing the new sets I don’t have much more interest in it.

It's got crazy depth, an amazing mod community, Bowiemancy, loads of skills, caters to both casual and hardcore types without sacrificing anything, and it's a roguelike that can be bought for a few bucks.

Magic Duels is a great way to learn to play mtg for inexperienced players, and also a great way for more experienced players to play Standard for free!
The visuals are wonderful and story mode is fantastic. Story mode is a wonderful resource which I strongly recommend to every player who wants to know more about Magic's story and lore. Story mode focuses on the first five members of the Gatewatch, all monocoloured Planeswalkers and provides excellent background for the flavour behind the game.

Not having the time or disposable income to keep up with the physical card game, Magic Duels is a good middle-ground. After playing through the various story battles, you should have enough cards to make and customize rudimentary decks, and enough in-game currentcy to purchace enough boosterpacks to get SOMETHING that will help elevate your decks into something more competetive.
In-game currency CAN be purchaced with real-world money, and it may be tempting to do so to unlock more rare/better cards - but I'd honestly reccomend investigating local hobby shops to find a group of players and investing in some physical cards as a better use of your money. But if that's not for you for whatever reason (time constraints, prefer to play casually while the local players are deep in the meta-game, etc) I could see dropping $15-$30 if only to support a well-made game.
The tutorials are handy to learn game mechanics, but if you're an old-hand at MTG (I started playing during the Mirrage block, and then played sporadically until the Ravnica block) most of it is tedious after you've learned how to control the game (And any card mechanics that may be new since you last played). But you don't want to ignore the tutorials completely, because completing the
Skill Quest for each mechanic nets you a small amount of in-game cash (about 2 boosterpacks worth, total). So even if they feel tedious and a bit condescending, you'll still want to complete them all.
I have only two complaints, and they are fairly minor:
1) The cash shop model, while fair, seems a bit off. Normally in free-to-play games like this, when you buy booster packs in bulk there is a small discount - usually to encourage players to save up, or incentivise them to purchace a larger pile of in-game cash. Not having this discount is fine, but it makes the pre-set bundle amounts seem odd. If there's no discounts on the bundles, why not let the players select how many boosters they want to purchace at once rather than the preset x1, x2, x8, x20 and x32? With no discount, if I only had the cash for 18 booster packs, Why should I have to select x8 twice then a x2, why not just let me input x18?
2) When creating/editing decks, the filters are helpful - but I wish there were more. You can filter by card type (Creature / Instant / Artifact / Sorcery / Land / Enchantment), by Colour, by converted mana cost, by rarity, by set, or by 'new' cards. There are all good filters, but it needs more - Like by Creature
- so that if you need to find all your elves/goblins/zombies/whatervers for synergies, you don't have to search through EVERY creature in one or multiple colours. Also helpful would be a way to search your card collection for certain effcts - like all cards that have (or grant) doublestrike, all cards that allow you to draw a card, all cards that give/use Energy tokens. I currently only have 3% of the Origins set, and 26% of the Kaladesh set, and the lack of these filters is getting annoying - it must be
for those with considerably more cards unlocked than me.
Other minor things that don't really detract from the game, but I'm not quite sure about or I find odd;
-Boosterpacks give you 6 cards each (at least 1 rare or better, 2 uncommons, and the rest commons). And you want multiples of many cards in your collection to be able to include more than one copy in a deck. But since your decks don't compete for cards (You can include a card you only have one of in any number of decks, but only once per deck) having more than 4 of any given card in your collection is pointless. So I'm not sure what happens you collect 4 of a card - is that card removed from the pool of possible cards? If you get more than 4, can you turn in the extras for credit towards more boosters? Or, like in real like, do you just end up with several virtual shoeboxes of worthless commons in your E-closet?
-In addition to daily quests that you can complete for in-game cash, there's a community quest that lasts about a week, and has absurdly high numbers (balanced by the fact that everyone playing can contribute). Since I've started playing, the community quest has usually completed the requirements with 4-5 days remaining on the timer. Unfortunately, it doesn't get REWARDED until the timer ends. Seems kinda odd - either make the goals higher so that the community has to work at them for longer, or award them on completion of the requirements, and queue up a new quest sooner.

Well....it just feels much more real.
I don't want to ruin anyones experience with spoilers, so I won't go into great detail about the story. I'll just leave it at stating that it leaves you plenty of room to decide the outcome, at the end of which I'll let you decide whether you feel satisfied or aggravated at the way things turn out.

It's a pretty generic horror game, but that isn't a bad thing. However there are many bad things about this game. I even made you a list!
-The tutorial level is unbelievably laggy compared to the rest of the game, maybe because the entire level loaded at once.
-Walk in the dark, pick up a thing, rinse and repeat. We're getting GOTY with these revolutionary mechanics.
-Jump scares are substituted for things that could actually be scary, you know, like a story.
-When the level loads a different area, there is no loading screen, the game cuts to black and fades back. It feels jagged.
-Some parts are just way too dark. Even with the gamma turned up, you won't be able to discern different symbols in front of you, symbols which will determine if you live or become a giant shishkabob.
But don't add this to your cart and delete it from your cart yet! This game has some redeeming factors!
-The setting is great, really. The maps aren't the most creative, but they serve their purpose well when they aren't dark.
-The sound is fun. It will make you feel as if there's someone around you or even BEHIND YOU RIGHT NOW! AAAHH!!
-Because it's a standard horror game, they don't waste time introducing quirky mechanics you'll use once and then never again. It takes 5 minutes for hem to teach you what you need to know and you're off.
-The first "monster" you come across (and the only one I've seen so far) has a pretty basic design, but still manages to be freaky after seeing it 500 times.
I'd only recommend this game to people who like horror games and only if they want something a little lighter. The story won't give you existential depression, the monsters won't give you nightmares, you won't have to sleep between mommy and daddy when you finish Chapter 1, it's a very relaxed horror game.

It's hard to describe. I don't want to compare it to other titles because it'd be unfair. It's immersive, keeps you wondering about the story and frightening, that's the feeling it gave me. I played through chapter 1 and couldn't stop playing. Chapter 2 looks great and Chapter 3 is installed and ready to play! If you like horror graphic adventures or horror altogether, you should buy Doorways! Oh, and don't spect combat, it's all about the story and the horror!

If your looking for a horror title, in my opinion, keep looking.
Doorways: Chapter 1 & 2 is a fun game with great atmosphere and some good puzzles but just not scary. I also thought the tutorial was a bit long. If you find this game on sale snatch it up but with only about 2 1/2 hours of gameplay, lack of scares, and some glitchy moments, this game is just not worth the original price. (Also the next chapters must be paid for)
Overall rating : 5/10

An excellent metroidvania all around, with very few flaws. Tight controls, good combat options, fun boss fights, an amazing, fluid artstyle... If these are the sort of things important to you, you won't be disappointed in this game. To me, though, the atmosphere was the truly exceptional element and the reason this game might be my favorite metroidvania.
The dark, morbid, beautiful atmosphere is a combination of the story, art, and sound design:
Story: You're given very little to go off of in the beginning. Your homeland has been affected by a curse, and you've come to  the capital city to seek an audience with the queen in hopes that she can aid you. The remainder of the story is conveyed by the scattered few NPCs, item descriptions, and hints from scenery, much like Dark Souls. Also, like Dark Souls, you can follow the stories of several NPCs as you progress through the game. Most bosses also have some amount of dialogue, giving them characterization and often revealing some small part of the story.
Art: Don't take my word regarding the quality - the trailer on the store page does a fine job showcasing the art and animations of the game, and also shows a diverse selection of the environments you'll explore.
Sound: One thing the trailer doesn't do a great job of is showcasing the way the art and sound design work together to deepen the atmosphere. Unfortunately, this is hard to demonstrate in just a few minutes, and will really only come out in full strength when you play the game yourself. The understated music is suited so well to the dark, hopeless environment.
Combat is good. The roll and airdash both give a generous amount of invincibility frames, and most bosses have a fairly limited moveset that is almost always telegraphed to some extent, so with some focus, practice, and timing, anyone experienced in the genre could probably beat most of the bosses on normal difficulty without taking a hit. I can't speak for the higher difficulties, but they're always there if the normal difficulty isn't challenging enough.
The only issue I can raise with the game is its length - it took me about 4 hours to finish my first playthrough. But, at this price, it was definitely worth it. New Game+, variable difficulty options, and a somewhat nonlinear progression should provide a solid amount of replay value as well. Highly recommended.

This is a sequel with - apparently - much more development time and budget then the first one, but worse. And painfully worse because it obviously could've been a good game.
Instead, this is some weird, pixel art, 2D-mashup of dark souls and the dev's favorite bunch of cute-girl-anime. The checkpoint system is copy-pasta'd and renamed from dark soul's bonfire system. Many items, such as a necklace and ring that boost your damage output when low on health are heavily influenced (or simply stolen, depending on how you wanna look at it). Dear Devs, why half♥♥♥♥♥it? You could've at least gone full way and give us different weapons to choose from while you're at it, that might've made it more interesting.
None of the characters are too interesting. They all seem hastily intro- and outroduced and none really matters anyway.  Everyone's got the above mentioned cute-anime-girl chibi style, but at the same time, the game wants to be this sinister and dangerous-feeling dark souls universe of its own.
Doesn't work. Then again, as long as it's cute anime girls, y'all buy it, don't you. I certainly did.
The ending's the really insulting part. No spoilers, of course. But basically, if you don't put in additional work (and finding the main bosses themselves already felt random and tiring), you get a♥♥♥♥♥♥and abrupt ending. The game doesn't hint at where to look for the classic "deep indie game" true ending too obviously so basically, you have to put in even more stupid backtracking in an actually quite cool world, which then completely destroys its own interestingness by putting you through the good old "check every wall if it's maybe just a ghost wall, now that's gameplay".
So I checked out the true ending on the internet and oh boy, am I happy not to have actually worked for it.
Still undecided? Here's my tip for you. Go play the one before this one (Momodora III, I think), not this one. It's short, it's entertaining, has the same decent fighting system and same great artwork but MINUS all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in this one.
Also it's cheaper. You're welcome.

Magic Duels is a great way to learn to play mtg for inexperienced players, and also a great way for more experienced players to play Standard for free!
The visuals are wonderful and story mode is fantastic. Story mode is a wonderful resource which I strongly recommend to every player who wants to know more about Magic's story and lore. Story mode focuses on the first five members of the Gatewatch, all monocoloured Planeswalkers and provides excellent background for the flavour behind the game.

Not having the time or disposable income to keep up with the physical card game, Magic Duels is a good middle-ground. After playing through the various story battles, you should have enough cards to make and customize rudimentary decks, and enough in-game currentcy to purchace enough boosterpacks to get SOMETHING that will help elevate your decks into something more competetive.
In-game currency CAN be purchaced with real-world money, and it may be tempting to do so to unlock more rare/better cards - but I'd honestly reccomend investigating local hobby shops to find a group of players and investing in some physical cards as a better use of your money. But if that's not for you for whatever reason (time constraints, prefer to play casually while the local players are deep in the meta-game, etc) I could see dropping $15-$30 if only to support a well-made game.
The tutorials are handy to learn game mechanics, but if you're an old-hand at MTG (I started playing during the Mirrage block, and then played sporadically until the Ravnica block) most of it is tedious after you've learned how to control the game (And any card mechanics that may be new since you last played). But you don't want to ignore the tutorials completely, because completing the
Skill Quest for each mechanic nets you a small amount of in-game cash (about 2 boosterpacks worth, total). So even if they feel tedious and a bit condescending, you'll still want to complete them all.
I have only two complaints, and they are fairly minor:
1) The cash shop model, while fair, seems a bit off. Normally in free-to-play games like this, when you buy booster packs in bulk there is a small discount - usually to encourage players to save up, or incentivise them to purchace a larger pile of in-game cash. Not having this discount is fine, but it makes the pre-set bundle amounts seem odd. If there's no discounts on the bundles, why not let the players select how many boosters they want to purchace at once rather than the preset x1, x2, x8, x20 and x32? With no discount, if I only had the cash for 18 booster packs, Why should I have to select x8 twice then a x2, why not just let me input x18?
2) When creating/editing decks, the filters are helpful - but I wish there were more. You can filter by card type (Creature / Instant / Artifact / Sorcery / Land / Enchantment), by Colour, by converted mana cost, by rarity, by set, or by 'new' cards. There are all good filters, but it needs more - Like by Creature
- so that if you need to find all your elves/goblins/zombies/whatervers for synergies, you don't have to search through EVERY creature in one or multiple colours. Also helpful would be a way to search your card collection for certain effcts - like all cards that have (or grant) doublestrike, all cards that allow you to draw a card, all cards that give/use Energy tokens. I currently only have 3% of the Origins set, and 26% of the Kaladesh set, and the lack of these filters is getting annoying - it must be
for those with considerably more cards unlocked than me.
Other minor things that don't really detract from the game, but I'm not quite sure about or I find odd;
-Boosterpacks give you 6 cards each (at least 1 rare or better, 2 uncommons, and the rest commons). And you want multiples of many cards in your collection to be able to include more than one copy in a deck. But since your decks don't compete for cards (You can include a card you only have one of in any number of decks, but only once per deck) having more than 4 of any given card in your collection is pointless. So I'm not sure what happens you collect 4 of a card - is that card removed from the pool of possible cards? If you get more than 4, can you turn in the extras for credit towards more boosters? Or, like in real like, do you just end up with several virtual shoeboxes of worthless commons in your E-closet?
-In addition to daily quests that you can complete for in-game cash, there's a community quest that lasts about a week, and has absurdly high numbers (balanced by the fact that everyone playing can contribute). Since I've started playing, the community quest has usually completed the requirements with 4-5 days remaining on the timer. Unfortunately, it doesn't get REWARDED until the timer ends. Seems kinda odd - either make the goals higher so that the community has to work at them for longer, or award them on completion of the requirements, and queue up a new quest sooner.

Getting through this game succesfully is not easy. Fortunately there is a great built-in modding community that allows you to customise your game experience, although I do recommend that you try the game "vanilla" first to experience its full impact.
The Little Ones DLC adds children into the mix, which to me made the game even more interesting. Interactions between the kids and the adults are endearing but also frequently heart-breaking.
Overall I would definitely recommend this game. It has given me an experience that is different from any other, and I expect that it will stay in the back of my mind for some time to come.

As someone who has had a life-long struggle with depression, I was curious about this game (partially due to the controversy surrounding it, which has been written about to death so I won't do it here).  When I stumbled upon it, I decided to try it out.
I'm a fan of visual novels which, for the uninitiated, the bulk of the "game" is reading text.  Visual novels tend to have images of the characters and backgrounds, which is part of its style and appeal.  Suffice it to say that it wasn't a great leap for me to switch over to the "gameplay" in Depression Quest.
This game seems to set out to give the reader a taste of what it's like dealing with depression, although realistically it can't cover every possible life scenario such as class, gender, orientation, race, etc.  It describes the struggles of whether or not to include those close to you in your treatment, to see a therapist, to get on or continue with medication.  Learning about things like the 'feedback loops' that were mentioned can be life savers to folks dealing with depression.  To quote the old GIJoe cartoon, "Knowing is half the battle" and insofar as presenting the information in an interesting, descriptive manner, I think this game does that quite well.  It's a well-crafted game, although I'm not sure how well its replay value would be.
My one gripe is very much with the music.  The piano riff put me in a negative mood before I read word one of the game.  I don't expect hyper anime-style music, but maybe something a little more neutral in tone would have been more suitable.
I will recommend this game as it did resonate with my own personal struggles with depression and presented the information in a straightforward, entertaining manner.

is a visual novel that has JRPG elements included.  You play as Ryou, a high school student attending Crystal Stream living in the fictional country of Sorayama.  He is best friends with Claire and Rina, and Ryou is in (sort of) a relationship triangle with them.  Rina likes Ryou but Ryou likes Claire even though she already has a boyfriend.  However, when Rina runs to Ryou one stormy night and reports that Claire's boyfriend has been physically abusing her, that's when things start to get more complicated.  Add in there Ryou's dreams of a time long ago involving princes and magical girls (yup, think like
lol) as well as reports of an actual magical girl fighting off shadow monsters in the nearby forest and you have Fading Hearts in a nutshell.
In regards to gameplay, there isn't much to explain.  As this is a visual novel, there are choices you make that do affect the story, such as whether Ryou will end up with Claire or Rina.  Also, there is a shopping element where you can purchase items.  Doing so can have Ryou learn spells, increase his HP, or make his physical attacks stronger.  These points are important when it comes to the JRPG aspect of the game although you can very well skip this part.  However, you won't be able to earn all of the achievements if you choose never to fight so just be aware of that.
Now it's time for the critique part of the review.  I had quite the difficulty in deciding whether I liked it or not.  Honestly, I would say that it deserves a neutral rating but since Steam doesn't have that option (it really should, though), I choose to give it a positive review.  Normally, I would skip writing a review for games I feel are neutral but I'm going to make an exception here, as this game ended up growing on me.  lol  I did like the concept behind the game and the ideas poured into it.  I could tell that the developer was trying really hard to convey the connections between the country of Sorayama and the kingdom that was depicted in Ryou's dreams and described in the mangas (an item you could buy once the cosplay cafe is made available).  The writing definitely could be improved upon despite that it has been proofread.  If it were rewritten to convey the story better, that would be a good start.  The art was fine, done in the usual anime style, and the music was fine as well although I felt that the tracks were too short so they would loop quite a bit.  However, I do keep in mind that this is a pretty old VN, made during the time when VNs in general were not as common as they are now.  Also, I will say that even though I found the writing could use improvement, at least it wasn't a Google machine-translated one.  Ok, now I know I'll get some attacks because of what I just said but that's fine.  Yes,
is considered an EVN (English Visual Novel) so the writing should have been better, right?  I did learn that the writer's native language is French, so English would be his/her second language.  Thus, I can give some allowance even though I still do feel that the writing should be reworked and that a good editor should be on hand to fine tune it.
Overall, despite some obvious flaws, I'm going to give
a positive rating.  I liked the concept of the game and with some fine tuning, it could be a really great VN.  Also, as it is the developer's first game, I'll give it another pass.  I appreciate the effort that was put in even though the execution could have been better.  Is it worth buying at its price?  I'd say that it's definitely best to wait for a sale.  There are Steam achievements and they all do work, and there are Steam trading cards as well.  On a final note, I will say that even though this game is presented to be taken seriously, it's best that it's not.
can be one of those games that it is so bad that it's good.  lol  If I had taken it seriously, I would not have enjoyed it but since I didn't (although I didn't make fun of it; just tried to enjoy the story and the game mechanics without being too critical), I ended up enjoying it.  It's definitely not the best VN out there but it's certainly not the worst, either.
(One thing I forgot to add but there is a bug in this game.  If you enter the Extras section and click on Achievements, some of the Steam achievements do get unlocked although this was obviously not the developer's intention.  lol  Just wanted to point it out there.  XD)

A puzzle platformer disguised as a psychological horror, Doorways is perfect for those who like a decent atmosphere and don’t mind hopelessly running around in the darkness.

Despite what the description states, Doorways is not a horror adventure but a first-person platformer/puzzle game with some eerie elements, including an overabundance of the most overused one, pitch black darkness.
To the game’s credit, it has a good place in there, since the levels are actually representing the subconscious of two deranged serial murderers, and the player’s job is to explore these psyches by solving various jumping puzzles and avoiding all kinds of traps: essentially this is Tarsem Singh’s The Cell without a framing plot and less artistic pretentiousness.
And with a shorter run time: an experienced player can run through the game under an hour. But the road there is paved with lots of hopeless wandering in the darkness and many attempts on the trial-and-error puzzles.
Still, if you get hooked on the atmosphere, it can be a good experience, especially if you can grab it at a discount price to compensate for the short length.

Short but sweet opening to a 4-chapter first person horror game in the vein of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which was the hell spawn that popularized the PC independent horror FPS side of things.

The controls, as per usual with this kind of games using Unity Engine, feel a bit clunky and extra problems come from the engine itself, which can be a resource hog when using dynamic lights and other effects.
I have no complaints, the game is around 3 hours long, you can 100% easily (something I love given how little time I have to play) but it suffered from Steam opening the floodgates and, of course, the really poor decision of separating the chapters into further releases instead of integrating them to the base game. However, still hope they can eventually finish the last chapter!
Give it a try if you got it during discount season, which was my case and I'm sure many others. For those who paid full price... yep, I can understand their fury as this is not an arcade game you can replay for hours and hours.
tl;dr: recommended, but newcomers or people with doubts, wait for the discount seasons just in case.

So, I'd definitely recommend reading the other reviews here, specifically the ones from people who bought into this game when it was in early access. Anyway, none of that affects me because I picked this up in a bundle.

Normally I struggle through games to the bitter end before leaving a review but sadly I just didn't feel like it was worth it in this case.
It's very (intentionally) dark. Whilst darkness can be used to add atmosphere, in this case it mostly just left me squinting at my screen as I fumbled my way through irritating... I don't really know what to call them... jump quests? jump on the tiles quests? etc etc I'm assuming these were the "puzzles" mentioned. I found my willingness to explore evaporating as I squinted into more and more dark corners. Stuck? don't know where to go? can't find a way on? retrace your steps. Even though the game appears to be very (very) linear it still wants you to wander through many obstacles into dead ends to collect things, so you can turn around and have to make your way through those same obstacles in order to get out.
It feels like a college project. It has some nice ideas but they're not well implemented. When you compare it to the other games available out there in this genre it really doesn't hold up. The storyline might have been fun but the game was too irritating for me to be able to appreciate it. The controls are clunky (as a KB/mouse user anyway).

Tower of guns is an incredible hidden gem.
There are very few first person shooter rogue like games currently on the market, and this game is proof that they can work very well. Tower of guns is a fantastic fast paced shooter, and is a serious test of reflexes. The sheer number of enemies trying to shoot at you at once can very quickly become overwhelming if you fail to react. The levels are, while mostly indoors, incredibly spacious and provide a good area to explore (as well as containing a massive amount of hidden rooms, mazes, and in some cases whole levels!)
My one criticism for ToG is a lack of content. While trying to find 100% of the secrets will keep you searching forever, the number of gouns your character can start with is somewhat limited. It should be noted that you are intended to find more guns as the game progresses, however these are very rare and most of the time you will have to complete the game with the gun you start with (although by that point it will be heavily upgraded from all the pickups.)
While it may not last you as long as some other games, I feel ToG is well worth trying for a very enjoyable FPS.

modeled off real-life weaponry, but instead over-the-top creative concepts. You not only have the ability to jump without needing to press your knees against a wall and vault over, but you can jump to your wildest dreams. No stop-and-pop cover-hugging here, get your♥♥♥♥♥out there soldier. Or grandmother. Or 80's gamer. Because even the storyline is randomly generated.
I normally try to be fair and critical in my reviews, but I can't help but rave here. A little indie game took me in its arms and told me that FPS was still alive and circle-strafe-bunnyhopping in the clouds, and I didn't have to wait for it to come back down. Contrary to my Steam play time.  I'm a 3rd Gen Mapler.  11 year vet.  In the past I've made many wonderful friends that are now very good friends in real life, but this game now in comparison back it's glory days is dead.
Pre-Big Bang, the game was Korean Level difficulty in terms of grinding.  Many rages, exploded gear, dying, etc it was still worth it because of the community.  What kept this game thriving was the community and after everything got dumbed down there wasn't anything left of that community.
I play once in a blue moon.  Maybe a handful of times a year just to see what's going on.  If you do decide to play this game go on Reboot as it's way more lively there.  Though, the game is still different.  There is just years of content I can talk about that supported in game interaction as opposed to now.  Just to name a few was the elimination of boat rides (you can now bypass with an airplane ticket).  Boat rides allowed people to meet often, sit on a boat ride and watch noobs get attacked by Crogs (Crimson Balrogs) while the Pros either laughed or switched channels to ride the boat to farm Crogs.  Party Quest nerfs was probably one of the biggest ones as PQs allowed you to play with others with a decent amount of XP.  They were the equivalent of dungeons in other games except more focused on puzzle solving with other players.  Props to anyone who remembers the sequence for Ludi PQ :P.
I can talk about the wippernsappers playing MS now and how the game has changed so much, but myself and others have every right to.  The reality was the original Maplestory was pretty much one giant AIM chat room that you just happened to be an actual video game.  It was community based.  I've seen other games' communities become stunted and/or drastically changed.  Unfortunately for Maple that was the only thing that was going for this game.  When I do play, I'll be honest, it's just the sheer desire to grind levels.  Though it's enjoyable it's nothing in comparison to what it was in it's glory days.
Chats being spammed by your almost full buddy list.  Walking up to random people and doing stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥  Walking up to noobs and dropping coins and watching them follow you, then you open a summoning bag with Mushmom in it and kill everyone.  Beating an Autoclicker in Kerning Party Quest or any party quest for that matter.  Scouring the FM for that ONE item.  Trying to find a training spot.  Trying to fend of KSers.  Defaming hackers.  Doing Guild Party Quest.  Blowing gear up.  Training for an hour to get 30%.  To put it [training] in perspective I made a character a few days ago before this review and got him to 150 in 2 days, my original character was a Hermit now NL.  Back when Leafre was released it took me an hour to get 7% on a fairly godly funded NL at that time with a Dragon Green Sleeve claw that was pretty ♥♥♥♥ing godly.
I wouldn't recommend this game.  If it went back to Pre-BB, yes, I would recommend it (yes I'm one of those players and rightfully so).
If you knew who Tiger was, watched Dray's Maplestory videos on YouTube like Maple Kombat, you'll all agree.
Point is the game isn't even important enough for people to make videos like Maple Kombat anymore.  They're literally all about training this and training that.

I look back on my Maple life with fondness as I still keep in touch with a lot of my friends from different parts of the world over social media.  I wouldn't take it back.

For a good challenge, turn off all UI and hints, make use of the great custom difficulty settings (no weapons, no KOs allowed, no damage allowed, etc.), and play non-lethal ghost style.  This makes for a much more immersive and intense experience.  Move slowly; allow yourself some time to learn to navigate the city.  The map is not extremely helpful (seemingly an intentional choice), and those short on patience may quickly become frustrated attempting to find side missions, in particular.
is not brilliant, but it is not 100% linear, either.  Contrary to the beliefs of those who rushed through, there are multiple paths to most objectives, but those paths may take a bit of exploration to discover.  That said, the game would certainly benefit from a more open, expansive touch, as being met with repeated denial upon attempted door, window, and ledge traversal is not exactly fun.  "Uh oh!  That guard may spot me.  Better scurry up this ledge...nope, game designers didn't want me to scurry up that ledge.  Loading quicksave..."  Also, loading screens when crawling through windows?  Let's nix that from the next game, please.
is terrible.  The localization of voices is so poor it seems unfinished (voices through a wall often sound like they're six inches from your ear), and vocal levels are all over the place (dialogue buried to the point of unintelligibility during some cut scenes).  Also, the extreme repetition of guard dialogue is inexcusable for a AAA game.  Pure laziness.  I laughed really hard when the Golden Joysticks Awards nominated Thief for Best Audio.  Anyhow, all other aspects of audio fare much better.  General atmosphere is certainly strong and enjoyable in its dark ambience.
are good, and sneaking around, distracting guards with bottles, navigating around noise-prone caged birds and dogs, creating shadow with water arrows, finding and disabling traps, and pick-pocketing are among the simple joys Thief presents.  The game truly shines when theft is the sole focus (this isn't always the case).  Do not skip the side missions, as they offer some of the best thieving and stealth opportunities.  AI is fair and as relaxed or challenging as the difficulty selected.  Failure always feels like your own fault rather than, "How'd that guard just see through a wall?!"  That said, you are underpowered against guards as an incentive to remain stealthy.
is something to skip through on subsequent replays.  As the supernatural stuff creeps in, you may find yourself saying, "But...I just want to be a thief and sneak around and steal things."  Or not.  This certainly depends on your expectations, or lack there-of, from a game titled "Thief".  With that said, the Outlast-style level, out-of-left-field and non-Thief as it may be, is genuinely creepy.
is high, particularly for obsessive completionists and speed-run attemptees.  The game does make this unnecessarily difficult in that each mission must be found in the city in order to replay, and none of these are marked on the map, so those short on time may spend the entirety of that time searching.  This may be a fun extra challenge for those with lots of time, patience, and practice navigating the city, but the additional option to quickly select and replay levels would certainly be welcome.
...many compare Thief to Dishonored.  Both are basically first person stealth.  Dishonored is clearly the better game as far as level design and story.  But for me, Thief is stronger in the shadow/darkness department, and I actually much prefer sneaking and being stealthy in Thief.  Though I opt to play Dishonored non-lethal, no KOs, and without "blink", I almost feel like the game would be more fun if played the opposite way.  How about Styx: Master of Shadows?  It's a fantastic hardcore stealth game with insane level design (but lower visual production values), and a clear winner as long as third person floats your boat.  If I found a game with the dark atmosphere of Thief, the art direction of Dishonored, and the level design of Styx, I wouldn't play anything else.

For lovers of the original classic series, this Thief game rings true. The Light Gem, treasures everywhere and a feeling of ultimate stealth keep this game in line with the series. It opts to branch out to a bit more of combat as an option, though I never found this effective and I enjoyed the variety of ways to move around The City and its various levels.
It falls short at the end, in my opinion. The last level feels exceptionally linear with a sharp spike in difficulty for various stealth desires. The story closure feels... weird, in my opinion (but that point is especially an opinion). Not unlike Human Revolution, Eidos' other baby, this game's ending felt a little rushed and didn't quite hold up to the classics many know and love.
Still, after the end you can continue to pursue side quests (of which there are plenty) and treasure hunting. The unique treasures that can be displayed in your safehouse give a great feeling of depth in how far you want to fill out the game, more so than a "x/100%" counter. The ambiance of the environment is top-notch; anyone who can run this game on near-max settings should further play in the dark with a headset. It's very easy to get immersed into the stealth, the fear, the tension, the joy of success. The game will throw a few curveballs (no spoilers) that may take veteran Thieves out of their comfort zone but it's only temporary and fits the point of the game.
Absolutely recommend for any stealth lovers. Take the end with a grain of salt, enjoy the rest of the game in its entirety.

It's a nice no nonsense action platformer/metroidvania. It has a story to give you a clear purpose but doesn't bombard you with much dialogues and jumps straight into action 99% of the time.
It has a nice aesthetics: The color palette unifies the overall feel of the game without feeling monotone. It's also heavily animated so each little cutscense feels alive.
It has a nice gameplay: It's got melee and ranged attack, but neither overpowers other. You'll smoothly alternate between them during any battles. The enemies got a countable amount of health and a perfect guard move so each battles requires you to formulate little strategies in real time. The dodge move also gives additional depth into battles without making it too complicated. Boss battles are a balance of player-sized nimble characters and humongous monsters to give it a variety.
The overall stage was a huge non-linear metroid-style map that is connected to each other and require you to figure out the directions by finding gate and keys. The stages are well-designed and intuitive: stage elements are consistently shared between different areas and doesn't contain punishing surprise elements. Even the secrets use a consistent mechanism to hide themselves and aren't impossible to find once you've got a certain item.
All in all, it's a very nice and polished game. The only problem is the length: it's too damn short! Rest assured tough, it's really worth all the pennies even at its length. I only complained about the length after it's over, meaning it could have been longer or have a deeper lore rather than having pacing problems.
Oh, also you can become a cat (!!).
The devs have no idea how idea how much I love them right now for adding this feature to the game.
