Tower of guns is yet-another-roguelike-like-like... and I like it! Basically, its a first person shooter with random elements. But I'll just stick to the pros and Cons.
Pros:
+UT2k4-ish movement and controls. High air control, double jumping, etc.
+Risk-of-Rain-esque difficulty scaling. Basically, don't kill hugbots, get difficulty-- when possible, make life easier on yourself. It'll get crazy hard eventually.
+Great feeling Guns (eventually, not your initial 2, but the following ones are quick to get)
+Acheivements/statistics - You know how you did, and you know what you're going for.
+Weapon modifiers are fantastic!
+Bonus levels for major achievements with significant power ups--- Some go crazy.
+Randomly selected storylines are pretty funny, and they are per 'run' and have internal continuity.
Meh:
Music is Ok, and gets the job done. Some music is great and fits the mood darn near perfectly (Hugbot Alley) but others just suffice
/At times, too chaotic. 50 spike balls flicking everywhere can be stressful. But its also a pro in that you need to change your approach, and either get the hell out of dodge and blitz through ignoring enemies (you don't have to kill any to proceed) or take it slow
Cons:
-Some balancing issues? Some items don't feel useful. Others seem unclear in how they will help you.
-Some repetitive enemies, There is only 1 mobile ground based non-boss enemy (that i have seen)
-It is unclear if there are any benefits to high difficulty
Overall? So far, 5/5, @ 50% 'total' completion with 5 hours played, I have beaten the game once.
The gameplay matters, and this game delivers. Not the best in everything, but serious fun that I haven't had in a shooter in a long time.

2. After sinking 11+ hours into beating the first campaign, I beat the final boss and was rewarded with a punishing bad end because I didn't collect 12 planks of fracking wood. The feeling of destroying a colossal dragon only to be rewarded with death because of a low lumber supply is unbelievably dissapointing. I feel robbed of my victory and my time.
3. The second campaign is a much more interesting setting - too bad I won't be able to see any of it because the sand shark fight is the most impossible garbage i've ever encountered. The fact that they only have a split second window of vulnerability would be enough. The fact that the ground beneath your feet is constantly shifting would be enough. But once you figure out a pattern to survive the fight, the monsters actually stop FREAKING ATTACKING YOU, and just buzz around the arena wasting your time and energy. I spent over an hour on one attempt of this fight, simply because the damn things wouldn't show their faces so i could hit them. The encounter literally just sits on its butt and waits for you to screw up and get caught in a sand trap or something long enough to kill you in 3-4 hits while you're trying to claw your way out.
All in all this game was a humongous waste of time and showed nothing but frustration and dissapointment time and again. I haven't played such a horribly unsatisfying game in a long time.

This is not a fun game.  This is not meant to be fun.  Don't misunderstand, it is definitely enjoyable, and worth the time put in, but more enjoyable like 'Things Fall Apart', or 'Crime and Punishment', or 'Heart of Darkness', or 'The Grapes of Wrath.'  This is an adult game that asks, "What is it like to survive in a war zone?", but instead of just telling you about it, like a novel, it sets up an experiment.  Here is the city.  Here are the people in the house.  Here is the story you make.  You must make them survive, make them get through.  Your reward is a roller coaster of the heart, as you are forced to make impossible decisions, challenged between altruism and selfish survival.  And your reward is a combination of knowledge of yourself, learning more of these people's lives, and maybe, just maybe, making it out the other side.  You only get a small snippet of what happens to everyone after the war, but at the same time, it is less important than the choices you made, how you tried to stretch out the food and medicine, how you tried to make your home more safe, and who you decided had to go to make your group survive.
Or, if you get the DLC, your family.  And the DLC really does expand in a grand way on this, mostly by showing children in the most realistic way I have seen in any game to date.  As smaller, weaker humans with less experience.  They will make you make hard choices.  They will then make you question your choices.  And even though you need to help them not be afraid of the very real monsters in the dark, they will help you not be afraid of the real monsters in your soul.
Also, pro parenting tip from the game... if you train kids in how to do household chores, they can help around the house.  Although, they still want to spend some time playing.

Sword of the Stars: The Pit is a harsh roguelike. Is it a good roguelike? Well, that's where opinions differ.
It seems to be missing that key roguelike experience that the community values. But what is it? It has hunger, a scarsity based ammo system, spell trees, randomized numbers and chances, and different classes. What's missing?
Fun. That's the statement of this review. SotS: The Pit is missing fun.
Roguelikes have always been a unique genre in which its fun to win OR lose. And losing in The Pit is not in the least fun. You either have enough ammo, or you don't. You have food to explore, or you don't. That computers skill roll works, or it doesn't.    There's no "mushroom" in this game of rock, paper, scissors. No surprise element to keep the early game from feeling like a grind; no hilarity to make bad runs enjoyable or memorable.
The Pit ends up being too binary. New roguelike players might not understand this, but The Pit definitely suffers from the poor design choice of bad or good. No middle. There's no crazy builds, no adaptation. You place your stats in nearly the same things, find your first weapon, and go from there. Experimentation is reserved for easy mode or not at all.
If you enjoy challenges, you'll enjoy this game. If you enjoy games, you won't enjoy SotS: The Pit. Even if you are the first of the two, you may find your frustration venting out at the developers for clearly not knowing how to balance roguelikes.
Fantastically punishing, and has a very cool mechanic to provide persistence across runs.

I seem to be on a glut of roguelike and roguelike inspired games lately.  Sword of the Stars: The Pit is an exceedingly competent entry into the genre that is well executed.  The graphics are a bit strange but familiar to those that have been with the series, and in the scope of it's own series are done fairly well if not extraordinarialy.  (The character animations definetely look to have been done on OpenCanvas or something similar and stand out against the rest of the game, though).
The roguelike elements are definetely the strength of the game.  Combat is intuitive, fair, and reasonably balanced.  The creature AI can be relied upon to act in a consistent manner which is fairly important for combat in roguelikes, and the different weapons actually add a variety of game mechanics rather than just being incrementally increased versions of the same guns, which is a pitfall of many roguelikes.  The random nature of the game can make things in some runs much more difficult, but I never felt the randomness broke a game in the way it can in many roguelikes.  If you got a bad roll on a level you can still have an entirely legitimate change of making it through the level if you play skillfully, such as utilising beserk mechanics to cause enemies to fight each other, luring enemies into environmental hazards, through grenades around corners, or placing traps.  Which also leads into another of the games strengths - there are a lot of mechanics such as those I just mentioned and they're fairly intuitive for the most part.  If you have any experience with roguelikes you likely don't need the tutorial or the manual, although both of those are actually quite well done.  The one mechanic I do have a gripe with is the idea of the crafting recipes.  It's supposed to be able to find recipes through some of the data panels but I have never done so.  Most of them can't be found this way and it turns the game either into experimentation with blind luck, or consulting a wiki.  There's some people that like their games like that however, and it's a subjective preference of mine that I don't.  The voice acted parts - albeit fairly rare - are actually pretty well done, as well.  The whole game just seems to be a game where a significant amount of time and effort has been taken on polishing the game, something sorely lacking from many releases big and small these days.
The biggest criticism I have about the game is that is very "safe".  It takes no risks and as such is very generic in the truest sense of the word.  However it's a well-executed implementation of the genre with an interesting background story and theme that offers a huge amount of replayability and a variety of different levels of challenge for someone to find their individual level of comfort.  Definetely a game to pick up if you enjoy the roguelike genre.

This is one of those games that changes very dramatically on a second playthrough, once you know the game mechanics better.
The first playthrough played like a standard Castlevania-like exploration adventure. Close range attacks, long range attacks, double jump, dodge. Use found items and abilities to progress to new areas. You know the drill.
I was very delighted by the art, music, and pacing. It's fantastic. It's a thrill to just wander around the map. But it's not just pretty aesthetics, unlike other indie games with retro aesthetics that get very bland very fast (90% of indie games on steam). Momodora has very polished game mechanics that makes combat very satisfying, and has depth that teaches itself which great storytelling sensibility, without hyperkinetically filling your screen with stats and hints like other games on this genre do (hello Valdis Story).
My first playthrough took me about five hours, and a healthy dose of retries over bosses that took me awhile to figure out. Then after finishing it it took me about two more hours to quickly rush through New Game+ to find all missing collectibles.
So far, great. Then I went for Hard Mode and Insane Mode.
At first, it seems a bit overwhelming (going from a huge lifebar to dying from a couple of hits, or just one hit in Insane mode), but there's a catch you most likely will miss on your first playthrough: you get VERY powerful equipments and items when defeating bosses without getting hit. Suddenly, equipping the right stuff at the right moment is everything, and the game's mechanics get a lot deeper than the first time around. You also realize just how non-linear the world is: after an introductory area, the four next main areas at the middle of the game can be tackled literally at any order before going for the final two. And figuring out the most efficient route reduces the average 5 hours of a first playthrough (according to howlongtobeat dot com) to as little as 1 hour. This might sound like a problem, but it's actually a design choice: it's a game designed to reward mastering. Similar to what made game like Castlevania Symphony of the Night and the first few Mega Man X so damn replayable.
To people familiar with the games that inspired this one, you'll feel right at home. It's a short but sweet ride that'll keep you comming back for more, wishing there were more new games as fine as this one around. It feels very polished, with lots of attention to details and replay value. I hope other small studios planning to take a chance at this genre are taking notes.

Tower of Guns is an extremely entertaining concept executed extremely well. It's a rogue like, randomized levels, enemy spawns, loot, and gets crazy difficult at any moment. But instead of being a top down shooter or a Diablo esque RPG, Tower of Guns is a fully fledged first person shooter, with the game mechanics geared towards the more retro side of things. Basically, It's Serious Sam meets Binding of Isaac. And this lovebaby is one heck of a rockstar.
The visual presentation is unique and varied, the cel shaded effect is quite nice and makes the incredible amount of things you'll be seeing on screen a lot easier to process. Every enemy is unmistakable in design, even if their textures are a little drab for my taste (request to developers, Fruity Textures Mode plz) The sound is zesty, guns sound intentionally weak at first, but sound awesome the more they level up.
Level design is linear but not confined or simple. Multiple elevated areas, loads of secrets and various ways to cross chasms. They are even comparable to levels from Portal. Typically there are 3 to 4 rooms then a boss room. It's quite intuitive and allows you to gauge how hard the level will be.
My only complaint with the game so far is the physics are wonky. Some of the platforming objects just do not work correctly. For example, the cog wheels with the platforms, Sometimes it lets you jump off them, sometimes it doesn't. Some objects like pipes and such end up being phased through a lot, which can make reaching some secret and high up areas impossible if the game doesn't like you that run.
Weapon designs are unique and varied. They all level up to be more powerful, and they all suit different styles of play and preference.
I rate the game so far an 8/10. I've yet to unlock Endless Mode, which is sure to be a treat.

You like towers? You like guns? You like long walks on the beach with british voiceovers? Then get ready for the ride of your life!
Tower of Guns is an indie made game that was recently published earlier this March after a year in being developed. In it, your only objective is to make your way through 15 floors to the top of the tower. Sounds easy? Well it would be, if it wasnt for all the guns trying to mow you over. Each floor is randomized, giving you the element of surprise and wonder as bullets, saw blades plasma, spikes, cannons and a whole lotta other stuff tries to kill you. At the end of each floor, you face down a boss, which is also randomized. Hopefully you dont take death too seriously, because not only will it happen, but you are tallied for it to boot. Its not like death is important or anything, right? :D
This doesnt mean you are entirely weak. Items and powerups you may find from beaten bosses, enemies, or capsules you cant open without enough money (also beaten from enemies) will offer a variety of upgrades to you or your weapon, which are also randomized. Sometimes you might score a good one, sometimes you wont, and sometimes you wont find any. The more you play, the more you can unlock. Collect all the different gun abilities, achieve perks and guns depending on what you do, level up your gun by collecting the blue orbs and stay alive by collecting the red orbs from fallen enemies, and get to the top of that tower!
Tower of Guns is a thrilling rush for its worth. I highly recommend taking it for a spin, because if the whole "Tower of Guns" thing doesnt appeal to you, you really are missing out dear viewer. Just remember to never be a sitting duck and keep your eyes open for anything. Theres a lot of flashing and a lot of bullets coming your way, so be ready for the biggest barrage from all sides coming your way! Also, be creative; You arent given any sort of instructions on "how to play", so if you see something interesting, follow up on it, it might take you to a secret, and there are a lot of secrets on each floor.
So go buy it. Do it! Do it now!

Even though it's a rather simple game, it's quite catchy.
You have to survive a war and only by night can you go out and collect stuff you need to survive, because during the day there are snipers and you might die (I haven't so far and it happened a few times that I didn't make it in time to get out of a building).
You start the game either with a pre-set pair of three different survivors, each of them with their own background, or you start your own story with one person alone. Over some time, other guys will join you and your house.
You have to collect food, material, wood, tools and other things, but you also have to be careful and might need weapons since there could be thieves and bandits or even normal people who try to defend whatever is left to them, so you could also die if you are not careful enough. Apart from that you could also die from wounds, probably from hunger or if winter is coming and it's cold and you don't heat, so in this respective it never gets boring and you really have to watch out for your guys.
That's basically the game in a nutshell.
For me personally one of the reasons why I like the game so much is the setting. It's not your everyday one or third person game, but the scenery, as you can see from the pictures, is more like a theatre, a stage or a puppet house so to speak. I find that quite appealing. I also like the characters and the fact that everything's random. Every time you start a new game, you could have a harsh winter or none at all, the places where you can go and collect your stuff change (say the church you went to in your last story was ready to trade, while in the next game bandits are living there, you just don't know) and the people you play with as well. It also takes some time to find out which way is the best to survive, so it never gets boring, though you need a certain amount of patience to start a game over and over again to find the best way to survive.
I personally have a lot of fun with it and can recommend it to anyone who's looking for a not too serious game to play in between.

Overall this is a very good game for the artistic representation of the oppression of war, however, as a game it has flaws as well.
Pros:
+ The atmosphere is very good.
+ The personalization of the story to a few people who vary different plays is well-designed.
+ The 'feel' of the game is very sad and effective for the topic - and I really like the art.
+ All of this adds up to a strong experience.
Not plusses:
- Like any game of the type, it has to invent some ways making it a 'game', and those aren't always enjoyable - do you have enough food, heat, morale, etc.
- That gaming side tends to take you out of the game a bit learning ways to 'game the system' - how best to do what the game wants more than relating to the situation depicted.
But that last point isn't as bad as it sounds. The game does well mostly at those gameplay elements, despicting issues and other people in the game, and providing options for different playstyles.
It's not a game I really feel warm and fuzzy about returning to, and I don't really look forward to parts like the combat side. But I think it's a great experience worth trying.

Thief follows the concept of Deadly Shadows (its predecessor released 10 years ago) with its City in the center of the game which is freely explorable between the story missions. The story consists of 8 chapters and while this number seems insufficient, these are great and interesting levels. There are two more clients in the City giving Garrett - our protagonist - additional missions and a guy in the local inn giving him several jobs.
Overall, it took me 25 hours to complete all missions but I missed a lot of collectibles, secret areas and other loot. In fact, the missions have optional criteria which can yield some extra gold so it's worth checking them again. And once the game is complete you are free to move about in the City and replay the missions for the missing items.
The good stuff:
-- Graphics. The game employs some excellent lighting and shadow effects. Since staying in the shadow away from the light sources is a must it is good to know the developers took this part of the game seriously. There are several cutscenes and not just Garrett but everybody else turning up in his story look very detailed and realistic. Accompanying voice acting is top notch. Locales during missions are diverse and interesting.
-- Atmosphere. Hiding and stealing has never been more fun! I like how you can take almost everything in the game: golden saucers, candles, silver cutlery and all kinds of jewels. Robbing has never felt better! You can look for secret doors by pulling books on shelves or lockpick a safe that is hidden behind a painting. These are regular activities coupled with the disabling of several deadly traps.
-- Equipment / AI. Rope arrows help you reach higher places, choke arrows eliminate dogs silently and water arrows will extinguish almost any fire you encounter. Enemies do notice them - guards can easily be distracted and the AI is clever enough to look for you even inside of a cupboard.
-- Longevity. As I have already mentioned above it takes a while to complete all missions and it takes even more days to find every lootable item scattered across the City and its surrounding areas.
The bad stuff:
-- Optimisation issues. Before being able to properly play Garrett's story I needed to tweak the game a little. In fact, it took me a while to realise it was not my rig that caused the problem; some effects are simply not worth being turned on. Interestingly, most of them were shadow-related and I barely noticed anything when I turned them off. The game looks just as good and the stuttering - for the most part - ceased to exist. I hate when I have to look up numerous websites for tweaking advice.
-- Audio issues. Sometimes you hear people speaking but you have no idea where the voices come from. Since you run on rooftops or ledges next to windows I gathered these could be people indoors. But then again sometimes you hear them as if they were next to you and at other times you don't hear them but the subtitles are shown. Occasionally more than one citizen speaks and the audio overlaps. Pretty annoying at times.
-- Stuttering / loading screens / hub system. The hub system the game uses requires a lot of time to get used to. The map can be annoying and you do have to remember if it is a door or a window that takes you to the next district. But these areas are not that big so I did not really get why the game was divided up into so many sections. Loading, therefore, is common, especially when a mission is complete and you have to get back to your client to terminate it for good. He, of course, stays at the other end of the map.
Sometimes you have to go ground level to find a pile of boxes that is the only means to access another area... this was annoying as hell! And once the next chapter begins Garrett always finds himself next to his Clock Tower hideout. This is the central part of the City and loading it up takes a lot of time and stuttering, as well. Some of the cutscenes also suffer from loading time - until it is done low resolution textures will appear for many secs.
-- Gameplay issues / nuisances. Garrett's blackjack. Really? A melee weapon to stun enemies usable in combat, as well? Where is his sword? Or a knife? The game already labels you a Predator if you kill someone with a bow from a distance. So, why cannot we do that close-up? Sometimes I felt like going with the failed stealth and dispatching the attacking guards option but when I saw how slowly it can be done with the blackjack I loaded up a previous checkpoint immediately instead of wasting my time with the soldiers. The developers should have looked at Dishonored.  With all the excellent arrow types Garrett just looks lame with his blackjack.
Moving can also be difficult at times. Sometimes Garrett jumps and grabs a rope in front of him while other times he falls and dies. Long jumps after running can only be used where the developers intended them to be used. Many times you'd like to jump down but Garrett crouches and looks down.
Overall, I liked Thief. But I found its stuttering, its optimisation issues very irritating at first. Its hub system - the navigation in the City - and its combat with the blackjack took me several hours to accept. I expected more from such a remake and from Eidos. I wish they had looked at other games such as Dishonored and borrowed some good ideas. Or simply look at the Dark Project from 1998 - the first Thief game that had no issues with Garrett wielding a sword.
I was not interested in the Bank Heist mission and Forsaken challenge DLCs, therefore, I cannot comment on those. I do not like that some of the content are intentionally pulled so that it can be sold later on.
Thief could have been much better. It is not a bad game but not a very good game, either. Once you have gotten used to its nuisances you can immerse yourself in the City's steampunk atmosphere. If you achieve that, long hours of gameplay are guaranteed. My rating for the game is 6/10 at best.

I loved, and still love, the original Thief series. That said, I'm not beholden to the original series so much that I'm closed to new interpretations, as long as they're done well. Sadly, in this particular case, the mark has been missed by an incredible amount. The game is beautiful, and the aesthetic is very well-realized. Beyond that, it's a travesty. The story is a mess: either they cut out a sizable portion of it or they changed the story at the last minute and struggled to make the existing pieces fit the new narrative. Either way, it's a hodgepodge of half-baked ideas and huge leaps of narrative logic. The sound design is all over the place, with characters being far too quiet in cutscenes, over-repeated incidental dialogue from NPCs, and sound positioning seems to be wrong most of the time.
I wanted to love the game, as while there are quite a number of stealth action games, very few really focus on the experience of being a master thief: sneaking around and stealing things. Most focus on assassination or some other kind of objectives. While it doesn't meet the criteria of playing a thief, I still would highly recommend you play Dishonoured instead of this if you're looking for a great Thief-like, even if it primarily concerns itself with being a sneaky killer more than a sneaky stealer.

Full review:
Fading Hearts is a VN, but it's also a dating simulator, which is quite a rare site on Steam.
Your choices in the game can essentially change the entire genre of the game. You'll have the choice of leading a life of adventure, or just a normal, laid-back life. During my play session, I chose the laid-back life (I am a fan of VNs like Clannad, Kanon, etc.) and generally had a good time.
That being said, this game is not for everyone. If you go into a game like this expecting much in terms of gameplay, you might want to look elsewhere. Most of the "gameplay" here is just reading. It is a VN after all, that should be expected.
I can recommend the game for its story. It may be short, but it was well worth the read!

To make this short -
Just so we're on the same page, as far as I'm concerned, Long Live The Queen and Magical Diary
games, as they offer plenty of interactive content, where you actually get to play, make decisions and influence what happens next. In Fading Hearts, though, the communication is mostly one-way - most of the time you watch and read, and occasionally make a choice. It took me around 20 minutes of scrolling through animations and text boxes, until I got my first choice, and that is only to have the game throw at me more and more information.
Obviously, I'm disappointed, as I was expecting more to do. Despite my disappointment, though, I'm not rating this game down, since it was completely my fault, that I didn't get what I wanted. I should've done some reading before buying something I had thought was something else. I just figured I'd post something about it, so others wouldn't make that mistake.

Much as it pains me, I can't give this game a good review.  It is nice to see games in this style being sold in Western markets, but regrettably this is not a particularly good example of the genre.  The story and characters are engaging, and have some depth, although the writing is mediocre (a real problem when the entirety of the game is read off the screen).
The real killer, however, is that the game is very poorly coded -- important events happen off-screen, without the player's involvement; interactions with characters reference events you have not experienced; and endings occur regardless of their triggers being hit (or not hit, as the case may be).
This game has a great concept, but its execution falls terribly short of the mark.  I wouldn't expect these errors in a free title, let alone a $15 game.  I do look forward to seeing future work from Sakura River -- possibly even a complete version of this title -- but I can't recommend this game to anyone but serious visual novel junkies looking for a fix, and even they are likely to be disappointed.

I don't often write reviews for games after I play them, but this game deserves some recommendation. When I first got the game, I played 5 minutes of it and it just seemed slow and not too great. It is so inconsistent in textures - between realistic and pixelated - but it somehow manages to create the perfect aptmosphere  that's easy to look at. A unique and admirable artstyle. The games story and art makes up for the slow and at times awkward gameplay by far.
I RECOMMEND THIS GAME IF:
You would like to get immersed in a twisted creepy depressing story.
You like puzzles.
You like simple, though quality games.
You're a fan of psyhcological horror games.
And I recommend it to anyone else who's interested. It is well worth $10 for sure.

Ill start with saying something few people have dared to say: This is a good game. Does it have bugs, glitches and overall annoyances? Yes, absolutely but the core is an amazing game with great potential.
You start out as a nobody, with a rank one class either beggar, merchant, militia or peasant. The beginning fase is rough, a mandatory crafting grind is necessary to reach better classes such as blacksmith or huntsman... but the pay off is huge. Once you reach these 2nd rank proffessions you will feel emersed in your role. As a blacksmith you promote your services on the server or you try to recruit newer players to work for you.
The dynamics of this game highly depend on the server population. Go in an empty server and you will miss out on 75% the black death has to offer. I encourage people to put themselves at risk and embrace your semi-perma death. I died several times but due to the fact that perks and houses are preserved it never felt brutal to the point i wanted to quit.
Certain things however need to be pointed out for this to be a fair review. The AI in this game is bad.. horrible really. Animals blink in and out of existance at random making hunting a nightmare. Guards sometimes randomly attack you. Bandits can suddenly pop in and start to attack you out of nowhere. Furthermore the bounty system is broken to the point that you can randomly aquire a massive bounty eventhough you are a saint in the game.
However once you see past all of this and immerse yourself in the world this game has to offer you can get an easy 20 - 30 hours out of it. Well worth the price i'd say.
So to conclude, are you a fast paced action FPS shooting kind of gamer with a craving of a large amount of content then dont get this game. Are you however someone that loves to Roleplay, immerse yourself in a character and live life like a medieval citizen then yes pick up this gem!

Caveblazers is a nice game. Fine-looking, polished, and with good original soundtrack and general audio.
One current issue that most negative reviews complain about difficulty being uneven. Let me clarify,
Say, health. Depending on starting loadout, you have anywhere between 60 to 150 health (mostly 100). Enemies hit for 10..20 damage at most. Healing items drop at random (from enemies, crates, bosses) and heal between 10 to 40 health per piece.
And it's generally fine, but the pure randomness of it has it that there's no amount of health you can expect to recover per stage. The game might rain healing items upon you, or you might get a single one for a level full of dangerous layouts. Even bosses may sometimes not drop health, which looks like mockery when you've already been on brink of death for a few levels.
Later on, if you want to get the real ending, you have to complete the game with a number of modifiers at once. One of these has it that items very rarely drop from enemies/crates and are instead bought in shops between every few levels. And, guess what - those shops may or may not have healing items as well! You can get a shop that has half of it's inventory be healing items, or you can get a shop that has none at all.
The issue is further complicated by other modifiers having player take more damage (2x from enemies, 4x from bosses - that means dying in two hits from boss), introducing hardy and heavy-hitting enemies, and adding a time limit (via a slowly descending ceiling of doom) to stages.
The enemies also have pretty good aim - even those that are restricted to 8-directional aiming (like player does) are generally warranted to land a hit on the player if both are standing on stable ground and the player did not jump out of the way as soon as noticing the "aiming indicator".
As result, despite the game positioning itself as an action-roguelike-platformer, on higher difficulty you have to play incredibly carefully as you do not know if the game is going to randomly and gradually starve you in terms of health or not.
Speaking of bosses, these seem to be picked largely at random and also vary in difficulty wildly - some can be hit continuously from afar, others can only be damaged at weakpoint states and require jumping around the stage to be able aim at them properly.
Then there are magic items. These grant various passive effects or active abilities, and, you guessed it, also vary in usefulness. Some can tremendously help by providing means to consistently heal or avoid getting hit, others are barely any use whatsoever, especially against bosses. As result, it is tempting to straight away restart the game after reaching the first shop on a "hard mode" session if there isn't anything useful on sale, and many people do just that. It's a grindy mechanic, somewhat reminiscent of running through level 1-1 over and over in Spelunky until you find a "good shop", except here you also have to collect as much as you can in case you
find something good.
Weaponry, "blessings" (positive modifiers), one-use items (bombs, potions), and rings also all vary in usefulness, though most don't bear noticeable impact on "hard mode" sessions except for when you get literally none of them (and thus are forced into a really stretched out fight with a boss, for example).
Overall, the game is good for playing casual sessions every now and then, but it's hard to imagine playing it "seriously" when success relies on staying lucky or playing completely flawlessly, which is a tiresome combination.

It does not make ANY sense!! So, this is the reason why Chapter 6, for me, ruined the whole horror scenario. Other than that scene, there are some more questionable scenes for the couple Joe and Ivy Davis that I think if you have not played the first game called Downfall, you won't be able to understand what is going on with them at all. They should have made it more intense than the phrase "Devil came through here" and the screams. I mean is that suppose to scare me?
In Chapter 5, things are good with the story-telling and finally, a revealation about Susan's past. What I didn't get was the pursuer. Why is he holding flowers and suddenly, attacked from nowhere? Open world, survival. Lot of potential for community feel and RP elements. Different classes will work well together for those that prefer a co-op style of play. Also potential to be hunted and hated or even be a spreader of the plague upon others.
This game won't hold your hand or draw pretty wisplike lines to guide you to your destination. That will be entirely your choice. Will you look for berries and loot barrels and crates for food? Or will you opt to be a thief and take what you want? Will you be a crafter or do you prefer to wield weapons and hunt animals for food or maybe even other players? The choices are all you.
There are bugs obviously, early release games always have them. The devs seem to address these quickly and have several ways for players to report them in and out of the game. Content is still lacking, but there's enough to do to keep most players entertained for several hours per game session.
What's lacking now is a large player base, we need more people to give this title a shot and experience how much fun and potential it has to offer. If you're undecided or can't stand bugs, you probably should wait a few months, but if you understand how early access works , there's already a lot of potential for fun, and the game is very playable as it stands right now. It can only get better.
The devs welcome constructive ideas and criticisms and are working hard to make this game a huge success. I'd suggest you watch some let's plays on Youtube and see if you feel like this title would be a good fit for you or your guild or gaming friends. Hope to see you all in Mercia soon!

I could sum this game up by saying, This game is amazingly addicting.. but I'll tack on a proper short review.
There are a variety of things that come together in this game, a mix of of retro-style graphics, with modern conveniences such as a well done musical score, a good auto-map and loads of replayability via the included editor and Community maps made from it.
The goal of the game is simple.. storm the evil castle, collect it's tasty treasures, and live! All of that is easier said than done, as you've got hoardes of fun-to-kill creatures intent on feasting on your intrails, various traps, and challenging boss encounters between you and success.
Controls 8/10
Controls can be abit sluggish occassionally, but definitely nothing to toss your keyboard through the window over.
Movement is with the WASD keys, and your various attacks are with the arrow keys. This game has controller support though I have never used it, I have heard some say the controller support is poorly implemented, but the keyboard controls just work, and they feel right after your first few OOOOH dude moments. Holding Space bar "locks" you into whatever direction you are facing while you move around, and holding Left Shift makes you stand in place so you can face any direction you want without moving. F key drinks whatever potion you may have from Rejuvination to temporary Invulnerability.
Sound 9/10
The music is what happens when 8 bit whackiness meets intense symphonic orchestration. It will be in your head, and matches the frantic pace of the gameplay perfectly.
Gameplay 8/10
This game is Amazing! You can set various 'challenges' before you begin a map, such as starting with 1 HP, or sharing HP, or set some 'crutches' or handicaps like unlimited lives and health regeneration so you can really tailor the already great experience to your own twisted needs. There are a a number of classes to choose from like the Paladin who is a defensive animal, hiding behind his shield blocking most projectile attacks while slashing away valiantly when monsters get foolish enough to get close to him, the ranger who can shoot from a good safe distance, the priest who can heal or deal damage with a beam of energy and drop some neato energy draining fields that will heal people who stand in it if monsters are getting damaged in it. Warlocks who can poison creatures with their dagger and toss some cool lightning around.. And mage, with his AoE short range fireballs, and ability to call in a meteor shower to rain in some arcane devastation. And each class really brings a different feel to the game. Everything is in a nice top down view which really helps in this type of game.
Overall I'd give this game 8½ / 10, and totally reccomend it.

If you are a fan of the older style of FPS games like Quake, then this is a game you should definitely look into.
As it advertises, the game is a bit of an FPS roguelite, both the level layouts as well as the enemy patterns are randomly generated.  However, you will not be picking up any new weapons during your run.  Instead you will choose a gun and a perk (things like triple jump, no fall damage...there are several unlockable ones as well) at the start and level it, also occasionally finding mods for it.  At first this seems a bit disappointing, but when you actually see some of the mods out there, you realize you'd be better off just trying to make your favorite gun super powerful.  You do have infinite ammo after all, there's no worrying about scavenging for bullets or running out here.  (Edit: It appears I was wrong, you *can* find new weapons, they are just ridiculously rare, because they are OP and really fun to use)
Also, yes, you really can have a ridiculous number of jumps just like the store ad says.  I've had a run where I can jump 16 times in midair, and had I found more items, I could have maybe went to 20 jumps.  The reason you can have so many jumps is because there really is no other way to reach things in some rooms.  Don't expect to find everything in any playthrough of Tower of Guns, there are just too many places either hidden behind fake walls or placed insanely high so you can't reach it without a ton of jumps.  However, do remember you can rocket jump in this game, so people who are better at it than me can probably find some cool secrets.
The performance is pretty good, game runs smoothly at all times.  This is the Unreal Engine though, I expect it to be capable of good performance like that.
Overall, this is a really fun game, and the dev should be proud of himself for making such a fun game considering he did it all by himself.  Props to his brother for the OST as well, while it's not something you're going to listen to for hours, it fits the game in my opinion.
(I should also mention I've had this for a few months before the steam release, it was fun even before it was finished, and it's even better now.)

Sometimes: Success Requires Sacrifice is a small game where your objective is to make it to the end. However, there are usually sacrifices along the way…
Sometimes: Success Requires Sacrifice has 5 gameplay modes for you to choose from. The main on, Classic, has you going through a set of levels trying to reach the end. However, the catch is that the room is pitch black and you can’t see where you’re going. So how are you supposed to find your way to the end?
As one might imagine from the title, death does play a decent role in this game. You have the choice to suicide your character, and the corpse of that character will leave a light for the next one to come on through. There’s unlimited lives available thankfully, so free to die as many times as you wish. As you get through to the later levels, sawblades are added and then eventually reapers. Hitting these will also kill your character and provide some needed light.
Endless has you going around collecting medals without any fear of actual death. Well, except for suiciding to provide light so you can actually see where you’re going. Definitely the “relax” mode in this game, since some of the later levels in Classic can start to really get hectic with trying to dodge blades and the reaper!
Trust Fall has you falling down an endless pit. The goal? See how far you can get before you hit a sawblade. The positioning of these is random, so sometimes you might just get the god run and get really far down.
Chips is like Pac-Man. You need to go around collecting up the chips, trying not to hit the “ghosts”. Like I said, it’s just Pac-Man. The final mode, Hearts, I haven’t actually tried out yet. From what I’ve read on the forums however, it takes you out of the game and into a browser-based thing. There’s no in-game warning that it does this either, so you’ve been warned now!
The game’s controls are your basic WASD. Unfortunately, there’s no controller support included. As of writing this review, there’s also no delay after you die. I think a good portion of my deaths in the run I did came from still holding a button when I died and running right into a blade. Needless to say I had many well-lit starts…
Is the game worth it? If you’re looking for a short diversion then check it out. You can challenge yourself against the in-game achievements to see how well you can do, should you wish to. With the levels in Classic being set and not randomly generated, mastering them just comes down to a matter of learning them all by heart. It’d be nice to see an option that does allow for randomly generated levels to keep it fresh, outside of Trust Fall of course. If anything though, the game is likely best found on sale for now since the main thing it provides is just a short diversion with the gameplay.

OVERVIEW
I have been playing WolfQuest for ages (since early 2.5), and more than my playtime says. This game is amazing!
You play a wolf, who has to find a mate, find a den, mark territory, have pups, grow your pups, train your pups, protect your pups, then take a journey across the world to the end of the game, the Rendezvous Site.
PROS
-Great wolf customisation, with around 20 coats, 2 coat shade/tint sliders, 8 howls, dragable speed, stamina and strength sliders, lots of injuries (ripped ears, limping), and a radio collar that can be worn
-Four large maps to explore
-The graphics are very good
-Lots to do - you can hunt, encounter and 'chat'/fight with stranger wolves, and explore the world, as well as completing achievements and the quests/missions
-Many easy and challenging achievements
-Lots of creatures - hunt elk, bull elk, hares, (and I think Moose have been added), and protect yourself from bears and cougars, kill coyotes, and watch the moths, butterflies, flies, and birds fly about. Vultures also fly above carcasses which is a nice touch
-Multiplayer - you can raise the cubs on multiplayer! You can also use emotes that your wolf does, like roll over, tail tucked behind legs, etc
-Lots of hidden things to find
-Lost River bonus map has a great mystery and great music!
-Nice soundtrack to listen to
-Educational, learn how wolves survive, and also about how wind direction has a part in hunting
-Cattle Ranch bonus level is fun
-Challenged keep you coming back (can you kill the Bull Elk?)
CONS
-Multiplayer people tend to want private rooms instead of public, but not a big deal, public games are still around and fun!
-Can be a bit repetitive with all of the running about
-The bonuses for lots of XP are so hard to get. You can unlock more powerful pee (yup), an albino pup, and a secret densite, however you need around 20,000 XP, and I usually have around 1000-2000 by the end of chapter 1, when the prizes are unlocked.
I would like to see...
Hunger (as well as health)
Thirst
Side quests (kill five coyotes, find this, kill an elk)
More bonus levels like the cattle ranch
Poachers
Overall great game, but can be slightly repetitive, however because I love this game I keep playing it.
NOTE: If you aren't sure, on the WolfQuest website you can download the old version 2.5 which is quite a few years old. It hasn't got as good graphics or AI and the hunting elk is a lot harder but it is free.

This game was easy enough for my six year old brother to pick up and play without trouble, and several years later it's not much more difficult. There's not much to it if you're looking for long-term gameplay unless you want to get all of the achievements, but that should not sway you from picking this up if it interests you.
There is a multi-player functionality, but as I have not played it I will not comment on it.
The game starts out easy enough. You play a wolf on the search for a mate. Earn points by taking down prey and predators, but beware bull elk and bears! You must find three packs in the map and play a "minigame" of sorts to interact with them. Successfully running off pack wolves will earn you points, but they can take your health down to near-death if they're stronger than you and you don't run away when they tell you too!
Once you find the three packs, you can start seeing "dispersal wolves". You can make these your mate. Once you have a mate, hunting becomes much easier, and you can continue playing in the first map or you can move on to raising pups. This game is very kid-friendly (with the exception of possibly prey corpses when you feed), so don't worry about any actual mating being depicted. You move straight from choosing a den in the next map to guarding your active pups.
One great thing since this game has come to Steam is that a lot of the bugs with the pup stage have been worked out. Before I found the game very difficult, as my mate would stand around doing nothing while predators attacked my pups literally every two seconds, leaving me no time to hunt to feed them.
Predators attack much less frequently, and your mate will run to carcasses to bring food to your pups. Playing on the easiest setting was easy but not brainless when it came to this stage, which was nice.
From here, you take your pups on a journey to the summer hunting ground, which means leading them across the map. I found this to be the most difficult stage, particularly carrying pups across the river without them drowning. The easiest thing I found was to take one pup across and then let my mate carry them all across the two parts of the river crossing. The hardest part of this stage is keeping all your pups fed throughout the journey, as you move far from any elk herds. Keep your belly full of "food for pups"!
If I remember correctly, the game ends here. You can, however, play as one of your surviving pups, or a new wolf altogether! You can play through the previous stages endlessly. Beyond this, there's not too much gameplay to be had unless you want to partake in the online multiplayer.
All in all, I recommend this game if you enjoy an occasional play here and there to relax. Don't expect to get hundreds and hundreds of hours out of this one without getting bored at some point! Otherwise, it's a great stress-relieving simulation game.

First things first - the game is not worth the money. Why?
because it's a mess.
Let's sum up the gameplay, before I get to the actual story.
There's so much stuff to do. The most important thing is, you can click to skip all of the boring walls of text and there really is a ton of them (75% of the game's text) and they have absolutely no meaning besides being annoying. Once in a while, you will have some dreams about magic and other epic stuff, although nobody in the game tells you why you're having the dreams (not even your "I" from alternative dimension) and what's actually happening. Oh, and the dreams make no sense whatsoever. Did you want a game with a satisfying, fun story? Then stop reading here.
You can read manga to learn some spells, but instead of just writing "You have learnt Cast Diarrhea spell", it reads part of some story. Those stories are boring and irrelevant to the main story line, so just skip through them.
You can work for three companies, but you don't really need the money, since there's not much stuff to buy. It's somewhat relevant to story, but the only difference between working and not working is that in the end it writes "You helped saving this company" or "You ruined this company". Yeah.
You can work out to make yourself stronger, but there's no point since you don't need to fight at all during the whole playthrough.
Yup, there's some "fighting". It's the well-know "click this ability to cast diarrhea" or "click this to attack". You can fight, but you don't have to. OH GAWD THE DECISIONS!!!
As for decisions, there're about 10 opportunities to choose from several (usually two) options and somehow change the story. The most game-changing decision for me was whether to choose strawberry or green tea jelly.
Working - pointless. Working out - pointless. Reading - pointless. Fighting - pointless. That's why I said it's a mess, in the beginning. There's a lot of stuff, but nothing works well.
Anyway, sooner or later you will just end up spamming left mouse button clicks
The writing is poor while the story idea is decent. It's full of cliché, the game was not made by Japanese people, but it tries really hard to look like a Japanese game. There's lot of talking about anime and manga stuff, there's some cosplay caffe and tea house. So it's pretty much Japan. BUT it's not. The story actually takes place in the "Trident City" (I think) in the Soroyuma country (?, Eh.. I don't even remember the names anymore, sorry). But yeah, still Japan.
Oh, one more thing. The game ends quite suddenly. I was having my usual work out rutine, then I went to sleep. I woke up, went somewhere outside the city and then the game ended. No explanation, nothing.
If you want to see the "quality" of the writing, go watch a video.
As for graphics, there're around 10-15 background images (=locations). That's not a lot. The characters sometimes change facial expressions and body language, but that doesn't make me like the game much more.
I had to turn the music off after some time, it gets rather annoying. Every tune keeps playing in a loop and they're not very original neither. I also tend to take "alt+tab" breaks while playing games like this and I'd probably go nuts within 10 minutes if I'd have to listen to that stuff over and over again.
The main story is decent and the game tries to make you replay it. And you probably will do so. All in all, it's quite short (2 hours-ish), but some decisions actually affect the story thus making the game replay-able. Will you talk to this person, or never meet her again? Will you try to save this person or forget her? Will you get to know this person or ignore her?
That's the good stuff about the game, I just don't understand why there has to be so much pointlessness in this game.
Characters are somewhat likeable. They all have some secrets, which makes them interesting and makes you want to progress further in the story.
I don't really like the magic stuff and the way the game handles it, but I guess it's acceptable.
The story itself isn't that much original, but the decisions and possibilities are what makes you want to play.
I'll do another playthrough and see if it changes my opinion about the game. I might edit my review if it does.
- It's a mess, but it's still playable. Not worth the price, 5€ would be more appropriate.
- The story concept is rather decent while the writing is terrible. The decisions are what makes you "want" (/suffer) to play and possibly re-play the game
- Graphics and music are mediocre
- Other aspects than the story are pointless and just serve as gametime "fillers"
All in all, the concept of the game is decent. But EVERYTHING is way too poorly executed.

Sweet game. It's a Zombie-survival rogue-like game without the zombies. This review is just about the points that stood out the most and make this game unique.  You could play to trade and survive or scavenge and conquer (kill those who stand in your way). I started with the first but then moved on to the second strategy after I learned the controls and could raid a house of army deserters who had kidnapped the owner and starved him to death. I have not yet finished the game so I don't know how that approach will affect the outcome.
Pros:
-Atmosphere and realism: You're constantly reminded that you're in a war and you're caught in the middle of it trying to make do whichever way you can (creating traps for rats, having to trade in order get more materials/components/things that you need and not just scavenge for them).
-Gameplay: Sneaking and fighting crudely resemble Mark of the Ninja in footstep sounds, hiding spots, stealth, and stealthy kills.
-Thrill: Because of the rogue-like mechanic and the gameplay mentioned above I really felt that I had to do my best to not get killed in every scavenge attempt. I had my heart-pumping every time I was sneaking in behind a shotgun-wielding thug while I was hoping he wouldn't turn around so that I could get to that room to see what it had.
Cons:
-Controls: They just suck. You have to use the left D-pad's left and right to choose which action you want and often these actions are not in order so you have to cycle through until you get it right. It's no problem in the shelter but during combat it's life or death (I'm looking at you, Cover). The game dev's should have prioritized the most-common sense options depending on the situation... but they didn't.
Neutral:
-No friend-foe distinction: You don't know whether killing that person who wants you to leave will not affect your scavenger guy until after you do it. And that's part of war... but the devs could've made some sort of distinguishing
-No load save: Adds to the realism of life (only one go), especially in a war. But sometimes the controls get you killed and you don't know how those controls will respond unless you try them...
Recommendation:
Overall, this is a good game to buy.  It's fun, thrilling, and memorable despite its cons. My recommendation is to have a try-run where you can experiment with the controls (especially in a fire-fight).

The problem with sequels, is that they rarely stick to the proven recipe. Thief 1,2 and 3 were very good, and don't get me wrong, Thief 4 is excellent, but the inclusion of side quests, focussing etc detracts from the original gameplay. Gone is Garret's remote viewing eye, moss arrows and gass arrows that knocks out opponents. Davenport of old was a ordered place where you could travel using only the roof tops, yet the new Davenport is disorganized and the layout is different from the old Davenport. What would remedy the situation. Well, a port of Thief 1,2 and 3 to the new engine, but please revert to the way things were and drop the focus bs. Thief is meant to be difficult, so stop sugarcoating it, and return it to it's 1998 glory days. Oh and by the way, why did the Hammers dissappear? Excellent game, highly recommended, yet flawed for not following from where the others left off.

WHY ARE YOU READING THE REVIEWS? Seriously, for the most part, they're worse than YouTube comments, they're written by the same kind of people, and with the same amount of careful thought and consideration. So that should tell you something.
Anyway, here's my real review: It's an interactive story. And while it is
exhaustive on the topic of depression (by the developers' own admission), it does educate on the subject. I really do think that people who really don't understand what depression is like, but want to change that, will benefit from this.
As one who does understand, I felt for the character (myself?) as I played. I worried. I chose honest answers and got pretty accurate results. I played through it several times. It made me realize some of the dumb mistakes I actively make and how I justify them to myself. I started a freaking notebook in Evernote just to write down what I was learning from this.
Again, it's not exhaustive. I would honestly have liked to have seen more. But it's free, and it's an attempt to venture into uncharted waters with the medium. It's a discussion starter. It's good.

A simple, addicting dungeon crawler. Reminiscent of the original Gauntlet games, but with a bit more spice to it.
You choose from a small selection of classes, each with their own unique attacks, abillities, and power-ups. Each class plays differently: the ranger fires arrows and lays bombs while the paladin blocks projectiles with his shield while slicing up enemies at close range, for example. The recent massive update (Temple of the Sun) added tons of class balancing and an entire new class, the priest, which suggests that more classes may come in the future (this is what I'm really hoping for, as learning all the ins and outs of the classes make the game a really fun experience).
Two main campaigns will soak up a few hours of gameplay each. The game also comes with a level editor, and the Steam community has already created some really polished campaigns (some better than others, of course). So there will always be new content coming out.
The game really shines with its multiplayer. I bought the 4-pack and gave the extra copies to friends, and we've been really enjoying the dungeon crawl together. Beating the first boss for the first time was a very rewarding experience. Single player is still fun, though can get a bit monotonous once you learn exactly how all the enemies respond to you and how to safely win each battle. It's more fun to have other players watchign your back or helping you pick up all the treasure.

Alright.  I played the game, beat it and even enjoyed it, honestly.  However:
The art style is pretty dated for what it is and felt pretty simple.  It was pretty, but I've played a number of VN's that
were much prettier.  6/10
The story had moments that were touching and was overall very relatable for the most part.  It was also rather simplistic and carried almost no twists or surprises.  There was *one* thing that I guessed incorrectly about at the very end.  Don't mistake this as being impressive, since the game only has 5
characters that you, the main character ever interacts with.
So it being easily predictable is pretty much a given. 4/10
Music is alright at first, it's gets rather monotonous since there is very little change or variety.  I never reached the point where I hated it, but it didn't exactly add much to the game at all, either.  5/10
The gameplay elements are also pretty simple.  Money quickly ceases being a concern with just a little fore-thinking and the right plan.  At the end, you are still chided for "not having enough, and maybe needing to work on that" by the game though.  Despite the fact that I could have bought every ingame asset with money to spare.
Combat is sort of interesting.  There are only something like 5 or 6 monster types though, so you will cycle through them all very quickly.  They just get stronger over time as you lvl up etc.  With a little work, you are also essentially invincible, so it's just a matter of wearing them down from your overly abundant, easily *re-fueled magic reserves.  So, stupidly easy.  4/10
I enjoyed the game for the most part.  I beat it with very little effort and it only took as long as it did because I deleted my first play through due to the common black screen problems.  Reinstalling fixed nothing.  Thankfully they are not widespread and don't harm the game overly much.
Overall, Fading Hearts is a 5/10 for me.  I can't in good conscience suggest it to people.  If you find a sale where it's $5 or less, consider maybe buying it.  Your time would be better spent with the plethora of freely translated VN's you can find elsewhere.  Much better spent.

I like the idea but it's visually busy and confusing, movement feels clunky and vague, and the weapons feel wimpy and insubstantial. Not really up to snuff. I'll happily take a look at Tower of Guns 2 if one comes along, though.

Who remembers Facing Worlds in Unreal Tournament? (I do! I do!) Though Tower of Guns bears little resemblance to Facing Worlds, while playing it I was nevertheless transported back to the year 2000, fondly remembering endless post-work capture the flag matches in which I would repeatedly get my butt kicked. The speedy-smooth Unreal engine is on fine display in Tower of Guns, and you've got plenty of that circle-strafey, stay-in-one-spot-and-you're-dead hyperfast shooting that UT popularized at the turn of the century. (There's even a flak cannon!) Of course, Tower of Guns is a single-player roguelike, so you won't be sniping noobs in this game. Quite the opposite: you are the moving target in a gigantic shooting gallery. As you progress up the tower, each room presents yet another assorment of turrets and robots that want to make you dead with their giant bullets and spiky balls of doom. The random map generation helps make each run feel fresh, but even still, don't expect tons of variety. This is a totally indie enterprise, after all. The visuals are interesting, vaguely reminiscent of a junkyard in Borderlands or a Death Star trash compactor level. Despite being a little lean on content, Tower of Guns is full of personality and the devs have laid the groundwork for plenty of expansion, if they so desire (and if the audience is there to justify it). Like Binding of Isaac (one of my favorite games ever), a single run usually takes 10 minutes, but I imagine it could take much longer if you get lucky (I'm not very lucky). Like firearms, Tower of Guns is best in short, controlled bursts. Highly recommended if you're looking to scratch that old school FPS itch.

Okay so in light of recent events Ive decide to change my review regarding The Black Death, and my opinions on the game and the development. So in Short this game is a survival game based on the interesting idea of surviving The Black Death. With me being a history nerd I was super excited for the Game to be realsed on Early Access.
When it was realsed the Game was Terrible, let's me completely honest about it. The characters looked like melted a barbie doll again a candle. The animations were poor and the enviroment was boring. Little to NO depth in the game with you basically run around the forest picking berries to survive.
With no sign of the developers working on the game this game died, faster than a person with the actualy Black Death (Sorry Bad Joke).
That was then and this game has been risen up from the grave with a complete and full patch that has basically chnaged the entire game. So when I join in the game they added Day and Night cycles which we amazing all be it very fast cycles but certainly welcome.
Graphics have been improved slihghtly here and there with the models still being gollums brother rather than King Arthur. The Music in this game is amazing which epicness that lacked in the original version. Sound and effects have been retuned with impacts sounds more punchy and combat sounding more deadly. The guards and Tradesmen have been improved with more lines of dialogue.
The Effects and the enviroment have been turned around with an extremely effective feel and look that makes you want to go to the winchester and wait for the Black Death to blow over. The General feel of the game has changed from a boring grind to an interesting battle of surivial.
The servers have been massively improved with timing out being cut down to a minium and the servers are slowly starting to return. The combat has been improved so much its unreckonisable to the previous version. Instead of guessing when the bandit pops up you have to fight with skill and control your stamina bar and blocks.
The crafting system has been slightly improved but that isnt really needed as the crafting is the best part of the game. Hunger, Thirst and infection have been overhauls into a nice slick UI with the food and thirst meter being tuned to a more realistic standard. Still your chareacter will need a drink like every 2 Mins tho.
All in all the game has a bad start but with the new improved version and a decicated team behind it this game is set to become as superb Survival EA game. Plus the developers are talking to the community as well which is a massive improvemant for the previous Hid and Seek the devs played.

Thought I would review this game to get an alternate opinion of it.
Depression Quest is an interactive fiction game and not a modern one. It is in the vein of early computer games that were entirely text-based and derived from narratives. I think that is one of the reasons reviews are mixed on it. It doesn't fit the mold of what a "modern" computer game is. Us old fart garmers will remember this type of gaming experience with fondness.
That being said, I can really only reccommend  the game for people who want to experience or learn about clinical depression or people who want to deal with their clinical depression in a positive way.
It is ingenious in its audacity and for tackling an often overlooked mental disease. It is innovative for its attempt to recreate the experience of a disease at a very realistic level. All the little things are there, such as the thought among many depressives that they don't actually have a disease when they are able to deal with it effectively (yes, that is a real thing) or excusing your tiredness for simply being tired, instead of the effects of a disease. Effects on concentration, focus, seeking diversion (as a result of the disease, not as a way to find enjoyment as it is with many people), social anxiety, interpersonal relationships, and others are all modeled. It takes the form of a choose-your-own-adventure (as interactive fiction generally is) and so there is some replay value to it. I personally played it several times and, since I don't know how the different paths of the game are determined, it's actually kind of fun (yes, in that ruminating depressive sort of way!) to tease out how the choices are rendered.
This is a game that does not have a wide appeal and is a very niche product. It is a game that has a therapeutic effect for suffers and/or is a way for the curious to "play" with the disease and challenge some preconceptions of yours or your preconceptions of those who suffer from the disease. If you are even remotely interested or intrigued, I'd suggest it because it is free. Just realize that the "fun" of the game is derived from  learning about something, not derived from entertainment.

This review is not going be focused on talking about the quality of the game or listing the pros and cons. Instead in this review I’m going to suggest what type of people would enjoy playing this game.
Anyways,
It is because some of the achievements are challenging (not because of luck) and also you probably enjoy doing them. There is also a hard mode option when you start your game. Another reason is that when you beat the game there is a New Game + (You start from the beginning but you have all of your items from the old game).  Finally, one thing that this game does that seems interesting to me is that the game rewards you with unique items for not being hit by bosses.
If you are skeptical of this game because of its pixel graphics, hear me out. The game has many animations to make movement and attacks feel real, the backgrounds in most areas are detailed, and despite the overall theme of the in-game world there is still a lot of color (which actually benefits the theme). The music in each areas matches the theme of that area and it also adds to the grim atmosphere of this game.
I say this because while there is some lore in the game (a lot of it is in favor text in items), the story is quite simple. When I was playing the game I didn’t feel like I had an emotional connection to any of the characters in the game. Even if there are some gloomy moments in the game, if you don’t care about any of the characters those moments won’t have much effect on you. There one more thing I want to tell you about. It is the ending of this game. When I beat the game the ending was too short and had no build up/foreshadowing to be meaningful to me.
The game does have an easy mode which gives you items that makes this game a lot easier however much of the game’s fun comes from the challenge. Another reason is that even with easy mode, I don’t think that causal players would enjoy that most of the save spots are spaced far away from each other and that many of them don’t have safe path to backtrack to get to them.
It's one of those games where it's short run time will leave you simply wanting more.

text: In all honesty, most games that claim to be "rogue-likes" are not that similar to the original game of the genre, the one it was founded on... Rogue. This game, on the other hand, feels like Rogue in its entirety. It just so happens to have newer graphics and a few cool new features. An acceptable roguelike in a too-crowded field.
There's nothing inherently wrong with SotS: The Pit. It does everything a roguelike is supposed to do. Procedurally generated levels with a high degree of randomization. A class based system that can radically alter your playstyle as well as your access to items. An unforgiving difficulty that is a mixture of luck and skill.
Frankly every roguelike does that, however, and this one has very little else going for it and a lot of strikes against it. For instance, you require food to survive, a resource which can be very limited. You get plenty of ingredients, but even if you do find a cooker it is most likely broken, requiring a skillcheck and a dice roll to fix. Even if you do fix it, you have to trial-and-error your way into a valid recipe, costing you precious resources with each failure. Even if you do find a valid recipe, that valid recipe can fail, consuming those resources anyways. It's a prime example of the artificial difficulty that plagues the game. Nearly every valuable item is secured behind some sort of skillcheck.
Combat is clean and simple, but boring. Warrior types are simply left-click to win, while psionics-- the game's version of magic users-- have more options, but most will be constrained to a single attack spell until well into the game. Weapons and armor have durability and proper replacements are precious, forcing you into sub-optimal strategies in order to preserve your most valuable equipment from an unseen acid trap or simply usage damage.
The greatest asset to the game is its unique genre, as scifi roguelikes are relatively rare, and are helped by the Sword of the Stars IP by allowing you to play varied races in the DLCs. Despite that, expect to spend your first couple of levels fighting rats and bats all the same.
All in all, simply average. Would only recommend it to people who have exhausted the many other roguelike options and strongly needed a fresh challenge.

It's a good little Metroidvania game.  Also, please do be aware that hard mode is actually HARD.  I'm talking you take two hits from anything: dead.  There's an Insane mode after that, where you start with most of your equippable items, and all the stuff you found is already found, plus you keep all the money you had (not much left to buy with it, though).  I haven't noticed a notable increase in difficulty in tht mode, but that could be because I'm far more familiar with the gameplay now, and the items from last game help out a lot, too, so I'll probably be suffering later on.
It's not hard like in games where there's a lot of "Gotcha!" surprises, where you just have to memorize the game to win (although there is a little of that, but only a little).  It's also not hard like in Dark Souls where the controls were designed by 1000 monkeys at keyboards, and if they'd just fix the controls it would be easy.  The controls are actually quite good.  It's a lot easier once you realize that every enemy telegraphs their next move in some way, many of those being a white circle the pulses outward (easy to miss if you're not looking for it).  I guess what makes it really hard is just how quicly you die.  I'm used to taking more than two hits before I die.  If you don't find all the health powerups, you'll just die in one hit.
Gameplay feels smooth, and there are some good abilities.  It doesn't tell you how to use air dodge (unlockable ability), but you just hit the Roll button while in the air, so now you know.  My complaints would be that you can't put notes in the map, the game doesn't pause while looking at the map, and if you let go of the map button, the map closes (it's not a toggle).  Also, when using the warp, it doesn't show you where these places are on the map, just gives you names, so until you memorize them, you have to warp around to see where you end up.  Also, if you're using a DirectInput controller, you'll need to use Joy2Key or XPadder to play with it, as it doesn't support them.
The ending kinda sucks.  It's just text and then credits roll.  It's not what we're playing the game for, I just expected a little more there.
Overall I highly enjoyed it.
Edit:  Insane mode is indeed harder as you go.  Having all the health powerups at the start made it easier then, but now I'm often dying to things in one hit when at full health.

It has 5 modes, which one takes you to your browser, 2 of them are copyed, one is pac-man clone and the other a game where you fall down endlessly while trying to avoid obstacles (for short: The let me try one more time type), and 2 modes which are unique. - Need to be able to shoot in any direction. Restricted available shooting angles is a somewhat primitive mechanic, and only serves to make the character control feel restrictive. - Hitting enemies with melee should knock them back at least as much as the character moves forward when attacking. Too often when chaining melee hits on enemies the character just moves right past them, leaving it akward to keep turning to face the enemy and try to get a hit, ultimately making the melee combat more dissatisfying than perhaps it could be.
- The money shouldn't fly so far when dropped from objects and enemies. This may seem a little petty, but when abundantly starting new characters upon death (as we all do in roguelikes) it's simply boring to spend so much time repeatedly hunting down money that's flown half a screen away from an object you destroyed with melee.
These may not seem like significant issues, but from my experience, they all contribute to making me not want to start a new character each time I die, grinding away my resolve far quicker than a roguelike should.
It's a real shame 'cause otherwise it's a well polished game, I just don't see it going down as a memorable rogulike with some of the current design aspects.
