Caveblazers is a nice little Rogue-like game. Its got a very good combat system combined with an enjoyable setting. However, the game has issues so far with progression, customization, and a few bugs.
The progression is inconsistent, with there being no hard leveling up of stats or abilites like you find in Rogue Legacy, but exp is instead used as a way to unlock perks (which are basically classes) and unlock cosmetics. Your first level requries little exp, but following levels require you to get 2000 per level up. Exp is earned by the typical how many baddies you killed, how far you go into the dungeon, and how much cool stuff  you get along the way. Its confusing, and while all progression being dependant on player skill is fine for some, for others its a turn off. I personally like it, as I get a strong sense of accomplishment when I do good, but my first several runs were♥♥♥♥♥♥
I personally hate the customization limits placed on me with the perks being locked mixed in with the limited cosmetics. For example, you can unlock either a new perk or a cosmetic when you level up, it doesn't give you a strong indication of which and you have to hope you get something you like. The cosmetics are limited, with me either becoming a generic person, or a member of the Yogscast. If Iwant to look like some dark overlord badass with a fancy hat, I cannot do that. My last 8 unlocks have been different colored shirts. If you like cosmetics like me, you will find this game to be frustrating.
The classes are each unique, but some are far more practical than others, there are definitely some classes you play as for         the sake of screwing around, and some which are more practical. For example, the brimstone perk so far is in my opinion the most powerful perk. Getting an auto-blocking weapon, and consistent early access to the extremely powerful demonic blessings is huge, at the cost of starting at 50/100 health, but the passive damage resistance you get is excellent, letting you squeak away far easier than with other classes. Then there is Sticky Pete, whose big perks are he gets more bombs, and all his bombs are sticky. Thats it. This isn't the only example of perk imbalance, but there is a place for all of them, and despite not all of them being practical, it is still fun to screw around with the less practical perks.
In terms of the actual gameplay, I do not own a controller, so my heavily biased opinion is that the controls suck for keyboard.  Yes I know that the game has a great big sticker that says "best played with a controller" but every other game I've ever played that said this at least let me customise my controls on my keyboard and mouse to be comfortable. This game lacks that, as the use of the punctuation keys is not permitted to be used as keybinds, only letters, and function keys (like space, control, etc). I hated having to come up with a whole new way to position my hands to play this from any of the formats I'm familiar with, and it just sucks on keyboard. The platforming is solid, with consistent and fun physics. The difficulty increases with level of the dungeon, and somewhat incorporates level design to make it more difficult, and its a very good difficulty model.
Map design is abysmal. The maps are repetitive as hell, with very few disginguishing features, and a couple repeating spots. Some things change from map to map, but once you've played the game three runs in each zone, you've seen everything it has to offer. There exists my most hated enemy, the little suicide bombers. No matter where you are, they will ♥♥♥♥ up your level. The platforming is so damn tight that even changing the location of one block can cut off your access to a huge area of the map, which is to me what makes those little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s a bigger problem than the bosses.
Speaking of which, they are relataively easy and stagnant, the only difference between early and late game bosses is their health pool and damge output. They also drop inconsistent loot, which ranges from meh to okay. I find the best gear to be the really cool weapons certain perks start with, and the boss loot often leaves me hoping more for a good blessing rather than the unimpressive weapons and magic items you get.
The big problem/attractive point of the game is that it is very heavily reliant on chance. I personally got the "bad luck" achievement on my fifth run (where you need to discover 5 bad potions in a row), so I found it unpleasant. There also is a lack of control over what blessings you get, and sometimes they just suck if you're going for a specific build. I wanted to do a melee focused build with the brimstone character, and my first 5 levels only gave me ranged oriented perks. I was doing good, but I hated not getting to play how I want. By the way, grab the pumice crystal as soon as you can, the AI adventurers are cancer. They steal kills, money, items, weapons, and are useless against bosses acting as a possible meat shield instead of doing good dps.
There are very few bugs present in the game, but they have all been annyoing as hell since they happen frequently. From my side, the game hates being minimized. It doesnt minimize though, it has to run in the background and not be accessible t hrough anything but the task manager, and the lack of an auto-pause feature has cost me several runs. I also have a few class specific issues like blood shrines on level one for the brimstone class still costing full health price, but those are insignificant. I have had no hard crashes and the games frames are smooth even on a crappy laptop.
The multiplayer is great. Local multiplayer is fun, and the camera while disorienting at first, is easy to get used to, and makes the game feel more nostalgic than watching cartoon network in your underwear.
Overall,the game feels like the best early access game in the world, its missing a few things I want such as online multiplayer and more weapon/class variety. However, pick it up, its a cheap and fun time waster, and ultimately you get what you pay for, and its not bad for $10.00.
Besides, its still better than anything EA has cranked out in the last few years.

Thief is an Action/Adventure/Role-Playing/FPS (First Person Sneaker) game, set in a Victorian Gothic world but, with primitive electric lights and machinery typical of the early 20th century, as well as some unique and very imaginative devices.  The characters are a blend of aristocracy, soldiers, commoners and beggers, some with British accents and, some who sound like they came from the streets of  Brooklyn.  The theme casts a hint of paranormal hope in a disease-ridden city of despair.  The player is a thief named Garrett, who lost his female counterpart, Erin, in an accident which resulted in Garrett's near death.  After his recovery, amnesia swallowed most of his memories of the past year.  So begins his search to find out what happened to him and, to learn Erin's fate.
Much of the city hub is hidden in darkness.  Dark alleys and dimly lit streets dominate Stonemarket. There are paths above ground level that take you past flats, through balconies and over rooftops, providing alternate routes across town.  But, many of the ground-level streets and alleys shown on the game map may look like a clear path with no walls or doors but, they sometimes bring you to a dead-end.  Trying to follow the map is confusing, until you get to know your way around town.
To get to the upper areas, you climb crates, walls, ladders or ropes but, only as the game permits. The game restricts where you can climb, e.g. you can climb one set of crates but not a nearby identicle set of crates.  Most climbable spots are identified by a faint blueish-white glow, which is a big help, when in a hurry.
Thief is comprised of 8 main chapters that will each take from a half hour to as much as 2 hours, depending on how much exploring you do.  Plus, there are 6 optional client jobs with specific items you must retrieve, and are somewhat smaller in scope than the main chapters.  Additionally, there are 25 side jobs that usually involve only one or two rooms and also have a specific item that you're after.
The promise of a fully stealthy play style prompted me to try Thief.  If you want the frontal assault gameplay of a good, old fashioned First-Person-Shooter game, Thief is not for you.  The main character is not a skilled CQB fighter and will often lose in hand-to-hand combat.
To play exclusively with a stealthy approach will require a great deal of time and patience.  However, a mixture of stealth, non-lethal takedowns and kills from a distance is common and a more fun way to play.  Remaining undetected will often depend on how you move and where you hide.  Swoop past a caged bird it becomes agitated by your sudden movement and will alert hostiles.  Dogs have keen senses and will see you when you get too close and give away your presence by barking.  Staying in the shadows and moving low and slow is your best practice for a stealthy approach.
There are a few DLC's that often come with Thief or, are available for a buck or two each.  They are very much worth the small price.  One is an added mission called, "The Bank Hiest".  Not as large as a normal chapter but, introduces a new component to the challenge.  Three others are "Ghost", "Opportunist" and "Predator".  These provide scoring of the three different play styles you can choose from.  You can play them exclusively or in any combination you like.  You decide as you progress.  There is no penalty for using one over another or, all three for that matter.  At the end of a mission, the game statistics will show a rating of your play style.
- Ghost:  Requires great patience.  Your intent is to avoid any interaction with hostiles or the environment.  Stealth is your primary concern.  Remain undetected and don't alarm anyone.
- Opportunist:  Interacting with or exploiting the environment, you try to remain undetected.  Putting out flames or dousing candles, will help you get past hostiles unseen.
- Predator: Use any means necessary to acheive your goal, taking out whoever is in your way.
A fourth rating of Hybrid is given if, "You equally blended a range of traits from all three play styles."
Thief has three difficulty levels...Rogue, Thief and Master, in successive order of difficulty.  There's also a Custom Settings menu that you can use to limit many of the features of the game, such as types of resourses, upgrades, HUD display features, abilities, tools, etc.  These self-imposed restrictions can make the game especially challenging.
Scattered throughout the game are a few puzzles that are moderately challenging.  However, I must confess, one of them was a little more so than I had patience for.  I ended up looking to a walkthrough for the solution and still didn't understand the logic of it.  All the rest, if you're paying attention to the story and reading the documents you fing along your way, will not be so hard.
I should warn you that, if you're trying to Ghost the game, you'll be challenged at almost every turn.  Especially if you're trying to grab all loot and collectables that are available.  Thief employs the usual scripted traps and...well...some cheap tricks as well.  And, many tasks require very precise timing to accompish successfully.  The devs have devised quite a repertoire of situations to foil your progress.  Occasionally, the game sets you up for a fall.  If you try to go slowly and, carefully watch for the hostiles and how they patrol, it will only postpone the inevitable.  In those situations, logic, reason and patience is of little help.  Basically, it's a game of surprises and a few seemingly impossible situations.  As in many games, getting through each chapter is generally a matter of trial and error.  So, until you learn the devs' tricks, frequent use of the Quick-save and Quick-load keys, is a necessity.
Then, we come to the Boss Fights.  As for the first one, you have two choices.  One; you can try to fight the Thief Taker General which will usually end in your demise, until you learn his patterns.  (More trial and error.)  Or, two; you can avoid confrontation entirely.  All you have to do is open the exit door and escape.  Well...of course it's not quite that simple.
The second Boss Fight is the last challenge of the game.  But, it's not so much a fight as it is a matter of evasion.  Not as difficult as the first one but, still not easy.  Fortunately, those are the only two Boss Fights in the game.
As for the story...it's kinda weak and convoluted.  I was never drawn into the plot as I have been in some games.  During the early chapters, I felt it had good potential.  Although, as I progressed, the plot began breaking down, changing and taking new directions.  For me,  it was a tremendous let-down.
Of course, what game is complete without bugs.  And Thief has its fair share of them.  Aside from a few technical problems of crashes and hangs that have been reported by a small percentage of players, there are some bugs during the gameplay that can be really annoying.  e.g. there are a few times, when you've figured out a guards patrol pattern, you'll try something that doesn't work and will reload a Quick-save, only to find that the guard now stands still in a spot that prohibits your further progress, and never moves.  When attempting to Ghost a chapter, this can be particularly frustrating, as you'll have little choice but to take action that causes a penalty.  Either that, or start the chapter all over again from the beginning.  Poor quality control.
In conclusion, I have to say, this was a fair attempt at a stealth type game but, they could have done much better. For me, Thief comes in only a little above average.  It offers variety in gameplay but, while claiming to be an open world, is still rather linear and restrictive.  On a scale of 1 to 10, I give it a 7.  It has pretty good graphics, a lot of atmosphere and a great deal of replay value.  I think it just needed more time in developement and testing.

This game represents everything I hate about modern games.
When I first installed the game, the first thing I noticed was the ridiculous size. 21 GB. This immediately sent up red flags as another poorly optimised PC port. I was right in that suspicion.
Starting up the game, the first thing I got was of course a prompt to use Uplay instead. This is annoying, but I understand. I played Far Cry 3 after all, and I had fun with what game there was.
When I sorted everything out with my Uplay account and got the game to actually run, what I noticed next was the horrible mouse acceleration. I immediately went to the settings to turn it off, only to notice that it was already set to off, the game is just like that by default.
After a brief googling session, I decided I couldn't be bothered to wait any more and just went along with it as it was. It then gave me an unskippable cutscene with no sound. Apparently, the prerendered cutscenes decided to just not work with audio. They also didn't look very good in the first place.
After that cutscene, I was treated to another unskippable cutscene, this one actually rendered real time. What I noticed then was how incredibly laggy it was. I have a decent computer, nothing spectacular, but okay. Games should not lag this bad. Take a look at Ground Zeroes for an example of a game that both looks and runs significantly better.
Once the cutscene was over, I could finally access the options menu to turn the quality down even more. I set it to medium, but it still ran pretty poorly. I decided to just roll with it and go further. After walking around some in the palace and scavenging some stuff, I finally got down and was treated to another "intense" action cutscene.
Finally able to walk out and finally allowed to actually do something after 20 minutes of doing nothing, I had to run to a vehicle where I was treated to a nice rail-shooting session. Finally something good, I thought. I was mistaken. The final nail in the coffin was aim assist.
This is just straight up unacceptable. I'm glad I didn't buy this game myself, though I feel bad someone had to give money for such a terrible product. Would not recommend to anyone. Do not buy.

This is a spoiler-free review.
This is a type of game that seems to have people that either really like it or just straight-up hate it. There's also a lot of curious people that want to know if the game is worth getting, so rather than just tell you "Oh yeah, I like this!" I'm going to list all of the various things a person may like or dislike about the game.
First of all, this is NOT a visual novel. This is a simulation game mixed with RPG elements. A visual novel is a game in which you only point and click to get story to continue. This is NOT that kind of game. It becomes a simulation game when there are stats to alter and daily choices to be made. It infuriates me that so many people called this a visual novel, when it's obviously a simulation game. Since you can go into a turn-based battle with HP & MP, level up, use a sword or magic, that's the part that's RPG-like. Although, I definitely wouldn't call this an RPG, since the battling is definitely not the focus of the game. In fact, you don't have to step foot in a battle if you don't want to. You can progress the story without participating in battle.
Is this a dating sim? I believe so. I've seen others argue that it isn't, but I would say *it is* mainly because the only good endings you can get require you to have a good romantic relationship with a girl. There are only two girls to choose from, by the way.
How's the storyline? The best word I'd give the storyline is that it's rather odd. This isn't to say that it's a bad storyline, but in all honesty, I find the plot to be a bit weird. I've only gotten 4 endings out of the possible 10, so the storyline could be explained more if I get more endings, but they don't seem to explain the "weirdness" of the storyline very well. For some people, this isn't a problem though.
Otherwise, the story involves getting to know one of (or both) of the girls that the main character knows. There are also two optional characters one can interact with, but they're strictly platonic.
The main goal of the story is to save Claire. Yes, Claire is one of the two girls you can be romantically involved with, but you must save her regardless of which girl you choose, otherwise you'll get a bad ending. Save her from what? That would be giving away spoilers.
How are the battles? Too easy, honestly. All one has to do is learn enough spells, and a person can very, very easily survive battles without much effort. In fact, you could learn ALL of the spells before even entering into your first battle, and you're pretty much guaranteed to win. As I mentioned earlier, there's HP, MP, basic attack (with a sword), and magic. It is turn-based, like any old-fashioned JRPG. There are times while in battle that certain mechanics of it don't make sense. For instance, if an enemy casts a shield on itself, it also casts a shield on the main character. I think this was a mistake in the game design, not intentional.
How long does one playthrough take? It's really only the first playthrough that should take a while. My first playthrough took about 5 or 6 hours. Of course, I read all of the dialogue. If you were to skip the dialogue, it would probably only take you an hour or two. If you're a fan of story (which I'm not sure why you wouldn't be if you're playing a game that's heavily focused on story), it's only long the first playthrough, because after that, you can skip any *already read* dialogue. There's also the option to skip all dialogue regardless of whether you've read it or not, but that seems like a rather silly thing to do.
Are there walkthroughs for this game? Yes, but the only ones I've ever found were incomplete. I suggest doing a Google search to find various walkthroughs if you really want tips on how to get through the game. Some walkthroughs have given false information though, so be careful about which ones you choose to follow.
It's difficult to write a walkthrough for this game, because of the high randomization of events. Two different people playing the game could make the *exact* same choices, but end up experiencing events on different dates in the game. Basically, the games event mechanics are not set to specific dates. You, the gamer, have to trigger them yourself through either persistence or mere chance.
What do I mean by "persistence"?  For example, the forest where your battles can take place has certain events within it. If you want those events to happen more quickly, then you need to keep exploring it over and over again until it triggers. However, if you're a patient person, you could just wait for it to happen by chance by exploring the forest every once in a while or something. Each time you explore the forest, the game randomly generates either a battle, a personal daydream of the main character's, or an event. Battles are the most frequent. Thus, you can have about a dozen battles before ever randomly getting an event or you could simply "luck out" and get an event straight off.
Is there any "ecchi" or nudity? Nope. Not even a little bit.
I think I've covered all the stuff most people ask/wonder about this game. I hope it helps the curious/unsure people about whether or not to get the game.

Dealing with stuff like managing your time: keeping your friends and support network relationships healthy while finding time to earn a paycheck, get swole, prep for upcoming combat, etc. and the entire time people aren't being completely forthcoming with you so you're actively trying to figure out which characters are trying to manipulate you and why. While at work or nurturing a friendship or training for something, prioritizing an important task or project can sometimes inadvertently cause another important thing to fail catastrophically, so it becomes a pretty challenging juggling act.
Anyway, game is VERY "anime". If you're okay with this, I absolutely recommend it.

(TL;DR @ bottom)
I've been playing the alpha versions of this program for a few months now. It's a very relaxed puzzle game, in which you link lines from different types of stations in order to allow passengers to reach their desired type of destination. As the game goes on the map slowly expands and adds/changes stations to force you to keep expanding/upgrading. I recommend just ignoring the score and let yourself just focus on trying to find the best way to flow the traffic for as long as possible. Mini Metro is great for when you just want to relax; personally it’s good for recovering from rage-inducing moments other games cause.
Pros:
-Simple, Zen-like game
-Minimalist graphics that are spot on for the theme.
-Easy to learn, plenty of ways to try and experiment with the growing map to keep going.
Cons:  (Since the game is beta, these will likely change in time)
-No tutorial yet, so most the ways you can interact with the board have to be figured out on your own.
-No sound effects/music. The music is simple to solve, but other audio effects would be nice.
-If you’re still reading, 15 points to Gryffindor. (Bloody gits)
My tip for figuring out the controls: Experiment of course. You can click-drag about anything (stations, ends of lines, mid-lines) you don't like, It'll Highlight/grey out if you can/cannot do something respectively.
Currently, the lack of audio is a downer, but the minimalist art style (and Zen theme) go well with a bit of Jazz. Just start
(or Pandora, etc.), theme search for jazz and hit play; I'm good for an hour.
TL;DR = Very relaxing puzzle game. Art-style can draw you in. Simple to play, enough challenge to keep it interesting with little stress. You’ll have to provide your own music (I recommend Jazz).

Arguably my favourite to date from the recent Roguelike revival, The Pit nails a perfect level of difficulty - punishing every lapse and failure, but still leaving you with hope that the next run and the right ace-up-the-sleeve will be the one that takes you to the bottom of the pit.  And of course, it won't be.
Even after a successful playthrough (finally!), I'm still finding myself spending hours painstakingly hacking my way through the levels all over again, this time on the next difficulty level, or with a different play-style.  Character classes that seem strangley overpowered at the start suddenly reveal their fatal flaws at inopportune times.  I found out the hard way the sudden vulnerability of a Liir without its moisture suit, which seemed so strong at the beginning, crashing through room after room of monsters, armed to the gills and backed with powerful psionics.  The Pit makes you feel strong and humble in the same breath.  To round out the whole experience, the game boasts a polished but simple old-school visual style, a deeply creative world (with enough backstory to make you curious about more, but not to much as to bog you down in reading), and just enough loot, crafting, and randomization to make opening every locked crate a genuinely exciting experience.

Despite its short length, Momodora is something really really special.  The game has this really wonderful, dreamlike atmosphere due to its minimalist soundtrack and the dark fairy tale meets Studio Ghibli art style.  Mechanically, the game is sound, with solid platforming and generally enjoyable combat.  The boss battles are pretty cool, although they could do with a bit more balancing with some being too easy and some very frustrating.  But overall, for me, this just came together to be something more than the some of its parts, and i loved it.
The only bad thing to say about this game is that you can get through it in about 4 hours.  I want more.  I want depth.  I want different weapons and armour.  I want a bigger game world.  i want more bosses.  And i'd have gladly sunk another 20 hours into this if the content was there.
that said, I'd still rather buy something like this over another generic ubi-sandbox game, as I've had a much more meaningful few hours in this than i have in a number of much larger games.  If you don't like these 16 bit style games, I doubt Momodora is the one to convert you, but if you do and don't mind the short run time, I can't see any reason not to give this my full recommendation (i did get it on sale though).

There were five game modes available when I played:
navigate through a series of progressively more dangerous mazes in the dark. Each of your deaths (including suicides, by pressing Spacebar) illuminates a small radius where you died, allowing you to see what's there, and this remains until you complete the level. At first the mazes are simple and consist of walls, but various hazards will be added as you progress through the levels.
I was in a wide open forest and had to collect medals. I could essentially choose between wandering blindly in the dark (to try to keep my death count low) until I found them, or repeatedly committing suicide at various places in the darkness until I located all the medals. When I eventually found them all, I was taken back to the title screen. I selected Endless mode again, and was taken to level 2, which appeared to be the same as the first one, as far as I could tell. This was as far as I progressed in this mode.
Goes to the webpage for the game "Sometimes You Lose Heart", the free promotional game promoting this game.
I was falling down a very deep, dark hole, and moving left and right to try to avoid blades. It was difficult to dodge them in time if I happened to be on a collision course with one, as there is little time to dodge.
I was in a rather large maze, and had to collect 316 star-like things that I assume were "chips", while avoiding monsters in the darkness. It reminded me of Pac-Man.
I spent most of my time in Classic mode.
I had initial confusion when reaching the first exit, since it looks somewhat spiky and intimidating, and when I touched it, I thought I'd died and respawned in a procedurally-generated level. I explored everywhere I could reach, trying to find another way out, before eventually realizing I may need to touch the big spinning spiky thing again, as it may be the exit--which it was.
A minor complaint: On the title screen, I expected that the "How To Play" button would display instructions regarding gameplay and objective, but it actually displayed controls.
PROS:
+ Interesting death mechanic
+ Pretty, relaxing backing piano music
+ Cute but simple graphics; your blood staining blades is a nice detail
+ Death count is displayed
+ A variety of modes available
CONS:
- Lack of instructions: What's the objective? How many levels? Unlimited? How do collectibles matter? What do the modes mean? How to play "well"? What am I trying to do? Presumably die as few times as possible and reach exit? Anything else I should know?
- Is my progress saved? I don't know how many levels there are (the game didn't tell me), so how long do I continue? When can I quit? Does it save? I can't remember the controls mid-game, and there's no way to check?
- Repetitive gameplay
- Couldn't find a way to rebind controls
- No indication of current progress
- Dying causes instant respawn: after an unexpected death, you may walk into spikes immediately after respawning, and add to your death count
- Pressing Esc to pause causes game to quit to main menu without warning, and didn't save my progress. Checked the controls to see if it tells you a pause button or warns you that Esc quits, and it doesn't.
- There's an xp bar on the title screen, but after playing for a while and then (unintentionally) quitting to the title screen, it still said "Lvl: 1" "XP: 0/10". No explanation of it provided.
- Every time I opened the game, a warning about save files was displayed, and then the option to reset data is displayed every time immediately after this, with the "Reset data" button being very close to where the button was that closed the initial warning message. It's actually possible to close the warning message with one click, and then click "Reset Data" with a second click, without even moving the mouse at all. This is unnerving, especially considering that when the "Reset Data" button is clicked, there is no warning about data being erased, so it seems that one accidental click means you would lose your progress.
Considering all the above, it feels a bit barebones. It's a nice effort and has potential, but could use some polish before I can genuinely recommend it, so that it feels more complete.

As someone who has battled depression within this past year (2014), I felt a connection to the character that you play out. There is a trigger warning on this game, so be warned. Some parts brought back up some memories of how I had felt and what I had gone through, which caused me to tear up and even cry at a few parts because those memories are still quite fresh and most definitly painful.
If you are looking for a fun game, look somewhere else. This game wasn't designed or intended to be fun. It's more about the experience that you get from playing this game that is truly what makes it worth a playthrough.

Real talk though, not even criticising it because of the whole backstory. I genuinely downloaded it wanting to like it; wanting  it to be a misunderstood gem which molded eloquence and painful personal experience into a story which communicated the pain of depression (note: the neurological chemical balance, not mere sadness) to a world which doesn't understand it. I wanted this game to thwart the multitude of self-diagnosed sufferers and create a better understanding for the harsh people who've misunderstood the sickness or mistaken it for weakness. What I found instead was material that will serve only to negatively fuel both parties.
It's a relatively small download and free so if there's a level of intrigue regarding the story feel free to pick it up but in terms of being a legitimately worthwhile piece of prose then this ultimately fails.

This is an impartial review of this game.  I'm aware of the Zoe Quinn Scandal and the bad publicity of this game, however, I wanted to try it on my own with as unbiased a few as possible.
First and foremost, this is certainly not a game by any means and should be treated more as a depression simulation and should be provided to those suffering with depression to share with those around them.  Though the game fails to provide any catalyst to explain the depression or to allow the player to empathize with the character, all of the activities, layouts, choices, and mindsets clearly depict depression as intended.  On this front, the "game" achieves what it intended to do.  Since it is free of charge, this depression sim should be recommended to anyone who knows someone suffering with depression.  Even if you hate Zoe Quinn for the scandal or want to blast this for not being a true game, think of the message of depression and the stigma it can help alleviate to help people.
Pros:
-Accurately depicts depression symptoms, feelings, actions, restrictions etc...
-Will accurately explain depression to someone who hasn't experienced it
-Spreads awareness of what true depression is and helps alleviate stigma of mental illness
-Costs nothing
Cons:
-Just like Coming Home, this isn't a game
-The player will only relate to the character if they are within the range of late teens through twenties, limiting audience
-There is no explanation for the depression, making the character appear to be a whiny privileged person with first world problems
-Anyone unaware that this is essentially a depression sim read-along may be in for disappointment
It helped me a lot.

It took me a long time before I felt brave enough to play through this game as I have found it very difficult to face up to my depression and having to relive it has been very difficult. All I've really been doing is watching Disney Princess movies and eating sweeties to try and keep myself sane so it took a lot of courage to play through it.
As I played through it I tried to choose the options that I have gone through in my own depression, a lot of them seemed like the more positive aspects which felt nice as I know that having to play this game 6 months ago I would have been selecting the worst ones. It is a very interesting piece of art work as there is no right or wrong way to play it and I applaud games like that. The best thing that I got from it though is how it went into very vivid detail about the way that the person deals with their day to day life and as I have been depressed for many years it was fascinating to draw parallels of how things that I had put down to my personality being broken being symptoms of the depression illness.
I feel that it really was a positive experience for me to go through it as difficult as it was because it does teach you that you are not alone and I think that's a very strong lesson. I feel that hope is pretty hard to come by for me at the moment and things like this are the startings of a glimmer of light through the clouds. It's hard to explain how it helped but the important thing is that it did and I really do want to thank Zoe as it is something that has helped me in a way that therapy and drugs haven't yet.
I don't keep up with gaming news, I have no idea what things like gamergate are or who Zoe Quinn is and really I don't want to know because I want to appreciate this as a piece of art untainted by anything political. Maybe one day when I am feeling better I will be able to form my own opinion on those things but for now let's end on a high note. I honestly feel that people who feel ready need this kind of thing and gaming needs similar projects to evolve as what it may one day become: the highest of high art.
As a transgender person suicide and depression isn't exactly uncommon with my community and I need all the help I can get. I really want to thank Zoe for the work she has done and to pass on my condolances for all the negative reviews this product has got. Self acceptance is such a challenging time and it is one that can take people years and possibly never happen for some and I am probably currenlty at the lowest I will ever be. Any little glimmer of hope that I can grab on to and anything that allows me to live another day and see if it really does get better is worht its weight in gold to me and this game has certainly helped with that. If you are dealing with depression you really do owe it to yourself to check this out...when you are ready. It's not an easy journey but it is one I am very glad to say I have taken and it will be interesting to play it again when I have fully transitioned and I am at a much higher stage to see how it turns out differently.

I almost feel guilty with how much I've enjoyed this entry to the Thief series. Folks have chewed the game up for not being very devout to the series and that it's another case of a cherished franchise getting screwed by corporate repackaging. While this game is far from perfect, I really don't think that's warranted at all. It's rare I have this much genuine fun with a game.
First, I'll mention the bad. This game was optimized by a twelve year old. I had some stuttering on my system even on lower graphical settings, a number of crashes, and the occasional sound-glitch that cut half the game's sound. The dialog and story can be really corny (I mean, someone literally uses the line "we're not so different, you and I" without joking. Seriously?), and there's a huge detriment to the fact that you can't jump. Yes, that's right, you can't jump. You need to go to ledges to jump down or to jump onto something, but you can't leap whenever you want.
So, with all that said, why do I like it? Well, I'm the kind of gamer who really, really likes stealth games, particularly in the case of FPS. I played a stick-to-the-shadows rogue in Skyrim, I snuck around throughout the Metro series, and I couldn't get enough of the earlier Thief titles. One of the most satisfying feelings I get is looting a room blind, slipping past guards just as they're about to catch me, and solving some tricky puzzles to get to a safe. This game is flooded with secrets, and between missions, you travel a huge city with a number of nooks and crannies waiting to be explored. There's also the stealth roll, which allows you to very smoothly leap from shadow to shadow, which is tremendously satisfying. One of the best aspects, though, is the environment. There's so much great atmosphere in this game, from a creepy abandoned asylum (with jump scares, be warned), to a burning bridge, to a lavish mansion. I got lost trying to look for so many secrets, and the rewards for finding them were pretty satisfying on their own. I even like the fact that Garrett is total crap in a fight. Makes it that much more terrifying when you're caught, because you can't defend yourself nearly as easy as other games.
All in all, I'd definitely say buy this beauty, even if you're a diehard fan of the earlier titles. Once you get over some of the more glaring aspects, this is a real diamond in the rough.

For a game with 10 endings, the game's length and replay value aren't much. That is unless you are like me and squeeze every last bit of a game's 'valued' cost in order to get back its moneys worth.
Out of all the endings, only about three of them are worth playing through. Other reviewers claim that the game is a highly intricate, interactive rpg-style simulation, but truthfully it's not so much different than a regular indie rpg game or dating sim; probably a few notches worst.
Most of the events are predetermined and are based on the limited selection of options made by everyday decisions. Rather, the interactions are quite bland at best and the action & adventure aspect drastically dulls after the tenth battle of the same-looking monster.
In conclusion, if you're looking for an extremely cheap-thrilled visual novel worth 5-10 hours of your time (possibly less), this may be your game. Just know that the story length is very short, and the story itself isn't what you'd call pulitzer prize-winning material. If you do decide to buy the game, get ready as you'll probably be spending more time pressing the skip button and reading white words off a black screen, than anything else.
Worth the $15? I think not.

Fading Hearts is a pure Visual Novel. Just like all the other big ones (Juniper's Knot, Katawa Shoujo, etc.) You read through the story and at certain points you have to make a choice. These choices have a certain effect on the story itself and make for a unique experience.
The writing is good and interesting. There're some failures in grammar, but they aren't that disturbing. But, one thing that IS disturbing are bugs that make you miss parts of the story. Maybe they're important, maybe they aren't. No matter what they're, it's disturbing, because it makes you feel left of the middle.
But, to be honest, Fading Hearts is of an acceptable length, it's written in a nice way and the story and characters are deep enough to keep you interested.
Price and quality are okay for this game, as are the graphics and music.
I would say that Fading Hearts is a nice addition to the Steam Visual Novel Library.

Over 185 hours...I've played over 185 hours in Dungeons of Dredmor, and I'm still not tired of this game.  It's kind of hard to be, because the key idea to the game as a whole is "randomness"  Every level, every enemy and item placement, even every skill if you choose to go that route is random, and it's awesome.
The randomness of it all creates a unique experience, even to the niche genre of roguelikes, that let's the player be cool with the experimentation of new character builds, new gameplay strategies, and new ways to die.  Dying happens a lot, by the way.  The game is so addictive though, you won't mind starting a new character, getting closer and closer to Lord Dredmor.  The humor of the game definitely helps that.  What also helps is the Steam Workshop feature, adding more depth to a game that already has it in spades.
Over 185 hours in, and I'm still not tired of the game yet.  Still haven't beaten it either.  Maybe next round.

I've been playing the alpha versions of this program for a few months now. It's a very relaxed puzzle game, in which you link lines from different types of stations in order to allow passengers to reach their desired type of destination. As the game goes on the map slowly expands and adds/changes stations to force you to keep expanding/upgrading. I recommend just ignoring the score and let yourself just focus on trying to find the best way to flow the traffic for as long as possible. Mini Metro is great for when you just want to relax; personally it’s good for recovering from rage-inducing moments other games cause.
Pros:
-Simple, Zen-like game
-Minimalist graphics that are spot on for the theme.
-Easy to learn, plenty of ways to try and experiment with the growing map to keep going.
Cons:  (Since the game is beta, these will likely change in time)
-No tutorial yet, so most the ways you can interact with the board have to be figured out on your own.
-No sound effects/music. The music is simple to solve, but other audio effects would be nice.
-If you’re still reading, 15 points to Gryffindor. (Bloody gits)
My tip for figuring out the controls: Experiment of course. You can click-drag about anything (stations, ends of lines, mid-lines) you don't like, It'll Highlight/grey out if you can/cannot do something respectively.
Currently, the lack of audio is a downer, but the minimalist art style (and Zen theme) go well with a bit of Jazz. Just start
(or Pandora, etc.), theme search for jazz and hit play; I'm good for an hour.
TL;DR = Very relaxing puzzle game. Art-style can draw you in. Simple to play, enough challenge to keep it interesting with little stress. You’ll have to provide your own music (I recommend Jazz).

Tower of Guns is a favorite of mine. The gameplay feels so much like Quake II when I'm running around dodging and firing. The levels are somewhat randomized, and there are secrets all over the place.
I, like many other people I know, used to play Quake and Doom over and over again on quick little binges, but the games did get old after a while. Bumping up the difficulty only does so much when the game is exactly the same each time. ToG gives me this same, "sit down for 20 minutes" experience while keeping the challenge high. Each play through, you pick your weapon and a perk to tweak your run.
In general, the pace of ToG is as frantic as you want it to be. You can try to slow down and look for secrets and such, or you can blast through and try to get under the par time for the level.
Some things to be aware of: There is no saving. You have to play to a death or win in one sitting. Also, you have only one gun, unless you happen to pick up an extra gun during your run. This means you're not worrying about ammo or weapon switching. This is a pure run, jump, and fire sort of game. And I love it.
Do you like roguelikes?  Do you like fast-paced first person shooters?  Do you like apples?  If you answered yes to two of those questions then you'll like Tower of Guns.

For starters, I've played this game LONG before it even appeared on Steam. Let me just say, besides RuneScape, this was also one of my top childhood games.
Pros:
+ Amazing global environment with lots of maps and worlds to explore
+ Very diverse amount of classes (a new one used to come out with each big update like every month or two)
+ Crazy amounts of monsters and special mobs to find (and capture too depending on your type of class)
+ Fair trading system in game with its own special economics for players looking to explore the "Free Market" of the game (includes loads of players buying and selling like a brokerage)
+ Very community-driven and GMs often hosted events for players to group up
+  Leveling system got easier with each major game-breaking update, which in turn reduced the grind issue
Cons:
- Quite lackluster content ideas with each update (could be improved but lack of players means lack of true quality down the road)
- Lack of playerbase and dying population over the past few years (I could be wrong on Steam's side but I'm pretty sure the numbers have dropped substantially after "Big Bang" came out)
- All classes end up becoming a hassle at earlier levels to unlock skills and items with (also costing you exp and gold eventually; the coolest looking classes and most unique ones are towards the end game with max levels)
- Painful scams involved in trading; people can throw in random♥♥♥♥♥♥you dont want and end up scamming you halfway through the transaction, but this had been somewhat fixed over time by Nexon, but not sure)
- Every time you play a class for a long time, then realize a new type of character/class is out, forcing you to reconsider why you bothered with your first option anyway
- Lots of spammers and bots in populated cities
- And the worst of all... being WIPED to the floor by random, big boss mob spawns that dumb players summon in the middle of nowhere while you are afk or in a trade
Let me just summarize everything and say.. this game used to be good, but not anymore because of the years that have gone by with little incentive to improve; I don't blame the developers as much as the playerbase itself for the abandonment, but that's just my personal take.

I tried to guys... I really tried to. I tried my best to enjoy the game, but I couldn't. I couldn't anymore. What I thought would be a game matching the likes of other rogue-like games from Risk Of Rain, The Binding of Isaac,to smart phone tops such as Pixel Dungeons and Soul Knight. I was attracted by Yogcast, thinking if they supported this, it had to be good. I was baited.
There are some good points to the game. I like the simple yet effective pixelated platformer art style, the characters well-designed, effects decent. And that's as much as I can go.
This game is boring. It took a few hours to realise this, and I honestly did enjoy the first 2 or 3, but the more I tried, the worse it gets. This game has so many areas lacking. Now let me begin:
The game is repetitive. Okay granted, it could be due to my many attempts at passing the first few levels that got me irritated, but what I'm saying is, the game IS really repetitive. It feels monotonous, the same few blessings, the same few weapons, the same few spells. The weapons and items are given too liberally (though sometimes in few to none, please balance this), and almost all the weapons feel the same. The melee weapons are really of no difference other than some small effects and damage. The range weapons have more interesting differences, which is a good point, but regardless, most of them do the same thing. Most of the spells are utterly pathetic. Most charge spells add nothing to gameplay. They are impractical in the fights. The passive spells are conversely, bit overpowered early game (and pointless late-game when their damage is insignificant). And the worst point of all, the playstyle feels the same regardless of what perk you pick (with the exception of a few with the weird starter weapons). This is because there is no way of specialisation. I do appreciate the times when they give the choice among 3 blessings, choose 1, but those are of little significance compared to the overall environment of the game. You will end up just going with the flow and ignoring what perk you've picked in the first place, which usually ends up with taking melee bashing around, a bow shooting randomly, and an OP passive spell, or useless charged spell. You'd think that the randomly-generated terrain will add replayability to the game, but it ends up making the whole map feel uniformed, simplistic, repeating, unrefined. Where ever you go, you see the same background, the same enemies, the same chests, the same colour. The first level will always be Cave, Cave, Cave, and you die, and Cave again, and Cave. And that background music... It's so overwhelming. It is so sharp and so pressing. And again... so repetitive. Ah my gosh.
The game is difficult, in the wrong way. Let's start with the weapons. Melee, swing short range. Good for the first few levels, not. In close quarters combat, there is not much you can do other than spam the attack key. And when you are that close, with a horde of random enemies, all with different attack styles, different movement styles, you can't predict which enemy will do what. There is no way you can, because their AI is erratic, incomplete, weird, random. So you take damage, not a big deal right? Yeah... no. The damage cannot be healed because there are so few options available. So far I've seen consumables (which heal really little compared to the damage dished out by the mobs, especially the 2 miniscule 'hearts' after the bosses. And they are rare too), and drains (but only available in melee! Which means more dmg which means why bother life stealing), and woah and behold! The all-or-nothing healing statue. Really? Heal once, and the statue is gone, for good. You either take it all, or you take none. Not even a "potion on sale" which sells for a lower price and heals lower, but straight up statue that heals to full, and costs more the more health you can heal, exarcebated by the fact that there are 1001 ways to increase your max health. Health is so difficult to come by, and that will be the case regardless of your skill level. At least in the Binding of Isaac, it is a choice to play certain characters which may be more difficult (eg. Blue Baby, The Lost), but oh my oh my, you are brought into a cave with no health, no game, no controls. Let me get back to weapons. So bows. Bows are probably one of the only viable weapons in the game. I mean, how are you gonna kill a flying monster with a melee weapon? You can't simple. At first, I thought the 8 directional shooting system is fine. And it really isn't. The Binding of Isaac is able to execute this well because it's a top down shooter, where fine tuning of position and aiming is possible. In Risk Of Rain, most enemies stay on the ground, so the dual directional attack is fine. But hey... Look, Caveblazers is a platformer with weird angles every where and enemies flying and jumping AND AIMING AT YOU FROM WEIRD ANGLES. The octadirectional shooting really can't work out here, and the bosses just makes it especially difficult. Flying enemies are a real pain to deal with with range weapons (and that's why the shotgun bow is probably one of the best weapons I have found). And as I mentioned before, the charge spells are just... impractical in most situations. Alright... where am I... okay now the blessings. The blessings are really cool, and some of them are fun, and some of them are garbage (I mean really... improve the downward melee stomp thing? Really?). What this game lacks is the OP blessings factor. In many other rogue-like games, you have this small chance to get something really powerful so you can progress the game and see the end. Not this game though. Even luck can't save you because there's nothing that can save you in the first place. The improvement of your stats and character is just not matched by increase in health, and that inevitabliy kills you too fast. Glass cannon yo, but not actually a cannon because the player lacks AoE factor. Oh yeaaah the bosses... right the bosses. The bosses are actually... a bit too predictable? But almost all of them are flying, and they have too much health, it gets painful to fight... Melee is almost always out of the option for boss fights. Good gosh. enough.
And one last point to make... This game actually made me feel lonely. Lonely in an abandoned way. Not abandoned by the game because it is well-designed to make me feel that way, but I feel abandoned and neglected by the developers. The game holds on to the player quite tightly at first, giving us "quests", and having some human interactions. I thought that was what the game was gonna be, because my first 5 to 6 play throughs involved interactions with the 'home cave'. We are introduced to the game with a guy for us to talk to, and there goes a dialogue for a good minute. Then we are introduced to perks, to outfits, to this weird purncian crystal thing which I still don't know does what, and introduced to records. Till this point, I feel involved with the game, I always had something to look forward to after 'Game Over'. But it stopped. Everything stopped. The game no longer progress. Nothing changes. This is unlike Risk Of Rain where there is already minimal human interaction from the start. I always felt alone but that's how the game is and I appreciated the loneliness. Caveblazers however, shows that they believe in friendships when the brought in random other human NPCs fighting about which you can make friends with (of course they die immediately a short moment later, and they are very rare... maybe just me). It really is not a nice feeling. That's all I can describe it.
So that's why I really felt disappointed by this game. This game has so much potential, so much of it thrown aside. So much of it wasted. I truly enjoyed the first few playthroughs, but I can't anymore. I'm sorry. I really wanted to.

This is probably one of my all-time favourites. I think the playtime in contrast to the actual length of the game speaks for itself.
It just keeps you interested so that you try to go through all the options and unlock all the endings (which will have you fuming at the mouth with rage sometimes. Took me over a year and several playthroughs to get them all). But it never gets boring, even if you know what to do by heart. Every scene seems perfectly captured by "its" music, the atmosphere is disturbing and great, the balance between beauty and ugliness/carnage is just right and the characters really grow on you (big plus: great voice acting.) There is really no reason not to play this - maybe if you're not willing to spend your free time on "deep♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; like this. But otherwise, there isn't really an excuse.
What I found striking was that even though it is full of morbid and depressing themes, there's really a lot of hope in it. Not that it's any way of therapy or even a healthy way of coping with problems, but I would say that it is uplifting and feels somewhat positive. Towards the end, that is.

The Cat Lady is a bittersweet story. It starts with suicide, anger, horror, pain, violence and despair. But it is all worth. You begin with no empathy for this sad bitter woman with strange habits. She looks like a coward who tried to kill herself, a person with no value. But then, just like it happens with a "cat person", you begin to understand her, to identify with her, and by the end, you will even love her. This is what most people want when they play this game. When I was looking into it I didn't go in blind. I'm no fanboy of the souls games, but I am a person who enjoys a good amount of difficulty. I'll talk about difficulty first, then get into mechanics.
Most of the bosses in this game have A LOT. OF. HP. If you do not upgrade your damage, you will be very sorry. Possibly. You fight with a leaf. And you are sometimes fighting a colassus harbinger of plague and scourge. So keep that in mind. I see a lot of people throwing around the "Fake" difficulty trope a good amount, but not explaining why this game has false difficulty. I'll do my best to explain why this is.
Reasons this game is falsely difficult: Being poisoned can kill you. You can kill yourself with items that "sacrifice HP". Most bosses have 100x the health of trash mobs in the area. Beating bosses without getting hit rewards you with awesome loot, but going into this game blind, you may or may never know. Some enemy placement is quite unique, but if I can just dash by everything after a certain point, then whats the problem? There were traps that reset just to troll kill you (and honestly killed me far more times than monsters). Some monsters with "tells" (before they will big attack) for some reason have a lag between the tell and action. They make take a few steps and then attack, or not. All bosses have 5 different attacks or fewer. They also tossed in the mob with the ol' many copies but one does a different thing. Lasers. Tracking missiles. and more or less was not very impressive. One miniboss had two attacks.
All in all this game has just a few sections.

Actual game play mechanics? Not bad, but nothing new. Double jump. Dodge roll. Melee. Ranged.
The biggest plus?
***

WolfQuest debuted in 2005 as part of a free educational campaign to teach us about wolves.  It was made by a comparatively small team in cahoots with the Minnesota Zoo. With that said, WolfQuest is impressive as it is.  It was a good game back then, but it is even better now since it was overhauled.
This game won't feel like other games; yes, you can tell that it was made by a small team, and yes, it can see a few bugs here and there.  The graphics are impressive, better than many other games actually, but not stunning or extraordinary.   The gameplay offers very little to do in terms of things to do.  Essentially, you are just a wolf running around a lot of hills, chasing down other animals and killing them in order to feed and protect your pups.  However, the game difficulty has four different settings that make the game much more difficult, respectively.  This alone adds a decent amount of replayability as you try your best to complete each phase of the game with all of your pups alive - not an easy task, especially on single player.
For those that appreciate simulators, WolfQuest is one of the few of its kind.  We sadly do not have near enough animal RPGs/ simulators on the market, and this one is a beautiful taste of the genre.  If you enjoy relaxing games, role play, or just really, really love wolves, this game will stay with you forever, and you won't regret buying it.

7. Staying alive is the only way to progress, how to survive is totally up to you. Callback to my fifth point.
8. Buy a house! It's a grind but well worth the effort. A safe place to stash your stuff. Except for that one time you forgot to lock the door and some pleb stole everything. Yes deeds transfer over.

Far Cry 4, like it's immediate predecessor, is a explosive, crazy, action-packed murder romp through another exotic location. It's greatest strength, sheer abundance of insane situations that occur, is also lifted straight from Far Cry 3. They're nearly identical, with all the faults and gameplay nitpicks of 3 being addressed. But for some, this is also FC4s greatest weakness. It's glorified DLC. Ultimately, your purchase is determined by one factor. Do you want more Far Cry!? Thankfully, I did.
Story: Welcome to Kyrat, an ancient Himalayan country torn apart by a civil war between it's despotic self-acclaimed King, Pagan Min; and the Golden Path. You are Ajay Ghale, returning to his barely-remembered homeland. Son of rebel leader Mohan Ghale, you will lead the fight against King Pagan Min, another amazing Far Cry villain. Like Vaas, but with a wry sense of humor, and spiffy pink suit; his unfortunate underutilization is one of the games downsides. We want more Min! Unlike Jason Brody, Ghale has no aversion to killing, no story of callusing. He's a blank paramilitary badass slate, a whiteboard for the player to impose themselves on, doesn't talk much, which is a blessing. Through a fairly intriguing storyline, you will decide the fate of Kyrat and direction of the Golden Path, through a series of choices. Do you save captured soldiers, or leave them to their fate to retrieve intel? Your choice has the illusion of consequence, and it works quite well. I cared about the characters, adored MIn (not so much his lieutenants) and the various moral dilemmas  had me deep in thought for a few minutes. Perfectly satisfactory.
Presentation: Beautiful. Sweeping wooded valleys, soaring mountain vistas, sun tinted water, the forest and steppe environments are breathtaking and gloriously realised with perfect background audio. Birds chirping, water lapping, prayer flags flapping in a swirling breeze. Wildlife from bears to honey badgers stalk their prey and yourself. Himalayan tundras are appropriately desolate and panther filled, this game is awe-inspiring and immersing. A well realised menu theme scatters colorful prayer dust across your settings menu. Supplemented by perfect voice acting, and crisp and shattering gunshots and explosions, the entire package is wrapped up in a exciting dubstep/Nepalese score, truly realising the setting. Welcome to Kyrat, and good luck setting down the controller.
Gameplay: See Far Cry 3.
Kidding.
Utilise a massive suite of weapons, ranging from rapid fire MG42 machine guns, volatile flamethrowers, devastating RPGs, workhorse AK47s to hi-tech Vector 45. ACP submachine guns, roaring magnum revolvers and explosive shotguns. Objective? Hunt animals to upgrade your equipment (3 bear skins= 1 extra weapon holster?). Scavenge herbs to craft health and sensory potions. Mostly, kill the soldiers of Min's Royal Army. Enemy types vary from standard 'duck in cover and spray' infantry, hulking heavy machine gunners with no regards for personal safety, bloodthirsty melee berzerkers, and elite snipers and stealthy hunters of Min's Royal Guard. Enemy AI is capable and brutal, expect calculated assaults and stalwart sieges from Min's troops. Utilize an incredibly realized stealth system, distracting guards, sneakily picking off stragglers with suppressed weapons and bows, and leaping into brutal melee kills and streaks, all without tripping the alarm. Like FC3, 4 has a brilliant and receptive FPS mechanics, firefights are exciting and harrowing, stealth is difficult but ever-so-rewarding. Plus, they finally added vehicle combat. Aside from all the killing, discover the awesome open world of Kyrat, takeover outposts, climb towers (ubisoft...), creep through caves, pursue side quests, etc. It's great. Even more so by the unpredictable nature of the DUNIA engine, firefights are often interrupted by animal attacks, Golden Path reinforcement. I've been hunting deer, and gotten ambushed by a pack of honey badgers, who are fleeing Royal Army soldiers blasting them from vehicle mounted machine guns. Chaos!
Technical: I'm running a GTX 760 and FX6300, alongside 8GB of RAM. Ran consistently at 60fps, at high and medium alternating settings, with AA on low. If you wanna run this on ultra, 8xAA, HBA0+; expect needing some serious hardware. But, even for mid range PCs, FC4 will run like a charm. It's just as beautiful on medium, I assure you. Occasional glitches pop up, but pop in is minimal, and  textures across the board are superb. This isn't Unity, fear not.
In conclusion, Far Cry 4 is a rewarding, and downright fun experience. I enjoyed every second of shenanigans, and the story was more than satisfactory. Plus, you can fool around in co-op with a friend! If you enjoyed Far Cry 3, I absolutely recommend Far Cry 4. If you haven't played Far Cry 3, what the hell are you waiting for!?!?
See you in Kyrat!

Played this game before it came to Steam and love it through and through!
There are visual novels with longer and deeper storylines, but Fading Heart managed to be more enjoyable than most of them; its characters are downright endearing, and the story is interesting with its share of twists and mysteries.
Among things that makes Fading Hearts favorably stand out among other VNs is that it gives you a lot of actual choice, rather then deciding the route for you based on often- unobvious dialogue choice. For instance, most VNs require the player to focus on pursuing specific girl, often at expense of being cold or downright rude to other girls to avoid getting unwanted “points” with them. Fading Hearts recognizes that being nice to a girl doesn’t mean you are romantically interested in her, and ultimately places decision of who to pursue into your hands. It encourages supporting all your friends regardless of your romantic interest, which I find a refreshing change from many other VNs.
Not to say that the plot can’t force something upon you, it sure can. But even when the choice is taken from you, it is the result of what you choose earlier – choose poorly!
To sum it up, I fully recommend Fading Hearts to everyone who enjoys VNs. And for people not familiar with the genre, I’d say it is a good choice of the first VN if they want to try them out.

One man decided to make an incredible old-school first person shooter.  He enlisted the help of another man to create one of the most kickass soundtracks in a game to date.
I cannot stress enough that this is the work of one developer and one musician.  Is it because I'm about to say, "Oh, this is pretty good for a small team."?
No.  This is not good for a small team.  This is nigh on black magic level for a single man and his brother-in-law.  If a full fledged STUDIO released this, I'd be giving it as much praise as I am now.  I can only imagine a sort of Faustian pact that enabled this game to be created.
Enough gushing.  Let me elucidate a little bit on the mechanics that make this game so gosh darn fun.
1.  Roguelike elements.  Permadeath, restart, randomly put together levels, perk unlocks and new guns to create a fresh feeling each playthrough.  The rooms in each level are handcrafted, and oh how lovingly handcrafted they are!  There are literally dozens upon dozens of secrets in each playthrough and they are DEVIOUS.
2.  Shooting is fun - Guns?  Yeah, this game has some guns.  It's got your pistols, machine guns, shotguns, Mini-large hadron colliders, and guns that shoot bouncing spikey balls and glowing discs of death.  Wait.  What?
3.  Weapon mods - Hey.  You have a rocket launcher.  What's this weapon mod do?  Oh.  It turns it into a machine gun rocket launcher.  That's pretty cool.  I like that.
4.  Fast, Quake/Unreal style gameplay - It starts off a little slow, plinking away with your little basic gun of choice.  Then you start picking up badges (powerups), weapon mods, and items.  Pretty soon you're jumping fifteen feet in the air with only ONE of your jumps.  I've personally gotten up to six jumps in one game.  Double jump?  Pfft.  Triple, quadruple, and quintuple jumps are where it's at.  You'll be gliding around a massive, beautiful arena, firing your glowing, machine gun razor blade shooting pizza launcher at dozens of robots trying to murder you.
5.  Boss Fights - Good lord.  Yeah, you got your Mama Spinbots, just bullet hell spinny robot death throwers that try to murder you through sheer brute force.  Then you've got the Egg Scrambler, the Gumball Machine, and Mr. Turret.  I cannot emphasize how cool the boss fights are.  The Egg Scrambler is one of my favorite boss fights in any FPS ever.  EVER.
6.  It's ten dollars right now, fifteen at full price.  Come on.  If you liked old school shooters, you will want to make a sweet, sweet baby with Tower of Guns.
Also, it's hilarious.

Choose a hero, hack through waves and waves of enemies, buy upgrades, kill even more enemies, get more upgrades, kill a boss, get to the next level, start the whole process over. However dull that may sound, player will often suffer from the "one more" syndrome - "I will wipe one more floor and I will go to bed", "I'll clear one more level and I'm going to do something else" - which prolongs the time one spends playing it.
Hammerwatch has a very pleasant art style. The graphics is pixelated (in a good manner) and generally looks quite pretty and also fits the dungeon crawler theme. The only problem would be some single coins being too small to notice when lying directly behind a wall.
The game seems to have lots of content - enemies, levels, secret areas, traps, puzzles, bosses, upgrades. But the gameplay itself is a little too shallow, so playing for more than 2 hours feels like a chore (and makes your fingers hurt for bashing the skill buttons). There is a level editor and Steam Workshop integration, so probably there are more fun scenarios to play rather than the original ones. There's also a multiplayer mode, which I had no chance to test and I deeply regret it because it looks like the game's value shines much brighter with it.
The game could use some improvements with loot system being the most important one in my opinion. Currently, there are only 4 things that can be picked up: gold, hp/mana pots, vendor coins and extra lives. Implementing some more interesting loot system could really improve the overall value of the game and increase the feeling of playing a good roguelike (luck based drops that sometimes set you up for a level and sometimes require specific play style to benefit). Lack of randomly generated worlds is also a little bit bummer, as it decreases replayability value a lot, however, it is understandable that some of the current elements (puzzles, secret areas) would just not work with generated floors so devs had to make a decision there.
As I said in the beginning, Hammerwatch is not a great game. However, it is often to be found at 90% discount (1€~), which is a crazy good price for a solid game like this one. I bought it on one of such occassions and I don't regret it. Paying the full price might be a bit to steep, though. All in all, I had some fun playing it and I will have some more, because I am not finished yet.

Depression Quest is a game that makes me really excited about where the medium of video games is now and direction it's going in the future. Depression Quest is an interactive educational simulation about living with depression. It attempts to use game mechanics to communicate to the player what living with depression feels like. The mechanics are simple and certainly nothing revolutionary. But what makes me excited about this game is that to me it serves as an indicator that the medium of video games is maturing to a point where games can start to cover serious topics like this and tell deeply personal stories.
The game of Depression Quest is basically a text-only roleplaying experience that repeatedly presents you with a scenario and then offers you several choices of how to deal with a the presented scenario. For instance, your in-game girlfriend may call you up and ask you if you'd like to attend a birthday party. You're then given several choices like "attend" or "politely decline" or "say you're not feeling well" or something like that. The catch is that while you can see all of the options, the ones you can actually select are almost always limited based on how depressed you're feeling. There's a few blurbs of text near the bottom of the screen which essentially serve as your "depression meter" and as you get better or worse, more or fewer options are available to you. As far as a simulation of depression goes, it was pretty effective. Sometimes you can see the option you'd really like to choose, but you just can't pick it, which is kind of frustrating.
The game states that its authors have personally struggled with depression before which makes Depression Quest's story feel very authentic. Now I'm not sure if it was the quality of the writing or how personal it felt, but I was alarmed at how many times the writing really struck a chord and resonated with me. There were many times where I was like "Oh wow, I think that to myself all the time". Again, I've never struggled with the serious, deep kind of depression this game is about, but those thoughts I had were a testament to how relatable the writing is even to someone who doesn't know much about the subject matter.
As someone who has never personally dealt with depression before, this game was a very educational tool for me and I'm very glad that this game exists. I hope it helps to raise awareness of what exactly depression is and how the people suffering from it can feel limited in their lives. I also hope that this can influence more developers to make more really personal experiences like this game. It's probably less than an hour long, but it's totally free and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a personal game or anyone who would like to try to roleplay what it's like to live life with depression

To be honest I don't get why this is MIXED reviewed and not a POSITIVE positive reviewed product. Although the game does have its cons it has a lot of pros. Not to mention this game has HUGE potential. I want to start off by saying that as of now the game is not worth 19.99, not because its bad but simply because its early access and lacks quite some content. On the other hand I have enjoyed this game a lot over the past 2 days and seriously its a game I can just come on and relax and enjoy. Now lets get to the pros and cons.
PROS:
- Amazing Graphics with little lag (Turn off post proccess to see what I mean):
The graphics on this game are beautiful. The enviornment is amazingly foilaged and the map is a decent size for 50+ people. Specially if many players stick to a few towns to make it prosper.
- All classes are dependent on eachother, therefore quite they balanced:
All of the classes currently available are very balanced. For example. The blacksmith requires the peaseant for increased sales, and food supply. If the peseants do not supply the local vendors (AI or other players) there will be no food to buy. The peasent requires the blacksmith for weaponry used in self defense when gathering resources and for sale of its resources it has gathered. Not to mention blacksmiths will sometimes hire peasents to carry their loads due to higher load or weight limits for peseants.
- Able to own property to call your own:
The ability to enter a contract and own your own house or piece of land is an amazing option within the Black Death. Not only does it give a sense of accomplishment but also a little place to rest, store valuables, sit down and talk with friends, etc. Choose to buy in the middle of a big town or a lonly house out in the prarie, its your choice.
- Varied amounts of resources (Which I've heard they plan to increase anyway):
There are plenty of resources in the Black Death. They are all different quality resources which in the end allow you to sell or build better end products. This allows for the ability to travel far and wide for good resources and set up collection routes which help you to produce money a lot quicker. Just to mention a few; cotten, stone, iron ore, granite, bones, raw meat, raw fish, pelts (depending on what you hunt; wolves, deer, fox, etc.), carrots, pumpkins, parsnips, onions, and a WHOLE wide variety of different things!
CONS: ( I don't even view them as cons, just because this game is so early in development)
- Very sluggish combat and AI system:
At the moment the combat system is very bad. Not only do the AI and players suddenly appear because it starts reading their movements a bit late, but also swinging swords or hatchets sometimes get stuck, they break suddenly, etc.  Although I know they plan to improve this in the future so far its one of the most frustrating things
- Fair amounts of small glitches and OCCASIONAL crashes:
Although crashing is not a very common occurance within the Black Death, it has happened. Luckily they have an automatic system that allows you to send them your dump files so they can take care of the issue as quickly as possible. A few other glitches that maybe occur is the blank list of items a AI will offer to sell you. Although this can be simply fixed by walking away and coming back a bit later, it gets quite annoying when your dying to sell an important valuable or trying to buy some much needed food.

As you explore, you will find desolate places, scary places, places where you feel watched. One of those places is a small overgrown valley where a small path weaves its way between the trees. Suddenly you notice something hanging over your head. Dead bodies. Apparently this is where the guards of a nearby castle hangs its criminals. Dead fruit hanging from old trees to remind everyone passing by to behave.
The Black Death offers a realistic medieval fantasy setting. There are no dragons here, no skeletons emerging from the ground. But that doesn't mean that the dead are not walking. The plague hangs like a dark shadow over everything and everyone can become infected. Maybe it is only a matter of time. Some places you will find people who have grown mad because of the disease - they got nothing to lose afterall.
No matter what class you choose for your character, you will be able to craft and explore and try to survive. You will discover that having friends is more valuable than having enemies. When your character dies, it is permanent - although any spent skill points will carry over to the next character you create. When death matters, staying alive matters. This makes your characters story matter.
The game truly encourages roleplay. I have met several people already who have talked to me as if they were the characters themselves. You can press the "V" key to voice chat and meeting another character who speaks to you as if he belonged inside the world is better than any D&D tabletop session.
This game got a huge potential and I cannot recommend it enough.
